strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A licensed nurse in her professional role.
Malpractice is a type of negligence.
Neither describes a standard-of-care failure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves malpractice.

questions.stem: A nursing expert is asked to testify in a case about a patient harmed on a medical unit. Against what standard will the nurse's conduct be judged?

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do in similar circumstances in that geographical area
options.rationale: The standard of proof, almost word for word. It is not the best possible nurse and it is not this nurse's own opinion.

options.text: What the most experienced nurse on the unit would have done
options.rationale: The standard is reasonably prudent, not exemplary. Holding everyone to the best performer would make the standard unreachable.

options.text: What the hospital's policy manual required at the time
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard and does not define it. A policy can itself fall below the standard.

options.text: What the nurse herself believed was appropriate at the time
options.rationale: The standard is external. Personal belief does not set it.

questions.takeaway: Standard of proof: what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the geographical area where the alleged breach occurred.
questions.strategy: Two distractors set the bar too high or too low. One substitutes policy for the standard itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same area.
Prudent, not exemplary.
One is evidence, one is internal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reasonably prudent nurse standard.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse assigns work among a registered nurse, a licensed vocational nurse, and a certified nursing assistant.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate the least qualified person who may appropriately perform it.

rows.text: Recording intake and output
rows.rationale: Named on her Delegation 411 slide among the assistant's tasks, alongside vitals, ambulation, position changes, bathing and eating.

rows.text: Initial admission assessment of a newly admitted patient
rows.rationale: Assessment belongs to the registered nurse. The licensed vocational nurse may perform secondary assessment and reinforcement.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the registered nurse has already provided to a stable patient
rows.rationale: Her slide gives the vocational nurse secondary and reinforcing roles: assess, teach, monitor, stable patients and discharge.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met an outcome
rows.rationale: Evaluation is named on her slide as a registered nurse function.

rows.text: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
rows.rationale: Ambulation is named among the assistant's tasks, and the patient is stable.

rows.text: Caring for a patient whose condition is unstable
rows.rationale: Unstable patients are named as a registered nurse responsibility.

questions.takeaway: RN: unstable patients, assessment, evaluation, teaching. LVN: secondary and reinforcing, stable patients, discharge. CNA: vitals, ambulation, positioning, bathing, eating, intake and output.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about teaching and assessment at different depths. First contact belongs to the registered nurse; reinforcement can go to the vocational nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is
steps.detail: Unstable goes to the RN.

steps.action: Ask whether it is initial or reinforcing
steps.detail: First assessment, or follow-up.
Vitals, ambulation, intake and output.

elimination.verdict: Two CNA, one LVN, three RN.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what a patient must receive for informed consent to be valid. Which elements are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: An explanation of the procedure
options.rationale: Named first. He must know what is proposed.

options.text: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting
options.rationale: Named, and it is the element most often omitted in practice.

options.text: A description of serious harm including death, and anticipated pain or discomfort
options.rationale: Named, and it must include death where that is a possibility.

options.text: An explanation of alternative therapies and the risks of doing nothing
options.rationale: Named, and doing nothing is itself an alternative with consequences.

options.text: Knowledge that he may refuse without losing other supportive care
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the fear that refusing one thing costs him everything else.

options.text: A guarantee that the procedure will achieve the intended result
options.rationale: No procedure can be guaranteed, and promising an outcome would invalidate rather than strengthen the consent.

questions.takeaway: Informed consent requires explanation of the procedure, who is performing it, serious harm including death, alternatives and the risks of doing nothing, the right to refuse without losing other care, and the right to withdraw even after the procedure has begun.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers a guarantee. Consent describes risk honestly; it never promises a result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Procedure, people, risks, alternatives, right to refuse.
No outcome can be promised.
He may refuse even after it has begun.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse stops at the scene of a road collision and provides care within her competence until paramedics arrive. Which law addresses her legal position?

options.text: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
options.rationale: EMTALA governs how hospitals must treat people presenting for emergency care. It does not apply at a roadside.

options.text: Good Samaritan laws, which limit liability and offer legal immunity
options.rationale: Named directly. They protect a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act, which permits emergency care
options.rationale: The practice act defines her scope. Good Samaritan laws address liability for helping outside employment.

options.text: Her employer's malpractice insurance
options.rationale: Employer coverage concerns care given in the course of employment.

questions.takeaway: Good Samaritan laws limit liability and offer legal immunity to a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a real emergency statute that governs hospitals rather than roadsides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At a roadside, not at work.
Governs hospital emergency departments.

steps.action: Cut the practice act and insurance
steps.detail: One is scope, one is employment coverage.

elimination.verdict: That leaves Good Samaritan laws.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the federal statutes affecting her practice.

The law requiring institutions to give patients written information about their right to refuse treatment and to formulate an advance directive is the [[1]].

The law giving patients rights over their health information and protecting employees is [[2]].

The law requiring insurers to cover mental health and substance use treatment is the [[3]].

The act prohibiting the purchase or sale of organs is the [[4]].

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires written information about the right to make decisions, refuse treatment, and formulate an advance directive such as a power of attorney or living will.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: Concerns consumer rights and protections, affordable coverage, access, and quality.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: Protects the rights of people with physical or mental disabilities.

options.text: Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act
options.rationale: Altered the way health care is provided to older adults.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: Provides rights to patients over their health information and protects employees.

options.text: HITECH
options.rationale: The near-miss. HITECH concerns health information technology and requires nurses to ensure protected health information is secured.

options.text: EMTALA
options.rationale: Governs emergency treatment and active labor.

options.text: the Mental Health Parity Act
options.rationale: Concerns insurance coverage for mental health and substance use.

options.text: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
options.rationale: Requires insurers to provide coverage for mental health and substance use disorder treatment.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: Broader coverage and access legislation.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: Concerns discrimination and access, not insurance coverage.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: Concerns health information.

options.text: National Organ Transplant Act
options.rationale: Prohibits the purchase or sale of organs.

options.text: Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
options.rationale: The near-miss. It provides the foundation for the national organ donation system; the Transplant Act is what prohibits sale.

options.text: Uniform Determination of Death Act
options.rationale: Determines actual death, cardiopulmonary or irreversible cessation of the entire brain and brain stem.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Concerns advance directives and the right to refuse treatment.

questions.takeaway: Self-Determination is advance directives. HIPAA is information rights. Parity is insurance coverage. Anatomical Gift builds the donation system; Transplant Act prohibits sale.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: HIPAA against HITECH, and the two organ acts. One builds the system, the other prohibits the market.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: HIPAA rights, HITECH security.
Foundation, or prohibition.
Directives, information, coverage, organs.

elimination.verdict: Self-Determination, HIPAA, Parity, Transplant Act.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication and the vial does not look like the one she usually uses. She is behind on her round. Which action reflects the lessons drawn from the RaDonda Vaught case?

options.text: Give it and document that the appearance was unfamiliar
options.rationale: Documenting a concern is not resolving it, and the patient receives the drug either way.

options.text: Stop, verify with a drug guide or the pharmacist before proceeding
options.rationale: Pause and verify when something does not look right, particularly with high-alert medications, and use resources when in doubt.

options.text: Proceed, since she selected it from the automated cabinet under the correct name
options.rationale: An override and a confirmation error were central to that case. The cabinet is not the verification.

options.text: Ask another nurse to check it while she moves to her next patient
options.rationale: The check belongs to the person giving it. Delegating the verification does not transfer the accountability.

questions.takeaway: Follow all the rights, pause and verify when something looks wrong, use resources, avoid workarounds, and report system failures.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats the automated cabinet as the verification step. That was central to what went wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Something does not look right.
An override and confirmation error caused the harm.

steps.action: Cut delegating the check and documenting
steps.detail: Neither resolves the doubt before administration.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping to verify.

questions.stem: A nurse discusses a patient's diagnosis in a hospital lift where visitors can hear. No harm was intended. Which category does this fall into?

options.text: An unintentional tort
options.rationale: The near-miss. Unintentional torts arise when someone is harmed and the person knew or should have known their actions fell below the standard of practice, which describes negligence.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent to cause the harm. She intended to speak, not to harm.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Acts where the person does not intend harm but causes it. Breach of confidentiality is the classic example.

options.text: A criminal offense under state law
options.rationale: Torts are civil wrongs. Criminal law concerns felonies and misdemeanors.

questions.takeaway: Torts are civil wrongful acts or omissions. Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known their conduct fell below the standard.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is unintentional tort. Both involve no intent, and they differ in whether a standard of care was breached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She did not intend harm.
Confidentiality, not a care standard.
One needs intent, one is a different body of law.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a quasi-intentional tort.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to reduce her personal legal risk. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Developing and using clinical judgment to identify patient needs
options.rationale: Named directly, and sound clinical decisions are what keep practice above the standard.

options.text: Remaining aware of current issues in health care
options.rationale: Named, and standards move.

options.text: Becoming involved in professional organizations and committees that define standards
options.rationale: Named, and it means she helps set the standard she is judged against.

options.text: Participating in risk management and quality improvement programs
options.rationale: Named. These identify potential hazards and eliminate them before harm occurs.

options.text: Documenting thoroughly and accurately
options.rationale: Named among the lessons drawn from the Vaught case, and an undocumented action is difficult to defend.

options.text: Carrying personal malpractice insurance instead of relying on the employer's
options.rationale: Insurance covers the cost of a claim. It reduces financial exposure rather than legal risk, and the question asks about the risk itself.

questions.takeaway: Reducing legal risk: clinical judgment, awareness of current issues, professional involvement, risk management and quality improvement, and thorough documentation.
questions.strategy: One distractor reduces what a claim costs rather than the chance of one. Read what the question asks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Practicing above the standard.
Covers cost, not risk.
All named actions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes her shift and no replacement has arrived for the next shift. She leaves at the end of her scheduled hours without notifying anyone. Which concern does this raise?

options.text: Patient abandonment, because she left without handing over responsibility
options.rationale: Named among the workforce guidelines. Leaving a scheduled shift without transferring care to someone qualified is abandonment.

options.text: None, because her contracted hours had ended
options.rationale: The end of her hours does not end her responsibility until care has been transferred.

options.text: A staffing ratio violation by the employer
options.rationale: The ratio problem is real and it belongs to the employer. Her own exposure comes from how she left.

options.text: A breach of her nurse practice act's scope provisions
options.rationale: Scope concerns what she may do, not how she ends a shift.

questions.takeaway: Nursing workforce guidelines cover staffing and ratios, assignments, patient abandonment, delegation, and nursing students.
questions.strategy: One distractor points at a genuine employer failing. The question asks what this raises for her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Left without transferring care.
Responsibility ends at handover.

steps.action: Cut the ratio and scope options
steps.detail: One is the employer's, one is unrelated.

elimination.verdict: That leaves patient abandonment.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss legal risk. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Malpractice is a type of negligence, and the person held liable must be a professional."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her definition.

options.text: "Risk management programs reduce legal risk by finding hazards before harm occurs."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is how they reduce exposure.

options.text: "A nursing expert will testify about the standard of care as applied to the facts."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is what nurse experts do in a nursing case.

options.text: "If I follow hospital policy exactly, I cannot be found negligent."
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard, not the standard itself. A policy can fall below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.

questions.takeaway: Policy is evidence of the standard of care, not a defense in itself. The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats policy compliance as complete protection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The reasonably prudent nurse.
Malpractice, risk management, expert testimony.
Policy as a guarantee.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the policy statement.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient she is listening while she continues to type and does not look up. The room is quiet and there are no interruptions. He stops mid-sentence and says it can wait. Which term describes what happened?

options.text: Ineffective feedback, because she did not respond to his message
options.rationale: Feedback is the response coming back. She did respond, and the problem is that her two responses contradicted each other.

options.text: A channel problem, since the message was spoken rather than written
options.rationale: The channel is the route a message travels. The spoken channel worked and he heard her clearly.

options.text: Environmental interference from competing demands on her attention
options.rationale: The environment is everything outside the two of them. The stem rules out noise and interruptions, and her typing comes from her rather than from the room.

options.text: Incongruent communication, where the verbal and nonverbal messages conflict
options.rationale: Congruence is whether words and body say the same thing. He received both and believed the behavior, which is why he withdrew rather than repeating himself.

questions.takeaway: Four different failures: the channel is whether words arrive, feedback is whether a response comes back, the environment is disruption from outside, congruence is whether words and body agree.
questions.strategy: When two options both look true, check which one explains his reaction. Interference stops a message arriving; he received it and withdrew.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He stopped talking rather than repeating himself.
The stem states the room is quiet.
Both worked and carried contradictory content.

elimination.verdict: That leaves incongruent communication.

questions.scenario: A nurse talks with a patient who has just been told his cancer has returned.
questions.stem: For each nurse response, indicate whether it is a therapeutic technique or a communication block.

rows.text: "You don't feel confident that you can manage this."
rows.rationale: Reflection. It directs his attention back to his own feelings and thoughts.

rows.text: "Why didn't you come in sooner?"
rows.rationale: Asking why puts him on the defensive and implies he did something wrong.

rows.text: "I am here with you. Let me sit down."
rows.rationale: Offering self. It demonstrates presence and reduces the sense of being alone with it.

rows.text: "My mother went through this and she was fine."
rows.rationale: Changing the subject to herself, and it also carries false reassurance.

rows.text: "So what worries you most is what this means for your work."
rows.rationale: Restating. It repeats his main idea in different words, which shows listening and verifies understanding.

rows.text: "If I were you, I would start the treatment right away."
rows.rationale: Unsolicited advice. It substitutes her judgment for his decision.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic: clarification, restating, reflection, silence, offering self, giving information. Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing, judging, stereotyping, approving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: Every block here is well-intentioned. Ask whether the response keeps him talking or shuts the conversation down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does he say more, or stop?
It always reads as an accusation.
Her mother, her advice.

elimination.verdict: Three therapeutic, three blocking.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says he does not understand any of it and that everyone uses words he does not know. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask what he does understand so far, to find where the gap begins
options.rationale: You cannot pitch an explanation without knowing where to start. Assessing before teaching applies here as it does everywhere else.

options.text: Explain heart failure again using plain language
options.rationale: The right eventual move, and starting there means guessing which part lost him.

options.text: Provide written material he can read at his own pace
options.rationale: Useful once you know his reading level and where the gap is. Handing over paper before assessing repeats the problem in a new format.

options.text: Reassure him that it will make more sense over time
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it closes the opening he has just given you.

questions.takeaway: Assess before teaching. Excessive medical jargon is the named barrier, and plain language is the remedy once you know where to begin.
questions.strategy: Two distractors deliver the teaching correctly and too early. One closes the conversation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That he is lost, not where.
Both act before assessing.
It ends the exchange.

elimination.verdict: That leaves finding where the gap begins.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to talk with a patient about a difficult diagnosis. Which environmental factors should she consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Noise in the room and corridor
options.rationale: Named, and it forces both people to work harder to be understood.

options.text: Privacy from other patients and visitors
options.rationale: Named, and it determines what he is willing to say.

options.text: The number of people present
options.rationale: Named, and an audience changes what gets disclosed.

options.text: How she and the patient are positioned
options.rationale: Named, and standing over someone communicates before anyone speaks.

options.text: The time available for the conversation
options.rationale: Named, and a conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: The patient's level of education
options.rationale: A genuine factor influencing communication and it is not environmental. The environment is what surrounds the exchange.

questions.takeaway: Environment: noise, privacy, lighting, temperature, number of people present, positioning, and time available.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real factor from the other list. Environment is what is around the conversation, not what either person brings to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Room, people, time.
A factor influencing communication, not environmental.
All named environmental considerations.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient stops talking and looks out of the window after describing his symptoms. The nurse waits without speaking. Which technique is she using and why?

options.text: Silence, which gives him time to think and allows emotions to surface
options.rationale: Named as a therapeutic technique. It feels uncomfortable because nurses feel they are supposed to be doing something.

options.text: Clarification, to allow him to correct what he has said
options.rationale: Clarification asks a question when a statement is unclear or incomplete. She has asked nothing.

options.text: Reflection, to direct him back to his feelings
options.rationale: Reflection names the feeling out loud. Silence makes room for it without naming it.

options.text: Offering self, to demonstrate presence
options.rationale: The near-miss. Offering self involves saying something like I am here with you. Silence is presence without words.

questions.takeaway: Silence gives the patient time to think, allows emotions to surface, and encourages communication. It is a technique rather than an absence of one.
questions.strategy: Three distractors require the nurse to say something. She has said nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing, deliberately.
Clarification, reflection, offering self.
Silence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves silence.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the communication process with a student.

The person who initiates the communication and encodes the message is the [[1]].

The route the message travels, whether spoken, written or electronic, is the [[2]].

The response that tells the sender the message was received is the [[3]].

Repeating a patient's main idea in different words is [[4]].

options.text: sender
options.rationale: Initiates the communication and encodes the message.

options.text: receiver
options.rationale: Receives, interprets and decodes the message.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: The route the message travels.

options.text: context
options.rationale: The environment the exchange happens in.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: Speech, writing, a phone or a screen. The route rather than the content.

options.text: message
options.rationale: The near-miss. The message is the content; the channel is how it travels.

options.text: feedback
options.rationale: The response coming back.

options.text: context
options.rationale: The surrounding environment.

options.text: feedback
options.rationale: What tells the sender whether the message arrived and how it was understood.

options.text: decoding
options.rationale: What the receiver does internally to interpret the message.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: The route, not the response.

options.text: congruence
options.rationale: Whether verbal and nonverbal messages agree.

options.text: restating
options.rationale: Repeats the main idea using different words, which demonstrates listening and verifies understanding.

options.text: reflection
options.rationale: The near-miss. Reflection directs attention to feelings and thoughts; restating repeats the idea.

options.text: clarification
options.rationale: Used when a statement is unclear, incomplete or misunderstood.

options.text: giving information
options.rationale: Supplying accurate, understandable information appropriate to the patient's needs.

questions.takeaway: Six components: sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context. Restating repeats the idea; reflection names the feeling.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: message against channel, and restating against reflection. Content against route, and idea against feeling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: What is said, and how it travels.
Feedback closes the loop.
Restating and reflection.

elimination.verdict: Sender, channel, feedback, restating.

questions.stem: A patient says he does not know whether he can manage his insulin at home. Which response is reflection?

options.text: "So you are unsure about the insulin injections specifically."
options.rationale: Restating. It repeats his idea in different words rather than naming the feeling underneath it.

options.text: "Can you tell me more about which part concerns you?"
options.rationale: Clarification. It asks a question to make an incomplete statement clearer.

options.text: "You are not feeling confident that you can manage this."
options.rationale: Reflection directs his attention back to his own feeling, which is her exact example.

options.text: "Most people find it easier after the first week."
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it is a block rather than a technique.

questions.takeaway: Reflection directs attention back to feelings, thoughts and ideas. Restating repeats the content.
questions.strategy: Restating and reflection are the pair that gets confused. One returns the idea, the other returns the feeling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is returned to him
steps.detail: His words, or his feeling.
Both work with the content.
A block.

elimination.verdict: That leaves reflection.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a relationship with a newly admitted patient. Which actions establish a therapeutic relationship? Select all that apply.

options.text: Introduce herself and explain her role
options.rationale: Named first. He needs to know who is in the room and why.

options.text: Address the patient properly
options.rationale: Named, and it means asking rather than assuming what he wants to be called.

options.text: Maintain privacy
options.rationale: Named, and it determines what he is willing to say.

options.text: Maintain professional boundaries
options.rationale: Named, and it protects the relationship from becoming something else.

options.text: Follow through on commitments
options.rationale: Named, and small promises kept are what make larger assurances believable.

options.text: Share a personal experience to build rapport
options.rationale: Moves the focus to the nurse. Changing the subject to yourself is among the named blocks.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic communication: introduce yourself, explain your role, address the patient properly, maintain privacy, demonstrate respect, maintain boundaries, be present and attentive, follow through.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds warm and moves the conversation to the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who the focus stays on
steps.detail: The patient.
Shifts the focus.
All named.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a patient's condition has changed but mentions it vaguely to the provider without giving the specific findings. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is acceptable, since the change was communicated in some form
options.rationale: Mentioning is not communicating. The findings are what let someone else act.

options.text: This is a safety concern, because professional communication supports safety and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Her slide names safety and clinical decision-making among what professional communication supports. A provider cannot act on information he did not receive.

options.text: The responsibility passes to the provider once he has been told something
options.rationale: She remains accountable for communicating clearly enough to be acted on.

options.text: The written record makes verbal communication less important
options.rationale: The record documents; it does not alert anyone in time.

questions.takeaway: Professional communication supports continuity, safety, collaboration and clinical decision-making. Miscommunication causes errors.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat partial communication as sufficient. Ask whether the provider can act on what he received.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he can do with it
steps.detail: Nothing specific.

steps.action: Cut the acceptable and transfer options
steps.detail: Neither makes the information usable.
Documentation does not alert.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the safety concern.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a frightened preoperative patient not to worry because the surgeon is excellent. Which block is this?

options.text: Minimizing feelings
options.rationale: The near-miss, and both are present. Minimizing dismisses the feeling as unimportant; false reassurance replaces it with a promise.

options.text: Changing the subject
options.rationale: She stayed on the topic. She answered it with a promise instead of an exploration.

options.text: Defending
options.rationale: Defending protects a person or the institution from criticism. Nobody has been criticized.

options.text: False reassurance
options.rationale: It promises an outcome nobody can guarantee, and it tells him the subject is closed.

questions.takeaway: Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing feelings, judging, stereotyping, approving and disapproving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is minimizing, and both elements are arguably present. The promise about the outcome is the defining feature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That it will be fine.
She stayed on topic.
Nothing was criticized.

elimination.verdict: That leaves false reassurance.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Nurse enters to discuss discharge medications with a 68-year-old. Television is on at volume. His daughter and two grandchildren are visiting. He is due to leave for a scan in ten minutes. He reports pain of 7 of 10 and has not had analgesia since 0600. He wears bilateral hearing aids, both in place. He is alert and oriented. The curtain is open and the adjacent bed is occupied. He speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should make the nurse defer or change this conversation.

segments.text: Television is on at volume
segments.rationale: Noise is a named environmental factor, and it is the easiest of these to fix.

segments.text: His daughter and two grandchildren are visiting
segments.rationale: The number of people present is named, and young children in the room affect what anyone will raise.

segments.text: Due to leave for a scan in ten minutes
segments.rationale: Time available is named. Starting a discharge medication discussion with ten minutes is worse than deferring it.

segments.text: Pain of 7 of 10, no analgesia since 0600
segments.rationale: Health status, specifically pain, is a named factor influencing communication. Nobody learns well at 7 of 10.

segments.text: The curtain is open and the adjacent bed is occupied
segments.rationale: Privacy is named, and medication discussions disclose diagnoses.

segments.text: Wears bilateral hearing aids, both in place
segments.rationale: A potential barrier that is already managed. Aids in place is the reassuring detail.

segments.text: Alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Cognitive ability is a named factor and here it is intact, which removes it as a barrier.

segments.text: Speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty
segments.rationale: Language and literacy are both potential barriers, and both are ruled out by this finding.

questions.takeaway: Factors influencing communication: developmental level, culture, language, health status, emotional state, cognitive ability, environment, previous experience, personal perceptions.
questions.strategy: Three findings are barriers that are already resolved or absent. They are there to be left alone, and each one tells you something useful.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate present barriers from absent ones
steps.detail: Hearing aids in, oriented, fluent.
Noise, people, privacy, time.
Pain at 7 of 10.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5: four environmental factors and his pain.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient whether the pain is worse today. He answers yes and says nothing further. Which change would improve the exchange?

options.text: Ask an open-ended question about how the pain has been
options.rationale: Open-ended questions encourage communication. A closed question produced exactly what it invited.

options.text: Ask whether the pain is sharp or dull
options.rationale: Another closed question. It narrows further rather than opening.

options.text: Ask why he did not mention it sooner
options.rationale: Asking why is a named block and it puts him on the defensive.

options.text: Tell him the analgesia will be due shortly
options.rationale: Moves to a solution before the assessment is complete.

questions.takeaway: Questions that encourage communication are open-ended. Closed questions have a place and they produce short answers.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is another closed question dressed as a follow-up. Ask which option cannot be answered in one word.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Test each for a one-word answer
steps.detail: Three can be.
A named block.
Acts before assessing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the open-ended question.

questions.stem: A nurse is told a patient from a particular cultural background will avoid eye contact and will want family present for decisions. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Plan the encounter around the described pattern
options.rationale: Applies a group generalization to an individual, which is how cultural knowledge becomes stereotyping.

options.text: Avoid eye contact throughout to show respect
options.rationale: Adopts the assumption as a rule. He may find it disconcerting.

options.text: Treat this as something to ask about rather than something to assume
options.rationale: Not all people from a particular culture communicate the same way, which is her opening line on the topic.

options.text: Ask the family what he would prefer
options.rationale: Asks about him without asking him. He is the person who knows.

questions.takeaway: Not all people from a particular culture communicate the same way. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: Two distractors act on the generalization. One asks the wrong person.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He does.

steps.action: Cut the two options acting on the assumption
steps.detail: Both apply a group pattern.
Bypasses him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking rather than assuming.

questions.stem: A nurse gives information to a patient about a new medication. Which characteristics should that information have? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accurate
options.rationale: Named, and information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped.

options.text: Appropriate to the patient's needs
options.rationale: Named, and it means relevant to him rather than comprehensive.

options.text: Understandable
options.rationale: Named, and information he cannot use has not been given.

options.text: Delivered in language free of excessive medical jargon
options.rationale: Named among effective verbal communication, and jargon is the named barrier.

options.text: Comprehensive enough to cover every possible side effect
options.rationale: Overloading with information is a named thing to avoid, and an exhaustive list is unusable at home.

questions.takeaway: Giving information: accurate, appropriate to the patient's needs, understandable. It decreases uncertainty and supports decision making.
questions.strategy: One distractor mistakes completeness for quality. Overloading is a named error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Accurate, appropriate, understandable.
Overloading is named as a thing to avoid.
All supported by her slides.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse sits at eye level, does not interrupt, repeats key phrases, and watches the patient's facial expression while he speaks. Which does this describe?

options.text: Therapeutic silence
options.rationale: Silence is waiting without speaking. She is repeating phrases and responding.

options.text: Clarification
options.rationale: One technique within the exchange rather than the whole approach described.

options.text: Active listening
options.rationale: Paying attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allowing him to speak, being mindful of interruptions, clarifying, and attending to nonverbal cues.

options.text: Offering self
options.rationale: Offering self means making yourself available: I am here with you. This describes how she listens.

questions.takeaway: Active listening: pay attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allow the patient to speak, mind interruptions, clarify and repeat phrases, reflect and validate, attend to nonverbal cues.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name a single technique. The stem describes several behaviors together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position, silence from interruption, repetition, observation.
Each is one part of it.
Active listening.

elimination.verdict: That leaves active listening.

questions.stem: A patient with expressive difficulty after a stroke struggles to find a word and the nurse finishes his sentence for him. Which problem does this create?

options.text: Interrupting, which is a named barrier and removes the time he needs
options.rationale: Being mindful of interruptions is part of active listening. For a patient with expressive difficulty, the time is the intervention.

options.text: Minimizing feelings, because his difficulty is dismissed
options.rationale: Nothing about his feelings is addressed or dismissed. The problem is the time taken from him.

options.text: Giving unsolicited advice about how to communicate
options.rationale: She supplied a word rather than advice.

options.text: Leading, because she directed his answer
options.rationale: The near-miss. She supplied a word he may or may not have wanted, and the core failure is that she did not let him finish.

questions.takeaway: Be mindful of interruptions. For a patient with expressive difficulty, allowing time is the intervention.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is leading, and supplying a word does steer him. What the technique names is the interruption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The time to find his own word.
Neither is described.
Related, and the named barrier is interrupting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves interrupting.

questions.stem: A nurse explains a procedure quickly, uses several abbreviations, and asks at the end whether the patient has any questions. He says no. Which error has she made?

options.text: Failing to obtain informed consent for the procedure
options.rationale: Consent is a separate process and is not what the stem describes.

options.text: Using a closed-ended question to end the conversation
options.rationale: Any questions is closed, and the deeper error is treating the answer as proof of comprehension.

options.text: Providing information that was not accurate
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the content was wrong. The problem is whether it landed.

options.text: Assuming understanding, which her slide names among the things to avoid
options.rationale: No questions is not evidence of understanding. Talking too fast, jargon, overloading and assuming understanding are all named together.

questions.takeaway: Avoid excessive medical jargon, talking too fast, overloading with information, and assuming understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real weakness in her closing question. Ask what she concluded from his answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That he understood.
Neither is described.
True, and secondary to the assumption.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assuming understanding.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old admitted with pneumonia has become withdrawn. He answers in single words, has not touched his meals, and turns toward the window when staff enter. His oxygen saturation is 95% and his pain is 2 of 10. His wife died three weeks ago. The unit is busy and the nurse has been documenting at the bedside computer while talking to him.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Sit down at eye level, stop documenting, and give him her full attention
options.rationale: Her own congruence example in reverse. Documenting while talking tells him she is not available, whatever she says.

options.text: Use reflection to name what he may be feeling, then allow silence
options.rationale: Reflection directs him back to his own feelings, and silence gives the time for them to surface.

options.text: Reassure him that he will feel better once the pneumonia clears
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it also attributes his withdrawal to the infection when his saturation and pain say otherwise.

options.text: Ask him why he is not eating
options.rationale: Asking why is a named block. It reads as an accusation to someone already withdrawn.

options.text: Withdrawal with a recent bereavement, and no one has been fully present with him
options.rationale: His emotional state is a named factor influencing communication, and the nurse's own incongruent behavior is part of why nothing has been said.

options.text: Hypoxia contributing to altered behavior
options.rationale: His saturation is 95%. The stem rules this out directly.

options.text: Uncontrolled pain limiting his willingness to talk
options.rationale: Pain at 2 of 10. Also ruled out by the stem.

options.text: Cognitive impairment affecting his ability to converse
options.rationale: Nothing suggests impairment. He answers, briefly, and turns away deliberately.

options.text: Whether he begins to say more than single words
options.rationale: The behavior that defined the problem, measured directly.

options.text: Whether he raises his wife or his situation without being prompted
options.rationale: Measures whether the relationship has become one he can use, which is what the actions aimed at.

options.text: Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%
options.rationale: A real parameter, and it evaluates his pneumonia rather than anything that was changed.

options.text: Whether he finishes his next meal
options.rationale: Intake matters and it is a downstream consequence rather than a measure of whether the communication worked.

questions.takeaway: Emotional state is a factor influencing communication. When the clinical numbers are reassuring, the withdrawal is telling you something the numbers cannot.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors are ruled out by values in the stem. The saturation and the pain score are placed there to eliminate the easy explanations.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation 95%, pain 2 of 10.

steps.action: Note what changed three weeks ago
steps.detail: His wife died.
Documenting while talking.

elimination.verdict: Sit and be present, reflect and allow silence, for withdrawal after bereavement, evaluated by what he says.

questions.stem: A nurse says to a patient, "You didn't take your medication again, did you?" Which two blocks does this combine?

options.text: Clarification and restating
options.rationale: Both are therapeutic techniques, and neither is present here.

options.text: A leading question and judging
options.rationale: The phrasing directs him to a particular answer, and again carries a verdict about him before he has spoken.

options.text: False reassurance and defending
options.rationale: Nothing is being promised, and nobody is being defended.

options.text: Changing the subject and stereotyping
options.rationale: The subject has not changed, and no group generalization is made.

questions.takeaway: Blocks include leading questions and judging. A single sentence can carry more than one.
questions.strategy: Two options list therapeutic techniques or blocks that are simply not present. Read the sentence for what it does to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Did you? invites one answer.
It carries a verdict.

steps.action: Cut the techniques and absent blocks
steps.detail: None appear in the sentence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a leading question with judging.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss communication. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "My nonverbal behavior may communicate more than my words."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her note on nonverbal communication.

options.text: "If the patient says he has no questions, I can record that he understood the teaching."
options.rationale: Assuming understanding is a named error. No questions may mean he does not know what to ask, or does not want to appear slow.

options.text: "Silence is a technique, not a gap I need to fill."
options.rationale: Accurate, and she notes that nurses find it uncomfortable because they feel they should be doing something.

options.text: "Therapeutic communication is purposeful rather than just being nice."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her framing.

questions.takeaway: Assuming understanding is a named error. Silence is a technique. Nonverbal behavior often says more than words.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats an absence of questions as proof of comprehension.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing about understanding.
Nonverbal, silence, purpose.
Assumed understanding.

elimination.verdict: That leaves recording that he understood.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to teach a newly diagnosed patient about his insulin. He reports pain of 8 of 10, his roommate's television is on, and his daughter is due in ten minutes. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach now and repeat the session before discharge
options.rationale: Two ineffective sessions rather than one effective one, and the first may leave him thinking he has already been taught.

options.text: Give him written material and review it later
options.rationale: Written material is a strategy, not a substitute for assessing readiness. He is unlikely to read it at 8 of 10.

options.text: Address the pain and the distractions, then teach when he is ready
options.rationale: Readiness asks whether pain is controlled, whether he is free from distractions, and whether he is interested. Teaching through 8 of 10 pain wastes the session.

options.text: Teach the daughter instead when she arrives
options.rationale: Family involvement is appropriate when he wants it and when they will provide the care. It is not a workaround for his pain.

questions.takeaway: Readiness to learn: is pain controlled, is he free from distractions, is he interested. Assess readiness before teaching.
questions.strategy: Three options proceed in some form. Ask what he is likely to retain at 8 of 10 with a television on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain uncontrolled, distractions present.
Neither addresses the barriers.
Not a substitute for teaching him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves addressing the barriers first.

questions.scenario: A nurse writes learning objectives for a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes.
questions.stem: For each objective, indicate which learning domain it belongs to.

rows.text: The patient will name three signs of hypoglycemia
rows.rationale: Knowledge and recall. The cognitive domain covers knowing, understanding and problem solving.

rows.text: The patient will draw up and inject the correct insulin dose
rows.rationale: A physical skill, demonstrated. Psychomotor covers physical skills and demonstration of procedures.

rows.text: The patient will express his concerns about injecting himself
rows.rationale: Feelings and attitudes. The affective domain covers feelings, values and motivation.

rows.text: The patient will decide what to do when his glucose reads 58 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Problem solving, which sits in the cognitive domain alongside knowledge.

rows.text: The patient will demonstrate rotating his injection sites
rows.rationale: Another physical skill performed and observed.

rows.text: The patient will state that managing his diabetes is worth the effort
rows.rationale: A value and a motivation rather than a fact or a skill.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing. Psychomotor is doing. Affective is valuing. The domain determines how the outcome is evaluated.
questions.strategy: Problem solving sits in cognitive rather than forming a domain of its own. Deciding what to do is still knowing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A fact, a movement, or a feeling.
It belongs to cognitive.
Both psychomotor.

elimination.verdict: Two cognitive, two psychomotor, two affective.

questions.stem: A nurse writes the objective that a patient will understand his new anticoagulant. Which revision is better?

options.text: The patient will state three foods to limit and two signs of bleeding before discharge
options.rationale: Observable, measurable and time-bound. Understand cannot be seen, and her slide gives exactly this contrast.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient about his anticoagulant before discharge
options.rationale: Describes what the nurse does. A learning objective describes what the patient will be able to do.

options.text: The patient will feel confident managing his anticoagulant at home
options.rationale: Confidence is no more observable than understanding. It replaces one unmeasurable verb with another.

options.text: The patient will comprehend the importance of consistent dosing
options.rationale: Comprehend is understand in different clothing.

questions.takeaway: Learning objectives describe what the patient will be able to do after teaching, and they must be evaluable.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap one unobservable verb for another. One changes the subject to the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One option is about the nurse.
Feel, comprehend, understand.

steps.action: Find the one you could watch
steps.detail: State three foods and two signs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the specific, observable objective.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to teach a patient before discharge. Which assessments belong to the period before teaching begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: What the patient already knows
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start.

options.text: Whether any barriers are present
options.rationale: Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy.

options.text: The patient's ability to learn
options.rationale: Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability.

options.text: Whether his pain is controlled
options.rationale: Named under readiness.

options.text: Whether he is interested
options.rationale: Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: Whether the teaching was effective
options.rationale: Evaluation comes after teaching. It cannot be assessed before anything has been taught.

questions.takeaway: Before teaching: assess what he knows, what barriers exist, and his ability to learn. Assess readiness: pain controlled, free from distractions, interested.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the end of the process. Place yourself in time before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing has been taught yet.
It comes afterwards.
All precede teaching.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a visiting daughter that her mother has hypertension exacerbated by failure to take her diuretic, that her systolic has been over 180, and that she is NPO pending an echocardiogram and an EKG. She then charts that the family was updated on the plan of care. Which problem does this create?

options.text: The nurse breached confidentiality by discussing the mother's care
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the daughter is not an appropriate person to speak with.

options.text: The jargon means the daughter may not have understood, so the chart entry may be inaccurate
options.rationale: Documenting that a family was updated records what the nurse said, not what they received. The entry is only true if the information landed.

options.text: The information given was clinically inaccurate
options.rationale: The content is accurate. The problem is that it was unusable.

options.text: The nurse should have waited for the provider to give this information
options.rationale: Explaining the plan of care is squarely nursing work. The failure is in how it was explained.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Never assume a patient or family understood, and documenting that you updated someone records your action rather than their understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor questions the accuracy of the content. Ask what the daughter can now do with what she was told.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Almost none of it.
Neither is the problem.
This is nursing work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves jargon making the chart entry doubtful.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse plans education for a patient going home with a new wound.

What the nurse does to facilitate learning is [[1]].

A change in knowledge, behavior, skill or understanding is [[2]].

Watching the patient perform the dressing change himself is [[3]].

A patient's ability to obtain, understand and use health information is [[4]].

options.text: teaching
options.rationale: Her definition: what the nurse does to facilitate learning.

options.text: learning
options.rationale: The near-miss. Learning is what happens in the patient; teaching is what the nurse does.

options.text: evaluation
options.rationale: Determining whether learning occurred.

options.text: health literacy
options.rationale: The patient's capacity to work with health information.

options.text: learning
options.rationale: Her definition, and it is measured by change rather than by exposure.

options.text: teaching
options.rationale: The nurse's activity. Teaching can happen without learning, which is why evaluation exists.

options.text: readiness
options.rationale: Whether the patient is in a state to learn.

options.text: reinforcement
options.rationale: The final step, repeating and strengthening what was learned.

options.text: return demonstration
options.rationale: The patient performs the skill back. It evaluates a psychomotor objective directly.

options.text: demonstration
options.rationale: The near-miss. Demonstration is the nurse showing; return demonstration is the patient doing.

options.text: teach-back
options.rationale: Teach-back has the patient explain in his own words. Useful, and it evaluates knowledge rather than a physical skill.

options.text: hands-on practice
options.rationale: Practice builds the skill. Return demonstration is where you assess it.

options.text: health literacy
options.rationale: Affects the ability to obtain, understand and use information, make decisions, and follow instructions.

options.text: readiness to learn
options.rationale: Whether he is able to engage right now.

options.text: cognitive ability
options.rationale: Closer, and health literacy is specific to health information rather than to general capacity.

options.text: the affective domain
options.rationale: Feelings, attitudes and motivation.

questions.takeaway: Teaching is what the nurse does. Learning is the change in the patient. Demonstration is the nurse showing; return demonstration is the patient doing.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: teaching against learning, and demonstration against return demonstration. In both, the question is who is acting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The nurse, or the patient.
Demonstration and return demonstration.
Health literacy is specific to health information.

elimination.verdict: Teaching, learning, return demonstration, health literacy.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient to use a new inhaler, then asks whether he understood. He nods and says yes. Which action should follow?

options.text: Ask him to use the inhaler while she watches
options.rationale: A psychomotor skill is evaluated by watching it performed. Never assume a patient understands because they nod.

options.text: Provide written instructions to reinforce the teaching
options.rationale: Reinforcement is a legitimate later step, and it does not tell you whether he can use the device.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the inhaler
options.rationale: Another closed question, and no questions is not evidence of competence.

options.text: Document that the patient verbalized understanding
options.rationale: Records the nod as evidence. Her slide names this assumption explicitly.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate learning by the method the objective requires. A physical skill is evaluated by demonstration, not by a nod.
questions.strategy: Three options accept a verbal answer as proof of a physical skill.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what kind of objective it is
steps.detail: Psychomotor.
Records an assumption.
Neither tests performance.

elimination.verdict: That leaves watching him use it.

questions.stem: A patient with a new abdominal wound cannot reach the site to change his own dressing. He lives with his son, who will perform the care. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach the patient thoroughly, since the education is for him
options.rationale: He cannot physically perform it. Teaching the person who cannot do the task leaves the person who will untrained.

options.text: Provide written instructions for the son to follow
options.rationale: Written material supports a skill. It does not establish that he can perform it.

options.text: Arrange home health so that nobody at home needs to be taught
options.rationale: May be appropriate and it does not remove the need for someone in the house to recognize problems.

options.text: Teach the son and confirm by return demonstration that he can perform it
options.rationale: Teaching should include the caregiver who will actually perform the care, and the confirmation is what makes it safe.

questions.takeaway: Ask who will provide care after discharge, who needs to learn the skill, whether the patient wants family involved, and whether the caregiver is an appropriate learner. Confirm by demonstration.
questions.strategy: One distractor keeps the teaching with the patient on principle. Ask who will be holding the dressing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The son.
He cannot reach the site.

steps.action: Cut home health and written material
steps.detail: Neither confirms capability at home.

elimination.verdict: That leaves teaching the son with return demonstration.

questions.stem: A nurse documents a teaching session about a new anticoagulant. Which elements belong in the entry? Select all that apply.

options.text: What was taught
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered.

options.text: The teaching method used
options.rationale: Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent.

options.text: The patient's response
options.rationale: Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning.

options.text: The level of understanding demonstrated
options.rationale: Named, and demonstrated is the operative word.

options.text: Any questions or concerns raised
options.rationale: Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: The amount of time the session took
options.rationale: Not among the named elements. Duration says nothing about whether learning occurred.

questions.takeaway: Document what was taught, the method, the patient or caregiver response, level of understanding, demonstrated skills, questions and concerns, and any additional teaching needed.
questions.strategy: One distractor records effort rather than outcome. Ask what the next nurse needs to know.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the next nurse needs
steps.detail: Content, method, response, gaps.
Effort, not outcome.
All named elements.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the same standardized diabetes teaching packet for a 20-year-old university student and a 74-year-old who lives alone. Which principle has she overlooked?

options.text: The younger patient requires less teaching than the older patient
options.rationale: Assumes from age in the other direction, which is the same error.

options.text: Written materials are inappropriate for older adults
options.rationale: Age does not determine whether written material works. Assessment does.

options.text: Diabetes teaching should always be delivered over multiple sessions
options.rationale: The number of sessions is not the principle at issue.

options.text: Teaching must be individualized rather than one size fits all
options.rationale: Her own example. The two patients differ in ability, resources, routine and what they need to manage.

questions.takeaway: Avoid one size fits all. Assess the individual, identify specific needs, match teaching to ability, use appropriate resources, and adapt the method.
questions.strategy: Two distractors make a new assumption based on age. That is the same error the question is about.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One packet for two different people.
Same error, reversed.
Not the principle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves individualization.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Nurse prepares discharge teaching for a 79-year-old going home with a new anticoagulant and a wound requiring daily dressing changes. Patient reports pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen. States he left his reading glasses at home. Says he stopped school at 14 and finds forms difficult. His wife, who will do the dressings, is present and attentive. He is alert and oriented. The room is quiet. He asks three specific questions about the medication. He has no prior experience of wound care.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should change how the nurse delivers this teaching.

segments.text: Left his reading glasses at home
segments.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods.

segments.text: Stopped school at 14 and finds forms difficult
segments.rationale: Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information.

segments.text: His wife will do the dressings and is present
segments.rationale: She is the person who will perform the skill, so she is the person who must demonstrate it back.

segments.text: No prior experience of wound care
segments.rationale: What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

segments.text: Pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen
segments.rationale: Controlled pain. Readiness on this count is satisfied, which is why it is here.

segments.text: Alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Cognitive ability intact, removing it as a barrier.

segments.text: The room is quiet
segments.rationale: Free from distractions, which is one of the readiness criteria met.

segments.text: Asks three specific questions about the medication
segments.rationale: Evidence of interest, and interest is the third readiness criterion. A strength rather than a barrier.

questions.takeaway: Four findings change the method: no glasses, limited literacy, a caregiver who will do the skill, and no prior experience. Four confirm he is ready.
questions.strategy: Every readiness criterion is met here and stated explicitly. The findings that matter are about how to teach, not whether to.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain, distraction, interest all satisfied.
Glasses, literacy, experience.
His wife.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: the four that change how you teach.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked whether patient education can be assigned to assistive personnel during a busy shift. Which response is accurate?

options.text: It may be delegated if the assistive personnel is familiar with the content
options.rationale: Familiarity with content does not confer the scope to assess or evaluate learning.

options.text: Patient education is within the nurse's scope and cannot be delegated
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly. Teaching requires assessment of learning needs and evaluation of learning, neither of which is delegable.

options.text: It may be delegated provided the nurse documents the education afterwards
options.rationale: Documenting something you did not do is a separate problem on top of the delegation error.

options.text: It may be delegated for routine topics such as diet
options.rationale: The topic does not change the scope. Reinforcing a message is different from teaching.

questions.takeaway: Patient education is in the nurse's scope of practice and is not something that can be delegated.
questions.strategy: Three distractors offer conditions under which it becomes acceptable. There are none.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Assessing needs and evaluating learning.
None changes the scope.
A second error on top.

elimination.verdict: That leaves education being non-delegable.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to teach a patient how to use a walker safely. Which teaching strategy best matches the objective?

options.text: A video showing correct walker technique
options.rationale: Better than text and still passive. Watching is not doing.

options.text: Written instructions with diagrams for reference at home
options.rationale: Useful as reinforcement. Nobody learns to walk with a device from a page.

options.text: Demonstration followed by hands-on practice and return demonstration
options.rationale: Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills, and practice with return demonstration is how the skill is built and confirmed.

options.text: A discussion about the importance of using the walker correctly
options.rationale: Discussion suits cognitive and affective objectives. It does not build a physical skill.

questions.takeaway: Match the teaching strategy to the learning goal. Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are strategies that would support the learning without producing it. Ask what the objective requires him to do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Psychomotor.
Suits knowledge and attitudes.
Both are passive.

elimination.verdict: That leaves demonstration with practice and return demonstration.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says he does not see the point of weighing himself daily because it will not change anything. Which learning domain should the nurse address first?

options.text: Cognitive, by explaining how daily weights detect fluid retention
options.rationale: Reasonable teaching and it addresses knowledge he may already have. He has not said he does not understand.

options.text: All three simultaneously, to be thorough
options.rationale: Spreads effort across two domains where there is no gap, and misses that his objection is about meaning.

options.text: Affective, because his attitude and motivation are the obstacle
options.rationale: He is not lacking the knowledge or the skill. Feelings, attitudes, values and motivation sit in the affective domain.

options.text: Psychomotor, by demonstrating correct use of the scale
options.rationale: Weighing is not the skill gap. He knows how to stand on a scale.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing, psychomotor is doing, affective is valuing. Address the domain where the gap actually is.
questions.strategy: One distractor is correct teaching aimed at a gap he has not shown. Ask what he actually said.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It will not change anything.
He has neither gap.
Effort where there is no gap.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the affective domain.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient going home after surgery. Which topics belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Medications and how to take them
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics.

options.text: Follow-up appointments
options.rationale: Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought.

options.text: Activity and diet restrictions
options.rationale: Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told.

options.text: Wound care
options.rationale: Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration.

options.text: Warning signs and when and how to seek help
options.rationale: Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: The names of the staff who provided his care
options.rationale: Courteous and not part of discharge education. Nothing about it affects his safety at home.

questions.takeaway: Discharge education: medications, follow-up appointments, activity, diet, wound care, warning signs, when and how to seek help, equipment, and self-management.
questions.strategy: One distractor is pleasant and changes nothing about how he manages at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he needs at home
steps.detail: Drugs, appointments, limits, wound, warnings.
No effect on safety.
All named topics.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse completes a teaching session and moves on to her next patient without checking what the patient took from it. Which error has she made?

options.text: Failing to individualize the teaching
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests the content was generic. The omission is at the end, not the start.

options.text: Teaching without evaluating learning
options.rationale: Her slide names this directly. Teaching and learning are separate things, and only evaluation tells you whether the second happened.

options.text: Failing to identify barriers before teaching
options.rationale: An error that happens before teaching. Hers happened after.

options.text: Failing to document the session
options.rationale: Documentation matters and it is a separate step. She could document accurately and still not know whether he learned.

questions.takeaway: Avoid teaching without evaluation of learning. Evaluation may be verbal explanation, demonstration, observation, or asking questions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real errors that occur at other points in the process. Place the omission in time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After teaching, before leaving.
Both precede teaching.
A separate step.

elimination.verdict: That leaves teaching without evaluation.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the sequence that effective patient education follows. Which order is correct?

options.text: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce
options.rationale: Her stated sequence. Assessment opens it and reinforcement closes it.

options.text: Teach, assess, practice, evaluate, communicate, reinforce
options.rationale: Places teaching before assessment, which is the error the whole chapter is built against.

options.text: Assess, teach, evaluate, communicate, practice, reinforce
options.rationale: Places evaluation before practice, so the skill is assessed before it has been built.

options.text: Communicate, teach, assess, reinforce, practice, evaluate
options.rationale: Assessment third and evaluation last with practice after reinforcement. The sequence is scrambled.

questions.takeaway: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce. Effective education depends on effective communication.
questions.strategy: Two things anchor the sequence: assessment comes first, and practice comes before evaluation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: First, always.
Build the skill, then assess it.
Each breaks one of those two rules.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce.

questions.stem: A nurse explains that a patient should ambulate three times daily, watch for edema, and remain NPO after midnight. Which change would most improve this?

options.text: Replace the clinical terms with words the patient uses
options.rationale: Ambulate, edema and NPO are all on her list of commonly used jargon. None of them means anything to most patients.

options.text: Repeat the instructions a second time before leaving
options.rationale: Repeating words he does not understand produces the same result twice.

options.text: Provide the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: The same jargon in a different format.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the instructions
options.rationale: He cannot form a question about terms he did not follow, and no questions would then be recorded as understanding.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Ambulate, edema, NPO, dyspnea, hypertension, PRN, EDD and SBA are all named as commonly used and commonly misunderstood.
questions.strategy: Three distractors deliver the same words again in a different way. Ask what he did not understand the first time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three clinical terms in one sentence.
Same words, different delivery.
He cannot ask about what he missed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves replacing the terms.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her own documentation of a teaching session with a colleague. Which entry requires correction?

options.text: "Patient education is in my scope and I cannot delegate it."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is stated directly on her slide.

options.text: "Teaching is what I do; learning is the change in the patient."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the distinction is why evaluation exists.

options.text: "A 20-year-old with diabetes needs different teaching from a 74-year-old."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her own example of individualization.

options.text: "Patient nodded and stated he understood; learning objectives met."
options.rationale: Never assume a patient understands because they nod. Learning is a change that has to be evaluated, not inferred.

questions.takeaway: Never assume understanding from a nod. Teaching is what the nurse does; learning is the change that has to be demonstrated.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats a nod as evaluation.
