options.text: Ask the provider and pharmacist to review the diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Medication dizziness is addressed by the RN with the pharmacist. The drug is a likely contributor.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest until the confusion clears
options.rationale: Fall prevention does not mean keeping her in bed. Immobility worsens weakness.

options.text: Raise all four side rails
options.rationale: A confused client may climb over them. Four rails up count as a restraint.

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints for the night
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for routine fall prevention.

question.takeaway: Match each intervention to a specific risk factor. The goal is safe mobility, not immobility.
question.strategy: The three wrong options all restrict her. Each one looks safe and each one raises her risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.action: Link each option to a risk factor
steps.detail: Urgency, bed height, vision, footwear, medication.
Bed rest, four rails and restraints.
They fix the cause instead of holding her down.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Pulling at IV tubing. Trying to climb over the raised side rail. Restless. Daughter cannot come until 0800. Charge nurse asks whether wrist restraints are needed.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints per agency policy
options.rationale: Restraints are a last resort. The chart shows no alternatives tried yet.

options.text: Assess whether she needs to void or is in pain
options.rationale: Ask why before you restrain. She said she had to go right now. Meeting that need often ends the behavior.

options.text: Request a prescription for a sedative
options.rationale: A sedative used to control behavior is a chemical restraint. It also adds to her confusion.

options.text: Raise the side rails at the foot of the bed
options.rationale: She is already climbing over a rail. More rails give her a higher fall.

question.takeaway: Before any restraint, look for the unmet need: toileting, pain, thirst, fear or a medication effect.
question.strategy: The charge nurse suggestion makes the restraint feel approved. The deck says to ask why first.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Priority key word

steps.detail: The question asks for the first action.
Physical restraint, chemical restraint and extra rails.
Find the cause of the behavior.

elimination.verdict: Assess for toileting need and pain.

entries.text: Voided 300 mL with assistance at 0430; resting quietly since. Toileted every 2 hours. IV covered with a stretch sleeve; not reaching for tubing. Bed alarm on. Glasses on; states "I know I am in the hospital." Night light on. No restraints used. Provider notified about diphenhydramine; discontinued. Used call light at 0615 to ask for help. Bed found in high position after 0545 linen change; lowered.

question.scenario: The nurse evaluates the fall prevention plan at the end of the shift.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the interventions were effective or not effective.

rows.text: Voided 300 mL with assistance at 0430; resting quietly since
rows.rationale: Meeting the toileting need ended the attempts to get up.

rows.text: Not reaching for IV tubing under the sleeve
rows.rationale: Covering the line was a restraint alternative that worked.

rows.text: Used the call light at 0615 to ask for help
rows.rationale: She is asking for help instead of getting up alone.

rows.text: Bed found in high position after the 0545 linen change
rows.rationale: The same process gap happened again. Add a bed height check after every linen change and reinforce it at shift report.

rows.text: States "I know I am in the hospital" with glasses on
rows.rationale: Reorientation with her glasses is improving her awareness.

question.takeaway: Evaluate each intervention against its goal. One gap in the environment can undo a plan that is otherwise working.
question.strategy: The bed height row is about staff, not the client. It still counts as a failure of the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each row to its goal
steps.detail: Toileting, IV protection, call light use, orientation, bed height.
A high bed means the environment plan failed.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, not effective, effective.

questions.scenario: A nurse assesses four patients experiencing stress.
questions.stem: For each set of findings, indicate which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome it represents.

rows.text: Pulse 118, respirations 26, diaphoretic and restless five minutes after being told his biopsy was positive
rows.rationale: Sympathetic activation within minutes of a perceived threat. Fight or flight.

rows.text: Six weeks into caring for her husband, she says she is managing and her blood pressure has risen from 118/74 to 146/88
rows.rationale: Functioning is maintained while stress hormones stay elevated. Patients may appear fine while carrying high stress.

rows.text: After eight months of financial strain: fatigue, irritability, poor sleep, and three chest infections
rows.rationale: Resources depleted, with frequent illness reflecting the immune suppression chronic stress produces.

rows.text: Pupils dilated, blood glucose 148, muscle tension, moments after a near-miss in traffic
rows.rationale: The full sympathetic picture, including the rise in glucose, immediately after the threat.

rows.text: Three months after a job loss she has stopped seeing friends, cannot concentrate, and has begun drinking daily
rows.rationale: Coping resources overwhelmed, with maladaptive coping and social withdrawal appearing together.

questions.takeaway: Alarm is the immediate fight-or-flight response. Resistance is adapting while hormones stay elevated. Exhaustion is depletion, with illness and maladaptive coping.
questions.strategy: Resistance is the stage people miss, because the patient looks well. Rising blood pressure with I am managing is the picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Minutes, weeks, or months.
Resistance hides behind functioning.
Frequent infection points to exhaustion.

elimination.verdict: Two alarm, one resistance, two exhaustion.

questions.stem: A patient has been caring for a disabled child for eleven years. Her blood pressure is now 152/94, she sleeps poorly, and she has developed reflux. Which concept explains the link between her circumstances and these findings?

options.text: The alarm stage, because her sympathetic nervous system is activated
options.rationale: Alarm is the immediate response to a threat. Eleven years is not an alarm response.

options.text: An adventitious crisis arising from an unplanned event
options.rationale: Adventitious crises are rare catastrophic events. This is sustained rather than sudden.

options.text: Allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear of repeated or chronic stress
options.rationale: Long-term stress produces hypertension, sleep problems, digestive problems and raised glucose. The load accumulates rather than resolving between episodes.

options.text: Secondary traumatic stress from exposure to another person's suffering
options.rationale: Secondary traumatic stress comes from repeated exposure to others' trauma. Hers is the ongoing demand of caregiving.

questions.takeaway: Allostatic load is the cumulative physiologic wear and tear caused by repeated or chronic stress. It produces hypertension, heart disease, sleep problems, digestive problems and raised glucose.
questions.strategy: Two distractors name real concepts that describe short or sudden stress. The stem gives you eleven years.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eleven years.
Both describe short-term events.
That is exposure to others' trauma.

elimination.verdict: That leaves allostatic load.

questions.stem: A patient whose home was destroyed in a wildfire three weeks ago tells the nurse her usual ways of coping are no longer working and she does not know what to do next. Which does this describe?

options.text: Exhaustion, the third stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome
options.rationale: Exhaustion describes physiologic depletion over prolonged stress. Crisis names the failure of coping specifically.

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder following a traumatic event
options.rationale: PTSD involves flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance. Nothing in the stem describes those.

options.text: A crisis, a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work
options.rationale: Her definition. A crisis is defined by coping failing, not by the size of the event.

options.text: Maladaptive coping, because her strategies are ineffective
options.rationale: Maladaptive coping means using strategies that harm, such as substance use or withdrawal. Hers have stopped working rather than become harmful.

questions.takeaway: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental, situational and adventitious are the three types.
questions.strategy: One distractor requires symptoms the stem does not give. One confuses coping failing with coping harming.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Her usual coping no longer works.
No flashbacks, avoidance or hypervigilance described.
Failed is not the same as harmful.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a crisis.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse works with several patients in crisis.

A first-time mother overwhelmed by the transition to parenthood is experiencing a [[1]] crisis.

A man whose business closed last month is experiencing a [[2]] crisis.

A family displaced by an earthquake is experiencing an [[3]] crisis.

A nurse who feels guilt and loss of confidence after a medication error caused harm is experiencing [[4]].

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Triggered by a normal life transition. Becoming a parent is expected and can still overwhelm coping.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: The near-miss. Situational crises come from external events rather than from expected life stages.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Unplanned, rare and catastrophic.

options.text: traumatic
options.rationale: Not one of the three named crisis types.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: Provoked by an external event such as job loss, a crash or serious illness.

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Developmental crises arise from normal life transitions.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Reserved for rare catastrophic events.

options.text: chronic
options.rationale: A type of stress rather than a type of crisis.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Unplanned, rare and catastrophic. A natural disaster is the standard example.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: The near-miss. Both are externally provoked; adventitious is reserved for the rare and catastrophic.

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Nothing about an earthquake is a life stage.

options.text: secondary
options.rationale: Not a crisis type.

options.text: second victim syndrome
options.rationale: Emotional and psychological trauma after involvement in an unexpected adverse event, error or injury. Guilt, shame, anxiety, fear and decreased confidence.

options.text: compassion fatigue
options.rationale: The near-miss. Compassion fatigue comes from repeated exposure to others' suffering; second victim syndrome follows a specific adverse event she was involved in.

options.text: secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Stress from repeated exposure to others' trauma.

options.text: moral distress
options.rationale: Knowing the right action and being constrained from taking it.

questions.takeaway: Developmental crises come from life transitions, situational from external events, adventitious from rare catastrophes. Second victim syndrome follows an adverse event you were involved in.
questions.strategy: Situational and adventitious both come from outside. Adventitious is reserved for the rare and catastrophic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A life stage, an event, or a catastrophe.
Rarity and scale.
Cumulative exposure, or one specific event.

elimination.verdict: Developmental, situational, adventitious, second victim syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse her diagnosis must be a laboratory error and that she feels completely well. Which defense mechanism is she using?

options.text: Compensation, making up for a weakness by excelling elsewhere
options.rationale: Compensation involves building up one area to offset another. Nothing here describes that.

options.text: Denial, refusing to accept that something is real
options.rationale: She is rejecting the reality of the diagnosis rather than reinterpreting it.

options.text: Projection, attributing her own feelings to someone else
options.rationale: Projection means putting your own feeling onto another person. She is not describing anyone else's feelings.

options.text: Dissociation, detaching from thoughts, feelings or surroundings
options.rationale: Dissociation involves separating from your own experience. She is present and arguing.

questions.takeaway: Five defense mechanisms: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, compensation.
questions.strategy: Ask what she is doing with the information. Rejecting it outright is different from reinterpreting it or detaching from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That the diagnosis is real.
No other person's feelings involved.
She is present, and nothing is being offset.

elimination.verdict: That leaves denial.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old who has been toilet trained for four years begins wetting the bed after his parents separate. Which defense mechanism does this represent?

options.text: Compensation, offsetting a loss in one area with achievement in another
options.rationale: Nothing here describes achievement elsewhere.

options.text: Dissociation, detaching from the situation
options.rationale: Dissociation involves separation from one's own thoughts, feelings or surroundings.

options.text: Denial, refusing to accept the separation is real
options.rationale: Denial rejects the reality. The bedwetting is a return to earlier functioning rather than a rejection of facts.

options.text: Regression, returning to an earlier stage of functioning under stress
options.rationale: A behavior appropriate to a younger age reappearing when coping is overwhelmed.

questions.takeaway: Regression is a return to an earlier stage of functioning under stress. It is common in children and it occurs in adults too.
questions.strategy: The signal is a skill that was established being lost. Ask what direction the behavior moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A skill held for four years.
Backward, to earlier functioning.
None describes going backward.

elimination.verdict: That leaves regression.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient who has just learned of a terminal diagnosis. Which findings represent the alarm stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate increased from 78 to 116
options.rationale: Sympathetic activation raises heart rate.

options.text: Respirations increased and shallow
options.rationale: Named among the alarm findings.

options.text: Pupils dilated
options.rationale: A classic sympathetic sign.

options.text: Blood glucose rising
options.rationale: Named, and it is how the body mobilizes fuel for fight or flight.

options.text: Restless and fearful
options.rationale: Alertness, restlessness and fear are all named alarm findings.

options.text: Increased bowel sounds and hunger
options.rationale: Digestion decreases during alarm rather than increasing. The body diverts resources away from it.

questions.takeaway: Alarm: raised heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, glucose, muscle tension, sweating, dilated pupils, increased alertness, restlessness, fear, and decreased digestion.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses a real alarm finding. Digestion goes down, not up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Everything speeds up except digestion.
Digestion decreases.
All named alarm findings.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient facing surgery organizes her questions, researches the procedure, and arranges childcare for the recovery period. Which type of coping is she using?

options.text: Emotion-focused coping, managing feelings related to the stressor
options.rationale: Emotion-focused coping addresses the feelings. Hers addresses the circumstances.

options.text: Problem-focused coping, taking action to change or solve the stressor
options.rationale: Every action she has taken alters the situation itself rather than her feelings about it.

options.text: Maladaptive coping, because she is avoiding her feelings
options.rationale: Nothing suggests avoidance, and problem-focused coping is not maladaptive.

options.text: Defense mechanisms operating unconsciously
options.rationale: Defense mechanisms are unconscious. Her actions are deliberate.

questions.takeaway: Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings about it. Neither is inherently better; effectiveness depends on the situation.
questions.strategy: One distractor reads deliberate practical action as avoidance. Ask what her actions changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The circumstances around the surgery.
She did not address her feelings.
Deliberate and constructive.

elimination.verdict: That leaves problem-focused coping.

questions.stem: A patient facing a diagnosis she cannot change spends time with family, prays, and uses a breathing exercise when she feels overwhelmed. A student asks whether this is less effective than problem solving. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Problem-focused coping is more effective in most situations
options.rationale: Neither type is inherently superior. The fit with the situation is what matters.

options.text: She should be encouraged to use both types equally
options.rationale: Balance sounds sensible and it ignores that some stressors offer nothing to solve.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping is a form of avoidance
options.rationale: Avoidance is maladaptive. Managing feelings deliberately is not the same thing.

options.text: Effectiveness depends on the person and the situation, and some stressors cannot be changed
options.rationale: Coping effectiveness depends on the person, the situation, culture, past experiences, resources and support. Where the stressor is fixed, emotion-focused coping is the appropriate strategy.

questions.takeaway: Coping effectiveness depends on the person, situation, culture, past experiences, resources and support systems.
questions.strategy: One distractor ranks the two types. Ask what problem-focused coping could do about a diagnosis that cannot be changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing about the diagnosis itself.
Neither type is superior.

steps.action: Cut avoidance and the equal-use option
steps.detail: One mislabels it, one ignores the situation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves effectiveness depending on the fit.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies maladaptive coping in a patient under prolonged stress. Which behaviors are examples? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoiding or denying the problem
options.rationale: Named first, and it provides short-term relief while the problem grows.

options.text: Substance use
options.rationale: Named, and it is the one most likely to produce a second problem.

options.text: Overeating or undereating
options.rationale: Named, and either direction counts.

options.text: Excessive sleeping
options.rationale: Named, and it is distinct from the sleep disturbance stress also causes.

options.text: Social withdrawal
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the support system that would otherwise help.

options.text: Talking through the problem with a trusted friend
options.rationale: An adaptive strategy using the support system. Maladaptive coping gives short-term relief at a longer-term cost.

questions.takeaway: Maladaptive coping provides short-term relief and is harmful or ineffective over time: avoidance, substance use, disordered eating, excessive sleeping, withdrawal, aggression.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses the support system rather than retreating from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five accumulate a cost.
Uses support rather than avoiding it.
All named.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 1530: Patient is 34, admitted following a house fire two days ago in which her partner died. Sitting upright, staring at the door. Has not slept since admission. Startles when the door opens. Says she cannot stop seeing it. Has not eaten. States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her. Declines to contact her sister. Vital signs stable. No injuries requiring treatment. Chart notes she has a supportive sister two hours away.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing action.

segments.text: States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her
segments.rationale: A statement suggesting suicidal ideation. Stay with the patient, complete screening per policy, ensure immediate safety, and notify the team. This is the finding that outranks everything else here.

segments.text: Has not slept since admission
segments.rationale: Two days without sleep worsens every other finding and is itself a safety issue.

segments.text: Has not eaten
segments.rationale: An immediate need. Identifying pain, food, rest, privacy and support is part of acute crisis care.

segments.text: Startles when the door opens and says she cannot stop seeing it
segments.rationale: Hypervigilance and intrusive images. Trauma responses are not overreactions and they need recognizing.

segments.text: Declines to contact her sister
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from an available support, and support systems are one of the factors that determine coping.

segments.text: Vital signs stable
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding, and it is what tells you the problem is not physiological.

segments.text: No injuries requiring treatment
segments.rationale: Also reassuring. She survived the fire physically intact, which is not the same as intact.

segments.text: Has a supportive sister two hours away
segments.rationale: A resource rather than a finding. It is what makes the declining to contact her actionable.

questions.takeaway: In acute crisis: ensure safety first, screen for self-harm when it is mentioned or suspected, then identify immediate needs of pain, food, rest, privacy, information and support.
questions.strategy: One finding outranks all the others and it is easy to read past because it is phrased indirectly. Everyone would manage without her is not a throwaway line.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Everyone would manage without her.
Sleep, food, support.
Stable, uninjured, sister available.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5, with the safety statement taking priority.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department after an assault says she does not want to talk about it and asks whether she can keep her coat on. Which response reflects trauma-informed care?

options.text: Tell her she can keep the coat on and ask what would make her more comfortable
options.rationale: Choice and safety are two of the elements. Offering options wherever possible restores control to someone who has just had it taken.

options.text: Encourage her to talk, since expressing what happened will help
options.rationale: Overrides her stated preference. Listening without minimizing does not mean requiring disclosure.

options.text: Arrange for a family member to stay with her to provide support
options.rationale: Well intentioned, and it decides for her who should be present.

options.text: Explain that the coat must be removed for the examination
options.rationale: May be true eventually, and stated as an instruction it removes the choice she has just asked for.

questions.takeaway: Trauma-informed care: safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, respect.
questions.strategy: Three distractors decide something on her behalf. Ask which option returns a decision to her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: To keep her coat, and not to talk.

steps.action: Cut the instruction and the encouragement
steps.detail: Both override her.
Decides who is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves offering choice.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient's stress and coping. Which questions belong in that assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether the patient is currently safe
options.rationale: Named first, and safety is prioritized before anything else.

options.text: How the patient perceives the stressor
options.rationale: Named, and appraisal determines the impact more than the event does.

options.text: What coping resources are available
options.rationale: Named, and it covers support, finances and problem-solving skills.

options.text: Whether maladaptive coping is being used
options.rationale: Named, and it changes both the risk and the plan.

options.text: Adherence to healthy practices
options.rationale: Named, and it covers sleep, eating and activity.

options.text: Which defense mechanism the patient is using
options.rationale: Defense mechanisms are useful to recognize and are not among the named assessment questions. They operate unconsciously and labelling them is not the assessment.

questions.takeaway: Assessment questions: patient safety, perception of the stressor, available coping resources, maladaptive coping used, and adherence to healthy practices.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real concept from the chapter that is not one of the five assessment questions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safety, perception, resources, maladaptive coping, healthy practices.
Not among the assessment questions.
All named.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit reports feeling emotionally drained and numb, irritable with colleagues, and less affected by patients' distress than she used to be. She has made no errors. Which does this describe?

options.text: A situational crisis provoked by an external event
options.rationale: No single external event is described. This is cumulative.

options.text: Compassion fatigue from repeated exposure to others' suffering
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from repeated exposure. Irritability, numbness, decreased empathy and reduced job satisfaction.

options.text: Second victim syndrome following an adverse patient event
options.rationale: Second victim syndrome follows involvement in a specific adverse event, error or injury. The stem states she has made no errors.

options.text: The alarm stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome
options.rationale: Alarm is the acute sympathetic response to an immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: irritability, trouble sleeping, emotional numbness, decreased empathy, feeling overwhelmed or detached, reduced job satisfaction.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is second victim syndrome, and the stem rules it out by stating she has made no errors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No errors, so no adverse event.
Requires a specific event.
Both require an identifiable trigger.

elimination.verdict: That leaves compassion fatigue.

questions.stem: A nurse involved in a medication error that harmed a patient reports guilt, shame and loss of confidence in her practice. Which support is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that errors happen to everyone
options.rationale: False reassurance. It minimizes what she is carrying and closes the conversation.

options.text: Recommend she take time away from clinical practice
options.rationale: May be appropriate and it is a decision, not a support. Offered first it can read as removal.

options.text: Recognize this as second victim syndrome and connect her with peer support
options.rationale: Emotional and psychological trauma after involvement in an adverse event. Naming it is what allows support to be offered rather than endured privately.

options.text: Advise her to focus on the system factors rather than her own role
options.rationale: System analysis is necessary and it does not address what she is feeling.

questions.takeaway: Second victim syndrome: guilt, shame, anxiety, fear and decreased confidence after involvement in an unexpected adverse event, error or injury.
questions.strategy: Two distractors redirect her away from the feeling. Ask what she has actually described.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Guilt, shame, lost confidence.
Both move past it.

steps.action: Cut time away as the first move
steps.detail: A decision rather than support.

elimination.verdict: That leaves naming it and connecting her with peer support.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a patient experiencing severe stress after a serious diagnosis. Which is the first priority in the plan?

options.text: Realistic, patient-centered outcomes
options.rationale: Named second. Outcomes matter once safety is established.

options.text: Including the patient in defining what better coping looks like
options.rationale: Named, and it follows safety rather than preceding it.

options.text: Collaborating with the health care team and support system
options.rationale: Named, and it is part of the plan rather than its first priority.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Prioritize safety first. Everything else in the plan depends on the patient being safe while it happens.

questions.takeaway: Planning for stress management: prioritize safety first, then realistic patient-centered outcomes, include the patient in defining better coping, collaborate, and set time frames that match the setting.
questions.strategy: All four appear on her planning slide. The question asks which comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safety is stated first.
All real, none first.

steps.action: Ask what everything else depends on
steps.detail: The patient being safe.

elimination.verdict: That leaves safety.

questions.stem: A nurse implements health promotion interventions for a patient with high stress. Which are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery.

options.text: Educating about stress triggers and self-management strategies
options.rationale: Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode.

options.text: Referring to counseling, therapy or a peer support group
options.rationale: Named, and it extends support beyond the admission.

options.text: Arranging a quiet space with reduced stimuli
options.rationale: Environmental modification, named directly.

options.text: Scheduling rest breaks
options.rationale: Named alongside environmental modification.

options.text: Advising the patient to avoid thinking about the stressor
options.rationale: Avoidance is named as maladaptive coping. It provides short-term relief and does not help over time.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion interventions: relaxation techniques, education on triggers and self-management, referral, and environmental modification. Tailor them to the patient.
questions.strategy: One distractor recommends the first item on the maladaptive coping list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Relaxation, education, referral, environment.
Named as maladaptive.
All named interventions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone tells the nurse she has stopped going out since her husband died, cannot get to the shops, and is worried about money. Which additional assessments does her age make important?

options.text: Depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts
options.rationale: Named specifically for older adults, and each of her stated concerns raises the likelihood of all four.

options.text: Cognitive function and memory
options.rationale: Relevant generally and not what her slide names for stress and coping in older adults.

options.text: Medication adherence and polypharmacy
options.rationale: Important in older adults generally and not what this chapter names for stress and coping.

options.text: Nutritional intake and weight
options.rationale: Worth assessing given she cannot reach the shops, and it is not among the four named.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, assess depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts when indicated. Daily stressors include health changes, transportation, finances, loss and home maintenance.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely important in older adults. The question asks what this chapter names for stress and coping.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loss, transport, finances.
Depression, loneliness, safety, suicidal thoughts.
Important, and from other chapters.

elimination.verdict: That leaves depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss stress and coping. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "A patient in the resistance stage is coping well and needs no intervention."
options.rationale: Patients may appear fine while carrying high stress, and stress hormones remain elevated. Looking well is not the same as being well.

options.text: "A crisis is defined by coping failing, not by how large the event was."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is what makes a developmental crisis possible.

options.text: "Trauma responses are responses to remembered threat, not overreactions."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her wording.

options.text: "Allostatic load is the cumulative wear and tear of chronic stress."
options.rationale: Accurate.

questions.takeaway: In the resistance stage the patient may appear fine while stress hormones stay elevated. Functioning is not the same as recovery.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth reads a stage as a resolution.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adapting while still under stress.
Trauma, crisis, allostatic load.
Appearing fine read as coping well.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the resistance statement.

questions.scenario: A 45-year-old is admitted for observation after a collapse at work. Tests show no physical cause. She tells the nurse she has been working double shifts for seven months since her divorce, sleeps about four hours a night, has lost 9 kg, and has had three chest infections this year. She says she is coping and does not want to worry anyone. She has stopped seeing the friends she used to see weekly.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Assess her safety, her perception of the stressor, and what support is available
options.rationale: The named assessment questions, and safety comes first. Withdrawal plus exhaustion plus I do not want to worry anyone warrants direct enquiry.

options.text: Explore with her what reconnecting with her support system could look like
options.rationale: Support systems are one of the factors determining coping, and she has withdrawn from one she had.

options.text: Reassure her that many people go through difficult periods after a divorce
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it normalizes seven months of physiological depletion.

options.text: Recommend she reduce her shifts and take time off work
options.rationale: Sensible advice offered before understanding why she is working doubles. The finances may be the reason.

options.text: Exhaustion stage with maladaptive coping and depleted resources
options.rationale: Seven months of sustained stress with fatigue, poor sleep, weight loss, frequent infection and social withdrawal. That is depletion, not adaptation.

options.text: Alarm stage with sympathetic activation
options.rationale: Alarm is the immediate response to a threat, measured in minutes.

options.text: An adventitious crisis following a catastrophic event
options.rationale: Adventitious crises are rare catastrophes. A divorce is a situational stressor, and this has been building for months.

options.text: An expected adjustment reaction following divorce
options.rationale: Three infections, 9 kg lost and four hours of sleep is not an expected adjustment. It is the physiology of exhaustion.

options.text: Whether she reports her stress feels more manageable
options.rationale: Asking the patient directly is the first evaluation step named on her slide.

options.text: Sleep, appetite and concentration at follow-up
options.rationale: The symptoms that defined the exhaustion, reassessed. Named among the evaluation measures.

options.text: Whether she can name three relaxation techniques
options.rationale: Tests recall of teaching. It does not measure whether her coping improved.

options.text: Whether her employer reduces her shift allocation
options.rationale: Evaluates the employer rather than the patient, and it may not be within anyone's control.

questions.takeaway: Exhaustion presents physically: fatigue, poor sleep, impaired concentration and frequent illness. I am coping is what people say while depleted.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors describe short-term responses. The timeframe of seven months and the three infections are what rule them out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Seven months.
Weight, sleep, three infections.
Alarm and adventitious crisis.

elimination.verdict: Assess safety and support, explore reconnection, for exhaustion with maladaptive coping, evaluated by her report and her symptoms.

questions.stem: A patient who managed independently at home has been kept in bed for six days during treatment for an infection. The patient now needs two people to move from lying to sitting. Which statement best explains this change?

options.text: Prolonged rest reduced muscle strength, and the patient is now unable to move safely without help
options.rationale: Deconditioning is the loss of strength and endurance that follows disuse. Muscle weakens quickly without load, which is why restriction is not a neutral choice and why immobility is itself a fall risk factor.

options.text: The infection has extended and is producing new neurologic weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic weakness comes from damage to nerves or the brain and usually appears in a pattern, such as one side or one limb group. A spreading infection is a real possibility to rule out, and nothing here points to it.

options.text: The patient has become unmotivated to participate in care
options.rationale: Motivation describes willingness. Substituting a judgment about the patient for a mechanism is how real causes get missed.

options.text: This degree of change is an expected part of aging and will resolve once the patient is home
options.rationale: Expected aging changes develop gradually over years. Attributing an acute functional loss to age leaves a reversible problem untreated.

questions.takeaway: Immobility produces the weakness that produces falls. A functional loss that appears over days has a cause you can name and usually reverse.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel tells the nurse that a patient 'looks strong enough to walk to the door alone today.' Which response does the nurse make?

options.text: If the patient seems steady once you are up, it is fine to let go partway
options.rationale: Letting go mid-ambulation is a change in the level of assistance. Judging readiness is nursing judgment and does not transfer with the task.

options.text: Walk with the patient at the assistance level on the plan, and tell me what you notice
options.rationale: Delegation transfers a task while the nurse keeps the decision and the outcome. The task proceeds at the specified level, and the observation returns to the nurse, who is the one who may change the plan.

options.text: Leave the patient in bed until I am able to get there myself
options.rationale: Deferring the activity means the patient does not move today. This sounds cautious and quietly chooses immobility.

options.text: Document that the patient walked independently today
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. Recording an outcome that was never observed is both inaccurate and unsafe for whoever reads it next.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel may assist with mobility according to the plan. Deciding what the plan should be, and deciding mid-task to change it, stays with the nurse.

questions.stem: A patient was kept in restraints in bed for two days because of severe agitation during an acute illness. The restraints were removed this morning. Which finding indicates a complication of the restraints rather than a feature of the illness?

options.text: The temperature is 38.0 C
options.rationale: Fever is a systemic response to infection or inflammation. This belongs to whatever brought the patient in.

options.text: The white blood cell count remains elevated
options.rationale: White blood cells rise in response to infection and inflammation. It tracks the underlying illness.

options.text: The patient cannot bear weight to stand and needs two people to pivot to the chair
options.rationale: Loss of mobility is one of the listed complications of restraint. Muscle strength falls quickly without load, and this is the deficit that was created by the treatment rather than by the disease.

options.text: The patient reports a dry mouth after taking nothing by mouth overnight
options.rationale: Dry mouth follows reduced oral intake. Hydration is a genuine monitoring area during restraint use, and this particular finding is already explained.

questions.takeaway: Restraints cause skin and neurovascular injury, increased agitation and confusion, loss of mobility, and injury sustained trying to escape. Two days held still is enough to cost a patient the strength to stand.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old has weak legs after a week in bed at home. She is oriented, sees well and has no urinary urgency. Which intervention should the nurse include in her fall plan?

options.text: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
options.rationale: Weakness is the risk factor she has. Assisted, progressive movement treats it.

options.text: Scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: This targets urgency. She has none.

options.text: Frequent reorientation with familiar cues
options.rationale: This targets confusion. She is oriented.

options.text: Brighter lighting with glasses within reach
options.rationale: This targets visual impairment. She sees well.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the patient's actual risk factor. Each correct intervention for another problem is a distractor.
questions.strategy: Every negative finding in the stem rules out one option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weak legs.
Oriented, sees well, no urgency cut three options.
Weakness needs assisted mobility.

elimination.verdict: A. Weakness is treated by supported movement.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient who has been on bed rest for five days is getting up for the first time. The patient has lost two pounds since admission and says the stay has been boring. Before standing, the nurse has the patient sit at the edge of the bed. The patient says the room is 'swimming,' and the heart rate rises from 78 to 106.

The finding that most increases the risk for injury at this moment is [[1]].

The nurse's next action is to [[2]].

The change that would show the plan is working is [[3]].

options.text: the patient's report of boredom during the stay
options.rationale: Boredom describes how the stay has felt. It is true and inert.

options.text: the five days of bed rest
options.rationale: Bed rest is the exposure that produced the deconditioning. This is the genuine near miss in the pair.

options.text: a two-pound weight loss since admission
options.rationale: A small weight change over a short admission is common and nonspecific. No, and it is the kind of measured value that looks meaningful because it has a number attached.

options.text: the dizziness and the rise in heart rate on sitting up
options.rationale: Together these describe the body failing to keep blood pressure stable when the patient changes position. Read as a pair they mean the patient is not ready to stand.

options.text: ask assistive personnel to walk the patient while you finish charting
options.rationale: Handing off an activity means transferring it at the assistance level on the plan. Delegating an activity the patient is not currently tolerating passes the risk to someone with less authority to stop it.

options.text: assist the patient to stand immediately so the episode passes
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart. This is the moment the patient is most likely to fall.

options.text: keep the patient sitting and supported until the symptoms settle, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: Sitting at the edge of the bed lets the circulation adjust to the upright position in stages. It treats the symptom, preserves the mobility plan, and creates a checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: help the patient lie back down and cancel the activity for the day
options.rationale: Canceling returns the patient to bed. The symptom needs managing, not the activity abandoning.

options.text: the patient agrees to get up again tomorrow
options.rationale: Agreement is a statement of intent. A patient can be entirely willing and still become dizzy on sitting.

options.text: the patient sits and then stands without dizziness and walks the planned distance with the planned assistance
options.rationale: An outcome is a change in the patient, stated in terms of what the patient can do. It names position change without symptoms, and distance with a specified assistance level, both of which can be observed and compared.

options.text: the bed alarm does not sound during the shift
options.rationale: A silent alarm means no unassisted movement was detected. Only that the patient stayed put, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.text: the family reports the patient seems more cheerful
options.rationale: Mood is worth knowing and is reported by someone else. Ask: does it measure whether the patient can change position and walk safely? No.

questions.takeaway: After a period of restricted movement, getting up is staged. Symptoms on sitting are the checkpoint, and the outcome is stated as what the patient can do, not as what the patient intends or how the patient feels.

questions.stem: A patient's right leg can slide across the mattress but cannot lift off the bed. The goal is movement against gravity. Which finding indicates the goal was met?

options.text: Lifts the leg off the bed but cannot hold against pressure
options.rationale: Clearing gravity without added resistance is grade 3. That is the goal.

options.text: Slides the leg across the bed with less effort
options.rationale: Sliding keeps the movement in a supported plane. This is still grade 2.

options.text: A visible thigh contraction when asked to lift
options.rationale: A contraction without movement is grade 1. This is worse than baseline.

options.text: Bends the knee while lying on the side
options.rationale: Side-lying takes gravity out of knee movement. This is still grade 2.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the hinge. Below it the limb moves only with gravity removed. Above it you add resistance.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the limb is lifting against gravity in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Movement against gravity is grade 3.
Sliding and side-lying remove gravity.
Only A raises the limb off the surface.

elimination.verdict: A. The leg clears gravity.

questions.stem: A nurse has just repositioned a patient from supine to a side-lying position. The patient has a nasogastric tube, a urinary catheter, and an intravenous line. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the time of the position change and the position used
options.rationale: Documentation records what was done. Charting follows the reassessment rather than replacing it, and a problem created by the turn would go unfound.

options.text: Reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and the ability to breathe comfortably
options.rationale: Reassessment after repositioning checks what the move itself changed. With three devices in place, a tube caught under the patient or pulled taut is the predictable harm, and it is found in the minute after the turn or not at all.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees to support breathing
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed supports lung expansion and is part of supported Fowler's positioning. Changing the position again undoes the turn before anyone has checked it.

options.text: Return in two hours to reposition the patient again
options.rationale: Scheduled repositioning limits the time any one area spends under pressure. Leaving now means any problem the turn created has two hours to develop.

questions.takeaway: Repositioning is not finished when the patient is moved. Alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and comfortable breathing are all reassessed afterward, because the turn is what put them at risk.

questions.stem: A patient on mechanical ventilation for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome is placed prone for persistent hypoxemia. Which finding indicates the positioning is effective?

options.text: Redness over the sacrum has resolved
options.rationale: Turning does relieve sacral pressure. Here proning treats the lungs, so a skin finding does not measure its goal.

options.text: The hips and shoulders remain in extension
options.rationale: Preventing contractures is a general goal of positioning. It is not why this patient was placed prone.

options.text: Oxygen saturation has risen from 86% to 94%
options.rationale: Prone positioning is first-line therapy for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. Rising saturation shows the hypoxemia it targets is improving.

options.text: The endotracheal tube is easier to suction
options.rationale: Airway access is harder in the prone position. It is not a goal of proning.

questions.takeaway: Prone positioning is a lung treatment. Judge it by oxygenation, not by skin or joints.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for 2 weeks has thinning thighs and a weaker grip. The plan adds high-protein meals and progressive activity. Which finding indicates the plan is working?

options.text: Serum calcium is rising
options.rationale: Rising calcium means unloaded bone is still losing mineral. That is not improvement.

options.text: Grip strength and thigh size are increasing
options.rationale: Lean mass is being rebuilt. Negative nitrogen balance is reversing.

options.text: Eats less at each meal
options.rationale: Falling appetite worsens protein loss. This is a problem, not progress.

options.text: Weight is stable while the thighs keep thinning
options.rationale: Muscle is still wasting. Stable weight hides it.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes negative nitrogen balance with loss of lean mass. Protein plus activity reverses it.
questions.strategy: The findings in the stem are muscle findings, so improvement must show in the muscle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lean muscle loss from negative nitrogen balance.
Calcium and appetite changes are getting worse.
Only B shows muscle returning.

elimination.verdict: B. Muscle is rebuilding.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient reports a fall at home last month with no injury. Has lived alone since a spouse died two years ago and says most days are spent in a recliner watching television. Reports smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinking three to four beers most evenings. Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device. Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement. Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days. Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade. Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that place this patient at risk for further loss of musculoskeletal health.

segments.text: reports a fall at home last month with no injury
segments.rationale: A prior fall is the strongest single predictor of a future fall. The event demonstrates that balance or strength already failed once, and the next fall may land differently.

segments.text: most days are spent in a recliner watching television
segments.rationale: Sedentary time is time without load on muscle and bone. Sitting for most of the day supplies neither, and disuse takes muscle and bone apart.

segments.text: smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years
segments.rationale: Tobacco use is named among the things to avoid in order to maintain musculoskeletal health. Four decades, which is a sustained modifiable risk rather than an incidental one.

segments.text: drinking three to four beers most evenings
segments.rationale: Excessive alcohol is to be limited for musculoskeletal health. Yes, it is a daily pattern well above moderate intake, and alcohol also contributes to falls and to poor nutrition.

segments.text: Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device
segments.rationale: Independent ambulation without an assistive device is preserved function. It is something to build on rather than a risk.

segments.text: Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement
segments.rationale: Appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake is one of the listed measures that promotes musculoskeletal health. No, it describes the patient already doing one of the right things.

segments.text: Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days
segments.rationale: Adequate nutrition supports bone and muscle. Combined with the supplement, intake appears adequate.

segments.text: Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade
segments.rationale: Height loss reflects vertebral compression from reduced bone density. It signals osteopenia or osteoporosis, which is the aging change most likely to produce a fracture, and it is measurable evidence that bone has already been lost.

segments.text: Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally
segments.rationale: Symmetry and strength on bilateral comparison are normal findings. Comparing sides is how you establish that, and both sides are equal and strong.

questions.takeaway: Musculoskeletal health is promoted by regular physical activity, weight-bearing exercise, adequate nutrition, appropriate calcium and vitamin D, avoiding tobacco, and limiting excessive alcohol. Each of those is a place a patient can be losing ground.

questions.stem: A patient with dyspnea is placed in supported Fowler's position. Which finding 20 minutes later indicates the positioning was effective?

options.text: Has slid down with legs flat on the mattress
options.rationale: Without hip and knee flexion the patient slides. Sliding causes shear.

options.text: Breathing easier with hips and knees flexed
options.rationale: Supported Fowler's flexes the hips and knees. Upright alignment lets the lungs expand.

options.text: Head resting forward on the chest
options.rationale: This loses the cervical curve. It narrows the airway.

options.text: Arms hanging over the side rails
options.rationale: Unsupported arms pull on the shoulders. Alignment is lost.

questions.takeaway: Supported means held in alignment, not merely propped up. Reassess breathing after repositioning.
questions.strategy: The goal has two parts, easier breathing and alignment. Only one option shows both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Easier breathing in alignment.
Slumping, head flexion and hanging arms break alignment.
Only B reports easier breathing.

elimination.verdict: B. Aligned and breathing easier.

questions.stem: A patient on prolonged bed rest says the days feel pointless and has stopped asking to sit in the chair. Which nursing response best addresses this finding?

options.text: Arrange activities the patient values and involve family in the daily routine
options.rationale: Boredom, isolation, and loss of independence are listed psychosocial effects. They matter because a patient who disengages stops doing the activity that reverses the physical decline.

options.text: Explain that the rest is medically necessary and will end soon
options.rationale: Reassurance that closes the conversation and leaves the isolation unaddressed.

options.text: Document that the patient is depressed and notify the provider
options.rationale: Charting a label in place of acting. Nothing changes for the patient today.

options.text: Limit visitors so the patient can rest more fully
options.rationale: Increases isolation, which is the problem rather than the treatment.

questions.takeaway: Psychosocial effects are not the soft part of the list. They become physical decline.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for 5 days has hypoactive bowel sounds and no bowel movement. The patient can now sit and stand. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Increase dietary protein
options.rationale: Protein addresses negative nitrogen balance. It does not move the bowel.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices
options.rationale: These prevent venous stasis. They do nothing for the gut.

options.text: Keep the patient flat to rest the bowel
options.rationale: More immobility slows peristalsis further.

options.text: Ambulate the patient as tolerated with fluids
options.rationale: Movement restores peristalsis. Fluid keeps slow stool from hardening.

questions.takeaway: Immobility slows gut motility. The fix is movement plus fluid.
questions.strategy: The hypoactive bowel sounds point to slowed motility. The ability to stand makes walking possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slowed peristalsis from immobility.
Protein and compression devices treat other effects.
Standing means walking is an option.

elimination.verdict: D. Movement moves the bowel.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients who have been on bed rest for 3 weeks. Which patient should the nurse see first?

options.text: The patient with 1,400 mL of urine in 24 hours
options.rationale: This is adequate output. Nothing suggests stasis.

options.text: The patient with pale urine after drinking more
options.rationale: This is an expected response to fluids.

options.text: The patient with flank pain and cloudy, foul urine
options.rationale: Stasis allows infection and stones. This patient shows both.

options.text: The patient with urine specific gravity of 1.015
options.rationale: This is in the normal range.

questions.takeaway: Urinary stasis from immobility raises the risk of infection and stones. Abnormal beats expected.
questions.strategy: Three patients have normal or expected findings. One does not.

strategies: Odd man wins
Priority key word

steps.detail: Output, color and specific gravity are normal.
Pain with cloudy, foul urine means infection or stone.
Abnormal findings take priority.

elimination.verdict: C. The only abnormal finding.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches isometric exercises to a patient in skeletal traction who cannot move the affected leg. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will bend and straighten my knee against the traction."
options.rationale: That is isotonic exercise. It moves the joint, which traction forbids.

options.text: "The nurse will move my leg through its range of motion."
options.rationale: Passive range of motion keeps flexibility. The muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: "I will lift light ankle weights with that leg."
options.rationale: Resistance training loads a moving joint. It is not possible or safe in traction.

options.text: "I will tighten my thigh muscle and hold it without moving my leg."
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. It keeps strength in a limb that must stay still.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint. Isometric does not, which is why it works in a limb that must stay still.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old widow living alone in a third floor walkup has rarely left home since her husband died. Her gait and blood pressure are normal. Which factor does not explain her low activity?

options.text: Loss of her main social support
options.rationale: Her husband's death removed help and encouragement to stay active.

options.text: Her normal gait and blood pressure
options.rationale: Her health status is not limiting her. Normal gait and blood pressure do not explain why she stays home.

options.text: Three flights of stairs at home
options.rationale: Her environment makes every trip out harder.

options.text: Grief affecting her motivation
options.rationale: Emotional health shapes behavior. Grief commonly lowers activity.

questions.takeaway: Activity is shaped by development, health status, lifestyle, culture, environment, behavior and social support.
questions.strategy: The word not flips the question. Three options come straight from her story as barriers. Pick the one that is not a barrier.

strategies: Negative polarity
Odd man wins

steps.detail: You are looking for the factor that does not belong.

steps.action: Match each factor to the story
steps.detail: Her husband's death, the stairs and her grief all limit activity.
Her normal gait and blood pressure do not limit activity.

elimination.verdict: B, her normal gait and blood pressure.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia has been in bed for 4 days. The nurse sits the patient upright to cough and deep breathe every 2 hours. Which finding indicates effectiveness?

options.text: No calf tenderness
options.rationale: This reflects venous stasis prevention. It does not measure the lungs.

options.text: Full range of motion in all joints
options.rationale: This reflects contracture prevention. Correct care, different system.

options.text: Clear lung bases with an effective cough
options.rationale: Upright position expands the lungs and coughing clears secretions. Clear bases show both worked.

options.text: Serum albumin within normal range
options.rationale: This reflects nutrition. It says nothing about the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Match the evaluation to the intervention. Expansion and coughing are judged by breath sounds and cough.
questions.strategy: Each distractor is a real outcome of immobility care for a different system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lung expansion and secretion clearance.
Calves, joints and albumin are not lungs.
Clear bases and a strong cough.

elimination.verdict: C. The lungs are clear.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for four days sits at the edge of the bed to ambulate. Blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 102/58, pulse rises to 104, and the room is spinning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the patient sitting and supported, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: This is orthostatic hypotension. Staying seated lets circulation adjust without abandoning activity.

options.text: Assist the patient to stand so the episode passes
options.rationale: Standing lowers cerebral perfusion further. This is when the fall happens.

options.text: Return to supine and cancel activity for the day
options.rationale: Cancelling deepens the deconditioning that caused the problem.

options.text: Give the ordered analgesic and retry in an hour
options.rationale: Nothing points to pain, and rest does not improve orthostatic tolerance.

questions.takeaway: Falling pressure with a rising pulse on position change is orthostatic hypotension. Stage the change, do not cancel it.
questions.strategy: Read the pressure and pulse as a pair. Then pick the option that keeps the patient safe and still moving.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Priority key word

steps.detail: Pressure down, pulse up, dizzy.
Standing is unsafe and cancelling is too much.

elimination.verdict: Stay seated, then recheck.

questions.stem: A patient with sequential compression devices ordered has been immobile for five days after a pelvic fracture. The left calf is 3 cm larger than the right, warm and tender. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply the sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Compression prevents venous stasis in a limb without a clot. Applying it now treats prevention as if it were treatment.

options.text: Encourage active ankle pumping in both legs every hour
options.rationale: Leg exercises are correct prevention and are not the response to a limb that already shows the complication.

options.text: Hold the sequential compression devices and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness suggests a thrombus has already formed. Compression on a limb with a suspected clot is applied only after evaluation, so the device is held and the finding is reported.

options.text: Measure both calves again in four hours to establish a trend
options.rationale: The difference is already measured and symptomatic. Waiting adds risk without adding information.

questions.takeaway: Prevention and treatment are different. Once one limb shows swelling, warmth, and tenderness, stop preventing and start reporting.

questions.stem: A patient who slides down in bed and is dragged back up several times a day has reddened, partially denuded skin over the sacrum. The bed is kept at 45 degrees. Which change most directly addresses the mechanism of injury?

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier ointment to the sacrum twice daily
options.rationale: Moisture management is appropriate skin care and does nothing about the sliding that is tearing tissue.

options.text: Turn the patient every two hours without changing the bed angle
options.rationale: Turning limits time under pressure. The injury here is produced by sliding, which continues at 45 degrees.

options.text: Place a pillow under the knees to improve comfort
options.rationale: Knee flexion does help resist sliding, and alone it does not address either the bed angle or how the patient is moved.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed when clinically possible and use a lift sheet to reposition
options.rationale: Elevation lets the skeleton slide while the skin stays fixed, which is shear, and dragging adds friction. Lowering the angle removes the driving force and lifting removes the surface drag.

questions.takeaway: Pressure pushes down, friction rubs, shear slides the tissue under fixed skin. A head-up bed plus dragging produces the last two.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for two weeks has a footboard in place. The nurse finds the feet resting with the toes pointed and a gap of several inches between the soles and the board. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The device is not in contact with the feet, so it is not preventing plantar flexion
options.rationale: A footboard works only when the soles rest against it at a neutral angle. A gap means the ankles are free to settle into plantar flexion, which is how foot drop develops.

options.text: The findings are expected and the device is working as intended
options.rationale: Toes pointed is the position the device exists to prevent, so the finding is evidence it is not working.

options.text: The patient has developed a permanent contracture that the device can now correct
options.rationale: Contractures are permanent shortening. Positioning prevents them and does not reverse them, and nothing here establishes one has formed yet.

options.text: The gap indicates the patient has been performing active ankle exercises
options.rationale: Active movement would show the ankles in varied positions, not both settled in plantar flexion.

questions.takeaway: A supportive device only works in contact. Check that the intervention is actually happening, not just present.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for 3 weeks eats a third of each meal. Albumin is 2.9 g/dL and the limbs look thinner. Which outcome is most appropriate for the plan?

options.text: Eats most of high-protein meals with albumin rising
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance plus poor intake caused the loss. More protein targets both.

options.text: Reduces calories to match lower metabolic demand
options.rationale: Demand is lower, yet cutting intake worsens protein loss.

options.text: Serum calcium stays 9 to 10.5 mg/dL
options.rationale: Calcium tracks bone loss. The findings here are muscle and protein.

options.text: Stays on bed rest to spare protein stores
options.rationale: Immobility is what breaks down protein. Rest makes it worse.

questions.takeaway: Low albumin, poor intake and thin limbs are one process. Treat intake and activity together.
questions.strategy: Each finding in the stem points to protein. The outcome should measure protein.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Poor intake, low albumin and wasting are protein loss.
Fewer calories and more rest worsen it.
Calcium is bone.

elimination.verdict: A. Intake and albumin should rise.

questions.stem: A patient two days after knee arthroplasty is on a weight-bearing restriction and reports the knee is too painful to bend beyond a few degrees. Which exercise best maintains quadriceps strength now?

options.text: Perform straight leg raises through the full range
options.rationale: Isotonic work through a full arc. The hip moves and the load on a painful healing knee exceeds what this patient tolerates.

options.text: Have the nurse move the knee through its full range twice daily
options.rationale: Passive range maintains flexibility and the patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Tighten the quadriceps and hold without moving the knee
options.rationale: Isometric contraction loads the muscle with no joint movement, which is why it is used around painful or healing joints. Strength and joint stability are preserved during the period the knee cannot move.

options.text: Walk short distances with a walker several times daily
options.rationale: Isotonic and limited by the weight-bearing restriction. Walking does not load the quadriceps the way a held contraction does while the knee cannot bend.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint, isometric does not. When the joint cannot move, isometric is the only way to keep the muscle.

questions.stem: An immobile patient is turned every 2 hours into a pillow-supported 30-degree side-lying position. Skin is intact. The hips and knees are becoming stiff. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Continue turning without changes
options.rationale: Intact skin shows turning works for skin. It does nothing for stiff joints.

options.text: Perform range-of-motion exercises to the hips and knees
options.rationale: Stiffness means joints are not moving through their arc. Positioning holds a joint but does not move it.

options.text: Place a pillow under the knees when supine
options.rationale: Constant knee flexion promotes contracture.

options.text: Lengthen the time between turns
options.rationale: Longer time under load threatens the skin. It does not help the joints.

questions.takeaway: Positioning protects skin and alignment. It does not replace movement.
questions.strategy: The intact skin is the distractor cue. The stiff joints are the problem to act on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin is fine. Joints are stiffening.
Continuing or stretching the schedule ignores the joints.
A knee pillow holds flexion.

elimination.verdict: B. Joints need movement.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old is on day 2 of an admission for a heart failure exacerbation. Furosemide 40 mg by mouth is scheduled at 1000 and 2200. Overnight the patient voided five times between 2300 and 0500. Staff found the patient walking to the bathroom alone twice. Once there was urine on the floor beside the bed. The patient has been alert and oriented x4 on every check. Glasses are on and within reach. Orthostatic vital signs at 0600: lying 132/78 with a pulse of 80, standing 128/76 with a pulse of 84, no dizziness. Weight is down 1.1 kg from yesterday. The fall risk score is high.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 risk factor the plan must target, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 1 to 2 hours overnight with assistive personnel
options.rationale: Getting the patient to the bathroom before the urge peaks removes the reason to rush. The deck pairs urgency with scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours.

options.text: Ask the provider and pharmacist whether the evening furosemide dose can be given earlier in the day
options.rationale: The 2200 dose is producing diuresis all night. Moving it earlier keeps the benefit and moves the voiding to hours when the patient is awake and staff are nearby.

options.text: Place a bed alarm and tell the patient to stay in bed until morning
options.rationale: An alarm tells you after the patient is already up. Telling someone with urgency to stay in bed sets up another solo trip or incontinence.

options.text: Reorient the patient to the room every hour overnight
options.rationale: This targets confusion. The patient has been oriented on every check, so it does not touch the actual risk.

options.text: Hold the 2200 furosemide dose tonight
options.rationale: Holding a prescribed diuretic in heart failure is not a nursing fall intervention. Timing changes go through the provider and pharmacist.

options.text: Urinary urgency and frequency from diuretic timing
options.rationale: Five voids overnight after a 2200 diuretic dose, solo trips and urine on the floor. The patient is rushing to the bathroom.

options.text: Medication-related dizziness
options.rationale: The orthostatic check is negative and there is no dizziness. The medication is causing urgency, not unsteadiness.

options.text: Confusion and disorientation
options.rationale: Oriented x4 on every check.

options.text: Visual impairment
options.rationale: Glasses are on and within reach.

options.text: Number of times the patient gets up alone overnight
options.rationale: This is the unsafe behavior the plan is meant to stop. If it keeps happening the plan is not working.

options.text: Nighttime voiding frequency after the dose timing changes
options.rationale: Shows whether moving the dose shifted the diuresis out of the night.

options.text: Orientation score each shift
options.rationale: Worth charting routinely. It does not measure the risk factor being treated.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure every 4 hours
options.rationale: Already negative. Repeating it every 4 hours overnight adds sleep disruption without measuring the target.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the actual risk factor. Urgency is handled with scheduled toileting and, when a diuretic drives it, with a conversation about dose timing.
questions.strategy: The scenario rules out confusion, vision and dizziness with specific data. Use each negative finding to cross off an option, then pick the actions that fit what is left.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Rule out the other risk factors
steps.detail: Oriented x4, glasses on, orthostatics negative.
Five overnight voids after a 2200 diuretic mean urgency.
Scheduled toileting and a timing review. Reject alarms, bed rest and holding the drug.
Solo trips out of bed and nighttime voiding.

elimination.verdict: Urgency from diuretic timing; scheduled toileting and a timing review; solo trips and nighttime voids.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old taking apixaban is found on the floor at 0300 with a red mark on the forehead. The nurse has called for help and is staying. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Return the patient to bed with enough staff and a lift
options.rationale: Moving before assessment can worsen a hip or neck injury.

options.text: Assess for injury, including the head, hips and consciousness
options.rationale: Find what is hurt before moving. The anticoagulant and forehead mark point to a head injury.

options.text: Notify the provider of the fall and the anticoagulant
options.rationale: The provider needs to know, after you have findings to report.

options.text: Document the event and complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: Documentation comes last.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: get help and stay, assess, move safely, notify, then document.
questions.strategy: Help is already coming. Ask what you must know before anyone moves the patient.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Priority key word

steps.detail: Help is called.
Assess before moving.

elimination.verdict: Assess for injury before moving.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old two days after hip repair pulls at her IV and tries to climb out of bed. Her last analgesic was 8 hours ago, and her bladder is distended. Which action is best?

options.text: Obtain an order for wrist restraints to protect the IV
options.rationale: A restraint is a last resort and treats neither pain nor a full bladder.

options.text: Raise all four side rails
options.rationale: Four rails are a restraint, and confused patients climb over them.

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative so she sleeps
options.rationale: A drug to control behavior is a chemical restraint and leaves the pain and full bladder untreated.

options.text: Assess pain and bladder, then give the analgesic and help her void
options.rationale: Overdue analgesia and a full bladder are fixable causes of the agitation.

questions.takeaway: Before a restraint, ask why. Pain and a full bladder often end the behavior once fixed.
questions.strategy: Two cues name unmet needs. Pick the option that meets them.

strategies: Odd man wins
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Three restrain physically or chemically.
Eight hours since analgesia and a full bladder.

elimination.verdict: Treat pain and bladder first.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old started a new antihypertensive at 0900. At 1000 her standing blood pressure is 108/64 and she feels lightheaded. By 1400 it is 128/76 without symptoms. Which intervention best targets her fall risk?

options.text: Keep her on bed rest until the drug is stopped
