options.rationale: Bed rest adds deconditioning as a second fall risk.

options.text: Raise all four side rails while she is in bed
options.rationale: Four rails are a restraint and are not used for routine fall prevention.

options.text: Assist her mobility after each dose and review dose timing
options.rationale: The drop tracks the dose and resolves, so plan around the dose.

options.text: Reorient her to the room every hour
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings suggests confusion.

questions.takeaway: A drop that follows the dose and resolves is a medication effect. Plan around the dose instead of removing mobility.
questions.strategy: Compare the two readings. The time course tells you the cause.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Priority key word

steps.detail: Low after the dose, normal by afternoon.
Assist when risk peaks.

elimination.verdict: Assist after doses and review timing.

questions.stem: A patient's fall plan calls for a gait belt and walker with one-person assist. A new sedative started today. Which task may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Reassess fall risk after the sedative
options.rationale: A new sedative calls for reassessment. Assessment is an RN responsibility.

options.text: Decide whether the patient can move to standby assist
options.rationale: Changing the level of assistance changes the plan. Planning belongs to the RN.

options.text: Walk the patient to the chair with the gait belt and walker
options.rationale: Assisting with mobility according to the plan is delegable.

options.text: Judge whether the plan prevented falls overnight
options.rationale: This is evaluation. It stays with the RN.

questions.takeaway: The RN assesses, plans and evaluates. Assistive personnel carry out the plan and report what they see.
questions.strategy: Look for the verb. Reassess, decide and judge are RN judgment.

strategies: Odd man wins

steps.detail: Reassess, decide, judge.
Walk the patient with the listed devices.
The new drug makes reassessment an RN task.

elimination.verdict: C. It is a task inside the existing plan.

questions.stem: A patient reports tingling in her hand each time she touched the metal rail of her electric bed. She is stable and not touching it now. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Unplug the bed, move her to a safe bed and tag it for biomedical check
options.rationale: Current is leaking to the frame. Removing the source protects her and the next person.

options.text: Tell her to avoid the rail until maintenance checks it
options.rationale: This relies on memory and leaves the hazard live.

options.text: Complete a full skin and cardiac assessment first
options.rationale: She is stable and out of contact while the hazard is still active.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: Required, but after the hazard is removed.

questions.takeaway: When equipment shocks a stable patient, remove the equipment first. Then assess and report.
questions.strategy: She is stable now. Ask what could still hurt someone.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Stable and not in contact.
The bed is still energized.

elimination.verdict: Remove the bed from service.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old in wrist restraints after bowel surgery is pulling harder and calling out. His last pain medication was 6 hours ago, and his lower abdomen is full. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Add a vest restraint
options.rationale: More agitation is a restraint complication, not proof more restraint is needed.

options.text: Assess the cause, starting with pain and his full bladder
options.rationale: Overdue analgesia and a full bladder both drive agitation, and both can be fixed.

options.text: Ask the provider for haloperidol
options.rationale: A drug to control behavior is a chemical restraint and skips the cause.

options.text: Remove both restraints now
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem shows the reason for the restraints has resolved. Find and meet his needs first, then remove them at the earliest safe point.

questions.takeaway: Worsening agitation in a restrained patient calls for a search for unmet needs, not more restraint.
questions.strategy: Two cues point to unmet needs. Find the option that looks for them.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Six hours since pain medication and a full bladder.
Vest and haloperidol add restraint.

elimination.verdict: Assess pain and bladder.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman with urinary urgency has gotten up alone twice at night to rush to the bathroom. The nurse adds scheduled toileting every 2 hours. Which finding indicates the intervention is effective?

options.text: The UAP documents offering toileting at every scheduled time
options.rationale: This shows the plan was carried out. It does not show her behavior changed.

options.text: She has not gotten up alone to reach the bathroom
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting aims to reduce urgency-driven unsafe movement. No unassisted trips means the goal is met.

options.text: She stays in bed all night with four side rails raised
options.rationale: Four rails up is a restraint. This describes a new problem, not fall prevention.

options.text: She states she understands why she is at risk for falling
options.rationale: Understanding is a step toward the goal. It does not show her behavior changed.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goal on the plan. For urgency the goal is fewer rushed, unassisted trips to the bathroom, not a completed task list.
questions.strategy: One option shows the plan was done and one shows it was understood. Only one shows her behavior changed.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Effective means an outcome in the patient.
A shows the task was done. D shows understanding only.
C confines her with four rails, which is a restraint.

elimination.verdict: B. No unassisted trips to the bathroom.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old patient walks with a walker after hip surgery. The nurse teaches his daughter about fall prevention. Which statement by the daughter indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll press the call light when Dad wants to walk."
options.rationale: This shows understanding. It specifies the help he needs.

options.text: "I'll keep his glasses and walker within reach."
options.rationale: This shows understanding. Keeping needed items within reach removes an unassisted reach or trip.

options.text: "I'll make sure Dad stays in bed so he can't fall."
options.rationale: Immobility worsens the weakness that put him at risk. The goal is safe mobility, not bed rest.

options.text: "I'll make sure he wears nonslip slippers when he gets up."
options.rationale: This shows understanding. Nonslip footwear is a universal fall precaution.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention aims at safe mobility. A family plan to keep the patient in bed shows the teaching did not work.
questions.strategy: The stem asks which statement needs follow up. Three statements support safe movement. The one that stops movement is the wrong lesson.

strategies: Negative polarity
Odd man wins

steps.detail: You are looking for the incorrect statement.

steps.action: Check each statement against the goal
steps.detail: A, B and D all support safe mobility.
C replaces mobility with bed rest, which worsens weakness.

elimination.verdict: C.

caseStudies.title: First time out of bed after bed rest
caseStudies.intro: A 68 year old man has been on bed rest for 5 days with pneumonia. Today the provider prescribes ambulation as tolerated.

entries.text: Lisinopril 20 mg given by mouth. Breath sounds clear bilaterally. Alert and oriented x4.
Reports his legs feel weak. Oral intake about 800 mL in the last 24 hours. Sacrum reddened; redness blanches with light pressure. Eager to get up.
Lying: T 36.9 C; HR 82; RR 16; BP 132/78; SpO2 96% on room air
BUN 26 mg/dL (7 to 20)
Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5)
Albumin 3.3 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0)
History of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Weight 104 kg. Walked independently before admission.

question.nursesNote: 0900: On bed rest for 5 days. Lisinopril 20 mg given at 0800. Reports his legs feel weak. Oral intake about 800 mL in 24 hours. Sacrum reddened; redness blanches with light pressure. Breath sounds clear bilaterally. SpO2 96% on room air. Alert and oriented x4.
question.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up before the client gets out of bed.

segments.text: On bed rest for 5 days
segments.rationale: Prolonged bed rest blunts the reflexes that hold blood pressure up when he stands.

segments.text: Lisinopril 20 mg given at 0800
segments.rationale: An antihypertensive at its peak adds to the risk of orthostatic hypotension.

segments.text: Reports his legs feel weak
segments.rationale: Disuse weakness. It decides how much help and what equipment the transfer needs.

segments.text: Oral intake about 800 mL in 24 hours
segments.rationale: Low intake with a high BUN suggests he is dry. Low volume makes orthostatic hypotension worse.

segments.text: Sacrum reddened; redness blanches with light pressure
segments.rationale: An early warning from lying in one position. Blanching means no injury yet, so this is the time to act.

segments.text: Breath sounds clear bilaterally
segments.rationale: His lungs are improving. Nothing to follow up.

segments.text: SpO2 96% on room air
segments.rationale: Normal oxygenation.

segments.text: Alert and oriented x4
segments.rationale: Normal. He can follow instructions for the transfer.

question.takeaway: Before a first ambulation, look for what lowers his blood pressure, what weakens his legs and what his skin is telling you.
question.strategy: The normal lung findings are there to see whether you stop at the admitting problem. The risk today is immobility.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Bed rest, lisinopril and low intake.
Weak legs.
Blanchable redness over the sacrum.

elimination.verdict: Bed rest, lisinopril, weak legs, low intake, sacral redness.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence:
After 5 days of bed rest, the reflexes that normally adjust his blood pressure are [[1]], so when he stands blood pools in the [[2]].

Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in systolic blood pressure of at least [[3]] within 3 minutes of rising.

options.text: slowed
options.rationale: Immobility reduces the autonomic response that constricts vessels when he rises.

options.text: exaggerated
options.rationale: The problem is a weak response, not a strong one.

options.text: unchanged
options.rationale: Bed rest changes them.

options.text: permanently lost
options.rationale: They recover as he becomes active again.

options.text: legs
options.rationale: Gravity pulls blood to the lower body, so less returns to the heart and brain.

options.text: lungs
options.rationale: Standing does not pool blood in the lungs.

options.text: brain
options.rationale: The brain gets less blood. That is why he feels dizzy.

options.text: abdomen only
options.rationale: The lower extremities are the main site.

options.text: 20 mm Hg
options.rationale: The textbook threshold. Diastolic drops of at least 10 mm Hg also count.

options.text: 5 mm Hg
options.rationale: A small change is expected with position.

options.text: 10 mm Hg
options.rationale: That is the diastolic threshold.

options.text: 40 mm Hg
options.rationale: Far larger than the definition requires.

question.takeaway: Immobility slows the blood pressure reflexes. Blood pools in the legs when he stands. A drop of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic is orthostatic hypotension.
question.strategy: The 10 mm Hg option is a real number. It belongs to the diastolic, not the systolic.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: "Permanently lost" is too strong.
Blood goes down to the legs.

steps.action: Match the number to the pressure
steps.detail: 20 systolic, 10 diastolic.

elimination.verdict: Slowed; legs; 20 mm Hg.

question.stem: Which problem is the nurse's priority during the client's first ambulation?

options.text: Risk for a fall from orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: The most immediate danger once he is upright. A fall can cause a serious injury in seconds.

options.text: Risk for a pressure injury over the sacrum
options.rationale: Real and important. Getting him up actually helps it, so it is not the danger during the walk.

options.text: Constipation from immobility
options.rationale: A hazard of bed rest that develops over days. It does not threaten him in the next few minutes.

options.text: Joint contractures from disuse
options.rationale: A slow complication that the walk itself helps prevent.

question.takeaway: Every hazard of immobility matters. The one that can hurt him in the next five minutes comes first.
question.strategy: All four are hazards of immobility. The words "during the first ambulation" narrow it to the acute risk.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: During the walk, not over the week.
Constipation and contractures take days.
Walking helps it rather than threatens it.

elimination.verdict: Fall from orthostatic hypotension.

question.scenario: The nurse plans the client's first ambulation.
question.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.

rows.text: Check blood pressure lying, then sitting, then standing
rows.rationale: Orthostatic readings show whether he tolerates each change in position.

rows.text: Have him dangle his legs for 1 to 2 minutes before standing
rows.rationale: Dangling is an intermediate step that lets you assess him before he stands.

rows.text: Apply a gait belt snugly around his waist over clothing, with room for two fingers
rows.rationale: Placed at the waist, the belt lets you steady him near his center of gravity.

rows.text: Use a sit to stand lift if he cannot bear his full weight
rows.rationale: Safe patient handling. Equipment protects him and the staff.

rows.text: Delegate the first walk to the assistive personnel alone
rows.rationale: The RN assesses tolerance on the first ambulation. Assistive personnel help with mobility according to the plan.

rows.text: Lift him by the gait belt if his knees buckle
rows.rationale: A gait belt is not used to lift or carry. Lower him to the floor while protecting his head.

question.takeaway: Assess in stages, use the right equipment and never lift a falling client with a gait belt.
question.strategy: Catching a falling client feels protective. The textbook says to guide him down instead, because catching injures you both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Lying, sitting, dangling, then standing.
Gait belt and lift as needed.

steps.action: Cut the scope and lifting errors
steps.detail: The RN handles the first walk; belts are not for lifting.

elimination.verdict: Indicated for rows 1 to 4. Not indicated for rows 5 and 6.

entries.text: Sitting on side of bed 1 minute: HR 104; BP 104/66. Reports dizziness still present after 90 seconds. Pale.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Return him to a lying position in bed
options.rationale: Dizziness lasting more than 60 seconds with a systolic drop of 28 means he goes back to bed immediately.

options.text: Stay with him while he lies back down
options.rationale: He is at risk for syncope. Do not leave him.

options.text: Recheck his blood pressure and heart rate once he is supine
options.rationale: Confirms that his pressure recovers when he lies flat.

options.text: Report the orthostatic hypotension to the provider
options.rationale: The skill steps call for reporting orthostatic hypotension. The lisinopril timing may need review.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids unless restricted
options.rationale: His intake is low and his BUN is high. Volume helps his pressure hold when he stands.

options.text: Have him stand up to see whether the dizziness passes
options.rationale: Standing makes the drop worse and invites a fall.

options.text: Leave the room to find another nurse to help him walk
options.rationale: Never leave a client who may faint. Use the call light.

question.takeaway: Dizziness past 60 seconds or a systolic drop of 20 means back to bed now. Stay, recheck, report and treat the cause.
question.strategy: Standing "to see whether it passes" sounds like assessment. It is the action that causes the fall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Dizziness over 60 seconds sends him back to bed.

steps.action: Keep him safe while you do it
steps.detail: Stay with him and recheck.
Report the drop and replace fluid.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Provider moved lisinopril to bedtime. Drank 600 mL since 1030. Lying BP 130/76. Dangled 2 minutes with no dizziness, then stood with gait belt; standing BP 124/74 after 2 minutes, no dizziness. Legs still weak; sit to stand lift used with two staff to transfer to chair at 1300.
Sat in chair from 1300 to 1600 without a position change. Returned to bed by manual lift; staff member reports back strain.

question.scenario: The nurse evaluates the afternoon mobility plan.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the interventions were effective or not effective.

rows.text: Standing BP 124/74 after 2 minutes, compared with lying BP 130/76
rows.rationale: A 6 mm Hg drop is within the expected range.

rows.text: No dizziness while dangling or standing
rows.rationale: Fluids and staged position changes worked.

rows.text: Transferred bed to chair with a sit to stand lift and two staff
rows.rationale: Safe patient handling protected the client and the staff.

rows.text: Drank 600 mL since 1030
rows.rationale: His intake is up, which helps his blood pressure hold when he stands.

rows.text: Staff member reports back strain after lifting him manually back to bed at 1600
rows.rationale: He needed equipment to return to bed too. Manual lifting of more than 35 lb risks staff injury.

rows.text: Sat in the chair for 3 hours without a position change
rows.rationale: Sitting still loads the sacrum and buttocks. He needs position changes in the chair as well.

question.takeaway: Getting a client out of bed does not end the plan. Equipment is used on every transfer. Position changes continue in the chair.
question.strategy: The last two rows happened after the successful transfer. Read every row to the end before you call the plan a success.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No drop of 20 systolic and no dizziness.
Equipment on the way out and on the way back.

steps.action: Check the fluid and skin plans
steps.detail: Intake improved; 3 hours in the chair without moving did not protect his skin.

elimination.verdict: Effective for rows 1 to 4. Not effective for rows 5 and 6.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews arterial blood gas results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: COPD: pH 7.36, PaCO2 58, HCO3 32
options.rationale: Two abnormal values with a normal pH is full compensation. This is the chronic baseline for many patients with COPD.

options.text: Postoperative on opioids: pH 7.28, PaCO2 60, HCO3 25
options.rationale: The CO2 is high with an acidic pH while the bicarbonate is still normal. Nothing has compensated yet, so this acidosis is acute.

options.text: Anxious before surgery: pH 7.44, PaCO2 36, HCO3 24
options.rationale: Every value is inside the normal range. This patient needs reassurance, not urgent assessment.

options.text: Pneumonia on oxygen: pH 7.40, PaCO2 40, HCO3 24
options.rationale: This is a normal blood gas. Oxygen therapy is working for this patient.

questions.takeaway: A normal pH with two abnormal values means the body has had time to compensate. An abnormal pH with a normal partner value means the problem is new.
questions.strategy: The COPD values look the most abnormal. Ask which patient's body has not caught up yet.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only B falls outside 7.35 to 7.45.
A has a high bicarbonate balancing the CO2. B has a normal bicarbonate.
No compensation means it happened recently.

elimination.verdict: B. Uncompensated acidosis outranks a compensated chronic pattern.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after 3 days of vomiting receives IV fluids and an antiemetic. Which arterial blood gas result indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: pH 7.52 with HCO3 34 mEq/L
options.rationale: Both values are still high. The alkalosis from losing stomach acid has not resolved.

options.text: pH 7.41 with HCO3 25 mEq/L
options.rationale: Both values are back inside the normal range. Stopping the acid loss let the alkalosis correct.

options.text: pH 7.30 with HCO3 18 mEq/L
options.rationale: This is acidosis, the pattern of losing bicarbonate through diarrhea. It is a new problem rather than a recovery.

options.text: pH 7.47 with HCO3 30 mEq/L
options.rationale: Both values are still above normal. The alkalosis has not resolved, so treatment is not yet effective.

questions.takeaway: Vomiting removes stomach acid and causes metabolic alkalosis. Improvement means the pH and bicarbonate fall back into range.
questions.strategy: Decide the starting direction first. Vomiting pushes the pH up, so success looks like the pH coming down to normal and stopping there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Vomiting loses acid, so the patient started alkalotic.
A and D are still alkalotic.
C has crossed into acidosis.

elimination.verdict: B. Normal pH with normal bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old patient with heart failure is taught how to detect fluid retention at home. Which statement indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will weigh myself every morning on the same scale in the same clothes."
options.rationale: Weight changes before any other sign because 1 kg equals about 1 liter of fluid. Same time, same scale, same clothing keeps the number honest.

options.text: "I will check my ankles for swelling each night."
options.rationale: Edema appears only after several liters have collected. It is a late sign.

options.text: "I will call the clinic if I start feeling very thirsty."
options.rationale: Thirst points to a deficit rather than an excess. It is also blunted at 76.

options.text: "I will weigh myself once a week at the pharmacy."
options.rationale: Weekly checks on a different scale miss daily gains. The numbers cannot be compared.

questions.takeaway: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of fluid overload. Daily weights on the same scale at the same time in the same clothing catch it first.
questions.strategy: Three options detect fluid late or not at all. Choose the one that catches fluid on the way in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Favor qualifiers

steps.detail: Weight changes before edema.
Weekly weights on a different scale are unreliable.
Thirst signals a deficit.

elimination.verdict: A. Daily weight under the same conditions.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is admitted after two days of poor oral intake during a heat wave. Which finding is the least reliable evidence of fluid volume deficit in this patient?

options.text: Heart rate 112 and blood pressure 96/58
options.rationale: The earliest compensation for a falling volume is tachycardia. The blood pressure drops once compensation is exhausted.

options.text: Urine output 15 mL/hr, dark and concentrated
options.rationale: Below 30 mL/hr is oliguria. The kidney is conserving everything it can. Concentrating the urine is how it does that.

options.text: Weight loss of 3 kg since last week
options.rationale: Three kilograms is about three liters. Acute weight change is fluid, not tissue.

options.text: Tenting of the skin on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Aging skin tents on the hand and forearm whether or not the patient is dry. Assess turgor over the sternum or the forehead instead.

questions.takeaway: Deficit shows up as tachycardia first, then hypotension, with concentrated low-volume urine, acute weight loss and new confusion. Hand turgor and thirst are both unreliable in older adults.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the least reliable finding. The wrong site for turgor is written to look like good assessment skill.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one finding that does not prove deficit in an 82-year-old.

steps.action: Keep the vital signs and the urine
steps.detail: Both fit a falling circulating volume.
Acute change of this size is water.
Aging hand skin tents in anyone.

elimination.verdict: D. Hand turgor is the wrong site for an older adult.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews IV fluid prescriptions for four patients.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the prescribed IV solution is appropriate or whether the nurse should clarify it with the provider.

rows.text: Vomiting for hours with low blood pressure: 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Isotonic saline stays in the vessels. It replaces the volume vomiting removed.

rows.text: Head injury with rising intracranial pressure: 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells. Brain cells would swell further inside the skull.

rows.text: Sodium 118 mEq/L with a new seizure: 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of swollen brain cells. It is given slowly with close sodium checks.

rows.text: Burns with low blood pressure: 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels for the cells. A hypotensive patient needs isotonic volume that stays in the circulation.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels. Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells. Hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells. Hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with high intracranial pressure or hypotension.
questions.strategy: Decide where the water needs to go for each patient. Then check whether the ordered fluid sends it there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vomiting and burns need fluid that stays in the vessels.
Swollen brain cells need water pulled out, never pushed in.
Flag any hypotonic fluid given to a swollen brain or a low blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 and 3 are appropriate. Rows 2 and 4 need clarification.

questions.stem: A nurse receives an order reading: potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push now for a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Administer it slowly over five minutes with the patient on a monitor
options.rationale: The trap. Administering a lethal route more carefully does not make it safe. There is no safe rate for IV push potassium.

options.text: Dilute it and infuse it over one hour through a peripheral line
options.rationale: Wrong twice. Diluting is the right idea and 20 mEq over one hour is 20 mEq/hr, double the peripheral maximum of 10 mEq/hr. Rewriting an unsafe order is also prescribing, which is not the nurse's to do.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the prescriber to clarify the order
options.rationale: Potassium is never given IV push. The nurse who recognizes an unsafe order stops and questions it, and carrying out an unsafe order does not transfer the responsibility.

options.text: Give it orally instead, since the patient can swallow
options.rationale: Changing the route is prescribing. The recognition is correct and the action exceeds the nurse's scope.

questions.takeaway: IV push potassium is fatal. The correct response to an unsafe order is to question it, never to carry it out more carefully or to substitute your own version.
questions.strategy: Three options all find a way to give the drug. Only one of them stops.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Potassium is never pushed.
A slower push and a nurse-chosen dilution are both still acting on an unsafe order.
That is prescribing.

elimination.verdict: Hold and clarify. An unsafe order is questioned, not adjusted.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient develops chills, a temperature rise from 37.0 C to 38.6 C, and low back pain. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the infusion and continue to monitor
options.rationale: Slowing keeps incompatible blood going in. Every minute of continued infusion adds to the hemolysis.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with normal saline using new tubing
options.rationale: Stop first. Then maintain access with saline through fresh tubing, because running saline through the existing set would push the blood remaining in the line into the patient.

options.text: Administer the prescribed acetaminophen for the fever
options.rationale: Treats a symptom of a reaction that is still running. The drug never comes before stopping the cause.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen to check for hemoglobinuria
options.rationale: It will be needed, and it is not first. Collecting a specimen while the transfusion continues is assessment at the expense of the patient.

questions.takeaway: When something goes wrong during an infusion or a transfusion, the first action is always to stop it. Assess, notify and document all come after.
questions.strategy: All four options are things that happen during this event. The question is only about order.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.
Reducing an exposure is not removing it.

steps.action: Cut the drug and the specimen
steps.detail: Both are correct later and neither is first.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion, then saline through new tubing to the hub.

questions.stem: A patient breathing 36 times a minute during a panic attack reports tingling around the mouth and in both hands. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for IV calcium
options.rationale: Total calcium has not changed. Alkalosis binds more calcium to albumin, so correcting the breathing corrects the tingling.

options.text: Coach the patient to breathe slowly with the nurse
options.rationale: Rapid breathing blows off carbon dioxide and causes respiratory alkalosis. Slowing the rate treats the cause of the tingling.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 4 L by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Hyperventilation raises oxygen levels. Nothing here suggests hypoxia.

options.text: Obtain a stat serum potassium level
options.rationale: Alkalosis moves potassium into cells. The respiratory rate already explains the tingling.

questions.takeaway: Tingling lips in a hyperventilating patient signal respiratory alkalosis. Treat the breathing, not the calcium.
questions.strategy: Tingling is a strong calcium cue, which is why the calcium option is there. Read the respiratory rate before you reach for an electrolyte.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 36 a minute is the finding the stem is built on.
Fast breathing raises oxygen.
Potassium and calcium options treat a number instead of the cause.

elimination.verdict: B. Slow the breathing to correct the alkalosis.

questions.stem: A patient with severe diarrhea for 4 days has an arterial pH of 7.30 with deep, rapid respirations. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Give the prescribed antidiarrheal with IV fluid replacement
options.rationale: Diarrhea removes bicarbonate from the intestine. Stopping the loss treats the cause of the acidosis.

options.text: Coach the patient to slow the breathing
options.rationale: The rapid breathing blows off acid to compensate. Slowing it would drive the pH lower.

options.text: Give a laxative to clear the remaining stool
options.rationale: More stool means more bicarbonate lost. The acidosis would worsen.

options.text: Hold IV fluids until the pH returns to normal
options.rationale: The patient has lost fluid along with bicarbonate. Waiting delays the treatment that corrects the pH.

questions.takeaway: Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and causes metabolic acidosis. Treat the cause and protect the fast breathing that compensates.
questions.strategy: The respirations tempt you to fix the breathing. Ask whether the lungs are the problem or the rescue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate.
Deep, rapid breathing removes acid. Cut B.
A laxative adds to it. Holding fluids delays the fix.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop the bicarbonate loss.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis has the findings below. Select the options that complete the nurse's plan.
questions.sentence:
pH 7.28, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L
Respirations 30, deep and regular

The nurse recognizes the rapid breathing as [[1]]. The nurse will [[2]].

options.text: compensation for metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is low with an acidic pH, so the problem is metabolic. The low CO2 is the lungs blowing off acid.

options.text: the cause of a respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis needs a high CO2. This CO2 is low.

options.text: hyperventilation from anxiety
options.rationale: Anxiety causes a high pH. This pH is 7.28.

options.text: a sign of respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: The pH is acidic. Nothing here is alkalotic.

options.text: report the results while avoiding anything that slows breathing
options.rationale: The breathing is the only compensation the patient has. Sedation would drop the pH further.

options.text: coach the patient to take slower breaths
options.rationale: Slowing the rate lets CO2 build up. The pH would fall.

options.text: have the patient rebreathe into a paper bag
options.rationale: Rebreathing raises CO2 for anxiety hyperventilation. It would worsen this acidosis.

options.text: hold the report until the next blood gas
options.rationale: A pH of 7.28 in sepsis is abnormal now. Waiting delays treatment.

questions.takeaway: The value that matches the pH, acidic or basic, is the cause. The value pointing the other way is compensation. Fast breathing in metabolic acidosis is a rescue you protect.
questions.strategy: Find the cause before you act. Fast breathing causes respiratory alkalosis but rescues metabolic acidosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.28 is acidosis. Cut the alkalosis choices.
The low bicarbonate matches the acidic pH, so it is metabolic.
Cut every action that slows breathing or raises CO2.

elimination.verdict: Compensation for metabolic acidosis. Report it and protect the breathing.

questions.scenario:
Patient A: calcium 7.6 mg/dL after thyroid surgery.
Patient B: calcium 12.4 mg/dL with cancer.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the patient whose plan of care should include this action.

rows.text: Keep the room quiet with limited visitors
rows.rationale: Low calcium makes nerves fire too easily. Less stimulation lowers the risk of tetany.

rows.text: Check for carpal spasm with the blood pressure cuff
rows.rationale: A positive Trousseau sign shows the excitability of low calcium. Thyroid surgery can damage the parathyroids.

rows.text: Assess calf circumference and warmth each shift
rows.rationale: High calcium raises clot risk. Calf changes can signal a DVT.

rows.text: Anticipate IV 0.9% sodium chloride with furosemide
rows.rationale: Saline with a loop diuretic promotes calcium excretion by the kidneys.

rows.text: Monitor bowel sounds for constipation
rows.rationale: High calcium slows gut smooth muscle. Constipation is expected.

questions.takeaway: Calcium is the brake on nerves. Low calcium means excitable, so reduce stimulation. High calcium means slow with clot risk, so hydrate and watch the calves.
questions.strategy: The calf row is the one students miss. Clotting belongs to high calcium because calcium is a clotting factor.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites. High calcium slows.
Quiet rooms and Trousseau checks go to the excitable patient.

steps.action: Place the clot and the fluids
steps.detail: Calf checks and saline with furosemide go to high calcium.

elimination.verdict: A, A, B, B, B.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L with new confusion. Fluids are restricted. Which finding indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: Sodium 132 mEq/L with clearer thinking
options.rationale: Less retained water means less dilution. Brain cells shrink back as the sodium rises.

options.text: Weight up 1 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: A gain means more water is being held. The sodium will stay dilute.

options.text: Sodium 121 mEq/L with lethargy
options.rationale: The sodium is falling further. Brain cells are swelling more.

options.text: Urine output falling below 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: Less urine means the kidneys are still holding water. SIADH is not improving.

questions.takeaway: SIADH holds water that dilutes sodium. Water moves into the concentrated brain cells, so restricting fluid lets the sodium and the thinking recover together.
questions.strategy: Picture the cause as extra water. Every sign of less water is improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: SIADH retains water, so sodium is dilute.
Weight gain and low urine output show retention.
121 is lower than 124.

elimination.verdict: A. Rising sodium with improving mental status.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with chronic kidney disease takes milk of magnesia nightly. He is hard to wake, respirations are 11, patellar reflexes are absent and magnesium is 4.6 mEq/L. Which plan of care is most appropriate?

options.text: Give IV magnesium sulfate, start seizure precautions, monitor the Chvostek sign
options.rationale: This plan treats low magnesium. IV magnesium makes his toxicity worse.

options.text: Stop all magnesium, prepare IV calcium, monitor respirations and reflexes
options.rationale: His kidneys cannot clear the magnesium from the laxative, so the source stops first. Calcium counters magnesium at the heart and muscle, and breathing and reflexes show whether it is working.

options.text: Stop all magnesium, start seizure precautions, monitor the Chvostek sign
options.rationale: Stopping the source is right, but seizure precautions and the Chvostek sign belong to low magnesium. He is sedated, not excitable.

options.text: Prepare IV calcium and monitor blood glucose every hour
options.rationale: Glucose checks belong to insulin for high potassium. This plan also leaves the magnesium source running.

questions.takeaway: Kidney failure plus a magnesium laxative or antacid means magnesium toxicity. Stop the source and give calcium. Watch the breathing and the reflexes.
questions.strategy: Seizure precautions sound safe, and they belong to low magnesium. Check every part of the plan against his sedated state.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Kidney failure plus a magnesium laxative and a level of 4.6 point to magnesium toxicity. That removes A.
Absent reflexes and slow breathing mean sedated, not excitable. That removes the seizure plan in C.
D gives calcium but never stops the magnesium.

elimination.verdict: B. Stop magnesium, give calcium, watch respirations and reflexes.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure receiving IV furosemide has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Which finding requires the nurse's follow-up first?

options.text: Reports her legs feel heavy and weak
options.rationale: Skeletal muscle weakness. It can progress to flaccid paralysis, but the limbs are not the first threat to life.

options.text: Respirations 22 and shallow
options.rationale: The breathing muscles are weakening. This is the most dangerous finding on the list.

options.text: Cardiac monitor shows prominent U waves
options.rationale: The classic ECG sign of hypokalemia and a warning of dysrhythmias. It is a warning, while the shallow breathing is a failure already underway.

options.text: Lungs with fine crackles in the bases, unchanged from admission
options.rationale: Her heart failure baseline, not a potassium finding.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens skeletal, respiratory and gut muscle. It also makes the heart prone to dysrhythmias. Check breathing before anything else.
questions.strategy: Every option is abnormal. The crackles are a trap because they involve the lungs. They belong to her heart failure and have not changed.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: 2.9 with an active loop diuretic.
Unchanged crackles belong to heart failure.

steps.action: Rank the rest by the ABCs
steps.detail: Breathing muscle weakness comes before a rhythm warning or weak legs.

elimination.verdict: B. Shallow respirations mean the breathing muscles are failing.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion and notify the provider?

options.text: Patellar reflexes 2+
options.rationale: Normal. Magnesium is not building up.

options.text: Absent patellar reflexes and respirations of 10
options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity. Reflexes disappear first, and breathing slows next. Stop the infusion; IV calcium is the antidote.

options.text: Blood pressure 118/74
options.rationale: Normal.

options.text: Reports feeling less shaky than this morning
options.rationale: The treatment is working.

questions.takeaway: During IV magnesium, check deep tendon reflexes. Lost reflexes and slow breathing mean the patient has swung from low magnesium to toxic levels.
questions.strategy: The patient started with low magnesium, so it is tempting to think only about hypomagnesemia. The danger during treatment is overcorrection.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Think about the drug, not just the starting lab
steps.detail: IV magnesium can overshoot.
Deep tendon reflexes go first.
Respirations of 10 make it urgent.

elimination.verdict: Absent reflexes with respirations of 10.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old has had fever and poor oral intake for three days. She is confused with muscle twitching, mucous membranes are dry and serum sodium is 154 mEq/L. Which prescribed action does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Administer 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline raises sodium. It is for severe hyponatremia.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting water makes a free water deficit worse. Fluid restriction treats the hyponatremia of SIADH.

options.text: Administer 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Fever, poor intake, dry mucosa and a sodium of 154 mean hypernatremia from free water loss. A hypotonic solution replaces free water, which is what she lost.

options.text: Assess for Chvostek sign and check the serum calcium
options.rationale: Twitching fits hypocalcemia. The sodium value and the story do not, so this chases the wrong electrolyte.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia in an older adult is usually water loss plus a thirst reflex that did not respond. Replace free water. Watch the sodium and the mental status as it comes down.
questions.strategy: 3% saline and fluid restriction are the hyponatremia treatments. They are offered to see whether you mix up the two directions.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the condition from the number and the story
steps.detail: Sodium 154 after fever and poor intake means she lost water.
3% saline and fluid restriction both push sodium the wrong way.
Twitching tempts you toward calcium. The sodium explains the whole picture.

steps.action: Pick the option that adds water
steps.detail: Hypotonic IV fluid replaces the free water she lost.

elimination.verdict: C. Hypernatremia from free water loss is treated with 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Serum sodium 128 mEq/L, alert, reports a mild headache
options.rationale: Needs follow-up. She is alert, and a headache is an early finding.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.2 mEq/L, receiving oral potassium, reports leg cramps
options.rationale: The low potassium is being treated, and the symptom is expected.

options.text: Receiving IV magnesium sulfate, respirations 9, patellar reflexes absent
options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity during an infusion that is still running. Breathing is failing, so stop the infusion now.

options.text: Serum calcium 11.1 mg/dL, reports constipation
options.rationale: Slightly high with an expected symptom.

questions.takeaway: When four patients all have abnormal labs, choose the one whose airway or breathing is failing, and the one whose problem is still being made worse by something running.
questions.strategy: No lab value is given in option C. The respiratory rate is the value that matters.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Respirations of 9 in C.

steps.action: Ask whether the harm is ongoing
steps.detail: The infusion is still running.
Headache, cramps and constipation all match their labs and are stable.

elimination.verdict: The patient on IV magnesium with slow breathing and absent reflexes.

questions.stem: The nurse receives morning lab results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Serum sodium 126 mEq/L, alert and oriented, reports a mild headache
options.rationale: Low and worth a call to the provider. She is alert, so the brain is coping for now, and a sodium this low usually got here over hours or days.

options.text: Blood glucose 30 mg/dL, diaphoretic and slow to answer questions
options.rationale: Brain cells run on glucose and have no reserve. A glucose of 30 with a neuro change can become a seizure or loss of consciousness within minutes, and the fix is fast and in your hands.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L, reports feeling tired
options.rationale: Just below range with a vague symptom. Replace it, but it is not the emergency.

options.text: Serum sodium 147 mEq/L, reports thirst
options.rationale: Mildly high with the body's normal response. Encourage water and recheck.

questions.takeaway: The most abnormal number is not always the priority. Rank by how fast the problem can harm the patient and whether symptoms are already showing.
questions.strategy: Sodium 126 looks the most abnormal on paper. Glucose 30 with symptoms is the one that turns into a seizure before you finish rounds.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for symptoms, not just numbers
steps.detail: Two patients have symptoms: headache in A, sweating and slowed thinking in B. Slowed thinking is the brain sign.

steps.action: Ask how fast each one harms
steps.detail: Hypoglycemia injures the brain in minutes. Hyponatremia usually develops over hours or days.
Potassium 3.4 and sodium 147 are small deviations with expected symptoms.

elimination.verdict: The glucose of 30. Treat it now, then call about the sodium.

questions.stem: A patient receiving IV magnesium sulfate now has a magnesium level of 7.5 mEq/L with absent deep tendon reflexes. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: High magnesium depresses nerves and muscles. Removing the source comes before anything else.

options.text: Slow the infusion and recheck reflexes in 1 hour
options.rationale: Absent reflexes signal toxicity. Continuing at any rate adds more magnesium.

options.text: Document the reflexes as an expected finding
options.rationale: Absent reflexes signal toxicity, not an expected finding. Respiratory depression can follow.

options.text: Encourage foods rich in magnesium
options.rationale: The level is already high. Diet adds to the problem.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium slows everything: reflexes first, then breathing and heart rate. Stop all magnesium, then anticipate fluids, a loop diuretic or IV calcium.
questions.strategy: Reflexes fade before breathing does. When they are gone, stop the source.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.5 is far above 2.1.
Absent reflexes mean toxicity.
Slowing, documenting or adding diet keeps magnesium coming.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop the infusion.

questions.stem: Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Serum calcium 7.4 mg/dL, new hoarse voice and stridor
options.rationale: Laryngospasm from low calcium. The airway can close in minutes.

options.text: Serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, reports constipation
options.rationale: Slightly high with an expected symptom. Stable.

options.text: Blood glucose 68 mg/dL, alert and eating lunch
options.rationale: Slightly low and she is already eating. Recheck in 15 minutes.

options.text: Serum sodium 134 mEq/L, reports mild fatigue
options.rationale: Barely low, with a vague symptom.

questions.takeaway: An abnormal lab with an airway finding comes before every other abnormal lab. Stridor is an airway emergency whatever the cause.
questions.strategy: Low glucose is a common first pick. This patient is alert and eating, so she is already fixing it herself.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Stridor is airway.

steps.action: Check whether each problem is already being handled
steps.detail: The low glucose patient is eating.
Calcium 10.9 and sodium 134 are close to normal.

elimination.verdict: Calcium 7.4 with stridor.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L has a prescription for 20 mEq potassium chloride in 100 mL over 1 hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Clarify the rate with the provider before hanging it
options.rationale: The class limit is 5 to 10 mEq per hour. This order runs twice as fast, which risks a dysrhythmia.

options.text: Infuse it by pump as prescribed with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: A pump and monitor are correct safeguards. They do not make an unsafe rate safe.

options.text: Give 10 mEq by slow IV push then infuse the rest
options.rationale: Potassium is never given by IV push. A bolus can stop the heart.

options.text: Infuse it by gravity over 2 hours instead
options.rationale: Changing the rate is outside the nurse's scope. Gravity also removes the control a pump gives.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium is diluted, on a pump, no faster than 10 mEq per hour, with the site checked hourly on a monitor. Never push, never IM.
questions.strategy: Do the math before you look at the safeguards. The rate in the order is the finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: 20 mEq over 1 hour is 20 mEq per hour.
The limit is 10 mEq per hour.

steps.action: Cut the unsafe and the unauthorized
steps.detail: IV push is never allowed. The nurse cannot rewrite the order.

elimination.verdict: A. Clarify the rate.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L. His weight is up 2 kg. Crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which prescription does the nurse expect?

options.text: Restrict fluids
options.rationale: His sodium is low because of extra water, so you remove water rather than add salt. The cause and the fluid volume status decide the treatment. Low sodium from too much water needs fluid restriction.

options.text: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adds volume to a patient who already has crackles. Saline is the fix for low sodium from losing sodium, not from too much water.

options.text: Encourage oral water intake
options.rationale: More water makes the sodium lower.

options.text: Give a potassium supplement
options.rationale: Does not address sodium or water.

questions.takeaway: Same sodium number, opposite fixes. Find the cause and volume status first. Then correct slowly so the brain can adjust.
questions.strategy: The crackles and weight gain decide it. He has too much water, so the right fix removes water.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight gain and crackles mean excess.

steps.action: Match the fix to the cause
steps.detail: Remove water. Do not add sodium.
Saline and oral water both add fluid to an overloaded patient. Potassium does not touch the problem.

elimination.verdict: A. Restrict fluids.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 7.2 mg/dL is twitching and reports painful hand cramps. The nurse places her in a quiet room to reduce stimulation. For acute tetany, which prescription does the nurse expect?

options.text: Oral calcium with the next meal
options.rationale: Too slow for tetany. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic cases. Vitamin D is added then because it helps the gut absorb calcium.

options.text: IV calcium
options.rationale: Severe or acute hypocalcemia needs IV replacement. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic cases.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: Furosemide increases calcium loss.

options.text: A calcitonin injection
options.rationale: Calcitonin lowers calcium.

questions.takeaway: For hypocalcemia, replace calcium: IV for tetany, oral for mild cases. Add vitamin D so it is absorbed. Reduce stimulation with a quiet room.
questions.strategy: Calcitonin and furosemide are hypercalcemia treatments. Check the direction before you pick a drug. Then let the word acute choose the route.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Priority key word

steps.detail: Calcitonin and furosemide lower calcium. She needs it raised.
Acute tetany needs the fastest route.

steps.action: Reject the right drug at the wrong time
steps.detail: Oral calcium fits mild or chronic cases, not tetany.

elimination.verdict: B. IV calcium.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney disease has a potassium of 6.9 mEq/L with peaked T waves and a widening QRS. The nurse has stopped the potassium infusion. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give IV calcium as prescribed
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart muscle within minutes. It does not lower the potassium; it buys time while the other drugs work.

options.text: Give regular insulin with dextrose as prescribed
options.rationale: Insulin moves potassium into cells. Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. It is the right drug at the wrong time, because the ECG changes mean the heart needs protection first.

options.text: Give a potassium binder as prescribed
options.rationale: Removes potassium from the body through the GI tract. It is slower, so it comes after the heart is protected and the potassium is shifted.

options.text: Recheck the potassium and blood glucose
options.rationale: Rechecking confirms the level is falling and catches rebound low potassium or low glucose. It belongs at the end. The ECG changes already confirm the danger.

questions.takeaway: Stop, protect, shift, remove, recheck. Calcium comes before insulin because the heart is what kills.
questions.strategy: Students often pick insulin because it lowers the number. Calcium comes first because it protects the heart while the other drugs work.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: The source is stopped. The key word is next.
Peaked T waves with a widening QRS mean the heart is at risk now. Calcium stabilizes it within minutes.
Insulin shifts, the binder removes, the recheck confirms. All three come after calcium.

elimination.verdict: A. Calcium protects the heart before anything lowers the level.

questions.stem: Eighteen hours after a total thyroidectomy, a patient reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Positive Chvostek sign
options.rationale: Confirms low calcium, and it is a warning sign. It is not yet the airway.

options.text: High-pitched noisy breathing and a hoarse voice
options.rationale: Laryngospasm. Low calcium is making the larynx spasm, and the airway can close. Call for help and prepare IV calcium.

options.text: Muscle cramps in her calves
options.rationale: Expected in hypocalcemia and uncomfortable. Not an airway threat.

options.text: Incisional pain rated 5 out of 10
options.rationale: Expected after surgery. Treat it after the airway is safe.

questions.takeaway: After thyroid surgery, low calcium can close the airway. Stridor or a new hoarse voice outranks every other calcium finding.
questions.strategy: Chvostek sign is the answer students remember, which makes it the distractor. It confirms the problem; stridor is the emergency.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: The parathyroid glands can be damaged during thyroid surgery.
Only one option is about breathing.
Chvostek sign and cramps confirm the problem; stridor is the danger.

elimination.verdict: Noisy high-pitched breathing. The airway comes first.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old taking hydrochlorothiazide has a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L. Which finding is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Reports mild nausea and a poor appetite
options.rationale: A real finding in hyponatremia, and it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous.

options.text: New confusion and difficulty staying awake since this morning
options.rationale: Cerebral change. Water is moving into brain cells inside a rigid skull, and confusion and lethargy are the steps before seizures and coma.

options.text: Urine output of 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. Nothing to act on.

options.text: Dry oral mucous membranes
options.rationale: Points to volume status, which matters for choosing treatment. It does not threaten her the way the brain change does.

questions.takeaway: In sodium imbalance, the brain is the organ at risk. A change in level of consciousness is the finding you act on first.
questions.strategy: Every option could appear in a patient with low sodium. Ask which one belongs to the organ that cannot swell safely.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Sodium moves water into and out of brain cells.
40 mL per hour is fine.
Nausea and dry mucosa are uncomfortable. New confusion is progressing.

elimination.verdict: New confusion and lethargy. Protect the brain first.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L has flat T waves and prominent U waves. After IV potassium replacement, which finding indicates the treatment was effective?

options.text: Tall peaked T waves with a widened QRS
options.rationale: This is the high potassium ECG. Replacement has overshot and needs follow up.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds with cramping
options.rationale: Increased motility is a high potassium finding. It suggests overcorrection.

options.text: Upright T waves with no U waves
options.rationale: The low potassium changes have resolved. The level has returned toward 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Hypoactive bowel sounds with leg weakness
options.rationale: A slow gut with weak muscles is a low potassium picture. The deficit persists.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium slows things: flat T, U wave, sluggish gut. High potassium irritates things: peaked T, diarrhea. Evaluate replacement for both undercorrection and overcorrection.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option is a real potassium finding. Sort each into still low or now too high before you choose.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Peaked T with wide QRS is high. Upright T without U waves is normal.
Hyperactive means too high. Hypoactive means still low.
Only one option shows neither extreme.

elimination.verdict: C. The low potassium ECG changes have resolved.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer has a serum calcium of 13.1 mg/dL. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate implementing first to lower the calcium?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Normal saline helps the kidneys excrete calcium and corrects the dehydration that often comes with it.

options.text: IV furosemide started right away
options.rationale: A loop diuretic increases calcium excretion. It is given once fluid volume is restored, because diuresing a dry patient worsens the dehydration.

options.text: A bisphosphonate as prescribed
options.rationale: It keeps calcium in the bone instead of the blood. It is part of the plan but does not come before hydration.

options.text: Hold oral calcium supplements
options.rationale: Stop every source of calcium. Holding a supplement does not remove the calcium already in the blood.

questions.takeaway: For hypercalcemia: flush with normal saline first, then add a loop diuretic once volume is restored. Stop the sources, keep calcium in the bone and put the patient on a monitor.
questions.strategy: All four options belong in the plan. The question is order. Furosemide is the correct drug at the wrong time if the patient is still dry.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what each option does to calcium
steps.detail: All four help lower it or keep it from rising.
Hydration comes before diuresis.
Holding a supplement and a bisphosphonate do not clear the calcium already in the blood.

elimination.verdict: A. Normal saline comes first.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use has a magnesium of 1.1 mEq/L with 4+ reflexes. After IV magnesium sulfate, which finding indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: Reflexes are now 2+
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes nerves excitable. Reflexes returning to normal show the level has corrected.

options.text: Reflexes are now absent
options.rationale: Absent reflexes signal too much magnesium. The treatment has overshot into toxicity.

options.text: Facial twitching when the cheek is tapped
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign shows nerves are still excitable. The magnesium is still low.

options.text: Tremors have increased
options.rationale: Tremors are excitability. Chronic alcohol use keeps draining magnesium, so this shows it is still low.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium looks like low calcium: brisk reflexes, tremors, Chvostek sign. Treatment works when reflexes return to normal, not when they disappear.
questions.strategy: Effective means normal, not the opposite extreme. Absent reflexes are toxicity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: 4+ reflexes mean excitable.
Absent reflexes mean too much.
Twitching and tremors show it is still low.

elimination.verdict: A. Normal reflexes.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L, heart rate 48, tall peaked T waves on the monitor
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes and bradycardia means the heart is already affected. The next rhythm may be ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.3 mEq/L, reports leg cramps, taking oral potassium with breakfast
options.rationale: Low, treated, and the symptom is expected. Stable.

options.text: Serum sodium 133 mEq/L, alert, eating breakfast
options.rationale: Just below range with no symptoms.

options.text: Serum potassium 5.3 mEq/L, normal sinus rhythm, no complaints
options.rationale: Mildly high with a normal rhythm. Recheck it and review medications, but the heart is not affected yet.

questions.takeaway: In hyperkalemia, ECG changes mean the heart is already involved. A high potassium with peaked T waves and bradycardia beats every other abnormal lab on the floor.
questions.strategy: Two patients have high potassium. The ECG tells you which one is unstable.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Only option A has rhythm changes.

steps.action: Compare the two high potassium patients
steps.detail: 5.3 with a normal rhythm is stable. 6.4 with peaked T waves is not.
Cramps with a low potassium that is being replaced are expected.

elimination.verdict: Potassium 6.4 with peaked T waves and bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and new cerebral edema has a prescription for 0.45% sodium chloride at 100 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Infuse as prescribed with hourly neurologic checks
options.rationale: Monitoring does not make the fluid safe. Hypotonic fluid will still move water into swollen brain cells.

options.text: Infuse at half the rate to limit plasma expansion
options.rationale: Most hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels. The danger is where the water goes, not how fast the plasma grows.

options.text: Clarify the order because hypotonic fluid can worsen brain swelling
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells. In a rigid skull, more water in brain cells raises intracranial pressure.

options.text: Request a colloid because only colloids are safe in brain injury
options.rationale: An absolute that is not true. Isotonic crystalloids are commonly used in neurologic patients.

questions.takeaway: Water follows solute. Hypotonic fluid swells cells, hypertonic fluid shrinks them. Colloids hold water in the vessels by oncotic pressure.
questions.strategy: Ask where the water in this fluid will end up, then ask whether that place is already swollen.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic, so water moves into cells.
His brain cells are already swollen inside a rigid skull.
Monitoring or a slower rate still delivers the wrong fluid.
"Only colloids" is not true.

elimination.verdict: C. Question hypotonic fluid in cerebral edema.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old receiving lactated Ringer's at 125 mL per hour after hip repair now has distended neck veins, crackles in both bases and urine output of 30 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give a 500 mL bolus because urine output is only 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: 30 mL per hour is the usual minimum, and her neck veins and crackles show overload. More fluid pushes her toward pulmonary edema.

options.text: Slow the infusion to the lowest prescribed rate and notify the provider
options.rationale: She is receiving more fluid than her heart and kidneys can handle. You stop adding to the problem first, then get a prescription such as a loop diuretic.

options.text: Recheck lung sounds, respiratory rate and SpO2 in 1 hour to confirm the trend
options.rationale: Distended neck veins with new crackles already show overload. Waiting an hour while the fluid runs lets her get worse.

options.text: Weigh her daily on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks overload over days. It does nothing for her lungs right now.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult receiving IV fluid, distended neck veins and new crackles mean overload. Stop adding fluid first, then notify the provider.
questions.strategy: Low urine output tempts you to add fluid. Read it beside the neck veins and crackles, which cannot be a deficit.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Neck vein distention and crackles during IV fluid mean fluid volume excess.
The bolus makes pulmonary edema worse.
Rechecking and daily weights are monitoring. The data already calls for action.

elimination.verdict: B.

questions.stem: A patient with low blood volume has increased aldosterone secretion. Which laboratory result requires follow up?

options.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: Aldosterone keeps sodium and water in exchange for potassium. The potassium has fallen below 3.5.

options.text: Sodium 139 mEq/L
options.rationale: Aldosterone keeps sodium. A normal sodium is expected.

options.text: Urine specific gravity 1.028
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is expected as the kidneys hold water. It is compensation.

options.text: Glucose 96 mg/dL
options.rationale: Aldosterone does not affect glucose. This value is normal.

questions.takeaway: Aldosterone keeps sodium with water and loses potassium. ADH keeps water alone. Natriuretic peptides excrete sodium and water.
questions.strategy: Ask what aldosterone trades away. The value it loses is the one to watch.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Sodium in, potassium out.
Normal sodium and concentrated urine are compensation.
Glucose is not part of the exchange.

elimination.verdict: A. Low potassium.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old taking hydrochlorothiazide is admitted with new confusion. Which assessment finding is a reliable sign of fluid volume deficit in this patient rather than an age-related change?

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand stays tented for several seconds
options.rationale: Aging skin loses elasticity, so the hand is unreliable. This finding may be present even with normal hydration.

options.text: States she is not thirsty
options.rationale: A blunted thirst reflex is an age-related cause of deficit named in class. It explains why she did not replace her losses. It is a cause, not a sign. It is not reassurance.

options.text: Lungs clear; no peripheral edema
options.rationale: Normal findings. They argue against overload but do not show a deficit.

options.text: Skin over the sternum stays tented
options.rationale: The sternum is the correct site in older adults. Tenting here points to a real deficit.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, check turgor at the sternum. Treat new confusion as a possible fluid problem. A lack of thirst is not reassurance.
questions.strategy: Hand turgor is the trap: aging skin makes it unreliable. Denying thirst is a blunted reflex that helps explain the deficit. It does not prove one. Ask which finding still means something in an 84-year-old.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Priority key word

steps.detail: Reliable sign, rather than an age-related change.
Hand and sternum are a pair. In older adults only the sternum counts.
Blunted thirst is itself an age-related change. It explains the deficit but does not confirm it.
Clear lungs and no edema rule out overload. They do not show a deficit.

elimination.verdict: D, sternal tenting.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L received IV calcium, regular insulin with dextrose and sodium polystyrene sulfonate. One hour later the nurse reassesses. Which finding requires immediate action?

options.text: Potassium of 5.9 mEq/L
options.rationale: Still above 5.0, but it is falling after treatment. The treatment is working, so this is a trend to keep watching.

options.text: Glucose of 54 mg/dL with sweating and shakiness
options.rationale: Correct. Insulin moves potassium into cells. It moves glucose in too. Dextrose was given to prevent exactly this, yet he is now hypoglycemic with symptoms. Low glucose can progress to seizures and loss of consciousness within minutes, so it needs treatment now.

options.text: Two loose stools since the binder was given
options.rationale: Expected. The binder pulls potassium into the gut. The stool is how it leaves the body. This means the drug is doing its job.

options.text: T waves that are still slightly peaked
options.rationale: The ECG is moving toward normal as the potassium falls. Calcium also protects the heart muscle while the level comes down. Improvement is not a reason to act.

questions.takeaway: After insulin and dextrose for hyperkalemia, watch the glucose as closely as the potassium. The deck names rebound hypoglycemia as a treatment risk.
questions.strategy: Three options describe hyperkalemia getting better. One describes a new problem caused by the treatment. The new problem wins.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.action: Read each value as a trend
steps.detail: Potassium is falling and the ECG is improving. Both show the treatment working.
Loose stools are the expected effect of the binder.
A glucose of 54 with symptoms is a complication of insulin that can quickly harm the brain.

elimination.verdict: Glucose 54 with symptoms. Treat the hypoglycemia the insulin caused.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old admitted with a sodium of 164 mEq/L is receiving D5W. Eight hours later the sodium is 151 mEq/L, and she has a new headache and is harder to rouse. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Increase the D5W rate because the sodium is still above 145 mEq/L
options.rationale: The number is still high, but lowering it faster is exactly what is causing harm. This moves in the wrong direction.

options.text: Stop or slow the D5W and notify the provider of the rapid fall in sodium and the neurologic change
options.rationale: The sodium dropped 13 mEq/L in 8 hours. Water rushed into brain cells that had adapted to the high level, and headache with falling consciousness signals brain swelling.

options.text: Give the ordered acetaminophen for the headache and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: This treats the symptom but leaves the cause running. Waiting an hour lets more free water reach the brain.

options.text: Encourage the patient to drink water to replace free water by mouth
options.rationale: Oral water adds more free water to a brain that is already swelling. A patient who is hard to rouse cannot safely swallow.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia is corrected slowly. New headache or a drop in consciousness during treatment points to cerebral edema from correcting too fast.
questions.strategy: The sodium is still high, yet the patient got worse. Ask what changed. The answer is the speed of the fall.

strategies: Priority key word
Assessment before intervention
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 164 to 151 in 8 hours is a fast drop.

steps.action: Link the trend to the findings
steps.detail: Headache and new drowsiness are signs of brain swelling.
Raising the rate and pushing oral water both speed the shift.
Acetaminophen for the headache leaves the cause in place.

elimination.verdict: Slow the hypotonic fluid and report it. The fall was too fast.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure is admitted weighing 88.4 kg with crackles in both lung bases. After 3 days of IV furosemide, which finding indicates the therapy is effective?

options.text: Weight of 86.1 kg with clear lung sounds
options.rationale: A loss of 2.3 kg means about 2.3 liters of fluid have left. Clear lungs show pulmonary edema is being prevented.

options.text: Intake 2,600 mL with output 1,800 mL in 24 hours
options.rationale: Intake still exceeds output by 800 mL. The balance is positive, so fluid is not leaving.

options.text: Bounding pulse of 102 beats a minute
options.rationale: A bounding pulse is a sign of fluid overload. The excess volume is still present.

options.text: Serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: Furosemide causes potassium loss. This is an adverse effect to report, not evidence the overload is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate diuretic therapy with daily weight, lung sounds and intake and output. A low potassium on a loop diuretic is a side effect to report, not a sign of success.
questions.strategy: The question asks whether the fluid problem is resolving. Choose the option where the admission findings improved. Cut the true side effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: Remove extra fluid and prevent pulmonary edema.

steps.action: Check each finding against the goal
steps.detail: A positive balance and a bounding pulse mean overload remains.
Low potassium measures harm from the drug, not the outcome.

elimination.verdict: A. Weight loss with clear lungs shows the fluid is leaving.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves. After IV calcium, insulin with dextrose and patiromer, which finding indicates the potassium has fallen?

options.text: Repeat potassium of 5.0 mEq/L with smaller T waves
options.rationale: Insulin shifts potassium into cells while patiromer removes it through the gut. A lower level with flatter T waves shows the plan worked.

options.text: No dysrhythmia on the monitor after the IV calcium
options.rationale: IV calcium stabilizes the heart muscle. It does not lower the potassium.

options.text: Blood glucose of 54 mg/dL with diaphoresis
options.rationale: This is hypoglycemia from the insulin. It needs immediate follow up.

options.text: Tingling progressing to weakness in both legs
options.rationale: Ascending weakness signals worsening hyperkalemia. The problem is progressing.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium protects the heart without lowering potassium. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into cells. Binders remove it. Confirm with a repeat level and the ECG.
questions.strategy: Only a lab value with a matching ECG change measures the potassium. The calcium option is the trap because it looks like success.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A lower serum potassium.
Calcium stabilizes the heart. It does not change the level.
Low glucose and ascending weakness need follow up.

elimination.verdict: A. The repeat level with smaller T waves is direct evidence the potassium fell.

caseStudies.title: Older adult with vomiting and diarrhea
caseStudies.intro: An 81-year-old woman is admitted from home after 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea. Her daughter brought her in because she seemed confused.

entries.text: Arrived by wheelchair with her daughter. Vomiting and watery diarrhea for 3 days; kept down only sips of tea.
Reports feeling dizzy when she sits up. Oral mucous membranes dry. Skin tents at the sternum.
Voided 90 mL of dark amber urine. Daughter states she has been confused since yesterday. Lungs clear.
Lying: T 37.3 C; HR 112, weak and thready; RR 20; BP 104/64; SpO2 97% on room air
Sitting on edge of bed: HR 128; BP 82/50
Hematocrit 51% (37 to 47)
Hemoglobin 17.0 g/dL (12 to 16)
BUN 32 mg/dL (10 to 20)
Serum osmolarity 304 mOsm/L (270 to 300)
Sodium 144 mEq/L (135 to 145); potassium 3.6 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0)
Glucose 96 mg/dL (70 to 100)
Hypertension, treated with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Osteoarthritis of both knees.
Lives alone. Walks with a cane. No known allergies.

question.nursesNote: 0830: 81-year-old with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea. Heart rate 112 and thready. Blood pressure 104/64 lying and 82/50 sitting. Reports dizziness when she sits up. Skin tents at the sternum. Oral mucous membranes dry. Voided 90 mL of dark amber urine. Daughter states she has been confused since yesterday. SpO2 97% on room air. Lungs clear. Temperature 37.3 C.
question.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 and thready
segments.rationale: The heart speeds up to keep output going when volume is low. A thready pulse means little volume behind each beat.

segments.text: Blood pressure 104/64 lying and 82/50 sitting
segments.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension. There is not enough circulating volume to hold her pressure when she changes position.

segments.text: Reports dizziness when she sits up
segments.rationale: The brain is briefly underperfused on position change. This is how she will fall.

segments.text: Skin tents at the sternum
