Oriented to person only. Asks what day it is several times. Hearing aid found in bedside drawer. Glasses were left at home.
Room blinds closed; TV off; no clock in room. No visitors since admission. Tearful; states "Nobody talks to me in here."
Leg wound dressing dry and intact. Ate 75% of breakfast.
T 36.9 C; HR 78; RR 16; BP 132/78; SpO2 97% on room air
Sodium 139 mEq/L (135 to 145)
Glucose 104 mg/dL (70 to 110)

question.nursesNote: 0200: Found sitting on the edge of the bed trying to stand. Did not use call light. 0800: Oriented to person only. Hearing aid found in bedside drawer. Glasses left at home. Room blinds closed; no clock in room. No visitors since admission. Tearful; states nobody talks to her. Leg wound dressing dry and intact. T 36.9 C. Sodium 139 mEq/L.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Found sitting on the edge of the bed trying to stand
segments.rationale: She tried to get up alone at night. That is an immediate fall risk.

segments.text: Did not use call light
segments.rationale: She did not call for help before trying to get up alone.

segments.text: Oriented to person only
segments.rationale: New since admission, when she was oriented x4. A sudden change is never assumed to be aging.

segments.text: Hearing aid found in bedside drawer
segments.rationale: Her main link to speech is sitting in a drawer.

segments.text: Glasses left at home
segments.rationale: Without them she cannot read a clock, a calendar or a face.

segments.text: Room blinds closed; no clock in room
segments.rationale: No light cues or time cues. These are the meaningful stimuli the slides name.

segments.text: No visitors since admission
segments.rationale: Absent social interaction feeds isolation and loneliness.

segments.text: Tearful; states nobody talks to her
segments.rationale: An affective effect of deprivation.

segments.text: Leg wound dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: Expected. Nothing to follow up.
Normal. Infection is not driving the confusion today.

segments.text: Sodium 139 mEq/L
segments.rationale: Normal. Rules out a common metabolic cause of confusion.

question.takeaway: New confusion in an isolated older adult is a finding to act on. Look at what she can see, hear and do in that room.
question.strategy: The normal labs and vital signs are there to be left alone. They also point you away from a medical cause and toward the environment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Oriented x4 on day 1 means the confusion is new.
No clock, no light, no visitors, no glasses, no hearing aid.
Dressing, temperature and sodium are fine.

elimination.verdict: Everything except the dressing, the temperature and the sodium.

question.scenario: The nurse sorts the client's findings by type of sensory alteration.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate the type of sensory alteration it represents.

rows.text: Hearing loss in both ears
rows.rationale: A loss of normal reception. It was present before admission.

rows.text: Needs glasses to see clearly
rows.rationale: A decline in normal vision.

rows.text: No visitors or conversation for 4 days
rows.rationale: Loss of meaningful stimulation. Isolation is the classic setting.

rows.text: Disoriented to time and place with no clock in the room
rows.rationale: A cognitive effect of deprivation.

rows.text: Tearful; says nobody talks to her in here
rows.rationale: An affective effect: boredom, anxiety and sadness.

rows.text: 11 hours of alarms and constant activity in the emergency department
rows.rationale: Excess stimulation the brain cannot filter. The ED is a named setting.

question.takeaway: Deficit is a problem with the equipment. Deprivation is too little input. Overload is too much input. Patients often have more than one.
question.strategy: Ask where the problem lives. In her ears and eyes is a deficit. In her quiet, empty room is deprivation.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hearing and vision loss are deficits.

steps.action: Separate too little from too much
steps.detail: The isolation room is too little. The ED was too much.
Confusion and tearfulness follow deprivation.

elimination.verdict: Deficit, deficit, deprivation, deprivation, deprivation, overload.

question.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence: The client is most likely experiencing [[1]]. The priority nursing concern at this time is [[2]].

options.text: sensory deprivation made worse by her sensory deficits
options.rationale: Too little meaningful input on top of hearing and vision loss. Normal labs make a medical cause less likely.

options.text: sensory overload
options.rationale: Her room is quiet and empty. Overload was the ED, days ago.

options.text: normal age related changes
options.rationale: She was oriented x4 on admission. A sudden change is never assumed to be aging.

options.text: progression of dementia
options.rationale: No history of dementia. The change came on over days in isolation.

options.text: risk for falls
options.rationale: She tried to stand alone at 0200 without the call light. Injury is the threat that can happen tonight.

options.text: impaired socialization
options.rationale: Real and she needs it addressed. It does not threaten her physically tonight.

options.text: risk for infection
options.rationale: She already has an infection that is being treated. It is not what changed.

options.text: imbalanced nutrition
options.rationale: She ate 75% of breakfast.

question.takeaway: Deprivation in isolation causes confusion. Confusion in an older adult causes falls. Safety comes first.
question.strategy: Impaired socialization is the emotionally compelling choice. It is true and it is not the priority.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Quiet room plus deficits plus normal labs means deprivation.
New change from baseline is never normal aging.
A fall can happen tonight.

elimination.verdict: Sensory deprivation; risk for falls.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the hearing aid in her left ear and check that it works
options.rationale: Restores her main route for speech and social contact.

options.text: Ask the daughter to bring her glasses and a family photo
options.rationale: Glasses correct the deficit. Photos are meaningful stimuli.

options.text: Place a large clock and a calendar where she can see them
options.rationale: Time cues support reorientation.

options.text: Open the blinds during the day and reorient her at each visit
options.rationale: Natural light and frequent reorientation are acute care basics.

options.text: Keep the bed low with the call light within reach
options.rationale: Directly addresses the fall risk.

options.text: Keep the TV on at high volume through the night
options.rationale: That swaps deprivation for overload and disrupts sleep.

options.text: Limit entering the room to reduce exposure to the infection
options.rationale: Contact precautions call for gown and gloves, not avoidance. Less contact deepens the deprivation.

options.text: Apply wrist restraints to keep her in bed
options.rationale: Not the least restrictive option. Restraints increase agitation and injury.

question.takeaway: Fix the deficits, add meaningful stimuli and keep her safe. Isolation limits germs, not people.
question.strategy: Watch for options that sound protective but isolate her more, such as fewer visits or restraints.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Hearing aid and glasses.
Clock, calendar, light, photos, reorientation.

steps.action: Reject too much or too little
steps.detail: Loud TV, avoidance and restraints make things worse.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Hearing aid in place and working. Daughter brought glasses and photos. Client asks the nurse to explain the dressing change.

question.stem: Which approach by the nurse is most appropriate when explaining the dressing change?

options.text: Face her directly in good light and speak slowly in a lower pitch
options.rationale: She can see your lips and expression. Slow, low pitched speech is easier to hear with the high frequency loss common in older adults.

options.text: Stand beside the window so the room is bright
options.rationale: Light behind you puts your face in shadow. She loses the visual cues.

options.text: Speak loudly into her left ear
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech. It does not make it clearer.

options.text: Explain the procedure to the daughter instead
options.rationale: The client is the one receiving care. Talking around her adds to her isolation.

question.takeaway: Face to face, good light, slow, lower pitch, no shouting. Talk to the client, not about her.
question.strategy: Bright light sounds helpful. The trap is where the light is: behind you it hides your face.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Louder is not clearer.
Light behind the speaker hides the face.
She asked. Answer her.

elimination.verdict: Face her in good light and speak slowly in a lower pitch.

entries.text: Oriented x4. Wearing glasses and hearing aid. Daughter visited last evening. Talks with the nurse about her cat and her daughter's visit.
Night nurse reports call light found on the floor out of reach at 0300; client sitting on edge of bed.

question.scenario: The nurse reviews the client's progress on day 6.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the interventions were effective or not effective.

rows.text: Oriented x4
rows.rationale: Back to her admission baseline.

rows.text: Wearing glasses and hearing aid
rows.rationale: Deficits are corrected, so she can take in stimuli.

rows.text: Talks with the nurse about her cat and her daughter's visit
rows.rationale: Engaged and social. Deprivation is lifting.

rows.text: Call light found on the floor out of reach at 0300
rows.rationale: The safety plan failed. She could not call for help.

rows.text: Sitting on the edge of the bed alone at night
rows.rationale: The fall risk is still present.

question.takeaway: Orientation can come back while safety still fails. Evaluate every goal separately.
question.strategy: Good orientation can make you skim past the night event. The call light out of reach is the finding that matters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: Met.
Call light out of reach means not met.
Secure the call light and increase night rounding.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, not effective, not effective.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

questions.stem: A teenage boy hands his intake form to the receptionist, who says the mother's and father's names are required and offers to fill them in. He looks away and says quietly that he has two dads. The receptionist becomes flustered and says loudly that he does not have a mother. Heads turn in the waiting area and he starts for the door. What would have prevented this?

options.text: An intake form that asks for parent or guardian names rather than mother and father
options.rationale: The form created the problem before anyone spoke. Updating policies and forms is one of the five ways to build a safe space, and it removes the assumption at the point it is made.

options.text: Displaying symbols of inclusivity in the waiting area
options.rationale: Part of an inclusive environment, and a rainbow sticker does not change what the form demands.

options.text: Training the receptionist to respond calmly when a patient discloses family structure
options.rationale: Worth doing, and it addresses the reaction rather than the assumption. He still has to correct a form that assumed his family wrong.

options.text: Having him complete the form privately with a nurse instead of at the desk
options.rationale: Reduces the audience for the exchange. The form still asks the wrong question.

questions.takeaway: Foster an inclusive environment: update policies and forms, display symbols of inclusivity, and build sexual orientation and gender identity into records.
questions.strategy: Three options improve what happens after the assumption is made. Only one removes the assumption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The form asked for a mother and a father.
Both improve the response to a problem still built in.
Moves the exchange, not the question.

elimination.verdict: That leaves changing the form.

questions.stem: During the exchange above, the receptionist realizes what she has said. Which response is most appropriate at that moment?

options.text: Briefly say sorry, correct the record, and continue with the check-in
options.rationale: A short correction keeps the attention on him and signals that the mistake is routine rather than a crisis he has to manage.

options.text: Offer to move him to a private room to finish the conversation
options.rationale: Well meant, and it makes the moment larger and marks him out further in front of the people already looking.

options.text: Say nothing further and complete the form as he has described it
options.rationale: Reads as not having noticed, or as not caring. Acknowledgment matters; length is what does not.

options.text: Apologize at length and explain that she did not mean anything by it
options.rationale: Makes him manage her distress. A long apology asks a patient in a waiting room to reassure the person who upset him.

questions.takeaway: Acknowledge briefly, correct, move on. The repair should cost the nurse something, not the patient.
questions.strategy: Every option except one enlarges the moment. Ask who ends up doing the emotional work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A long apology puts him in charge of her feelings.
Reads as indifference.
Makes a small moment into a scene.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the brief correction.

questions.stem: A clinician asks a patient whether she is sexually active with men, women, or both. She answers that she is sexually active with one woman. He skips the questions about condom use. Her partner is a transgender woman. Which error has he made?

options.text: He used outdated terminology in the question itself
options.rationale: The question was reasonably framed. What went wrong came after her answer.

options.text: He should not have asked about sexual activity at all
options.rationale: The sexual history is appropriate care. The failure is in the reasoning that followed her answer.

options.text: He failed to ask about the number of partners
options.rationale: She told him there is one. The omission is about what happens, not how many.

options.text: He inferred the anatomy involved from the gender of the partner
options.rationale: Sexual health risk follows anatomy and practices, not the gender of either person. Assuming from the label is what skipped a question she needed.

questions.takeaway: Assess anatomy and practices rather than inferring them from gender or orientation. Avoid assumptions.
questions.strategy: Three options criticize the question. The stem tells you the question was answered, then something was skipped.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Condom use was not discussed.
He assumed what her partner's body was.

steps.action: Cut the options about the question
steps.detail: The question was asked and answered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the inference from gender to anatomy.

questions.stem: The clinician in that encounter is openly gay and had recently skipped his center's training on LGBTQ+ care, saying he already knew the subject. What does this illustrate?

options.text: The training should have been mandatory rather than optional
options.rationale: A reasonable policy conclusion, and it names an administrative fix rather than what the case shows.

options.text: Belonging to a community does not substitute for training in its health care needs
options.rationale: Personal identity gives lived experience, not clinical knowledge of every population under an umbrella. Ongoing training is the first of the five safe-space practices.

options.text: His error was one of attitude rather than knowledge
options.rationale: His attitude let him skip the training, and what harmed the patient was a specific knowledge gap.

options.text: Clinicians who are themselves LGBTQ+ should not care for LGBTQ+ patients
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he should be excluded. The point is that identity did not supply what training would have.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself: learn the terminology, know the specific health issues, and take part in ongoing training. Every team member needs it.
questions.strategy: Two options draw policy or personnel conclusions. Ask what the missing training would actually have given him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He did not know to assess anatomy over label.
Nothing supports it.

steps.action: Cut the policy and attitude options
steps.detail: Neither names the clinical gap.

elimination.verdict: That leaves identity not substituting for training.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to admit a patient whose chart lists a legal name different from the one on the referral letter. Which actions create a safe space? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask what name and pronouns the patient uses and record them where staff will see
options.rationale: Affirming language starts with asking rather than guessing, and recording it means every subsequent staff member gets it right.

options.text: Keep the legal name in the record for billing and identification
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record. The legal name is needed for insurance and identification; the used name is needed for care.

options.text: Use the name the patient gives from that point on, in every interaction
options.rationale: Consistency is what makes it affirming. Asking and then not using it is worse than not asking.

options.text: Explain to colleagues why the patient's name differs from the chart
options.rationale: Discloses information that is the patient's to share. Respect privacy is part of affirming communication.

options.text: Ask which surgeries the patient has had, to know how to refer to them
options.rationale: Surgical history is relevant when it bears on the care being given. Asking to satisfy curiosity about someone's body is not assessment.

options.text: Wait for the patient to raise the difference before mentioning names
options.rationale: Leaves the patient to correct staff repeatedly, which is the burden the practice exists to remove.

questions.takeaway: Affirming communication: use preferred names and pronouns, avoid assumptions, be mindful of nonverbal cues, and respect privacy.
questions.strategy: Two distractors involve telling someone else, or asking about a body without a clinical reason.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staff need the name, not the explanation.
Privacy is part of affirming care.
No clinical reason is given.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.scenario: A clinic manager reviews practice after two patients did not return following a first visit.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate which of the five safe-space practices it represents.

rows.text: Adds a field for gender identity and pronouns to the electronic record
rows.rationale: Building identity into records and forms is part of the environment, not of any single conversation.

rows.text: A nurse notices she assumed a patient's partner was a man and examines why
rows.rationale: Examining your own assumptions and holding yourself accountable for them.

rows.text: Sends a survey asking patients what would make the clinic feel safer
rows.rationale: Seeking patient feedback rather than deciding for them what would help.

rows.text: Schedules quarterly training on terminology and population-specific health issues
rows.rationale: Ongoing training, terminology, and awareness of specific health issues.

rows.text: Introduces herself with her own pronouns before asking the patient's
rows.rationale: Makes the question routine rather than singling anyone out, and it avoids the assumption.

rows.text: Displays a visible inclusivity symbol at the reception desk
rows.rationale: A signal built into the space, which is what the environment practice covers.

questions.takeaway: Five safe-space practices: educate yourself, self-reflection, affirming communication, inclusive environment, prioritize patient needs.
questions.strategy: Two rows are both environment. Ask whether the action changes the space, the conversation, or the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The space, the words, or the nurse herself.
Forms and symbols are both environment.
Asking patients is prioritizing needs.

elimination.verdict: Environment, self-reflection, patient needs, education, communication, environment.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria attends clinic with a parent and asks when hormone therapy can start. Which response is accurate according to current practice?

options.text: Hormone therapy may be started at any age once dysphoria is diagnosed
options.rationale: A diagnosis does not by itself start hormones, and the typical threshold is 18.

options.text: Hormone therapy requires the parent's consent regardless of the patient's age
options.rationale: Consent requirements vary, and it is not what determines the timing described here.

options.text: Hormone therapy is typically not prescribed until at least 18 years of age
options.rationale: That is the threshold, and the intervening years involve mental health care, medical care, and social services rather than nothing.

options.text: Hormone therapy is unsafe for anyone under 18 and should not be discussed
options.rationale: Her slide states it is safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision. The threshold is about prescribing practice, not a safety prohibition on the conversation.

questions.takeaway: Hormone replacement therapy is typically not prescribed until at least 18. It is safe for youth and adults with supervision and appropriate management.
questions.strategy: One distractor removes the threshold, one turns it into a safety prohibition, one substitutes a consent rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Typically 18.
Diagnosis alone does not start it.
Her slide calls it safe with supervision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the threshold of at least 18.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why gender-affirming care is described as medically necessary rather than elective. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is potentially life-saving for transgender people
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly, and it reflects the mortality associated with untreated dysphoria.

options.text: It is supported by strong scientific evidence
options.rationale: The evidence base is what moves it out of the elective category.

options.text: It improves mental health and overall wellbeing
options.rationale: Reduction in dysphoria, depression and anxiety is the measured outcome.

options.text: It reduces suicidal ideation and suicide attempts
options.rationale: Named explicitly as an outcome, and it is the clearest basis for the word necessary.

options.text: It restores fertility that was lost through hormone therapy
options.rationale: Fertility is part of the informed consent discussion because it may be affected, not something the care restores.

options.text: It is limited to surgical procedures
options.rationale: It covers a wide range of services including mental health care, medical care, and social services.

questions.takeaway: Gender-affirming care is medically necessary and potentially life-saving, supported by strong evidence, and it spans mental health, medical, and social services.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses what the consent discussion says about fertility. One narrows the care to surgery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mental health, medical, and social services.
Far broader than that.
Consent covers fertility risk, not restoration.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted for a hip fracture. Her partner of 41 years is not listed as next of kin, and she declines to say who should be contacted. Which factor most likely explains her hesitation?

options.text: Her partner's own preference not to be involved in decisions
options.rationale: Possible, and the stem describes her decision rather than her partner's.

options.text: Reluctance to burden family during an acute admission
options.rationale: A real reason people give, and it does not explain a 41-year relationship going unnamed.

options.text: A lifetime of discrimination that has taught her disclosure carries risk
options.rationale: This generation lived through criminalization and open hostility. Historical discrimination and lifetime exposure to stigma shape whether disclosure feels safe today.

options.text: Cognitive changes affecting her recall of who to contact
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests impairment, and she is declining rather than failing to remember.

questions.takeaway: LGBTQ+ older adults carry historical discrimination and lifetime exposure to stigma and violence. Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services at all.
questions.strategy: Two distractors offer ordinary explanations that do not account for the length of the relationship.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Forty-one years, unlisted.
She is declining, not forgetting.

steps.action: Cut the partner and burden options
steps.detail: Neither explains the omission.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a lifetime of learned risk around disclosure.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that several LGBTQ+ patients have not returned after a first visit, and two described feeling judged by staff. Which consequence should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Outcomes will be unaffected, since the clinical care given was appropriate
options.rationale: Care that is clinically correct and delivered in a way that stops someone returning has not worked.

options.text: Patients will seek the same care from a different provider promptly
options.rationale: Optimistic. Avoidance after a bad experience is more often avoidance of care generally, not a smooth transfer.

options.text: Conditions will present later and at a more advanced stage
options.rationale: Lack of affirmation discourages service utilization. People who stop coming still get ill, and they arrive when the illness is harder to treat.

options.text: The clinic's satisfaction scores will fall, prompting a review
options.rationale: People who stop attending often stop responding to surveys too, so the scores may not show it at all.

questions.takeaway: Lack of affirmation discourages service utilization, and delayed presentation is how that shows up in outcomes.
questions.strategy: One distractor assumes people move smoothly to another provider. One assumes the problem will announce itself in the data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what happens to someone who stops attending
steps.detail: The illness continues.
Avoidance generalizes.
Those who leave stop responding.

elimination.verdict: That leaves later presentation at a more advanced stage.

questions.nursesNote: 0930: Patient is 31, admitted for elective surgery. Transgender man. Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use; he asks to be called Sam. Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns since arrival. He is on testosterone therapy and has not had a cervical screening in six years. He has no documented primary care provider. He says he stopped going to clinics after a receptionist argued with him about his name. Vital signs stable. He has arranged his own transport home and has a friend staying overnight.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require nursing action before this admission proceeds.

segments.text: Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use; he asks to be called Sam
segments.rationale: Both names belong in the record. Recording the name he uses is what stops the next staff member repeating the error.

segments.text: Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns since arrival
segments.rationale: A pattern rather than a slip. It needs correcting with the staff, briefly and away from the patient.

segments.text: Has not had a cervical screening in six years
segments.rationale: Screening follows the organs a person has, not their gender. Reproductive and sexual health needs are frequently overlooked in this population.

segments.text: No documented primary care provider
segments.rationale: A gap in continuity, and with the clinic history it points to avoidance of care rather than preference.

segments.text: Stopped going to clinics after a receptionist argued with him about his name
segments.rationale: Explains the screening gap and the missing provider. It is the finding that connects the others.

segments.text: On testosterone therapy
segments.rationale: Part of his medical history and relevant to his care. It is not in itself a finding requiring action.

segments.text: Vital signs stable
segments.rationale: A normal finding, included to be left alone.

segments.text: Has arranged his own transport home and has a friend staying overnight
segments.rationale: The discharge arrangements are in place. This is the part that is going well.

questions.takeaway: Screening follows anatomy. Avoidance of care after a bad encounter shows up as missed screening and no regular provider.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal, planned, or part of his history. One finding explains two others, and all three belong in the selection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Testosterone is history.
The clinic argument explains the gaps.
Vital signs and discharge plan.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5: name, pronouns, screening, no provider, and the reason behind them.

questions.stem: A nurse is taking a sexual history from a new patient. Which approach best reflects the recommended practice?

options.text: Ask about anatomy and specific practices rather than inferring from gender
options.rationale: Risk follows what a person has and what they do. Her flowsheet notes that transgender and non-binary patients may prefer non-gendered terms for their sex organs.

options.text: Ask whether the patient is sexually active with men, women, or both, and proceed from the answer
options.rationale: A reasonable opening that becomes a problem when the answer is used to infer anatomy, which is exactly what happened in her case study.

options.text: Ask only the questions relevant to the presenting complaint
options.rationale: Narrows the history to the reason for the visit and misses screening needs, which is how this population's needs get overlooked.

options.text: Defer the sexual history until a relationship has been established over several visits
options.rationale: Well intentioned, and it delays screening for a group already presenting late. The way to make it safe is how you ask, not whether.

questions.takeaway: Assess anatomy and practices. Avoid inferring what a person has, or what they do, from how they describe themselves.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the exact opening from her case study. It is not wrong as a question; it is wrong as a basis for inference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Organs and practices.
That is the case-study error.
Both produce missed screening.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking about anatomy and practices directly.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses a transgender patient's care with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Gender-affirming care includes mental health and social services, not just surgery."
options.rationale: Accurate. It spans a wide range of services.

options.text: "Transitioning is private, personal, and individualized, so I should not assume the steps."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her exact wording.

options.text: "I should ask what name and pronouns he uses and put them in the record."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is what makes the affirmation consistent across staff.

options.text: "Since he takes testosterone, he no longer needs cervical screening."
options.rationale: Screening follows the organs a person has. Hormone therapy does not remove a cervix, and this is precisely the overlooked need her slide names.

questions.takeaway: Reproductive and sexual health needs are frequently overlooked in this population. Screening is determined by anatomy, not by hormones or identity.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth uses hormone therapy to cancel a screening need.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The organs present.
Names, scope of care, individualized transition.
Testosterone does not remove a cervix.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the cervical screening statement.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews factors contributing to poor birthing experiences and outcomes among LGBTQ+ patients. Which factors are recognized? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bias or discrimination during care
options.rationale: Named directly, and it shapes whether a person returns for the rest of their care.

options.text: Heterocentric policies
options.rationale: Policies written around an assumed family structure exclude before anyone speaks.

options.text: Invalidation as parents
options.rationale: Having a parental role questioned or dismissed during the perinatal period.

options.text: Disruptions in hormone therapy
options.rationale: A specific barrier for transgender and non-binary parents during pregnancy.

options.text: Inexperienced physicians
options.rationale: Named as a contributing factor, and it connects to the training gap her case study shows.

options.text: A higher rate of underlying obstetric complications in this population
options.rationale: The poor outcomes trace to how care is delivered and received, not to an inherent obstetric difference.

questions.takeaway: Contributing factors include bias and discrimination, heterocentric policies, invalidation as parents, hormone therapy disruption, birth trauma, postpartum difficulties, dysphoria, and inexperienced clinicians.
questions.strategy: One distractor locates the problem in the patients' bodies rather than in the care they receive. That distinction runs through the whole chapter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: In the delivery of care.
Places the cause in the patient.
All six are named factors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague refer to a patient by the wrong pronoun during handover. The patient is not present. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the patient afterwards that the error occurred
options.rationale: Hands him a problem he can do nothing about and adds to the burden the practice exists to remove.

options.text: Correct it briefly at the time and continue the handover
options.rationale: The correction has to happen where the error happened, or every nurse on the next shift inherits it. Brief keeps it about the patient rather than the colleague.

options.text: Raise it with the manager after the handover is complete
options.rationale: Appropriate for a repeated pattern, and it leaves the incoming shift with the wrong information tonight.

options.text: Say nothing, since the patient is not there to hear it
options.rationale: The pronoun used in handover becomes the pronoun used at the bedside. An uncorrected error propagates.

questions.takeaway: Affirming language has to be consistent across the team. Correct briefly, in the moment, and move on.
questions.strategy: Two options defer the correction. One transfers it to the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what happens to an uncorrected pronoun
steps.detail: It travels to the bedside.
The next shift acts on it tonight.
Adds a burden he cannot act on.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the brief correction during handover.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked which ethical basis obliges her to provide affirming care. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Facility policy requires staff to use patients' stated names and pronouns
options.rationale: Policy may well require it, and policy is not the ethical basis. Policies vary; the code does not.

options.text: The Code of Ethics requires compassion and respect for the dignity and worth of every patient
options.rationale: It is not conditional on agreement, comfort, or the nurse's own views. The obligation attaches to every patient.

options.text: State law protects patients from discrimination in health care settings
options.rationale: Legal protections differ by state and by year. The professional obligation does not.

options.text: Affirming care improves patient satisfaction scores
options.rationale: True and irrelevant as a basis. Dignity is not owed because it scores well.

questions.takeaway: The Code of Ethics: compassion, respect for dignity, and the worth of every patient. Not conditional and not variable by jurisdiction.
questions.strategy: Three options name real reasons to do it. Ask which one is the professional obligation rather than an external requirement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The code applies everywhere.
Both differ by place.
A consequence, not a basis.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the Code of Ethics.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse prepares to care for a transgender patient.

Gender-affirming care is the treatment for a diagnosis of [[1]].

A nurse who examines her own assumptions before an encounter is practicing [[2]].

Adding pronoun fields to the intake form is an example of [[3]].

Deciding what screening a patient needs is based on [[4]].

options.text: gender dysphoria
options.rationale: Her slide defines gender-affirming care as treatment for a diagnosis of gender dysphoria.

options.text: gender identity
options.rationale: Identity is who a person is. It is not a diagnosis and does not require treatment.

options.text: gender expression
options.rationale: How a person presents outwardly, and again not a diagnosis.

options.text: sexual orientation
options.rationale: Who a person is attracted to, which is unrelated to gender identity.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Examining personal biases and assumptions, and holding yourself accountable for them.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Learning terminology and specific health issues, which is outward rather than inward.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: What happens in the conversation itself.

options.text: prioritizing patient needs
options.rationale: Listening, respecting, and seeking feedback from patients.

options.text: fostering an inclusive environment
options.rationale: Updating policies and forms, and building identity into records.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: The near-miss. Pronouns are used in communication, and changing the form changes the space rather than the conversation.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Inward work on the nurse's own assumptions.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Training and terminology.

options.text: the organs the patient has
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy. A transgender man with a cervix still needs cervical screening.

options.text: the patient's gender identity
options.rationale: Identity does not determine which organs are present.

options.text: the sex recorded at birth
options.rationale: Closer, and still wrong after surgery. What matters is what is there now.

options.text: whether the patient takes hormone therapy
options.rationale: Hormones change physiology and do not remove organs.

questions.takeaway: Gender dysphoria is the diagnosis. Identity, expression and orientation are not diagnoses. Screening follows anatomy.
questions.strategy: Blank 3 has a genuine near-miss: pronouns belong to communication, and putting a field on a form changes the environment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only dysphoria is a diagnosis.
The nurse, the words, or the space.
What is physically present.

elimination.verdict: Gender dysphoria, self-reflection, inclusive environment, organs present.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews why LGBTQ+ health matters specifically to nursing. Which reason is most accurate?

options.text: Nurses are often the first point of contact, so the encounter shapes whether a patient returns
options.rationale: First point of contact, improving health outcomes, and ethical responsibility are the three reasons her slide names, and the first is what makes the others possible.

options.text: Nurses are responsible for prescribing gender-affirming therapies
options.rationale: Outside the registered nurse's scope. The nurse's role is assessment, support, education, and advocacy.

options.text: Nurses must document sexual orientation for every patient on admission
options.rationale: Incorporating identity into records is a system practice, and it is not a mandatory field for every patient.

options.text: Nurses should refer LGBTQ+ patients to specialist clinicians where possible
options.rationale: Reasonable-sounding and it routes patients away from the care in front of them, which is how needs get overlooked.

questions.takeaway: Three reasons: nurses are the first point of contact, they improve health outcomes, and they hold an ethical responsibility.
questions.strategy: One distractor exceeds nursing scope. One routes the patient elsewhere, which is the opposite of the point.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: First contact, before anyone else.
Outside scope.
One overstates, one deflects.

elimination.verdict: That leaves being the first point of contact.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she has delayed a mammogram for three years because the last time she attended, staff repeatedly questioned her about her partner. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that staff attitudes have improved since then
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot keep and that asks her to trust an institution that has already failed her.

options.text: Document that the patient declined screening for three years
options.rationale: Records the gap without addressing it, and declined misstates what happened.

options.text: Explain the importance of regular screening and the risks of delay
options.rationale: Correct teaching that assumes the barrier is knowledge. She knows; she is avoiding.

options.text: Acknowledge what happened and arrange the screening with the concern addressed
options.rationale: The barrier is the previous encounter. Naming it and changing what happens this time is what makes the screening possible.

questions.takeaway: Avoidance after a bad encounter is an access problem. Address what happened before addressing the screening.
questions.strategy: One option teaches, one documents, one reassures. None of them changes what she is afraid will happen again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The previous encounter, not knowledge.
Neither addresses avoidance.
An unenforceable promise.

elimination.verdict: That leaves acknowledging it and arranging the screening differently.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old is admitted for a scheduled procedure. She lives with the woman she calls her partner of 30 years, who is not listed anywhere in the record. During admission she asks twice whether her partner will be allowed to stay, and says a previous hospital sent her partner home at the end of visiting hours while family members of other patients remained. She has not had a primary care visit in four years.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Ask who she wants documented as her support person and record it where staff will see
options.rationale: Records that assume a family structure are what produced the previous exclusion. Documenting her stated support person is what prevents it repeating.

options.text: Confirm with her what the visiting arrangements are and tell the team
options.rationale: Answers the question she has now asked twice, and makes the arrangement known to the people who will enforce it.

options.text: Reassure her that this hospital does not discriminate
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot enforce, offered instead of the documentation and communication that would actually secure it.

options.text: Document that the patient appears anxious about visiting policy
options.rationale: Records her anxiety as a finding and leaves the cause of it untouched.

options.text: Anticipated exclusion of her partner, based on a previous experience
options.rationale: She has asked twice and told you why. The problem is a reasonable expectation built from what happened before.

options.text: Anxiety related to the upcoming procedure
options.rationale: Plausible and not what she asked about. Both her questions concerned her partner.

options.text: Knowledge deficit regarding hospital visiting policy
options.rationale: Frames it as not knowing the rules. She knows what happened last time; the issue is whether it happens again.

options.text: Lack of family support during hospitalization
options.rationale: She has support. The risk is that the institution will not recognize it.

options.text: Whether her partner is recorded and treated as her support person by all staff
options.rationale: Measures whether the documentation actually changed how the team behaved.

options.text: Whether she raises the question again
options.rationale: She asked twice. If she stops asking, the concern has been answered.

options.text: Whether her vital signs remain stable before the procedure
options.rationale: A real parameter, and it does not evaluate anything the actions changed.

options.text: Whether she can state the hospital's visiting policy
options.rationale: Tests recall of a rule. The problem was never that she did not know one.

questions.takeaway: Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services. A partner unrecognized by the record is how that exclusion happens in practice.
questions.strategy: Two problem options relocate the issue into her, as anxiety or as not knowing. She told you it is about what happened last time.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Twice, about her partner, with a reason.

steps.action: Cut the options that relocate it
steps.detail: Anxiety and knowledge deficit.
You documented and you told the team.

elimination.verdict: Document and communicate, for anticipated exclusion, evaluated by staff behavior and whether she asks again.

questions.stem: A patient receiving furosemide has a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which assessment finding does the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Constipation and abdominal distention
options.rationale: A real finding in hypokalemia and not the one that kills. Smooth muscle slows along with everything else.

options.text: Shallow respirations with a weak cough
options.rationale: Hypokalemia weakens every muscle including the diaphragm and the intercostals. Respiratory muscle weakness is the finding that turns a laboratory value into an emergency.

options.text: Generalized fatigue and leg weakness
options.rationale: Expected and important, and it is the background against which you look for the breathing.

options.text: Prominent U waves on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: The classic electrocardiogram change in hypokalemia, and it belongs in the report. It is still not the finding that takes priority over ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Weakness is a respiratory finding until you rule it out. Hypokalemia, hypermagnesemia and hyponatremia all weaken the muscles that breathe.
questions.strategy: Every option is a genuine finding in hypokalemia. The question is which one threatens the airway and breathing.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option is about breathing.

steps.action: Note that U waves are tempting
steps.detail: They are the textbook sign, which is exactly why they are offered.

steps.action: Cut the gut and the fatigue
steps.detail: Both are expected and neither is immediately dangerous.

elimination.verdict: Shallow respirations. Assess the breathing, not just the grip.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 7.1 mEq/L and peaked T waves received IV calcium gluconate. A repeat potassium is 7.0 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Report that the calcium failed and request another dose
options.rationale: Calcium was never meant to lower potassium. The unchanged level is expected.

options.text: Anticipate regular insulin with dextrose
options.rationale: Insulin shifts potassium into cells. Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. This is the step that lowers the level.

options.text: Document that the cardiac risk has resolved
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart only for a short time. A potassium of 7.0 is still dangerous.

options.text: Discontinue cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: The patient still has a lethal potassium. Continuous monitoring is required.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium protects the heart but does not change potassium. Insulin with dextrose shifts it. Binders or dialysis remove it.
questions.strategy: The unchanged level is the trap. Expect it. Then choose the drug that actually moves potassium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It stabilizes the heart only.
7.0 is still critical.
Shift potassium into cells.

elimination.verdict: B. Insulin with dextrose.

questions.stem: A patient has been receiving potassium replacement for two days and the serum potassium remains 3.0 mEq/L. Which laboratory value does the nurse check next?

options.text: Serum magnesium
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes the kidney waste potassium and blocks it from staying in the cell. Potassium will not come up while the magnesium is low, no matter how much you give.

options.text: Serum albumin
options.rationale: Albumin matters for interpreting a calcium level, not a potassium one.

options.text: Serum phosphorus
options.rationale: Phosphorus moves inversely with calcium. It has no direct role in potassium replacement failing.

options.text: Serum chloride
options.rationale: Chloride tracks sodium and acid-base status. It does not explain refractory hypokalemia.

questions.takeaway: When a level will not respond to correction, the first question is which related electrolyte nobody checked. Potassium will not correct while magnesium is low.
questions.strategy: The stem is not asking about hypokalemia. It is asking why a correct treatment is not working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two days of replacement with no movement.
Magnesium, every time.
Albumin and phosphorus belong to a different pairing.

elimination.verdict: Magnesium. Read labs as a set, not one line at a time.

questions.stem: A patient who had a thyroidectomy yesterday has a serum calcium of 7.6 mg/dL. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: Sore throat when swallowing
options.rationale: Expected after neck surgery with intubation. It does not signal low calcium.

options.text: Incision pain rated 3 out of 10
options.rationale: Mild pain is expected the day after surgery.

options.text: Carpal spasm when the blood pressure cuff is inflated
options.rationale: A positive Trousseau sign shows nerve overexcitability from low calcium, likely from parathyroid injury, and it can progress to tetany and laryngospasm.

options.text: Drowsiness one hour after an opioid dose
options.rationale: An expected opioid effect. Low calcium excites nerves rather than sedating them.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium excites nerve and muscle: tingling, spasm, brisk reflexes and a long QT. After thyroid surgery, watch for it.
questions.strategy: Three options are expected after surgery. Keep the one that sounds excitable and fits the low calcium.

strategies: Odd man wins
Priority key word

steps.detail: Thyroid surgery can injure the parathyroid glands.
Sore throat, mild pain and opioid drowsiness are normal after surgery.
Carpal spasm is the low calcium cue.

elimination.verdict: C. A positive Trousseau sign.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L, 3+ pitting edema and a weight gain of 4 kg this week. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL/hr
options.rationale: Saline into a fluid-overloaded hyponatremic patient makes both problems worse. The sodium is low because there is too much water, not too little salt.

options.text: Fluid restriction with daily weights
options.rationale: This is dilutional hyponatremia. The sodium is diluted by retained water, so removing water is what raises the number.

options.text: Encouraging salty broths and adding salt to meals
options.rationale: Adds sodium to a patient who is already retaining water and will retain more with it.

options.text: Rapid infusion of 3% sodium chloride over two hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures or coma, given slowly and with close monitoring. Correcting fast causes osmotic demyelination.

questions.takeaway: Find the volume status before you treat the sodium. A low sodium with edema and weight gain is too much water, and the treatment is restriction rather than replacement.
questions.strategy: Two options add sodium and one adds volume. The edema and the weight gain tell you which direction the patient needs to move.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3+ edema and 4 kg of gain.
Adding fluid to an overloaded patient.
Sodium follows water in, and there is already too much water.

elimination.verdict: Fluid restriction. Hyponatremia is not automatically a sodium deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia becomes drowsy, and the nurse finds absent patellar reflexes with a respiratory rate of 10. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: Reflexes go first, then respirations, then rhythm. The progression has already reached breathing, and the first action is to stop what is causing it.

options.text: Administer calcium gluconate as the antidote
options.rationale: Calcium is the antidote and it comes after stopping the infusion. Giving the antidote while the drug keeps running is treating around the cause.

options.text: Notify the prescriber of the assessment findings
options.rationale: Necessary and not first. Notification follows the action that stops the harm.

options.text: Place the patient on continuous pulse oximetry
options.rationale: Monitoring a patient who is being poisoned does not stop the poisoning.

questions.takeaway: Hypermagnesemia progresses reflexes, then respirations, then rhythm. Checking the patellar reflex before each hour of infusion is how you catch it before the breathing.
questions.strategy: Three of the four options are correct actions and only one of them removes the cause.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.

steps.action: Note that the antidote is tempting
steps.detail: It is right and it is second.
Both follow the intervention.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion, then calcium gluconate, then notify.

questions.stem: A patient has a total calcium of 7.8 mg/dL with a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL. The patient has no tingling, no spasm and a normal QT interval. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient has significant hypocalcemia and needs replacement now
options.rationale: Treating the number instead of the patient. Nothing in the assessment supports a functional deficit.

options.text: The low albumin has lowered the total calcium without lowering the active calcium
options.rationale: Roughly half of serum calcium travels bound to albumin. Less albumin means less bound calcium and a lower total, while the ionized fraction that actually does the work is unchanged.

options.text: The result is a laboratory error and should be redrawn
options.rationale: The two values are consistent with each other, which is the opposite of an error.

options.text: The patient is developing hyperparathyroidism
options.rationale: That raises calcium rather than lowering it.

questions.takeaway: Low albumin lowers the total calcium without lowering the calcium that is working. Check the albumin, or ask for the ionized calcium, before treating a number.
questions.strategy: The absence of symptoms is the finding the question is built on. A truly low ionized calcium would show itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calcium is reported with albumin for a reason.
No tingling, no spasm, normal QT.
Nothing functional is wrong.

elimination.verdict: A dilutional artifact of low albumin. Ask for an ionized calcium.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old has a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L after prolonged fever and poor intake. Which plan of care does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Restrict free water until the sodium normalizes
options.rationale: This patient is short of water. Restriction makes the deficit worse.

options.text: Correct the sodium to normal within the first 8 hours
options.rationale: Lowering sodium fast pulls water into brain cells and causes cerebral edema.

options.text: Infuse 3% sodium chloride with hourly sodium levels
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline raises sodium further. It treats severe hyponatremia.

options.text: Infuse a hypotonic solution slowly with frequent neurologic checks
options.rationale: The water deficit is replaced gradually, and level of consciousness shows whether the brain is tolerating the change.

questions.takeaway: Both sodium extremes are brain problems, and both are corrected slowly. High sodium after fever means a water deficit.
questions.strategy: Speed is the trap in every sodium question. Pick the option that adds water slowly and watches the brain.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: High sodium after fever and poor intake means a water deficit.
Water restriction and 3% saline both raise sodium.
An 8-hour correction risks cerebral edema.

elimination.verdict: D. Slow hypotonic fluid with neurologic checks.

questions.stem: Two hours into an IV infusion, the patient says the site feels tight. The area is cool, pale and swollen, spreading outward from the catheter. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply warm compresses and continue the infusion at a slower rate
options.rationale: Warmth is for phlebitis. Continuing any rate keeps pushing solution into tissue.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and elevate the extremity
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen and spreading is infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

options.text: Massage the area to disperse the fluid and reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Massage forces more solution into the tissue and can worsen the injury.

options.text: Aspirate from the catheter and flush with 10 mL of normal saline to confirm patency
options.rationale: A flush adds volume to tissue that already has too much, and patency is not the question. A catheter can flush perfectly while it sits outside the vein.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration runs cool and spreads around the site. Phlebitis runs warm and follows the vein. A streak or a palpable cord is always phlebitis.
questions.strategy: The temperature and the direction of spread are the two cues that separate the two complications, and the stem gives you both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That rules out phlebitis and infection.
Not along the vein, so not a cord.
Both belong to the other diagnosis or make this one worse.
Patency is not safety.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

questions.scenario: The nurse reassesses four patients receiving treatment for an electrolyte imbalance.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the new finding shows the condition is improving or worsening.

rows.text: Calcium 7.4 mg/dL on replacement: new facial twitching when the cheek is tapped
rows.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign shows nerves are more excitable. The low calcium is not corrected.

rows.text: Magnesium 4.8 mEq/L after magnesium was stopped: reflexes now 1+ from absent
rows.rationale: High magnesium blocks reflexes. Their return shows the level is falling.

rows.text: Potassium 6.4 mEq/L after a binder: cramping with diarrhea has stopped
rows.rationale: High potassium makes the gut irritable. Calmer bowels show the level is falling.

rows.text: Calcium 12.6 mg/dL on IV saline: more lethargic than this morning
rows.rationale: High calcium slows nerves. More lethargy means the level is not coming down.

questions.takeaway: Calcium and magnesium are brakes: low excites, high slows. Potassium is the opposite: high excites. Improvement moves each finding back toward normal.
questions.strategy: Decide whether each imbalance excites or slows. Then ask whether the new finding moves toward or away from that state.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites. High magnesium slows. High potassium excites. High calcium slows.
Twitching is more excitement. Returning reflexes and calmer bowels are less.
Moving toward normal is improving. Moving further is worsening.

elimination.verdict: Worsening, improving, improving, worsening.

caseStudies.title: Heart failure with low potassium and fluid overload
caseStudies.intro: A 72-year-old man with heart failure was admitted 2 days ago for shortness of breath. He receives furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily.

entries.text: Reports his legs feel weak and heavy. Deep tendon reflexes decreased in both legs.
Crackles in both lower lobes. Neck veins distended with head of bed at 45 degrees. 2+ pitting edema in both ankles.
Weight 88.4 kg, up 1.8 kg from yesterday on the same scale. Admits he ate canned soup his wife brought in.
Bowel sounds hypoactive. Alert and oriented x4.
T 36.8 C; HR 104, irregular; RR 24; BP 154/92; SpO2 91% on room air
Cardiac monitor shows flat T waves, prominent U waves and frequent premature ventricular contractions
Potassium 2.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0)
Magnesium 1.2 mEq/L (1.3 to 2.1)
Sodium 137 mEq/L (135 to 145)
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2)
Heart failure and hypertension for 10 years.
Home medications: furosemide 40 mg by mouth daily; lisinopril 10 mg daily.
Eats few fruits or vegetables. Lives with his wife.

question.stem: Which findings require immediate follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Potassium 2.9 mEq/L
options.rationale: Well below 3.5 while he still receives a loop diuretic twice a day.

options.text: SpO2 91% with RR 24
options.rationale: Fluid in the lungs is impairing gas exchange.

options.text: Prominent U waves with frequent premature ventricular contractions
options.rationale: The ECG signs of hypokalemia plus an active dysrhythmia.

options.text: Weight up 1.8 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of fluid overload.

options.text: Weak legs with decreased deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Low potassium makes muscle less responsive. It can progress to paralysis.

options.text: Sodium 137 mEq/L
options.rationale: Within range.

options.text: Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
options.rationale: Normal kidney function.

options.text: Alert and oriented x4
options.rationale: Normal mental status.

question.takeaway: Two problems are running at once: too much fluid and too little potassium. Each has its own cues.
question.strategy: The normal labs are there to test whether you read the ranges. Sort each option into abnormal or normal before you decide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Apply the ABCs

steps.action: Check each lab against its range
steps.detail: Potassium is low. Sodium and creatinine are normal.
SpO2 91% and a dysrhythmia threaten him now.
Weakness in the legs tracks the potassium.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

question.scenario: The nurse sorts the client's findings.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is most consistent with fluid overload or hypokalemia.

rows.text: Crackles in both lower lobes
rows.rationale: Excess fluid has moved into the lungs.

rows.text: Distended neck veins
rows.rationale: Too much volume in the venous system.
More volume raises pressure. Hypokalemia tends to lower it.

rows.text: Flat T waves with prominent U waves
rows.rationale: The classic ECG pattern of low potassium.

rows.text: Decreased deep tendon reflexes in both legs
rows.rationale: Low potassium makes skeletal muscle and nerves less excitable.

rows.text: Hypoactive bowel sounds
rows.rationale: Smooth muscle in the gut slows too.

question.takeaway: Overload shows in the lungs, neck veins and pressure. Low potassium shows in the ECG, the skeletal muscle and the gut.
question.strategy: Ask whether each finding is about volume or about muscle and nerve firing. Volume findings belong to overload.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Crackles, neck veins and pressure.
ECG, reflexes and bowel sounds.
Low potassium lowers pressure, so high pressure here is volume.

elimination.verdict: Overload, overload, overload, hypokalemia, hypokalemia, hypokalemia.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence:
The client's most life threatening risk is [[1]].

This risk is driven by [[2]].

If the fluid overload is not corrected, the client is at risk for [[3]].

options.text: a lethal cardiac dysrhythmia
options.rationale: Low potassium disrupts the heart's electrical activity. He already has frequent premature ventricular contractions.

options.text: paralytic ileus
options.rationale: A severe GI effect of hypokalemia. It is not what kills first.

options.text: a pressure injury from ankle edema
options.rationale: A real risk and a slow one.

options.text: dehydration from the diuretic
options.rationale: He is overloaded, not dry.

options.text: a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L together with a low magnesium
options.rationale: Potassium and magnesium are closely linked. Low magnesium makes low potassium harder to correct and adds to dysrhythmia risk.

options.text: a sodium of 137 mEq/L
options.rationale: Normal.

options.text: a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL
options.rationale: Normal kidney function.

options.text: the 2+ ankle edema
options.rationale: A sign of overload, not of electrical risk.

options.text: pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Preventing pulmonary edema is the priority in fluid overload. His crackles and SpO2 of 91% show fluid is already reaching the lungs.

options.text: hypovolemic shock
options.rationale: The opposite volume problem.

options.text: hypernatremia
options.rationale: His sodium is normal.

options.text: tetany
options.rationale: Tetany comes from low calcium or magnesium, not from fluid overload.

question.takeaway: Both hypokalemia and hyperkalemia can cause life threatening dysrhythmias. Low magnesium often travels with low potassium.
question.strategy: The magnesium is easy to overlook because potassium is the headline. The deck links them; look for both.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: The heart rhythm.
Low potassium with low magnesium.
Fluid in the lungs becomes pulmonary edema.

elimination.verdict: Dysrhythmia; low potassium with low magnesium; pulmonary edema.

question.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: He has a dysrhythmia and a potassium of 2.9.

options.text: Potassium replacement as prescribed
options.rationale: Corrects the cause of the electrical risk.

options.text: Restrict fluid and dietary sodium
options.rationale: Removes the source of the overload. The canned soup is part of this story.

options.text: Weigh daily on the same scale at the same time in the same clothing
options.rationale: Tracks fluid change reliably.

options.text: Fall precautions
options.rationale: Leg weakness from hypokalemia makes a fall likely.

options.text: Encourage 3,000 mL of oral fluid daily
options.rationale: Adds volume to a client who is already overloaded.

options.text: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour to protect his kidneys
options.rationale: His kidneys are working. Extra saline worsens the overload.

question.takeaway: Treat both problems at once: protect the heart and replace potassium, then remove fluid and sodium and measure the result.
question.strategy: The saline option offers a reason that sounds protective. Check it against the chart: his creatinine is normal and he is overloaded.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Monitor and replace potassium.
Restrict fluid and sodium, track with weights.
Oral fluid push and a saline infusion both add to the overload.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Provider prescribes potassium chloride 20 mEq in 200 mL IV over 2 hours and oral magnesium. Premixed bag received from pharmacy. Peripheral IV in left forearm.

question.stem: Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Infuse the potassium using an IV pump
options.rationale: IV potassium is a high alert drug. A pump controls the rate.

options.text: Confirm the rate is 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: 20 mEq over 2 hours is 10 mEq per hour, the top of the safe range of 5 to 10.

options.text: Check the IV site every hour for burning or pain
options.rationale: Potassium irritates veins and can cause phlebitis.

options.text: Keep him on the cardiac monitor during the infusion
options.rationale: Watches the rhythm while the level changes.

options.text: Give 10 mEq by slow IV push first to raise the level quickly
options.rationale: Never give potassium IV push. It can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Run the bag over 30 minutes because his level is 2.9
options.rationale: That is 40 mEq per hour, four times the safe rate.

options.text: Give the dose intramuscularly if the IV infiltrates
options.rationale: Never give potassium IM or subcut. It causes tissue necrosis.

question.takeaway: IV potassium goes diluted, on a pump, at 5 to 10 mEq per hour, with hourly site checks and a cardiac monitor. Never push, never IM.
question.strategy: A low number creates urgency. Urgency does not change the rate. "Slow" push is still a push.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Favor qualifiers

steps.detail: IV push and IM.
20 mEq over 30 minutes is 40 mEq per hour.
Pump, rate, site checks, monitor.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

entries.text: Potassium 3.3 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). Magnesium 1.5 mEq/L (1.3 to 2.1).
Monitor shows sinus rhythm at 86. No U waves. No premature ventricular contractions in 2 hours.
Intake 600 mL and urine output 1,400 mL since 0700. RR 18; SpO2 95% on room air; fewer crackles at the bases. Reports legs feel stronger. 2+ pitting edema in both ankles.

question.scenario: The nurse evaluates the client's response to treatment.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows that treatment has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: Potassium 3.3 mEq/L, up from 2.9
rows.rationale: Rising but still below 3.5 while he continues a loop diuretic. Replacement continues and the level is rechecked.

rows.text: Sinus rhythm with no U waves or premature ventricular contractions
rows.rationale: The rhythm has settled as the potassium rises.

rows.text: Output 1,400 mL with intake 600 mL
rows.rationale: He is losing more fluid than he takes in, which is the goal.

rows.text: SpO2 95% with RR 18 and fewer crackles
rows.rationale: Less fluid in the lungs means better gas exchange.

rows.text: Legs feel stronger
rows.rationale: Muscle strength is returning as potassium rises.

rows.text: 2+ pitting edema in both ankles
rows.rationale: Unchanged since 0705. Interstitial fluid is still in excess, so diuresis and restriction continue.

question.takeaway: Evaluate each problem with its own cues. Potassium and rhythm answer the electrolyte question. Output, lungs, weight and edema answer the volume question.
question.strategy: Compare each finding to its goal, not to its starting point. A potassium that is rising but still below 3.5 has not met the goal. The edema has not changed since 0705.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Rhythm and leg strength improved; potassium is rising but still low.
Output, lungs and SpO2 improved.
Ankle edema is still 2+.

elimination.verdict: All effective except the low potassium and the unchanged ankle edema.

questions.stem: A patient has lost an estimated 1200 mL of blood during surgery and has a blood pressure of 88 over 52 with a pulse of 118. While blood is being crossmatched, which solution does the nurse expect to infuse?

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia and for expanding intravascular volume. It also carries risks of cell dehydration and hypernatremia that are unnecessary when an isotonic fluid will do the job.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so most of the infused water leaves the vasculature and enters cells. A fluid that moves water out of that space is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does expand intravascular volume by pulling water out of cells, and it is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Using it here treats the volume at the cost of dehydrating cells for no reason.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic at 273 mOsm/L, so infused volume stays in the extracellular space and expands circulating volume without shifting water into or out of cells. Volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation are the listed uses for isotonic fluids.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhage empties the vascular compartment, so the fluid that fixes it is the one that stays there. That is the definition of isotonic.

questions.stem: Two nurses are verifying a unit of packed red blood cells at the bedside. One reads the label aloud while the other listens and agrees. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Have each nurse check the unit and the band independently
options.rationale: Independent verification means each nurse checks the documents and the patient separately. A listener cannot catch an error she never looked for.

options.text: Sign the transfusion record and start the infusion
options.rationale: The signature records a check. It does not replace one that was done incorrectly.

options.text: Ask the patient to state his name and date of birth
options.rationale: Patient identification is good practice. It does not fix the missing independent check of the unit.

options.text: Let the nurse who will hang the unit finish the check
options.rationale: Who hangs the unit does not change how the check was done.

questions.takeaway: Two nurse verification means two independent checks, not one check with a witness.

questions.stem: A student scrubs an IV site with chlorhexidine for 30 seconds, lets it air dry, then palpates the vein again. Which action does the supervising nurse take?

options.text: Have the student repeat the skin prep before inserting
options.rationale: Touching the cleansed skin with an unsterile finger recontaminates it. The prep must be redone.

options.text: Allow insertion because the scrub lasted 30 seconds
options.rationale: A correct scrub is undone by touching the site afterward.

options.text: Have the student wipe the site with sterile gauze first
options.rationale: Wiping does not restore antisepsis. The antiseptic must be reapplied and dry.

options.text: Allow insertion because the student wore clean gloves
options.rationale: Clean gloves are not sterile. The site is still contaminated.

questions.takeaway: Scrub with friction for 30 seconds, let it air dry completely, then do not touch the site. Confirm the vein before the prep.
questions.strategy: The scenario shows two correct steps before the error. Do not let them distract you from the last one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 30 seconds with friction is correct.
Air drying is correct.
Repalpating recontaminates the site.

elimination.verdict: A. Repeat the prep.

questions.stem: A patient has a midline catheter placed for a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours
options.rationale: An antibiotic is a non-vesicant medication with an osmolarity well within peripheral limits. Antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration therapy are the listed indications.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr
options.rationale: Normal saline is isotonic at 308 mOsm/L. Yes, it is one of the named indications.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition at 60 mL/hr
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a highly concentrated solution of dextrose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins, and trace elements. Parenteral nutrition is explicitly excluded from midline use and requires central access, because its osmolarity far exceeds the peripheral limit and would damage the vein.

options.text: Morphine sulfate 2 mg intravenously every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: Morphine is an analgesic and is not a vesicant. Analgesics are listed among the appropriate therapies.

questions.takeaway: A midline is a long peripheral catheter, not a central line. Its tip ends below the axilla, so it obeys peripheral rules no matter how far up the arm it was inserted.

questions.stem: An IV site has cool, pale skin with moderate swelling. The drip has slowed with no blood return. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Fluid is leaking into the tissue. Stopping it prevents more damage before the catheter is removed.

options.text: Flush the catheter to restore flow
options.rationale: The catheter is out of the vein. Flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue.

options.text: Apply a warm compress while the infusion continues
options.rationale: A compress comes only after the infusion is stopped and the catheter is out, and warm or cool depends on the solution. Continuing the infusion adds fluid to the tissue.

options.text: Slow the rate and reassess in 1 hour
