options.rationale: Any rate keeps fluid leaking. Waiting worsens the infiltration.

questions.takeaway: Cool, pale, swollen skin with no blood return means infiltration. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, elevate the limb and document the grade.
questions.strategy: Warm and red with a cord would be phlebitis. Cool and pale means fluid has left the vein. Both start with stopping the infusion.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool, pale, swollen, slow, no blood return points to infiltration.
Flushing or continuing the infusion worsens it.
Stop the source.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop the infusion.

questions.stem: While the nurse changes the cap on a central venous catheter, the patient suddenly reports chest pain and severe shortness of breath. A churning murmur is heard over the precordium. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Position the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract so it cannot be pumped into the lungs. It manages the air already inside while clamping prevents more.

options.text: Administer 100 percent oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen improves saturation and helps the trapped air be reabsorbed. It is part of the response and it does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Clamp the catheter tubing
options.rationale: Clamping closes the pathway between room air and the venous system. Stopping the source is the first action because every additional second adds volume to the embolus, and the remaining steps treat what has already entered.

options.text: Activate the rapid response team
options.rationale: A rapid response brings additional expertise to the bedside. Calling is essential and it is not the first action when a one-second intervention stops the cause.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a mill-wheel murmur during line manipulation is air embolism. Clamp, position in left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response and give 100 percent oxygen.

questions.stem: A patient's nontunneled central line was placed 6 days ago for IV antibiotics. She now takes all her medications by mouth. Which action by the nurse best reduces her infection risk?

options.text: Change the transparent dressing today
options.rationale: Dressing care is needed maintenance. It does not shorten how long the line stays in.

options.text: Ask the provider whether the line can be removed
options.rationale: Dwell time is a primary infection risk. She no longer needs IV access, so removal is the strongest step.

options.text: Flush each lumen every shift
options.rationale: Flushing keeps the line patent. It does not prevent infection.

options.text: Label the tubing with the date it was hung
options.rationale: Labeling supports tubing changes. It does not address dwell time.

questions.takeaway: Ask every day whether the line is still needed. A line with no purpose only adds infection risk.

questions.stem: An AP reports that a patient's IV site looks puffy. The LPN is flushing another patient's established saline lock. Which action does the RN take?

options.text: Assess the site before deciding on removal
options.rationale: Interpreting a site finding is RN judgment. The AP reports what the site looks like.

options.text: Ask the AP to remove the catheter
options.rationale: Removal is an intervention based on assessment. It is not an AP task.

options.text: Have the LPN evaluate the site and decide on removal
options.rationale: The LPN may do routine monitoring. Interpreting a new problem stays with the RN.

options.text: Tell the AP to recheck the site in 1 hour
options.rationale: A puffy site may be infiltrating now. Waiting lets more fluid leak.

questions.takeaway: The RN keeps assessment, interpretation, blood product starts, high alert drugs and teaching. LPNs flush established lines. APs report site appearance. The RN stays accountable.
questions.strategy: The LPN's task is appropriate and is not the question. Focus on who interprets the AP's report.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flushing an established lock is delegable.
Deciding a site is infiltrated is RN assessment.
Rechecking later risks more fluid in the tissue.

elimination.verdict: A. The RN assesses the site.

questions.stem: On day 3 of IV antibiotics and potassium-added saline through a right forearm catheter, a patient reports burning along the arm. The vein is red with a palpable cord, and blood return is good. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Slow the infusion to 50 mL per hour and reassess the site in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing the rate keeps the irritating solution flowing into an inflamed vein. The slide intervention for phlebitis starts with stopping the infusion.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress and start a new line in the left arm
options.rationale: This is phlebitis. The cord shows an inflamed vein wall, and potassium is a likely chemical irritant. Stop, remove, apply warm moist heat and restart in the other arm, away from the damaged vein.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and start a new line in a hand vein below the current site
options.rationale: Removal is right. The new site is wrong. The slide lists sites distal to prior phlebitis as contraindicated because fluid entering below the inflamed vein must travel through it.

options.text: Flush the catheter with 10 mL of saline to confirm patency before deciding on removal
options.rationale: Patency is not the question. Blood return is already good. A patent catheter can still be sitting in an inflamed vein. Flushing adds more irritation.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis means stop, remove and apply warm moist heat. When you restart, choose a site that does not route fluid through the damaged vein.
questions.strategy: Two options remove the catheter. The tie breaker is where the new line goes. Ask which direction the fluid will travel from the new site.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness, a palpable cord and burning with good blood return is phlebitis, not infiltration.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the line
steps.detail: Slowing the rate and flushing both leave the inflamed vein in use.
A hand vein below the site sends fluid through the inflamed vein. The other arm avoids it.

elimination.verdict: Stop, remove, warm moist compress and restart in the opposite arm.

questions.stem: A patient receiving TPN through a left arm PICC reports the arm aches. The upper arm circumference rose 3 cm since morning, and the flush meets resistance. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Flush the PICC with a 10 mL syringe using steady firm pressure to clear the occlusion
options.rationale: Flushing against resistance can rupture the catheter or push a clot into the circulation. The PICC teaching slide is clear: do not use the line if resistance is felt.

options.text: Stop the infusion, avoid flushing against resistance and notify the provider of a suspected catheter-related thrombosis
options.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a rising circumference and a line that resists flushing is the slide picture of thrombosis. You stop using the line and report. The provider decides on imaging, anticoagulation, or removal. Stopping TPN suddenly can drop the glucose, so hang D10W peripherally per protocol and check the glucose.

options.text: Draw two sets of blood cultures and anticipate IV antibiotics
options.rationale: This is the response to a bloodstream infection. Nothing here suggests infection, and infection does not explain the swelling or the occlusion.

options.text: Elevate the arm, apply a warm compress and restart the TPN at a lower rate
options.rationale: Elevation is reasonable comfort care. Restarting the infusion through a line with a suspected clot is not safe. A slower rate does not treat the cause.

questions.takeaway: A swollen, painful limb plus a line that resists flushing points to thrombosis. Stop using the catheter, never force a flush and call the provider.
questions.strategy: First decide which complication fits. A swelling limb with a resisting line points to a clot. Then pick the action that stops harm without forcing the line.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Circumference rose 3 cm on the PICC side.
Limb swelling, pain and resistance fit thrombosis, not infection.
Firm flushing against resistance risks rupture or embolism.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion, do not flush against resistance and report suspected thrombosis.

caseStudies.title: Swollen forearm at a peripheral IV site
caseStudies.intro: A 79 year old woman is on day 2 of admission for pneumonia. She has a 22 gauge peripheral IV in her left forearm with 0.9% sodium chloride infusing at 75 mL per hour.

entries.text: IV site in left forearm clean, dry and intact. Flushes easily with blood return. No redness or swelling. Transparent dressing dated yesterday.

Client reports her left forearm feels tight and sore. Skin around the IV site is cool and pale. Swelling about 4 cm around the insertion site. Infusion pump alarming for occlusion. No blood return when checked. Right arm without swelling.
T 37.6 C; HR 88; RR 20; BP 132/78; SpO2 94% on 2 L nasal cannula
T 37.4 C; HR 90; RR 20; BP 134/80; SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula
Community acquired pneumonia. Receiving IV antibiotics every 12 hours. History of hypertension. Thin, fragile skin on both forearms. Right handed.

question.nursesNote: 1000: Client reports her left forearm feels tight and sore. Skin around the IV site is cool and pale. Swelling about 4 cm around the insertion site. Infusion pump alarming for occlusion. No blood return when checked. Right arm without swelling. SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Client reports her left forearm feels tight and sore
segments.rationale: New discomfort at the site. The 0800 note recorded no redness or swelling.

segments.text: Skin around the IV site is cool and pale
segments.rationale: Cool pale skin means fluid is collecting in the tissue instead of the vein.

segments.text: Swelling about 4 cm around the insertion site
segments.rationale: Edema at the site was not present at 0800.

segments.text: Infusion pump alarming for occlusion
segments.rationale: The fluid cannot flow freely into the vein. A slowed drip or an occlusion alarm is a sign of infiltration.

segments.text: No blood return when checked
segments.rationale: At 0800 the line had blood return. Losing it suggests the catheter tip is no longer in the vein.

segments.text: Right arm without swelling
segments.rationale: Normal. It helps you compare sides and needs no follow up.

segments.text: SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula
segments.rationale: Stable and slightly better than at 0800. This relates to her pneumonia, not the IV site.

question.takeaway: Compare the site with its last assessment. New pain, cool pale skin, swelling, a slowed or alarming pump and lost blood return all point to a problem at the site.
question.strategy: The oxygen saturation is abnormal for a healthy adult, which makes it tempting. It is stable for her pneumonia and has nothing to do with the IV.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Every IV finding changed since the last check.
Pain, cool pale skin, swelling, alarm and no blood return describe one problem.
The other arm and the stable SpO2 need no action.

elimination.verdict: Tight and sore, cool and pale, swelling, occlusion alarm, no blood return.

question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with infiltration or phlebitis.

rows.text: Cool, pale skin around the site
rows.rationale: Room temperature fluid is sitting in the tissue, so the skin feels cool and looks pale.

rows.text: Red streak along the path of the vein
rows.rationale: The vein wall is inflamed, so redness follows the vein.

rows.text: Swelling around the insertion site
rows.rationale: Fluid leaking out of the vein collects in the surrounding tissue.

rows.text: Warmth over the vein
rows.rationale: Inflammation brings more blood flow, which makes the area warm.

rows.text: Palpable cord along the vein
rows.rationale: An inflamed vein can feel firm like a cord under the skin.

rows.text: Slowed flow with no blood return
rows.rationale: The catheter tip is out of the vein, so fluid meets resistance and blood cannot flow back.

question.takeaway: Infiltration is cool, pale and swollen because fluid is in the tissue. Phlebitis is red, warm and tender along the vein because the vein wall is inflamed.
question.strategy: Both conditions cause pain, so pain alone does not tell them apart. Use temperature and color: cool and pale means infiltration, warm and red means phlebitis.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid in the tissue is infiltration. Inflammation of the vein wall is phlebitis.
Cool goes with infiltration. Warm goes with phlebitis.
A streak or cord follows the vein, which is phlebitis.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration, phlebitis, infiltration, phlebitis, phlebitis, infiltration.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence: The client is most likely experiencing [[1]] as evidenced by [[2]].

options.text: infiltration
options.rationale: Fluid is leaking into the tissue around the catheter.

options.text: phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is warm and red along the vein. Her site is cool and pale.

options.text: hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma shows bruising from blood in the tissue. This is clear IV fluid.

options.text: catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: That is systemic, with fever, chills and hypotension. Her temperature is falling and her BP is stable.

options.text: cool, pale skin with swelling and no blood return
options.rationale: These are the deck signs of infiltration.

options.text: a red streak with a palpable cord
options.rationale: These signs describe phlebitis. They are not in her chart.

options.text: a temperature of 37.4 C
options.rationale: Her temperature is improving and reflects her pneumonia.

options.text: thin, fragile skin on both forearms
options.rationale: Fragile skin raises her risk. It is not evidence that the problem is happening now.

question.takeaway: Name the complication from the signs at the site. Cool, pale, swollen and slow means infiltration.
question.strategy: Fragile skin is true and relevant. It explains why this happened, not what is happening. Pick the finding that proves the problem.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match the cluster to a complication
steps.detail: Cool, pale and swollen is infiltration.
No fever or hypotension, so it is not a bloodstream infection.
Fragile skin is a risk factor, not a sign.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration; cool, pale skin with swelling and no blood return.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care for this IV site? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Every milliliter that keeps running goes into the tissue.

options.text: Remove the catheter
options.rationale: The tip is out of the vein. The catheter cannot be saved.

options.text: Elevate the left arm
options.rationale: Elevation helps the extra fluid move out of the tissue.

options.text: Apply a warm or cool compress based on the solution type and facility policy
options.rationale: The deck says the compress for infiltration depends on the solution that leaked.

options.text: Document the site appearance and the infiltration grade
options.rationale: Grading and documenting lets the next nurse see whether it is improving.

options.text: Flush the catheter firmly to clear the occlusion
options.rationale: The problem is not a clot. Flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue.

options.text: Start the new IV in the left hand below the current site
options.rationale: Avoid sites distal to a prior infiltration. Fluid can leak out of the damaged vein above it.

question.takeaway: For infiltration: stop, remove, elevate, compress per solution, document and reassess. Restart the IV in a different site, not below the damaged one.
question.strategy: Flushing sounds like troubleshooting an occlusion alarm. When there is swelling and no blood return, the catheter is out of the vein and flushing makes it worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter.
Elevate the arm and use the correct compress.

steps.action: Reject actions that add fluid or reuse the vein
steps.detail: No forceful flush. No new site below the infiltration.

elimination.verdict: Stop, remove, elevate, compress per solution, document.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Stopping the fluid ends the injury. Everything else follows.

options.text: Elevate the left arm on a pillow
options.rationale: Helpful. It comes after the fluid stops.

options.text: Notify the provider
options.rationale: Not the first step for infiltration of an isotonic fluid. Stop the source first.

options.text: Start a new IV in the right forearm
options.rationale: She needs new access for her antibiotics. That comes after you stop and remove the failed line.

question.takeaway: When an IV site goes bad, stop the infusion first. You cannot treat the tissue while fluid is still flowing into it.
question.strategy: All four options are reasonable at some point. The question asks what comes first.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid is still running into her tissue.
Stopping the infusion ends the harm.
Remove, elevate, compress, then restart elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion.

entries.text: Infusion stopped. Catheter removed intact. Left arm elevated on a pillow with compress applied per policy. New 22 gauge IV placed in right forearm by RN.

Left forearm swelling decreased to about 1 cm. Skin warm with normal color. Client rates left arm pain 1 out of 10. Right forearm IV flushes easily with blood return. No redness at the right site. Left arm off the pillow and hanging at her side; slight new swelling over the left hand.

question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the interventions were effective or not effective.

rows.text: Left forearm swelling decreased to about 1 cm
rows.rationale: Swelling is going down, so the fluid is leaving the tissue.

rows.text: Left forearm skin warm with normal color
rows.rationale: Cool pale skin has resolved.

rows.text: Left arm pain rated 1 out of 10
rows.rationale: Her discomfort has almost gone.

rows.text: Right forearm IV flushes easily with blood return
rows.rationale: The new line is patent and in the vein.

rows.text: Slight new swelling over the left hand with the arm hanging at her side
rows.rationale: The arm is no longer elevated, so fluid is draining down into the hand. Re-elevate the arm and reassess.

question.takeaway: Evaluate by comparing with the original cues. Swelling, color and pain improved. New hand swelling shows the elevation was not maintained.
question.strategy: Most of the note is good news. Read each line separately so one abnormal finding does not get lost in the improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Match each finding to a cue
steps.detail: Swelling, color and pain were the problems at 1000.
Patent with blood return is the goal.
The arm is off the pillow and the hand is swelling.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, effective, not effective.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for Older Adults

questions.stem: A 91-year-old admitted two days ago for a urinary tract infection is oriented in the morning and cannot say where she is by evening. Her daughter says she manages her own finances at home. Which finding most strongly supports delirium?

options.text: Her age of 91, which makes confusion expected
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Confusion is never an expected finding, at any age.

options.text: The acute onset with attention that fluctuates through the day
options.rationale: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and marked by inattention. Waxing and waning within one day is what separates it from the other two.

options.text: The gradual loss of her ability to manage daily activities
options.rationale: Gradual decline over months to years points to dementia. Her daughter describes her managing finances until now.

options.text: Long-standing memory impairment noted on previous admissions
options.rationale: Chronic and stable memory loss describes dementia, and nothing in the stem reports it.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and inattentive. Dementia is progressive and chronic. Depression brings mood change and withdrawal.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe a slow decline and one blames her age. Ask how fast this appeared and whether it holds steady.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented this morning, disoriented by evening.
Both describe dementia.
Age never explains confusion.

elimination.verdict: That leaves acute onset with fluctuating attention.

questions.scenario: A nurse completes an annual assessment on an 84-year-old who lives alone.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age-related change or a red flag requiring further assessment.

rows.text: Takes slightly longer to respond when asked a question
rows.rationale: Slower reaction time is a normal age-related change and does not indicate impairment.

rows.text: Became disoriented to place over the past two days
rows.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag. Think delirium and look for the cause.

rows.text: Reports food tastes blander than it used to
rows.rationale: Decreased taste and smell is expected, and it matters because it can lead to poor intake.

rows.text: Has fallen twice in the past month with no clear explanation
rows.rationale: New unexplained falls are a red flag. A fall is a clinical clue, not an event to record and move past.

rows.text: Needs more light to read than she did five years ago
rows.rationale: Changes in sensory perception are expected, and they raise fall risk, which is assessed separately.

rows.text: Stopped attending her weekly card group and snaps at her daughter
rows.rationale: A new significant change in behavior is a red flag, and withdrawal with irritability may point to depression.

questions.takeaway: Expected: slower reaction time, sensory change, gradual mobility change. Red flags: sudden confusion, sudden functional decline, new unexplained falls, new behavior change.
questions.strategy: The word that sorts them is sudden. Gradual and mild belongs to aging; abrupt and unexplained belongs in an assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two findings appeared over days.
Slower, blander, needs more light.
New withdrawal is never expected.

elimination.verdict: Three expected, three requiring assessment.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is admitted after a fall at home. The nurse reviews what she takes: lisinopril, metformin, furosemide, zolpidem at night, ibuprofen most days for knee pain, a herbal sleep supplement, and a multivitamin. Which concerns should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: She meets the definition of polypharmacy
options.rationale: Five or more medications at once, and the count includes over-the-counter drugs and supplements.

options.text: The zolpidem and the herbal sleep supplement may duplicate each other
options.rationale: Duplicate therapy is a named polypharmacy concern, and two sedating products together raise her fall risk further.

options.text: The over-the-counter items may not be on her provider's list
options.rationale: Over-the-counter drugs and supplements are not regulated like prescriptions and are frequently omitted when patients list what they take.

options.text: A sedative at night in a patient who has fallen needs review
options.rationale: Medications are one of the named fall risk factors, and a hypnotic in an older adult who is already falling is the clearest example.

options.text: Taking a multivitamin indicates she is not eating adequately
options.rationale: A supplement is not evidence of poor intake. Intake is assessed by asking about eating, not by counting bottles.

options.text: The number of prescribers is the definition of polypharmacy
options.rationale: Multiple prescribers is a real risk for duplication, and polypharmacy is defined by the number of medications, not the number of providers.

questions.takeaway: Polypharmacy is five or more medications at once, counting over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Concerns include the number, duplicates, difficult dosing, and unregulated products.
questions.strategy: One distractor redefines polypharmacy by prescribers. One reads a vitamin as evidence about her diet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Seven items, including two over-the-counter.
A bottle is not a dietary assessment.
The count is of medications.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old moved into her daughter's home three weeks ago after living in the same house for 40 years. She is tearful, has stopped her morning walk, and is disoriented to place in the evenings. Her cognition was intact at her last clinic visit. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep her usual daily routines where possible and involve her in decisions
options.rationale: Relocation stress comes from lost surroundings, lost routines, and lost control. Restoring the routine and the control addresses the cause.

options.text: Request a cognitive screening tool to establish the degree of impairment
options.rationale: Measures the deficit without looking for its cause, and the stem tells you her cognition was intact three weeks ago.

options.text: Reassure the daughter that confusion is expected after a move at this age
options.rationale: Normalizes a red flag. Confusion is never expected, and calling it so means nobody looks for what is driving it.

options.text: Arrange a referral for placement in an assisted living facility
options.rationale: A second relocation for a woman whose problem is the first one.

questions.takeaway: Relocation stress produces anxiety, confusion, and withdrawal. Maintain routines, include the patient in decisions, and promote orientation.
questions.strategy: One option measures the problem, one normalizes it, one repeats it. Ask what changed three weeks ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She moved after 40 years in one house.
Measures rather than addresses.
One normalizes a red flag, one moves her again.

elimination.verdict: That leaves keeping her routines and including her in decisions.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old has lost 6 kg over four months. The nurse asks what a typical day's eating looks like. Which response reflects the best nursing approach?

options.text: Teach her the importance of adequate protein and calorie intake
options.rationale: Correct nutritional teaching that assumes the barrier is knowledge. Telling someone to eat more does not work if you do not know why they stopped.

options.text: Explore what is making eating difficult before offering any solution
options.rationale: Poor intake in an older adult has many possible causes: taste changes, dentures, constipation, fatigue, cost, and loneliness among them. The cause decides the intervention.

options.text: Request an order for a high-calorie oral supplement
options.rationale: Treats the weight loss without finding its cause, and a supplement she also cannot chew or afford changes nothing.

options.text: Document the weight loss and recheck at the next visit
options.rationale: Records a significant change and delays acting on it for another interval.

questions.takeaway: Poor intake is a symptom with many causes. Find out why before deciding what to do about it.
questions.strategy: Two options intervene before assessing. Ask what you would need to know to choose between a supplement, a dental referral, and help with groceries.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Taste, teeth, constipation, fatigue, cost, loneliness.

steps.action: Cut the teaching and supplement options
steps.detail: Both act before knowing the cause.
A 6 kg loss is already the finding.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring what is making eating difficult.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: A 77-year-old attends clinic with an adult grandson who manages her finances and answers most questions directed at her. She has lost 9 kg since her last visit four months ago. Her antihypertensive was last filled in March. She flinches when the grandson moves toward her chair. There is bruising on both upper arms. Her clothing is soiled and she has a sacral pressure injury. When asked how she spends her day she looks at the grandson before answering. She wears a hearing aid in the left ear. Blood pressure 158/94, pulse 88.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that raise concern for abuse or neglect.

segments.text: The grandson answers most questions directed at her
segments.rationale: A caregiver controlling communication is a named red flag, and it means she cannot disclose in his presence.

segments.text: Lost 9 kg since her last visit four months ago
segments.rationale: Unmet basic needs over time. Unintentional weight loss of this size is a core indicator of neglect.

segments.text: Antihypertensive last filled in March
segments.rationale: Withheld medication is neglect, and it raises the question of where the money went when someone else manages her finances.

segments.text: Flinches when the grandson moves toward her chair
segments.rationale: Fearfulness of a specific person is a red flag and is not explained by any medical finding here.

segments.text: Bruising on both upper arms
segments.rationale: Bruising in a location consistent with being gripped, unexplained, is an unexplained injury.

segments.text: Clothing is soiled and there is a sacral pressure injury
segments.rationale: Poor hygiene and a pressure injury together point to prolonged unmet care needs.

segments.text: The grandson manages her finances
segments.rationale: Managing money for a relative is common and lawful. It becomes a concern only when her needs go unmet because of it, which the other findings establish.

segments.text: Wears a hearing aid in the left ear
segments.rationale: A device she uses. Sensory change is expected with aging and this is being managed.

segments.text: Blood pressure 158/94, pulse 88
segments.rationale: An elevated pressure explained by the unfilled prescription. It is a consequence of the neglect rather than a separate red flag.

questions.takeaway: Red flags: unexplained injuries, poor hygiene, unmet basic needs, fearfulness, sudden behavior change, financial concerns, inconsistent explanations, and a caregiver controlling communication.
questions.strategy: Two findings describe an arrangement rather than a finding, and one is a consequence of another finding you have already selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Managing money is an arrangement.
Weight, medication, hygiene, skin.
She flinches, and she checks his face before answering.

elimination.verdict: Six findings selected: communication, weight, medication, fear, bruising, hygiene and skin.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a 77-year-old admitted for pneumonia finds her disoriented on day three. She was oriented on admission. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air and her temperature is 38.4 C. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to settle her overnight
options.rationale: Medications are themselves a contributing factor for delirium, and sedating a hypoxic patient makes the oxygenation worse.

options.text: Document the confusion and report it at handover
options.rationale: Communicates the change on a timescale that does not match a saturation of 88%.

options.text: Address the oxygenation and temperature as likely causes of the delirium
options.rationale: Hospital-acquired delirium appears around day two or three, and poor oxygenation, fever, and infection are all named contributing factors. The confusion is a symptom of something treatable.

options.text: Reorient her and place a bed alarm for safety
options.rationale: Reasonable supportive measures, and they manage the confusion without touching what is causing it.

questions.takeaway: Hospital-acquired delirium appears around days two to three. Look for infection, fever, poor oxygenation, medications, and acute illness.
questions.strategy: Three options manage the confusion. Ask what the saturation and the temperature are telling you about why it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation 88%, temperature 38.4 C.
Both manage the symptom.
Worsens both the delirium and the hypoxia.

elimination.verdict: That leaves treating the oxygenation and the fever.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses fall risk for an 81-year-old admitted after tripping at home. She takes seven medications including a nightly sedative, has cataracts, fell once last year, and her daughter says she eats very little and drinks few fluids. Which of her findings increase her risk of falling? Select all that apply.

options.text: Seven medications including a nightly sedative
options.rationale: Five or more is polypharmacy, and a sedative adds drowsiness and slowed reactions on top of the count.

options.text: Cataracts
options.rationale: Vision problems are a named risk factor. She cannot avoid a hazard she cannot see.

options.text: A fall in the past year
options.rationale: A previous fall is the strongest single predictor of another one.

options.text: Poor fluid intake
options.rationale: Dehydration causes dizziness and confusion, both of which precede falls.

options.text: Living with a daughter who checks on her
options.rationale: Support reduces risk rather than raising it.

options.text: Being 81 years old
options.rationale: Age itself is not a risk factor. The age-related changes that come with it are, and the stem names them separately.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk factors: age-related changes, chronic conditions, vision problems, cognitive impairment, previous falls, nutritional deficiency, and dehydration.
questions.strategy: One distractor is protective and one is age itself. Age is not a diagnosis and it is not a risk factor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Medications, cataracts, a previous fall, poor intake.
Support is protective.
Not a risk factor on its own.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 88-year-old for an elective hip replacement. The daughter says her mother has become much more forgetful over the past three years and now needs prompting to dress. Her attention is steady throughout the interview. Which condition does this pattern suggest?

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Progressive, chronic cognitive decline over years, with attention intact. That combination is dementia.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention. Three years is not acute and her attention is steady.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Depression brings mood change, withdrawal, and loss of interest. The stem describes function and memory, not mood.

options.text: Expected age-related memory change
options.rationale: Needing prompting to dress is a functional decline, and functional decline is not an expected change.

questions.takeaway: Dementia is progressive and chronic. Delirium is acute and fluctuating. Depression centers on mood and withdrawal.
questions.strategy: The two things that decide it are the timeline and whether attention holds steady.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three years, gradually worsening.
Steady throughout the interview.
Needing prompting to dress is decline.

elimination.verdict: That leaves dementia.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old tells the nurse she has three glasses of wine most evenings, the same as she has for thirty years, and adds that she now feels it far more than she used to. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Her tolerance has increased over thirty years of regular use
options.rationale: Reverses what she is describing. She reports feeling it more, not less.

options.text: Three glasses is within safe limits for an adult of any age
options.rationale: Limits are lower for older adults precisely because of the metabolic change, and the interaction with her medications matters too.

options.text: Alcohol use typically resolves on its own as people age
options.rationale: Substance use does not disappear with age. It is described as an invisible epidemic because it goes unrecognized.

options.text: Aging slows how the body breaks alcohol down, so the same amount has a stronger and longer effect
options.rationale: Changes in metabolism and excretion mean the same dose behaves differently. The same drug and the same dose does not mean the same response.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows the breakdown of alcohol and drugs, so effects come on faster and last longer at the same dose.
questions.strategy: She has told you the finding herself. Ask what changed, given the amount has not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirty years at the same amount.
How strongly she feels it.

steps.action: Cut tolerance and the safe-limit option
steps.detail: One reverses her report, one ignores age.

elimination.verdict: That leaves slowed metabolism with age.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
An 84-year-old is admitted from home. The nurse uses two frameworks to organize the assessment.

Asking whether she has been sleeping, eating, staying continent, becoming confused, falling, or developing skin breakdown uses the [[1]] framework.

Asking what she wants her recovery to look like addresses the [[2]] element of the 4 Ms.

Reviewing the seven medications she takes at home addresses the [[3]] element.

Her new confusion on day three belongs to the [[4]] element.

options.text: SPICES
options.rationale: Sleep, Problems with eating, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown. The six areas named are the acronym.

options.text: STEADI
options.rationale: STEADI is the fall framework: screen, assess modifiable risk factors, and intervene.

options.text: BMAT
options.rationale: A mobility assessment tool, and it covers movement rather than these six areas.

options.text: the 4 Ms
options.rationale: The 4 Ms are What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility. Four elements, not six.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: The patient's own goals and preferences, and the element that anchors the rest of the plan.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Mentation covers delirium, dementia and depression.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Mobility covers function and safe movement.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: Medication covers safety and review of what she takes.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: Medication safety and review, which at seven items is also a polypharmacy assessment.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: Her goals, not her prescriptions.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Cognition rather than pharmacy, though medications can affect it.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Function and movement.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Mentation covers delirium, dementia and depression, and new confusion on day three points to delirium.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Movement and function, though confusion will affect both.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: Her preferences, which should still be sought even when she is confused.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: A medication may well be causing the confusion, and the element the finding belongs to is mentation.

questions.takeaway: SPICES: Sleep, Problems eating, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown. The 4 Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility.
questions.strategy: Count the elements. Six areas is SPICES, four is the 4 Ms, and the fall-specific one is STEADI.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Six areas, so SPICES.
Goals, drugs, cognition, movement.
A drug may cause the confusion, and the finding is still mentation.

elimination.verdict: SPICES, What Matters, Medication, Mentation.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old who walked independently on admission has needed two people to transfer her since day four. She is medically improving and her infection has resolved. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The decline is expected with hospitalization at her age
options.rationale: Hospital-associated decline is common and frequently does not reverse on its own, which is why it is assessed rather than accepted.

options.text: The functional decline needs investigating, because it is not explained by her improving illness
options.rationale: A decline of this speed signals something treatable. Deconditioning from bed rest, a new medication, or an unrecognized problem all need excluding.

options.text: Function should be reassessed once she is fully recovered from the infection
options.rationale: Sensible-sounding, and it loses the window in which the decline can be reversed.

options.text: The decline reflects her age, since function naturally declines after 90
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Function does not fall from independent to two-person assist in four days because of a birthday.

questions.takeaway: A rapid decline in function is a symptom, not aging. Mobility is independence, and deconditioning starts within days.
questions.strategy: Each distractor offers a reason to wait. Ask what four days of immobility does on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Independent to two-person assist in four days.
Both defer assessment.
Age does not explain the rate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves investigating the decline.

questions.stem: A nurse performs medication reconciliation for an 80-year-old on admission. Which errors is this process designed to prevent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Omissions, where a home medication is not continued
options.rationale: A drug she has taken for years disappearing from the list is one of the three named errors.

options.text: Duplications, where two products do the same thing
options.rationale: Particularly likely when several prescribers are involved and over-the-counter products are in use.

options.text: Dangerous interactions between what she takes and what is newly ordered
options.rationale: Comparing the two lists is exactly what the process exists to do.

options.text: Incorrect administration technique by the nurse
options.rationale: Technique is a medication administration concern. Reconciliation compares lists rather than watching a dose being given.

options.text: Nonadherence with the regimen after discharge
options.rationale: Adherence is affected by many things and reconciliation addresses the accuracy of the list, not whether she takes it.

questions.takeaway: Medication reconciliation compares the current list against newly ordered drugs to prevent omissions, duplications, and dangerous interactions.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe real medication problems that a list comparison cannot catch.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Home list against new orders.
That is administration, not reconciliation.
A separate problem, after discharge.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a 76-year-old admitted with a hip fracture. Which approach best reflects patient-centered care for an older adult?

options.text: Apply the standard hip fracture pathway, which is evidence-based
options.rationale: Evidence-based and identical for every patient, which is the opposite of individualized.

options.text: Ask her daughter what goals would be realistic for a woman of her age
options.rationale: Substitutes the family's judgment for hers, and anchors the plan to her age rather than her function.

options.text: Set a goal of returning to her prior level of function in all activities
options.rationale: A reasonable-sounding goal set without her, and it may be neither what she wants nor achievable.

options.text: Ask what she wants her recovery to look like and build the plan from her answer
options.rationale: What Matters is the first of the 4 Ms, and patient-centered independence means having control over decisions and keeping the highest possible level of function.

questions.takeaway: Patient-centered care for older adults starts with What Matters: her goals and preferences, not her diagnosis or her age.
questions.strategy: Three options produce a plan made about her rather than with her. Ask who supplied the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pathway, the daughter, or the nurse.
Individualization is the point.

steps.action: Cut the daughter and the blanket goal
steps.detail: Both bypass her.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what she wants recovery to look like.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old attends clinic with fatigue, reduced appetite, and new weakness. Her laboratory results are unremarkable and no single diagnosis accounts for the findings. She takes six medications. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Further testing should continue until one diagnosis accounts for the findings
options.rationale: Assumes a unifying diagnosis exists, which is precisely what geriatric syndromes lack.

options.text: The six medications should be reviewed before anything else is pursued
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is a genuine contributor, and starting there assumes the answer before assessing the whole picture.

options.text: The reduced appetite should be corrected first, since it explains the weakness
options.rationale: Plausible and premature. Reduced intake may be a symptom rather than the cause.

options.text: Several factors are likely contributing and a comprehensive assessment is needed
options.rationale: Geriatric syndromes arise from multiple interacting causes across several body systems, which is why no single test explains them.

questions.takeaway: Geriatric syndromes involve multiple factors and several body systems. Assess broadly rather than chasing one explanation.
questions.strategy: Two distractors pick a real contributor and promote it to the cause. Ask whether one factor can account for all of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No single diagnosis, unremarkable labs.
Each names one contributor as the whole.
Assumes a unifying diagnosis.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a comprehensive assessment.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses caring for older adults with her preceptor. Which statement by the student indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Some confusion is expected at her age, so I would document it and continue."
options.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag at any age. Normalizing it means nobody looks for the infection, hypoxia, or medication causing it.

options.text: "I should count her supplements when I review how many medications she takes."
options.rationale: Accurate. Polypharmacy counts over-the-counter products and supplements.

options.text: "A change from her baseline matters more than where that baseline sits."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is why knowing the baseline is the second of her key points.

options.text: "If she falls, I need to find out why rather than just recording that it happened."
options.rationale: Accurate. A fall is a clinical clue.

questions.takeaway: Age is not a diagnosis. Never explain a new finding by how old the patient is.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her key points correctly. The fourth uses age as an explanation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Baseline, falls, supplements. All accurate.
Confusion attributed to her age.
A red flag treated as expected.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement normalizing confusion.

questions.stem: A nurse works with an 82-year-old who wants to remain in her own home. Her daughter is concerned about safety and is pushing for assisted living. The patient is oriented, manages her own medications, and has had no falls. Which action best supports aging in place?

options.text: Support the daughter's request, since she knows her mother's abilities best
options.rationale: Overrides a competent woman's stated wish. Her daughter's concern is real and it is not her decision to make.

options.text: Tell the daughter her mother has the right to decide and end the discussion
options.rationale: Accurate about autonomy and it abandons the daughter with an unaddressed worry, which usually means the pressure continues.

options.text: Assess what specifically concerns the daughter and address those risks in the home
options.rationale: Aging in place means staying independent at home as long as possible. Family concerns usually attach to specific things like transportation and daily activities, and those can be worked on.

options.text: Arrange a cognitive assessment to determine whether she can live alone safely
options.rationale: The stem states she is oriented and manages her own medications. Testing for a deficit nobody has observed treats the daughter's anxiety as a clinical finding.

questions.takeaway: Aging in place means growing older at home and staying independent as long as possible. Family concerns usually center on safety, transportation, and daily activities.
questions.strategy: One option overrides her, one dismisses the daughter, one tests for a problem nobody has found.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented, independent with medications, no falls.
Overrides a competent decision.

steps.action: Cut the dismissal and the testing
steps.detail: One abandons the daughter, one invents a deficit.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assessing the specific concerns and addressing them at home.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old is admitted from home after a fall. She lives alone. Her daughter reports she has seemed 'a bit vague' for a week and has stopped cooking. On admission she is oriented to person only, her temperature is 38.1 C, and she reports burning on urination. She takes five medications including a nightly sedative. Her last documented cognitive assessment, six months ago, was normal.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen and notify the provider of the fever and confusion
options.rationale: Infection is the most common reversible cause of delirium in an older adult, and the burning and fever point straight at it.

options.text: Review the sedative with the provider as a contributing factor
options.rationale: Medications are a named contributor to delirium, and a nightly hypnotic in a confused woman who has fallen is the clearest candidate.

options.text: Reorient her frequently and place familiar objects at the bedside
options.rationale: Supportive and worth doing, and it manages the confusion without touching the cause.

options.text: Request a referral for long-term placement given her decline
options.rationale: Acts on a change that has not yet been investigated, and her cognition was normal six months ago.

options.text: Delirium from a reversible cause
options.rationale: Acute onset over a week, fluctuating, with fever and urinary symptoms. The cause is findable and treatable.

options.text: Early dementia
options.rationale: Dementia is progressive over months to years. Her assessment was normal six months ago and this developed over a week.

options.text: Depression presenting as withdrawal
options.rationale: Stopping cooking could fit depression, and the fever and urinary symptoms do not.

options.text: Expected cognitive change for her age
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and disorientation to place and time is never an expected finding.

options.text: Orientation compared with her baseline
options.rationale: The finding that defined the problem, measured against what she was six months ago.

options.text: Temperature and urinalysis results
options.rationale: Measures whether the suspected cause is resolving, which is what the actions targeted.

options.text: Whether she can name three fall prevention strategies
options.rationale: Measurable, and it tests teaching that nobody identified as the problem, in a woman who is currently confused.

options.text: Her daughter's satisfaction with the admission
options.rationale: Worth knowing and it does not evaluate whether the delirium is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion is delirium until you have looked for a cause. Infection, fever, poor oxygenation, medications and acute illness are the places to look.
questions.strategy: Two actions manage the confusion rather than treat it. Evaluate the cause you targeted, not a teaching outcome nobody identified.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vague for a week, normal six months ago.
Too fast, and age explains nothing.
You treated infection and reviewed a drug.

elimination.verdict: Urine and provider notification, sedative review, for delirium, evaluated by orientation and infection markers.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a 75-year-old's chart before an annual visit. Which piece of information tells the nurse most about her nursing needs?

options.text: That she falls into the baby boomer age band
options.rationale: A demographic grouping, and a healthy 67-year-old and a frail 97-year-old do not have the same needs.

options.text: That her last blood pressure was 138/82
options.rationale: A useful clinical value and it describes one system rather than how she is managing.

options.text: That she stopped driving last year and now relies on a neighbor for groceries
options.rationale: Functional ability, independence and social situation are what shape the plan. This single fact touches nutrition, access, and isolation at once.

options.text: That she is 75 years old
options.rationale: Chronological age gives a number and tells you almost nothing about the person.

questions.takeaway: Chronological age gives a number. Functional ability, health status, cognition, independence, social situation and preferences describe the person.
questions.strategy: One option is a number, one is a demographic band, one is a single system. Ask which one changes what you would plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Function, independence, social situation.

steps.action: Cut age and the age band
steps.detail: Neither describes her.
One system, not her situation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the loss of driving and reliance on a neighbor.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for an 87-year-old on a medical unit is planning priorities for the shift. Which set of concepts should guide her?

options.text: Safety, mobility, nutrition, cognition, skin integrity and function
options.rationale: Hospitalization creates additional risk in these specific areas, and each is something nursing can protect during the admission.

options.text: Diagnosis, prognosis, and the medical treatment plan
options.rationale: Describes the medical management. Nursing priorities concern how she is functioning through it.

options.text: Discharge date, insurance coverage, and placement options
options.rationale: Administrative concerns that matter and do not organize bedside care.

options.text: Family preferences, visiting arrangements and communication
options.rationale: Family involvement matters and it is part of patient-centered care rather than the framework for priorities.

questions.takeaway: In acute care, prioritize safety, mobility, nutrition, cognition, skin integrity and function, all delivered as patient-centered care.
questions.strategy: Three options name things that are genuinely relevant to her admission. Ask which set describes what nursing protects.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Function, skin, cognition, nutrition, mobility.
That is the treatment, not the nursing priorities.
Both matter and neither organizes care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves safety, mobility, nutrition, cognition, skin and function.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old reports headlight glare at night and colors that look faded. It came on over about two years without pain. Which teaching should the nurse include?

options.text: Seek emergency care today
options.rationale: Emergencies such as detachment or angle closure are sudden. This onset is gradual.

options.text: Surgery is considered when vision limits daily activities
options.rationale: Glare, faded color and gradual painless onset fit cataract. Surgery is the only treatment.

options.text: Daily eye drops will restore lost vision
options.rationale: Drops lower pressure in glaucoma. Nothing restores glaucoma vision loss.

options.text: New glasses will fully correct the problem
options.rationale: Patients often blame their glasses at first. A clouded lens is not corrected by new lenses.

questions.takeaway: Cataract is painless and gradual with glare and faded color. Surgery is offered when daily activities are affected.
questions.strategy: Recognize the condition from the cues first. Then pick the teaching that fits it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two years without pain is not an emergency.
Glare and faded color point to the lens.
Surgery is the only cataract treatment.

elimination.verdict: B. Cataract teaching.

questions.stem: A patient with open-angle glaucoma says he stopped his latanoprost because "it wasn't doing anything and my eyes feel fine." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Let me arrange for a different drop that will work better for you."
options.rationale: Accepts a false premise. The drop was working; the disease has no symptoms to relieve.

options.text: "Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms until it is late. The drops protect the vision you still have."
options.rationale: Names the reason adherence failed. In a silent disease, feeling no different is the drug working, and lost vision never returns.

options.text: "You should restart it right away or you could go blind by next month."
options.rationale: Frightening and inaccurate about the timeline. Fear-based teaching tends to reduce adherence rather than improve it.

options.text: "Many people find these drops uncomfortable. Would you like something for that?"
options.rationale: Answers a complaint he did not make. He said the drop was ineffective, not that it bothered him.

questions.takeaway: When a client says a drug was not doing anything, ask what they expected it to do. For a preventive drug in a silent disease, feeling no different is the drug working.
questions.strategy: One option agrees with him, one frightens him, one answers a different complaint. Only one corrects the belief that caused the behavior.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He thinks no symptom means no benefit.

steps.action: Cut the agreement and the scare
steps.detail: Neither changes the belief.
He never mentioned discomfort.

elimination.verdict: Explain the silent disease. That conversation is the intervention.

questions.stem: A patient arrives reporting sudden severe eye pain, nausea, blurred vision and halos. The eye is red and the cornea looks cloudy. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply a cool compress and place the patient in a darkened room
options.rationale: Comfort measures for an emergency. The pressure keeps rising while you do them.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately and prepare for urgent pressure-lowering treatment
options.rationale: Acute angle-closure glaucoma. The optic nerve is being damaged by the hour, and permanent vision loss follows within hours without treatment.

options.text: Instill lubricating eye drops and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Lubricating drops do nothing for a pressure problem, and waiting 30 minutes costs vision.

options.text: Administer an antiemetic and reassess the pain
options.rationale: Treats a symptom of the emergency. The nausea is caused by the intraocular pressure.

questions.takeaway: Sudden, painful, red, with a cloudy cornea and halos is angle-closure glaucoma, and it is an emergency. Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive first-line treatment.
questions.strategy: Three options are comfort measures. The word sudden in an eye question almost always means emergency.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain plus sudden in an eye is an emergency until proven otherwise.

steps.action: Cut the compress and the antiemetic
steps.detail: Symptom relief for a pressure problem.
Lubrication will not touch a pressure problem.

elimination.verdict: Notify now. Vision is lost in hours, not days.

questions.stem: A patient calls the clinic reporting a sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light and a shadow across part of the vision. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Advise lubricating drops and a call back in one week
options.rationale: Treats it as dryness and delays care while the retina keeps detaching.

options.text: Reassure that floaters are common with aging
options.rationale: Floaters alone can be benign. With flashes and a shadow they are not.

options.text: Schedule a routine eye exam within the month
options.rationale: A routine visit is far too late for a detaching retina.

options.text: Arrange to be seen today and avoid jarring the head
options.rationale: Flashes, floaters and a curtain are retinal detachment until proven otherwise, and time to treatment decides how much vision is saved.

questions.takeaway: Flashes, floaters and a curtain equal retinal detachment. It is sudden, painless and still an emergency.
questions.strategy: Three options delay care. Any option that sends a sudden visual change home to wait is wrong.

strategies: Odd man wins
Priority key word

steps.detail: Flashes, floaters and a shadow.
Drops, reassurance and a routine visit all wait.
Same-day care with limited jarring.

elimination.verdict: D. Same-day emergency evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient going home after cataract surgery says, "I'll be back to weeding the garden and lifting my grandson tomorrow." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your vision will be at its best by tomorrow, so that should be fine."
options.rationale: Vision improves gradually over four to six weeks, and the plan itself is unsafe.

options.text: "Those are safe as long as you keep the eye patch on."
options.rationale: A patch does not prevent the pressure rise from bending and lifting.

options.text: "Avoid bending at the waist and lifting over 10 pounds until your surgeon clears you."
options.rationale: Bending and lifting raise intraocular pressure, which threatens the fresh wound and the lens position.

options.text: "You can return to them once the redness clears and you stop your drops."
options.rationale: Drops are finished as prescribed, and redness clearing does not mean pressure is safe.

questions.takeaway: After eye surgery, never raise the intraocular pressure. Bending, straining, lifting, coughing and vomiting are all on the list.
questions.strategy: Match the patient's plans to the mechanism that harms a fresh eye. Only one option names it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.action: Find the risk in his words
steps.detail: Weeding means bending, and lifting a child means strain.
Both raise intraocular pressure.
A patch, a timeline or stopping drops does not change pressure.

elimination.verdict: C. No bending or heavy lifting.

questions.stem: Testing pupils, the nurse finds they are 3 mm and equal. Both constrict to light in either eye. Neither changes as a finger nears the nose. Which finding requires follow-up?

options.text: Pupil size of 3 mm
options.rationale: This is a normal size.

options.text: Pupils equal in size
options.rationale: Equality is normal.

options.text: Both pupils constrict with light in either eye
options.rationale: This shows intact direct and consensual responses.

options.text: No change as the finger approaches
options.rationale: Pupils should constrict and converge on a near target. Accommodation is absent.

questions.takeaway: Accommodation is the letter of PERRLA students drop. A near target should bring constriction with convergence.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal. Test each against what PERRLA expects.

strategies: Odd man wins

steps.detail: 3 mm and equal are normal.
Direct and consensual responses are intact.
No constriction on a near target is abnormal.

elimination.verdict: D. Accommodation is missing.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma is newly prescribed timolol eye drops. Which teaching point is most important?

options.text: "Shake the bottle vigorously before each dose."
options.rationale: Applies to suspensions and is not the safety issue here.

options.text: "Press on the inner corner of your eye for a minute after the drop goes in."
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion blocks the tear duct so the drug stays in the eye rather than draining into the nose and being absorbed systemically. Timolol is a beta blocker and can cause bronchospasm.

options.text: "Store the drops in the refrigerator between doses."
options.rationale: A storage detail rather than a safety one, and it is not universally required.

options.text: "Stop the drops if your vision becomes blurred right after instillation."
options.rationale: Brief blurring after a drop is expected and not a reason to stop a sight-preserving medication.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma drops are systemic drugs. The eye holds one drop and the rest is absorbed through the nasal mucosa, skipping the liver. Beta blockers can cause bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm.
questions.strategy: The patient's asthma is in the stem for a reason. Ask which option protects the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is the only comorbidity given.
Timolol is a beta blocker.

steps.action: Cut the storage and shaking options
steps.detail: Neither touches systemic absorption.
Expected and transient.

elimination.verdict: Punctal occlusion, and the drop belongs on the medication reconciliation.

questions.stem: A construction worker arrives with a metal fragment protruding from the right eye after a grinding injury. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Gently remove the fragment and irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: Never remove a protruding object. Removing it can extrude intraocular contents and blind the eye.

options.text: Stabilize the object, shield both eyes, and arrange urgent ophthalmology evaluation
options.rationale: The object stays where it is, the eye is shielded rather than patched, and both eyes are covered because the uninjured eye tracking causes the injured one to move.

options.text: Apply a pressure patch to the injured eye to control bleeding
options.rationale: Pressure on a penetrated globe forces contents out. Shielding is not patching.

options.text: Send the patient for an MRI to determine the depth of the fragment
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected, because the magnet can move it. X-ray or CT is used instead.

questions.takeaway: Never remove a protruding object, never apply pressure, shield both eyes, and no MRI when metal is suspected. Imaging is X-ray or CT.
questions.strategy: Three options involve doing something to the eye. In penetrating eye trauma, the correct action is almost always to protect and refer.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The object is not the nurse's to remove.
Pressure extrudes contents.
Contraindicated with metal.
Covering only one leaves the injured eye tracking.

elimination.verdict: Stabilize, shield both eyes, refer urgently.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews four clinic patients who have never had an eye exam. Which patient does the nurse refer for glaucoma screening first?

options.text: A 42-year-old African American man
options.rationale: Glaucoma screening starts at 40 for African American clients because the disease starts earlier in this group.

options.text: A 50-year-old Hispanic woman with no family history
options.rationale: Screening for Hispanic and Latino clients starts at 60. She has no other listed risk.

options.text: A 25-year-old who wears contact lenses
options.rationale: Contact lenses raise corneal infection risk. They are not a glaucoma risk factor.

options.text: A 45-year-old taking antihistamines for allergies
options.rationale: Anticholinergic drugs can trigger angle closure in narrow angles. That is not a reason for screening.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma screening age depends on the population. African American clients start at 40. Hispanic and Latino clients start at 60.
questions.strategy: Match each age to its risk threshold. Two options name eye risks that belong to other problems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A cornea risk, not a nerve risk.
An angle closure trigger, not a screening indication.
Hispanic starts at 60, so 50 is early. African American starts at 40, so 42 qualifies.

elimination.verdict: A. He is past his threshold.

questions.scenario: A 71-year-old with diabetes sees rings around streetlights and has stopped driving at night. He says his eyes feel fine, so he filled his prescribed eye drops only once in six months. Intraocular pressures are 26 mm Hg right and 24 mm Hg left, with bilateral peripheral field loss. A1c is 9.1%.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Have him demonstrate instilling a drop, and teach punctal occlusion
options.rationale: Adherence is the problem in front of you, and technique is the part a nurse can fix in the room. Punctal occlusion also reduces systemic absorption.

options.text: Explain that the drops protect remaining vision in a disease with no symptoms
options.rationale: Names the belief that caused him to stop. Without this, better technique on a drug he does not believe in changes nothing.

options.text: Refer him for cataract evaluation for the glare and night driving
options.rationale: Reasonable on the surface and it misses the thing destroying his optic nerve. He may well have a cataract too, and it is not the priority today.

options.text: Document the missed doses and address adherence at the next visit
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. Every month of nonadherence costs visual field that does not come back.

options.text: Uncontrolled open-angle glaucoma with nonadherence to therapy
options.rationale: Halos, raised pressures in both eyes and peripheral field loss in eyes that feel fine. The nonadherence is why it is uncontrolled.

options.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: That is sudden, painful, with a red eye and a cloudy cornea. None of those findings is reported.

options.text: Diabetic retinopathy
options.rationale: A real risk with an A1c of 9.1% and it does not explain a pressure of 26 or the pattern of peripheral loss.

options.text: Age-related macular degeneration
options.rationale: Macular disease takes central vision first. His loss is peripheral.

options.text: Intraocular pressure at follow-up
options.rationale: The direct measure of whether therapy is working. Target is at or below about 21 mm Hg.

options.text: Visual field testing results over time
options.rationale: Field loss is what the treatment exists to stop. Stability is success; further loss means the plan is failing.

options.text: Snellen visual acuity in each eye
options.rationale: Central acuity stays normal in open-angle glaucoma until very late, so it will look reassuring while the disease progresses.

options.text: Absence of eye pain at follow-up
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is painless throughout. Comfort tells you nothing, and believing it is exactly why he stopped the drops.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma is silent, takes peripheral vision first, and lost vision never returns. Evaluate it with pressure and visual fields, never with acuity or comfort.
questions.strategy: Two of the parameters will look normal while the disease progresses. Ask which measurement would actually change if the treatment failed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Peripheral loss with raised pressure names the condition.
One filled prescription in six months.
Both stay normal until the disease is advanced.

elimination.verdict: Fix the adherence and the belief behind it, and follow pressure and fields.

caseStudies.title: Cataract surgery and discharge teaching
caseStudies.intro: A 74 year old man comes to the outpatient surgery center for phacoemulsification with a lens implant in his right eye.

entries.text: Blurred vision in the right eye getting slowly worse over 2 years. No pain.
Trouble driving at night; colors look faded. Has changed glasses twice without improvement.
Takes prednisone daily for COPD. Hypertension controlled with lisinopril.
Right eye: absent red reflex; pupil appears bluish white. Visual acuity 20/100 right, 20/30 left.
IOP 16 mmHg both eyes. PERRLA.
T 36.8 C; HR 72; RR 16; BP 134/80; SpO2 95% on room air
Lives with wife. Helps care for his 2 year old grandson. Enjoys woodworking.
Surgery complete. Eye shield in place over right eye. Denies pain. Plan: discharge home with wife this afternoon.

question.nursesNote: Blurred vision in the right eye getting slowly worse over 2 years. No pain. Trouble driving at night. Colors look faded. Changed glasses twice without improvement. Takes prednisone daily. Hypertension controlled with lisinopril. Right eye absent red reflex. IOP 16 mmHg.
question.stem: Which findings are consistent with a cataract or a known cause of cataract? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Blurred vision in the right eye getting slowly worse over 2 years
segments.rationale: Gradual blurring is the classic presentation.

segments.text: No pain
segments.rationale: Cataracts are painless. Sudden pain points to something else.

segments.text: Trouble driving at night
segments.rationale: Glare and scatter from the cloudy lens.

segments.text: Colors look faded
segments.rationale: The yellowed lens decreases color perception.

segments.text: Changed glasses twice without improvement
segments.rationale: Patients often blame their glasses first.

segments.text: Takes prednisone daily
segments.rationale: Corticosteroids are a named toxin cause of cataract.

segments.text: Hypertension controlled with lisinopril
segments.rationale: Hypertension is a general eye health risk factor. It is not a named cause or a sign of cataract.

segments.text: Right eye absent red reflex
segments.rationale: Sign of a mature cataract.

segments.text: IOP 16 mmHg
segments.rationale: Normal. A cataract does not raise IOP.

question.takeaway: Cataract: painless, gradual, blurred, faded colors, poor night vision, absent red reflex. Steroids are a cause worth spotting.
question.strategy: The medication list hides a cause. Prednisone is easy to skip past.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Painless and gradual.
Steroids cause cataracts.
IOP 16 and controlled BP are not cataract findings.

elimination.verdict: Everything except the hypertension and the IOP.

question.scenario: The nurse compares this client's findings with other eye conditions seen in the clinic.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate the condition it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Faded colors with gradual painless blurring
rows.rationale: The lens is clouding.

rows.text: Absent red reflex with a bluish white pupil
rows.rationale: The opaque lens blocks the reflex.

rows.text: Slow loss of peripheral vision with halos around lights
rows.rationale: Nerve damage moves from peripheral to central.

rows.text: IOP 28 mmHg
rows.rationale: Deck range for OAG is 22 to 32.

rows.text: Sudden flashes of light and new floaters
rows.rationale: Photopsia and floaters are classic early signs.

rows.text: Feels like a curtain is coming down over part of the vision
rows.rationale: Sudden and painless. An emergency.

question.takeaway: Cataract clouds, glaucoma narrows from the outside in, a detachment arrives suddenly like a curtain.
question.strategy: Halos appear with glaucoma and night glare with cataract. Tie it to the rest of the row: peripheral loss means glaucoma.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden means detachment.
Peripheral first means glaucoma.
Cloudy and faded means cataract.

elimination.verdict: Cataract, cataract, glaucoma, glaucoma, detachment, detachment.

question.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence: After surgery, the complication the nurse's discharge teaching most needs to prevent is [[1]]. For this client, the activity that places him at greatest risk is [[2]].

options.text: increased intraocular pressure
options.rationale: Pressure strains the fresh incision. The deck lists activities that raise IOP.

options.text: presbyopia
options.rationale: An age related change, not a surgical complication.

options.text: dry eyes
options.rationale: A LASIK complication on the deck.

options.text: faded color perception
options.rationale: A cataract symptom that surgery corrects, not a postop complication.

options.text: lifting his 2 year old grandson
options.rationale: A toddler weighs well over 10 lb. Lifting him means bending too.

options.text: watching television
options.rationale: Safe after surgery.

options.text: walking with his wife
options.rationale: Safe and good for him.

options.text: sleeping on his left side
options.rationale: Keeps pressure off the operative eye.

question.takeaway: After cataract surgery, protect the eye from pressure. Bending, lifting over 10 lb and straining all raise IOP.
question.strategy: The chart told you he cares for a toddler. Personal details in the notes are often there to be used.

strategies: Priority key word
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: IOP rises with strain.

steps.action: Search the chart for his life
steps.detail: Grandson and woodworking.
Lifting a toddler.

elimination.verdict: Increased IOP; lifting his grandson.
