question.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in the discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear dark glasses when outdoors or in bright light
options.rationale: Protects the eye and reduces light sensitivity.

options.text: Avoid lifting anything heavier than 10 lb
options.rationale: Straight from the deck postop list.

options.text: Bend at the knees rather than the waist
options.rationale: Bending at the waist raises IOP.

options.text: Avoid straining during a bowel movement
options.rationale: Straining raises IOP.

options.text: Report sudden eye pain or sudden loss of vision right away
options.rationale: Warning signs of a complication.

options.text: Expect your best vision by the next morning
options.rationale: Best vision comes at 4 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Return to woodworking in the shop tomorrow
options.rationale: Dust, flying debris and bending put the eye at risk.

options.text: Rub the eye gently if it itches
options.rationale: Rubbing puts pressure on the eye and risks injury.

question.takeaway: Protect from light, protect from pressure, report sudden change, expect 4 to 6 weeks.
question.strategy: Timeline options are a classic trap. Know the number: 4 to 6 weeks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Lifting, bending, straining.
Dark glasses, sudden pain or vision loss.

steps.action: Cut the wrong timeline and the risky activity
steps.detail: Next morning is too soon.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Client calls the surgery center. Reports sudden severe pain in the right eye with nausea after lifting his grandson into a car seat. States vision in that eye is suddenly worse.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Instruct the client to come in to be seen by the surgeon now
options.rationale: Sudden pain with nausea and a sudden vision change must be reported immediately. The surgeon assesses him today.

options.text: Advise him to take acetaminophen and rest with his eyes closed
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and delays care for a possible complication.

options.text: Tell him to keep his follow up appointment next week
options.rationale: Waiting risks permanent vision loss.

options.text: Tell him to apply a warm compress to the eye
options.rationale: It does not treat this problem. It also delays care.

question.takeaway: Sudden pain, nausea or vision change after eye surgery is reported right away. No home remedies.
question.strategy: Rest and acetaminophen sound reasonable for pain. The word sudden is what makes this urgent.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Sudden pain with nausea and vision change.
Rest, compress and next week all delay care.
The surgeon needs to see him now.

elimination.verdict: Come in to be seen by the surgeon now.

entries.text: Follow up visit. Complication treated on day 1. Right eye visual acuity 20/30. No pain. Reading the newspaper again. Wearing sunglasses outdoors.
Wife reports he has been using his table saw without safety glasses.

question.scenario: The nurse reviews the client's status at the 5 week follow up.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the outcome is met or not met.

rows.text: Right eye visual acuity 20/30
rows.rationale: Improved from 20/100. Expected at 4 to 6 weeks.

rows.text: No eye pain
rows.rationale: No sign of a new complication.

rows.text: Reading the newspaper again
rows.rationale: ADLs restored, which was the reason for surgery.

rows.text: Wearing sunglasses outdoors
rows.rationale: Following the teaching.

rows.text: Using his table saw without safety glasses
rows.rationale: Flying debris threatens the healing eye. The deck calls for eye protection around occupational hazards. Teach again.

question.takeaway: Vision is back. He is still running power tools without eye protection. One unmet behavior means more teaching.
question.strategy: The good visual acuity makes the whole picture feel resolved. Read to the last line of the note.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: 20/30 and reading again.
Sunglasses yes, safety glasses no.
Teach eye protection for woodworking again.

elimination.verdict: Met, met, met, met, not met.

questions.stem: A patient's Weber test is louder in the left ear. On the left, bone conduction lasts longer than air conduction. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Inspect the left ear canal for cerumen
options.rationale: Both tests point to a conductive loss on the left. Cerumen is the most common correctable cause.

options.text: Review the medication list for ototoxic drugs
options.rationale: Ototoxic drugs cause sensorineural loss. The tests show a conductive block.

options.text: Tell the patient hearing is normal
options.rationale: Normal is equal on Weber with air outlasting bone. Neither is present.

options.text: Explain that a cochlear implant may be needed
options.rationale: Implants treat sensorineural loss. Conductive loss is often correctable.

questions.takeaway: Weber lateralizes toward a conductive loss. Bone beating air confirms a block, so look for the block.
questions.strategy: Interpret both tests first. The action follows the type of loss.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Louder on the left fits conductive left.
Bone beats air on the left, which is a block.
A conductive block starts with the canal.

elimination.verdict: A. Look for the block.

questions.stem: A patient on day three of gentamicin and furosemide reports new ringing in both ears. The creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Document the tinnitus and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. By the time hearing loss is measurable, aminoglycoside damage is often permanent.

options.text: Notify the prescriber of the tinnitus together with the rising creatinine
options.rationale: Both drugs are ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Tinnitus is the early warning of ototoxicity, and the rising creatinine is the same injury in a second organ.

options.text: Reassure the patient that ringing is a common and harmless side effect
options.rationale: It is common and it is not harmless. Reassurance here delays the only action that can prevent permanent loss.

options.text: Hold the next dose of gentamicin and continue the furosemide
options.rationale: The recognition is right and holding a drug is a prescriber decision. It also leaves the second ototoxic drug running.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus is the early warning of ototoxicity, not the injury. An aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic is worse than either alone, and the ear and the kidney go down together.
questions.strategy: One option waits, one reassures and one exceeds scope. Only one reports the two findings as a single problem.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ear and kidney, same two drugs.
Both delay.
A prescriber decision, and it misses the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Notify now, with the creatinine, and ask about trough levels.

questions.stem: A child taking amoxicillin for acute otitis media has been crying with ear pain for two days. This morning the parent reports the pain stopped suddenly and there is yellow drainage on the pillow. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The antibiotic has taken effect and the infection is resolving
options.rationale: The emotionally compelling answer, and the family will have already reached it. Nothing about the infection was treated by what happened.

options.text: The tympanic membrane has perforated and the finding must be reported
options.rationale: Pressure built until the drum gave way. The pain stops because the pressure is released, and the drainage is the contents of the middle ear.

options.text: The child has developed external otitis in addition to the middle ear infection
options.rationale: External otitis produces pain with movement of the pinna, not sudden relief with purulent drainage from behind the drum.

options.text: The drainage is normal cerumen loosened by the fever
options.rationale: Cerumen is waxy and brown, and a fever does not liquefy it into purulent drainage.

questions.takeaway: Otitis media progresses retracted, red, bulging, perforated, and the pain stops when it ruptures. Sudden relief with drainage is perforation, not recovery.
questions.strategy: The relief is real and the family will present it as good news. Ask what changed physically.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It built for two days and then stopped abruptly.
A rupture.
Antibiotics do not produce sudden relief with new purulent drainage.

elimination.verdict: Perforation. Document the drainage, notify, and the antibiotic course still finishes.

questions.stem: A patient with impacted cerumen and a suspected tympanic membrane perforation asks the nurse to flush the wax out. What is the nurse's response?

options.text: Irrigate gently with body-temperature water to avoid dizziness
options.rationale: Temperature control is a real technique point and it does not make irrigation safe here.

options.text: Explain that irrigation is not done when a perforation is suspected, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Irrigating past a perforated drum drives contaminated fluid into the middle ear and spreads the infection.

options.text: Instill a ceruminolytic and then irrigate after 15 minutes of softening
options.rationale: The softening step is correct in general, and it does not remove the contraindication.

options.text: Use a cotton-tipped applicator to remove the visible wax first
options.rationale: Swabs push wax deeper and risk injuring an already compromised drum.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate with a suspected perforation or active otitis media, never with vegetable matter, and never a live insect. Ceruminolytic first, then removal by the provider.
questions.strategy: Three options are safer versions of the same forbidden action. A contraindication is not cancelled by good technique.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Suspected perforation.
Warm water, softening first and swabs are still going in.
Doing an unsafe thing more carefully is the recurring distractor.

elimination.verdict: Do not irrigate. Notify.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an 80-year-old with presbycusis. Which communication technique by the nurse requires correction?

options.text: Facing the patient directly at eye level with the light on the nurse's own face
options.rationale: Appropriate. A large part of what a hearing-impaired person understands is read from lips and expression. Standing in front of a window makes your face a silhouette.

options.text: Lowering the pitch of the voice while speaking at a moderate pace
options.rationale: Appropriate. Presbycusis takes the high frequencies first. Lowering pitch moves your voice into the range still intact.

options.text: Raising the voice to a near shout so the words carry
options.rationale: Needs correction. Shouting raises pitch into exactly the range that has been lost. It also distorts the words.

options.text: Rephrasing a sentence that was not understood rather than repeating it
options.rationale: Appropriate. Different words carry different frequencies. Repeating the same words louder rarely works.

questions.takeaway: Face them, lower your pitch, slow down, cut the background noise, rephrase and verify with teach-back. Never shout.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong technique. Shouting is the reflex everyone has and the thing that makes it worse.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the one technique that fails.
High frequencies are gone.

steps.action: Find the one that raises pitch
steps.detail: Shouting raises pitch and distorts. The rest work with a high-frequency loss.

elimination.verdict: C. Shouting pushes the voice into the range that is lost.

questions.stem: The day after a stapedectomy, a patient preparing for discharge says he plans to fly to a family wedding this weekend. Which instruction does the nurse emphasize?

options.text: "Your hearing should be back to normal by the time you get home."
options.rationale: Hearing improves over about four to six weeks. Promising an immediate result makes a normal recovery look like a failure.

options.text: "Ask for help when you get up, and avoid straining, nose-blowing and air travel."
options.rationale: Air travel, straining and nose-blowing raise middle ear pressure against a fresh prosthesis, and vertigo makes falls likely right after surgery.

options.text: "Irrigate the ear canal daily to prevent a wax buildup."
options.rationale: Nothing goes into a postoperative ear canal, and irrigation after middle ear surgery is contraindicated.

options.text: "A drooping mouth on the operative side is expected for a few days."
options.rationale: Facial asymmetry means facial nerve injury, because CN VII runs right past the surgical field. That is reported, never normalized.

questions.takeaway: After a stapedectomy: assist ambulation because vertigo risk is high, avoid anything that raises middle ear pressure, watch CN VII, and expect hearing to improve over four to six weeks.
questions.strategy: One option normalizes a complication, one promises a timeline, one puts fluid in a fresh surgical field. The correct one is the only one about safety.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is dangerous for him
steps.detail: Flying raises middle ear pressure, and vertigo risks a fall.
That is CN VII injury and gets reported.
Never in a postoperative canal.
Four to six weeks, not immediately.

elimination.verdict: Assist ambulation and avoid pressure-raising activities.

questions.stem: A patient with Meniere disease is admitted during an acute attack with severe vertigo, vomiting and nystagmus. Which nursing action takes priority?

options.text: Encourage oral fluids to replace losses from vomiting
options.rationale: Fluid is not the intervention here, and sodium restriction is the dietary principle in this disease.

options.text: Keep the side rails up, the call light in reach, and instruct the patient to lie still
options.rationale: The priority is preventing injury. Movement worsens the vertigo, and a fall during an attack is the realistic harm.

options.text: Ambulate the patient in the hall to prevent deconditioning
options.rationale: Movement during an acute attack is what causes the injury. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, not during one.

options.text: Place the patient in a brightly lit room for orientation
options.rationale: Light and visual stimulation worsen vertigo. A darkened quiet room is what helps.

questions.takeaway: Meniere is a safety diagnosis. The classic triad is vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss, and the fall is the emergency, not the vital sign changes.
questions.strategy: Nothing here threatens the airway, so the ABCs do not decide it. Safety and risk reduction does.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safety, not ABCs.
Both make vertigo worse.
Sodium restriction is the dietary rule.

elimination.verdict: Injury prevention: rails, call light, lie still, darkened room.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with Meniere disease is taught what to change at home. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will follow a low-sodium diet."
options.rationale: Correct. Sodium drives fluid retention. The disease is excess endolymph. Sodium restriction is the first lifestyle intervention.

options.text: "I will not drive or climb ladders when an attack could occur."
options.rationale: Correct. Tumarkin drop attacks come without warning, so the environment has to be safe in advance rather than relying on the patient to notice symptoms.

options.text: "I will drink more fluids to dilute the fluid in my inner ear."
options.rationale: The problem is too much fluid, not fluid that is too concentrated. Adding volume works against the treatment.

options.text: "My diuretic will reduce the amount of fluid in my inner ear."
options.rationale: Correct. Diuretics lower endolymph volume, which is the mechanism of the disease.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium, avoid triggers, fall precautions, diuretics. Surgery is last resort and labyrinthectomy costs the hearing on that side.
questions.strategy: One statement sounds like sensible hydration advice. Ask whether more fluid helps a disease of too much fluid.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Need for further teaching means you want the wrong statement.
Excess endolymph distending the labyrinth.

steps.action: Keep everything that removes fluid or prevents falls
steps.detail: Low sodium, diuretic, safety.
More fluid adds volume to a disease of too much fluid.

elimination.verdict: C, increasing fluids.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has sensorineural hearing loss. His properly fitted hearing aid makes speech louder but not clearer. Which option is most appropriate for the nurse to discuss with him?

options.text: A more powerful hearing aid
options.rationale: A stronger aid still only amplifies. Louder sound has not helped a cochlea that cannot convert it.

options.text: A cochlear implant
options.rationale: An implant bypasses the damaged cochlea to stimulate the nerve directly. It is the device for sensorineural loss.

options.text: A personal sound amplification product
options.rationale: This is another amplifier. It adds volume without fixing conversion.

options.text: A tympanoplasty
options.rationale: Tympanoplasty repairs the eardrum or ossicles for conductive loss. His loss is sensorineural.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aids amplify and help conductive loss more. Cochlear implants bypass the damaged cochlea in sensorineural loss.
questions.strategy: Two options only add volume. One repairs the wrong part of the ear. Only one bypasses the cochlea.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensorineural, so the cochlea or nerve is damaged.
A stronger aid and a PSAP only add volume.
Tympanoplasty fixes the middle ear.

elimination.verdict: B. Amplify versus bypass is the whole question.

questions.nursesNote: 0830: Patient is 74, admitted yesterday with pyelonephritis, receiving IV gentamicin and furosemide. Reports new bilateral ringing in the ears that began overnight. Asks the nurse to repeat questions twice and turns the left ear toward the speaker. No prior history of hearing difficulty and wears no hearing aids. Nursing assistant reports the patient was unsteady walking to the bathroom this morning. Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, up from 0.9 on admission. Temperature 37.2 C. Blood pressure 124/72. Reports flank pain improved from 7 to 3 out of 10.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate a developing drug toxicity.

segments.text: Receiving IV gentamicin and furosemide
segments.rationale: An aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic. Both are ototoxic and both are nephrotoxic, and together they are worse than either alone.

segments.text: New bilateral ringing in the ears that began overnight
segments.rationale: Tinnitus is the earliest sign of ototoxicity and precedes measurable hearing loss.

segments.text: Asks the nurse to repeat questions twice and turns the left ear toward the speaker
segments.rationale: Behavioral cues of hearing loss, and they are new. Behavior is assessment data.

segments.text: Unsteady walking to the bathroom this morning
segments.rationale: CN VIII carries hearing and balance together, so vestibular symptoms belong in the same picture rather than being filed as deconditioning.

segments.text: Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, up from 0.9 on admission
segments.rationale: The same drugs damaging the same two organs. A rising creatinine in this patient is also an ear warning.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2 C
segments.rationale: Normal, and evidence the infection is responding.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/72
segments.rationale: Normal and unrelated.

segments.text: Flank pain improved from 7 to 3 out of 10
segments.rationale: The pyelonephritis is improving. A reassuring finding that has nothing to do with the toxicity.

questions.takeaway: When a new symptom appears in a patient on a known toxic drug, the drug is your first hypothesis, not your last. Aging, deconditioning and anxiety are the three explanations that get older adults hurt.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or improving and are there to reward you for reading the whole note. Everything else converges on two drugs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gentamicin and furosemide.
Ringing, repeating, unsteadiness, and a creatinine that nearly doubled.
Temperature, blood pressure and improving flank pain.

elimination.verdict: Five findings, all pointing at ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity from the same two drugs. The negative hearing history is context that makes the change new, not a manifestation you highlight.

caseStudies.title: Hearing loss and ototoxic drugs
caseStudies.intro: A 71 year old retired carpenter is on day 3 of admission for pneumonia. He is receiving IV gentamicin and oral furosemide.

entries.text: Worked 40 years in construction with power tools; rarely wore hearing protection.
Wife says he has turned the TV up for years. Does not own a hearing aid.
Type 2 diabetes; heart failure.
Otoscope: right canal occluded with dry cerumen. Left canal clear; tympanic membrane intact.
Tilts head toward speaker; says "What?" often. Answered a question about pain by talking about breakfast.
New ringing in both ears since yesterday. States his hearing has gotten worse over the last 2 days.
Reports fullness in the right ear. Lungs with crackles in the right base, improving.
T 37.2 C; HR 84; RR 18; BP 128/74; SpO2 95% on room air
Glucose 142 mg/dL (70 to 110)

question.nursesNote: Tilts head toward speaker; says what often. Answered a pain question by talking about breakfast. New ringing in both ears since yesterday. Hearing worse over the last 2 days. Fullness in the right ear. Crackles in the right base, improving. BP 128/74.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up related to the client's hearing? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Tilts head toward speaker; says what often
segments.rationale: Behavioral cues of hearing loss.

segments.text: Answered a pain question by talking about breakfast
segments.rationale: A mismatched response. He cannot report pain accurately if he cannot hear the question.

segments.text: New ringing in both ears since yesterday
segments.rationale: New tinnitus while on an aminoglycoside.

segments.text: Hearing worse over the last 2 days
segments.rationale: A sudden change is never assumed to be age related.

segments.text: Fullness in the right ear
segments.rationale: Matches the cerumen found in the right canal.

segments.text: Crackles in the right base, improving
segments.rationale: Pneumonia finding that is getting better. Not a hearing cue.
Normal.

question.takeaway: Watch for the behavioral cues of hearing loss. New tinnitus on an ototoxic drug is never ignored.
question.strategy: The stem says related to hearing. The crackles are abnormal but belong to the pneumonia.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: Head tilt, what, mismatched answers.
Tinnitus and worse hearing over 2 days.
Gentamicin and furosemide are both ototoxic.

elimination.verdict: Everything except the crackles and the BP.

question.scenario: The nurse identifies which type of hearing loss each factor causes.
question.stem: For each factor, indicate the type of hearing loss it causes.

rows.text: Cerumen impaction in the right canal
rows.rationale: A blockage of sound transmission. Often correctable.

rows.text: 40 years of power tool noise
rows.rationale: Noise damages the inner ear.

rows.text: IV gentamicin
rows.rationale: Aminoglycosides are ototoxic to the inner ear and CN VIII.

rows.text: Furosemide
rows.rationale: Diuretics are on the ototoxic list.

rows.text: Presbycusis
rows.rationale: Age related degeneration of the cochlear nerve.

rows.text: Fluid behind the eardrum from otitis media
rows.rationale: Fluid blocks the ossicles from vibrating.

question.takeaway: Conductive is a blockage on the way in and is often fixable. Sensorineural is damage to the inner ear or nerve and is often permanent.
question.strategy: He likely has both types. That combination is called mixed hearing loss.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Canal or middle ear means conductive.
Noise, drugs, aging mean sensorineural.
Both types means mixed.

elimination.verdict: Conductive, sensorineural, sensorineural, sensorineural, sensorineural, conductive.

question.stem: Which problem should the nurse report to the provider first?

options.text: New tinnitus and worsening hearing while receiving gentamicin
options.rationale: Possible ototoxicity. Sensorineural damage is often permanent. Stopping the drug early can prevent more loss.

options.text: Cerumen blocking the right ear canal
options.rationale: Needs treatment. It is correctable and not getting worse by the hour.

options.text: Years of turning the TV up loud
options.rationale: Long standing and chronic.

options.text: No hearing aid at home
options.rationale: Worth a referral at discharge. Not urgent.

question.takeaway: Report the hearing change you can still stop. Ototoxic damage keeps building while the drug runs.
question.strategy: Cerumen is the finding you can see and fix. The priority is the one that is new and permanent.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: TV and no hearing aid are old news.
Cerumen is correctable. Nerve damage is not.
He is still receiving the gentamicin.

elimination.verdict: New tinnitus and hearing loss on gentamicin.

question.stem: Which strategies should the nurse use when communicating with this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Face the client directly in a well lit area
options.rationale: He can use lip movements and facial cues.

options.text: Speak clearly and slowly in a lower pitch
options.rationale: High frequencies are lost first. A lower pitch is easier to hear.

options.text: Speak toward his left ear
options.rationale: His right canal is blocked. Use the better ear.

options.text: Write down key information such as medication teaching
options.rationale: Written information backs up what he may have missed.

options.text: Ask him to repeat back what he heard
options.rationale: Confirms he actually understood rather than nodded along.

options.text: Shout so he can hear clearly
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and raises the pitch.

options.text: Stand in front of the window while talking
options.rationale: Light behind you hides your face.

options.text: Direct all questions to his wife
options.rationale: He is the client. Effective communication with him is a legal and ethical duty.

question.takeaway: Face him, good light, slow, lower pitch, better ear, write it down, check understanding. Never shout.
question.strategy: Talking to the wife feels efficient. It removes the client from his own care.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Face him in good light.
Slow and lower, not louder.

steps.action: Use the good ear and a backup
steps.detail: Left ear, written notes, teach back.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Provider stopped gentamicin and started a different antibiotic. Prescribed carbamide peroxide drops for the right ear followed by irrigation.
Client reports right ear pain. Yellow drainage noted on the pillow. T 37.9 C.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Withhold the ear irrigation and notify the provider
options.rationale: Pain with purulent drainage suggests otitis media or a perforated eardrum. Irrigation could spread the infection.

options.text: Irrigate the ear with warm water to flush out the drainage
options.rationale: Never irrigate when a perforation or otitis media is suspected.

options.text: Place a cotton swab deep in the canal to absorb the drainage
options.rationale: Swabs cause canal trauma and push material inward.

options.text: Proceed with the drops and irrigation as prescribed
options.rationale: The new findings change the plan. The prescription was written before them.

question.takeaway: No irrigation if perforation or otitis media is suspected. New findings mean you hold and report.
question.strategy: Following the order looks correct. The trap is ignoring a new finding that makes the order unsafe.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Priority key word

steps.detail: Pain, drainage and a rising temperature.
Irrigation spreads infection through a perforation.
Let the provider reassess.

elimination.verdict: Withhold the irrigation and notify the provider.

entries.text: Discharge teaching completed with client and wife. Audiology referral scheduled. Client states his teaching back in his own words.

question.scenario: The nurse evaluates the client's understanding of discharge teaching.
question.stem: For each client statement, indicate whether the teaching was effective or needs further teaching.

rows.text: "I will wear earplugs when I use my power tools."
rows.rationale: Noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss.

rows.text: "I will tell the pharmacist about my hearing before I start a new drug."
rows.rationale: Helps avoid another ototoxic drug.

rows.text: "I will ask my wife to face me when she talks."
rows.rationale: Uses visual cues.

rows.text: "I will clean my ears with cotton swabs every morning."
rows.rationale: Swabs push cerumen deeper and injure the canal.

rows.text: "I can take ibuprofen as often as I want for the ringing."
rows.rationale: NSAIDs are ototoxic and can worsen tinnitus.

rows.text: "A hearing aid will make my hearing just like it used to be."
rows.rationale: Hearing aids help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss. They do not restore normal hearing.

question.takeaway: Protect the ears from noise, drugs and swabs. Hearing aids help, but they do not restore normal hearing.
question.strategy: Ibuprofen sounds harmless for comfort. NSAIDs are on the ototoxic list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Earplugs, pharmacist, facing him.
Swabs and unlimited NSAIDs.
Just like it used to be is a false promise.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, needs further teaching, needs further teaching, needs further teaching.

questions.stem: During the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool, a patient passes sit and shake and stretch and point but cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Stop testing and plan transfers at a moderate assist level
options.rationale: Failing the stand test makes this Level 3, moderate assist. The level chooses the handling equipment, so testing stops here.

options.text: Ask the patient to march in place at the bedside
options.rationale: Marching in place is the walk test. A test is never attempted after the patient fails the one before it.

options.text: Walk the patient to the chair with a gait belt
options.rationale: Walking fits Level 4 only. This patient could not even rise from the bed.

options.text: Plan total assist care with no attempts to sit up
options.rationale: Total assist is Level 1. This patient has seated balance with some leg strength, so Level 1 understates the ability.

questions.takeaway: The first failed test names the level. The level then decides the equipment used for every transfer.
questions.strategy: Find the first test the patient failed. Pick the action that matches that level without skipping ahead or falling back.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: Cannot lift the buttocks means the stand test failed.
Failing the stand test is Level 3, moderate assist.
B and C belong to Level 4. D belongs to Level 1.

elimination.verdict: A. Testing stops and transfers are planned at Level 3.

questions.stem: An older adult completes BMAT Level 1 and Level 2 successfully. Before the nurse asks him to stand, which finding requires follow up?

options.text: He uses a walker at home
options.rationale: Assistive devices may be used during the stand test. This is useful to know, not a reason to stop.

options.text: He cannot state where he is and picks at the air
options.rationale: The stand test calls for checking cognition and delirium first. A confused patient with working legs may stand and fall.

options.text: His grip is firm in both hands
options.rationale: Grip was checked in Level 1. It is a normal finding.

options.text: He reached across midline without losing balance
options.rationale: Reaching across midline showed seated balance in Level 1. It is a normal finding.

questions.takeaway: Strength and judgment fail separately. Check cognition before Level 3 because a patient whose legs work but whose thinking does not will stand and fall.

questions.stem: A patient has left-sided weakness after a stroke. The patient can raise the left arm about halfway toward shoulder height and then cannot lift it any further. Which exercise does the nurse use to maintain shoulder mobility?

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the arm through the whole arc
options.rationale: Passive range of motion means someone else moves the joint while the patient's muscle does nothing. Taking over the whole arc wastes the muscle activity the patient still has, and passive work maintains flexibility without building strength.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the patient raising the arm through the full arc unaided
options.rationale: Active range of motion means the patient performs the entire movement alone. The joint would never reach full range, and stiffness would develop in the part that is never used.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the patient raising the arm as far as possible and the nurse completing the movement
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion means the patient moves the joint as far as they can and the nurse supplies the remainder. The muscle works through the portion the patient controls, which preserves strength, and the joint still reaches full range, which preserves flexibility.

options.text: Isometric exercise, with the patient tightening the shoulder muscles without moving the joint
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. Isometric work builds static strength and joint stability and does nothing for range.

questions.takeaway: Whenever a patient can contribute any part of a movement, they do that part. Active-assistive is the choice that keeps muscle working and still carries the joint through full range.

questions.stem: A patient has a long arm cast after a forearm fracture and will wear it for six weeks. The patient asks how to avoid losing strength in that arm. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Move the elbow and wrist through their full range several times daily
options.rationale: Range of motion carries a joint through its arc. Joints above and below a cast are exercised where they are free, and the joints inside it are immobilized on purpose while the bone heals.

options.text: Lift a light hand weight with the casted arm
options.rationale: Lifting a weight through an arc is isotonic exercise, in which the muscle contracts while the joint moves. This is the correct exercise for building dynamic strength and the wrong one for a limb that must stay still.

options.text: Rest the arm completely until the cast is removed
options.rationale: Complete rest means no muscle activity at all. Resting sounds protective and guarantees the outcome the patient asked how to avoid.

options.text: Tighten and release the muscles inside the cast without moving the joints
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement. It increases static strength and builds joint stability, and it can be used safely around painful or healing tissue, so the muscle keeps working for the six weeks the joint cannot.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise is the answer when a joint must not move. The muscle can still be loaded, so strength and joint stability survive the period of immobilization.

questions.stem: A patient walks the length of the hallway with a nurse. Which findings indicate that the patient exceeded activity tolerance? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient becomes light-headed and reaches for the handrail
options.rationale: Dizziness is a listed tolerance parameter and it signals that perfusion to the brain has dropped. A patient who needs the handrail to stay upright is at the point where the activity becomes a fall.

options.text: Heart rate remains 118 ten minutes after returning to the chair
options.rationale: Recovery is the last item on the list of things to evaluate and the one most often skipped. A sustained elevation says the patient did more than the cardiovascular system could absorb, even if the walk itself looked acceptable.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 92 during the walk and returns to 80 within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is judged by the response to activity and by the recovery afterward. This is the body working correctly, not failing.

options.text: Oxygen saturation falls from 96 percent to 87 percent during the walk
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Oxygenation is one of the listed tolerance parameters, and a drop of nine points into the eighties means demand has outrun the patient's ability to supply it.

options.text: The patient stops twice and says it is hard to catch a breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea is the subjective sense of not getting enough air. Having to stop is the functional version of the same finding.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20 and settles back to 16 after three minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is one of the tolerance parameters. A modest increase during walking that resolves on sitting is the expected response.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and the ability to recover afterward. Rises during exertion are expected; what matters is how large they are and whether they resolve.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a neurovascular assessment on a patient six hours after surgical repair of an ankle fracture. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Capillary refill of four seconds in the toes with new numbness of the foot, compared with two seconds and normal sensation on the other side
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressure on the nail bed, normally under three seconds, and numbness is loss of sensation. Absent or diminished pulses, a cool or pale extremity, new numbness, and sudden loss of movement are all findings to report.

options.text: Moderate swelling at the surgical site
options.rationale: Swelling is fluid accumulating in injured tissue. What would concern you is swelling that is rapid or increasing quickly, and the stem describes neither.

options.text: Bruising visible along the lateral ankle
options.rationale: Bruising is blood that has escaped into the tissue from the injury and the surgery. It is an expected finding after a fracture and its repair.

options.text: Pain rated 5 of 10 that decreases after the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Pain is one of the neurovascular parameters. This pain responded to the ordered dose, which is the reassuring version of the finding.

questions.takeaway: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, and pain, and it is always compared side to side. Two abnormal findings in the same limb with a normal opposite side is the pattern that gets reported.

questions.stem: A patient immobile after a spinal cord injury receives ankle supports and range of motion twice daily to prevent foot drop. Which finding at 2 weeks indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: The ankles move easily to a neutral position
options.rationale: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture. An ankle that still reaches neutral has not shortened.

options.text: The feet rest with the toes pointed down
options.rationale: Toes pointed down is plantar flexion, the position foot drop locks in. This finding shows the plan is failing.

options.text: The calf muscles look the same size as on admission
options.rationale: Muscle size reflects atrophy, a separate effect of disuse. Range of motion maintains flexibility rather than bulk.

options.text: The lower legs show no swelling
options.rationale: Swelling relates to venous stasis with thrombus risk. It says nothing about joint mobility.

questions.takeaway: Contracture prevention is judged by joint movement. An ankle that still reaches neutral is the outcome that counts.
questions.strategy: Name what the intervention prevents. Pick the finding that measures that exact problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Foot drop is a fixed plantar flexion contracture.
A shows the ankle reaching neutral. B shows it stuck in plantar flexion.
C measures atrophy. D measures venous stasis.

elimination.verdict: A. A mobile ankle means the contracture was prevented.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest after spinal surgery has diminished breath sounds at both bases with oxygen saturation of 92 percent. After hourly upright deep breathing, which finding indicates improvement?

options.text: Breath sounds are clear at both bases
options.rationale: Diminished sounds meant collapsed alveoli at the bases. Clear sounds show air is reaching them again.

options.text: Crackles are now heard at both bases
options.rationale: New adventitious sounds suggest retained secretions or developing pneumonia. That is a change for the worse.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 18 to 26
options.rationale: A faster rate means the patient is working harder to breathe. It signals decline.

options.text: Oxygen saturation stays at 92 percent
options.rationale: An unchanged saturation shows no gain in gas exchange.

questions.takeaway: Atelectasis resolves when air reaches the bases again. New crackles signal a slide toward pneumonia instead.
questions.strategy: Tie the outcome to the original cue. Diminished sounds were the problem, so returning sounds are the proof.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diminished basal sounds with a low saturation fit atelectasis.
Clear basal sounds reverse the original cue.
Crackles and a faster rate show decline. A saturation stuck at 92 shows no gain.

elimination.verdict: A. Air is reaching the bases again.

questions.scenario:
Day 10 of bed rest.
Weak cough with diminished breath sounds at both bases.
Dizzy when the head of the bed is raised quickly.
Right foot rests in plantar flexion.
questions.stem: The nurse reviews these findings for a patient on bed rest. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.

rows.text: Sit upright to cough and deep breathe every 2 hours
rows.rationale: The weak cough with diminished basal sounds points to atelectasis. Upright deep breathing reopens alveoli.

rows.text: Raise the head of the bed in stages before standing
rows.rationale: Dizziness with a quick position change is orthostatic hypotension. Gradual changes let the circulation adjust.

rows.text: Place a support against the soles to keep the ankles neutral
rows.rationale: The plantar flexed foot is heading toward foot drop. Neutral support prevents the contracture.

rows.text: Keep the patient flat to prevent dizziness
rows.rationale: Lying flat further limits lung expansion. It also deepens the deconditioning behind the dizziness.

rows.text: Limit fluids to reduce trips to the bathroom
rows.rationale: Dehydration worsens the orthostatic dizziness and adds to venous stasis with thrombus risk.

rows.text: Tuck the top sheet tightly over the feet
rows.rationale: A tight sheet pushes the feet into plantar flexion. It worsens the foot drop risk already present.

questions.takeaway: Each immobility finding points to its own prevention. Match the cue to the mechanism before choosing the action.
questions.strategy: Link each action to one finding in the excerpt. Reject any action that makes that finding worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The cough fits row 1. The dizziness fits row 2. The plantar flexed foot fits row 3.

steps.action: Test each action against its cue
steps.detail: Row 4 worsens the lungs. Row 5 promotes stasis. Row 6 pushes the foot down.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: 1, 2, 3. Not indicated: 4, 5, 6.

questions.stem: A patient's knee gives way with weight bearing after a twisting injury. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
The x-ray shows no fracture, but the knee keeps giving way. The nurse anticipates [[1]].

Point tenderness over the tibia persists despite the normal x-ray. The nurse anticipates [[2]].

After that second study, the nurse teaches the patient to [[3]].

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: CT adds bone detail for complex fractures. Ligaments are soft tissue.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan shows areas of increased bone activity. A ligament tear does not show on it.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: MRI is best for soft tissue such as ligaments. Instability with a clear x-ray points to ligament injury.

options.text: a DEXA scan
options.rationale: DEXA measures bone mineral density. It says nothing about a ligament.

options.text: a DEXA scan
options.rationale: DEXA reports bone density. It does not show whether a bone is cracked.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan can detect occult fractures, meaning breaks not visible on ordinary images.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles and fluid. It is not used to find a hidden break.

options.text: an arthroscopy
options.rationale: Arthroscopy looks inside a joint. It does not survey the bone for a hidden fracture.

options.text: handle urine with radiation precautions
options.rationale: The radioisotope leaves in stool and urine. No special precautions are needed for handling excreta.

options.text: lie flat for 24 hours
options.rationale: No activity restriction follows a bone scan. The patient lies still only during the scan.

options.text: report any iodine contrast reaction
options.rationale: Iodine contrast allergy is a concern with CT contrast. A bone scan uses a radioisotope.

options.text: increase fluid intake
options.rationale: The radioisotope is excreted in the urine. Extra fluids speed its removal.

questions.takeaway: Match the study to the tissue in question. MRI shows soft tissue. A bone scan finds a hidden fracture. Push fluids after a bone scan.
questions.strategy: Ask which tissue each new finding points to. Pick the study built to see that tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Instability with a clear x-ray points to ligament, a soft tissue. MRI sees soft tissue.
Bone tenderness with a normal x-ray raises an occult fracture. A bone scan detects it.
A bone scan uses a radioisotope excreted in urine. Fluids speed excretion.

elimination.verdict: MRI, then a bone scan, then increased fluids.

questions.stem: A patient has 5 of 5 leg strength and stands steadily with eyes open but sways and grabs the bedrail with eyes closed. Which plan for walking is most appropriate?

options.text: Walk independently since leg strength is full
options.rationale: Full strength does not make a patient safe. The sway shows balance is the failing part.

options.text: Walk with a gait belt and standby assist in a well-lit hall
options.rationale: Swaying only with eyes closed means proprioception is impaired. Good light lets vision compensate while the gait belt guards against a fall.

options.text: Begin leg strengthening exercises before any walking
options.rationale: Strength is already full. More strength will not restore position sense.

options.text: Keep the patient on bed rest until balance improves
options.rationale: Bed rest adds the harms of immobility. The patient can walk safely with support.

questions.takeaway: Strength and balance fail separately. A patient with poor position sense relies on vision, so keep the lights on and stay close.
questions.strategy: Name the system that failed when vision was removed. Pick the plan that protects that system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Full strength with sway only when the eyes close points to proprioception.
A and C treat strength, which is already normal.
D adds immobility when supported walking is safe.

elimination.verdict: B. Supported walking where vision can compensate.

questions.stem: A patient slumped in bed reports low back ache and tiredness. The nurse repositions her in supported Fowler's position with her spinal curves aligned. Which finding indicates the intervention was effective?

options.text: She reports her back ache and tiredness have eased
options.rationale: Proper alignment minimizes joint stress and reduces fatigue. Both of her original complaints improved.

options.text: Her upper arm muscles appear larger
options.rationale: Muscle bulk comes from loading the muscle. Posture does not build it.

options.text: The skin over her sacrum shows no redness
options.rationale: Skin integrity is an outcome of pressure relief over time. It is not the complaint the alignment was meant to treat.

options.text: She eats more of her lunch tray
options.rationale: Appetite is not an outcome of alignment.

questions.takeaway: Alignment promotes efficient movement, minimizes joint stress, reduces fatigue and improves balance. Evaluate it against the complaint you were treating.

questions.stem: A patient rated Level 1 total assist on the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool has had a week of therapy. Which finding shows that seated balance has improved?

options.text: Sits unsupported at the bedside for 3 minutes, reaching across midline
options.rationale: That passes sit and shake, the test failed at Level 1. Trunk strength with seated balance is now adequate.

options.text: Holds the bedrail to stay upright at the bedside for 1 minute
options.rationale: Needing support means seated balance still fails. The test requires more than 2 minutes unassisted.

options.text: Tolerates the head of the bed raised to high Fowler's
options.rationale: The bed is still supporting the trunk. Sit and shake is done at the side of the bed.

options.text: Straightens each knee while lying supine
options.rationale: Knee extension belongs to stretch and point, done sitting. That test comes only after sit and shake is passed.

questions.takeaway: Improvement is proven by passing the test that was failed. For Level 1, that means sitting unassisted over 2 minutes while reaching across midline.
questions.strategy: Name the test the patient failed. The right finding is the one that passes it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Level 1 means sit and shake was failed.
Sitting unassisted over 2 minutes while reaching across midline.
B uses support. C is in bed. D is a later test done in the wrong position.

elimination.verdict: A. The patient now passes sit and shake.

questions.stem: The nurse performs passive range of motion twice daily for a patient unconscious after a traumatic brain injury. Which finding at 2 weeks indicates the intervention is effective?

options.text: Grip strength has increased in both hands
options.rationale: Passive motion builds no strength. The patient does no muscle work.

options.text: The patient moves the fingers on command
options.rationale: Following commands reflects neurologic recovery. It is not an outcome of passive exercise.

options.text: The elbows and knees still extend fully
options.rationale: Passive range of motion maintains joint flexibility. Full extension shows no contracture has formed.

options.text: Arm muscle size is unchanged from admission
options.rationale: Passive motion does not prevent atrophy. It moves joints without muscle contraction.

questions.takeaway: Passive range of motion is chosen when the patient cannot move. Judge it by joint flexibility, never by strength.
questions.strategy: Ask what passive exercise can do. It moves the joint, so the outcome must be about the joint.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Passive range of motion maintains flexibility when the patient contributes nothing.
A and D depend on muscle work the patient is not doing.
B reflects brain recovery, not the exercise.

elimination.verdict: C. Full joint extension shows flexibility was kept.

questions.stem: The nurse completes a musculoskeletal assessment on a 78-year-old woman. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Mild muscle wasting in both thighs
options.rationale: Expected. Muscle tissue atrophies with age.

options.text: Symmetric decrease in shoulder range of motion
options.rationale: Expected. Cartilage becomes less elastic with age, so joints move through a smaller arc.

options.text: Slowed but steady gait
options.rationale: Expected. Movement slows with age.

options.text: New loss of movement in the left leg
options.rationale: Aging changes are gradual and symmetric. A new one-sided loss of movement is a red flag, not aging.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes are gradual losses in muscle, bone and cartilage. A new or sudden change is never assumed to be aging.
questions.strategy: Three options are gradual symmetric losses. One is new and one-sided.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Atrophy, less motion and slower gait are gradual aging losses.
Only one change is new and on one side.
New or sudden is not age related.

elimination.verdict: D.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a casted arm and cannot palpate the radial pulse. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the finding and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Delays confirmation of whether blood is reaching the hand.

options.text: Elevate the arm above the level of the heart
options.rationale: Raising a limb that may already be underperfused reduces arterial inflow further.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to improve circulation
options.rationale: Does not address a possible obstruction and delays the assessment.

options.text: Use a Doppler to check for flow, then compare with the other arm
options.rationale: A Doppler detects flow that cannot be felt. Comparing sides turns an uncertain finding into a clear one.

questions.takeaway: Absent or diminished pulses is a red flag. Confirm with Doppler and always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wants to begin an exercise program. Which modification does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Shorter sessions paced to the patient's tolerance with rest periods
options.rationale: Activity plans are modified rather than cancelled in chronic illness, and tolerance sets the pace.

options.text: Avoid all physical activity to conserve oxygen
options.rationale: Inactivity worsens deconditioning and breathlessness over time.

options.text: High-intensity intervals to build endurance quickly
options.rationale: Exceeds tolerance and risks severe dyspnea.

options.text: Exercise only while receiving nebulizer treatments
options.rationale: Not a standard modification and unnecessarily restricts when the patient can move.

questions.takeaway: Activity plans are modified in coronary artery disease, hypertension, COPD, diabetes, and immobility.

questions.stem: An older adult is admitted with weakness after a fall at home. To plan mobility care, which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "Are you afraid of falling again?"
options.rationale: Fear after a fall is worth knowing. It does not establish his baseline function.

options.text: "Do you use any assistive devices at home?"
options.rationale: This identifies what he normally relies on. Baseline comes first, then the nurse looks for what is new.

options.text: "Would you like help getting up now?"
options.rationale: This offers help before any assessment has been done.

options.text: "Has anyone in your family broken a hip?"
options.rationale: Family history says nothing about his current function.

questions.takeaway: Start every mobility assessment at the patient's baseline, then look for what is new.

questions.stem: Three days after abdominal surgery, a patient sits and shakes hands well but cannot straighten either knee or point the toes. The patient insists on standing. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document maximum assist and use a lift or extra staff for any transfer
options.rationale: Failing stretch and point means the legs cannot yet support a stand. The patient's eagerness does not change the level, and the level sets the equipment.

options.text: Allow a standing attempt with one person, since sitting balance is intact
options.rationale: Sitting balance passed but leg strength did not. Standing is the next test, and the patient failed the one before it.

options.text: Document moderate assist and attempt a stand with a gait belt
options.rationale: Moderate assist is assigned after a failed stand. This patient never reached the stand test.

options.text: Repeat the sitting test before going further
options.rationale: Sitting was already passed. Repeating it delays the transfer without adding information.

questions.takeaway: The mobility tool stops at the first failure, and that failure sets the equipment. Willingness to try is not a level.
questions.strategy: The patient's insistence is the emotional pull. The leg test result is the data that decides.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sit and shake passed. Stretch and point failed.
A failure at stretch and point means maximum assist.
A stand before passing the leg test risks a fall.

elimination.verdict: Maximum assist with a device or extra staff.

questions.stem: During a mobility assessment, a patient stands, marches in place and steps forward and back. He keeps letting go of his walker and says he does not need it. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document him as independent and remove the walker
options.rationale: Strength was shown but safety awareness was not. Removing the device acts on half the assessment.

options.text: Assign a lower mobility level because he let go of the walker
options.rationale: The level reflects what he can physically do. Releasing the walker is a safety finding to address.

options.text: Walk with standby assist and address his safety awareness
options.rationale: He met the stepping criterion, but the walking level also weighs judgment. Supervision continues until safety awareness is shown.

options.text: Keep him in bed until physical therapy evaluates him
options.rationale: Bed rest causes the weakness the assessment is meant to prevent. He just showed he can step.

questions.takeaway: Mobility is judged on strength, balance, gait and safety awareness. A strong patient with poor judgment is not independent.
questions.strategy: Two options swing to extremes, independence or bed rest. The answer keeps him moving with supervision.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: He stood, marched and stepped.

steps.action: Name what he did not show
steps.detail: He does not use the walker safely.
Walk with standby assist while you teach.

elimination.verdict: Standby assist and address safety awareness.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a patient's left arm moved only when slid across the bed. After two weeks of therapy, which finding indicates improved strength?

options.text: Slides the arm farther across the bed
options.rationale: Movement with gravity removed is still grade 2. Distance does not change the grade.

options.text: Lifts the left arm off the bed against gravity
options.rationale: Movement against gravity is grade 3. The arm has moved up from grade 2.

options.text: Shows a flicker of contraction when asked to lift
options.rationale: Trace contraction is grade 1. That would be a decline.

options.text: Tolerates full passive range of motion without pain
options.rationale: Passive motion uses no strength. It says nothing about the grade.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the gravity hinge. Clearing the bed is the first sign a grade 2 limb is getting stronger.
questions.strategy: Grade the starting finding first. Then pick the option one grade higher.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Moving only when slid across the bed is grade 2.
Grade 3 is movement against gravity.
A stays at grade 2. C drops to grade 1. D involves no strength.

elimination.verdict: B. The arm now clears gravity.

questions.stem: Six hours after a below-knee cast is applied, a patient has pain of 9 of 10 unrelieved by analgesia, cool toes with capillary refill of 5 seconds and new numbness. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Elevate the leg above heart level to reduce swelling
options.rationale: Elevation helps a limb with good perfusion. Raising an underperfused limb lowers arterial inflow further.

options.text: Give the next analgesic dose and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Analgesia already failed, which is a cue in itself. Thirty minutes is time the limb does not have.

options.text: Apply ice over the cast and document the findings
options.rationale: Cold constricts vessels in a limb that is already losing circulation.

options.text: Notify the provider now and keep the leg at heart level
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion with slow refill, coolness and numbness means perfusion is compromised. Heart level keeps arterial inflow while help comes.

questions.takeaway: Pain unrelieved by analgesia in a casted limb is a circulation problem until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Elevation and ice are usual cast care. The neurovascular findings make them the wrong action now.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Severe unrelieved pain, slow refill, coolness and numbness.
Elevation and ice reduce flow to a failing limb.
More analgesia delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now with the leg at heart level.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews four clinic patients. Whose findings indicate the need for a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan?

options.text: A 25-year-old whose knee gives way after a twisting injury
options.rationale: Instability after a twist points to a ligament. MRI images soft tissue.

options.text: A 70-year-old with 5 cm height loss and a wrist fracture from a fall from standing height
options.rationale: Height loss with a fracture from a low-energy fall suggests low bone density. DEXA measures bone mineral density.

options.text: A 40-year-old with an ankle fracture from a motorcycle crash
options.rationale: High-energy trauma explains this fracture. X-ray or CT maps the break.

options.text: A 50-year-old with hip pain after a fall and a normal x-ray
options.rationale: An occult fracture is the concern here. A bone scan can detect it.

questions.takeaway: DEXA answers one question: is the bone thin? A fracture from a minor fall plus height loss asks exactly that.
questions.strategy: For each patient, name the tissue problem. Pick the one where density is the question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A is ligament. C is trauma. D is a possible hidden fracture.
Only B has height loss with a fragility fracture.
DEXA measures bone mineral density.

elimination.verdict: B. The findings point to low bone density.

questions.stem: A man reports weeks of weakness when climbing stairs and lifting his arms overhead. Which laboratory result requires follow-up?

options.text: Serum calcium 9.4 mg/dL
options.rationale: This is within 9.0 to 10.5. Calcium reflects bone rather than muscle.

options.text: Alkaline phosphatase 90 units/L
options.rationale: This is within 30 to 120. It rises with bone or liver damage.

options.text: Serum phosphorus 3.6 mg/dL
options.rationale: This is within 3.0 to 4.5. It is a bone mineral marker.

options.text: Creatine kinase 480 units/L
options.rationale: This is well above the male range of 55 to 170. Injured muscle releases CK, which fits proximal weakness.

questions.takeaway: Proximal weakness points to muscle. CK, LDH, AST and aldolase are the muscle enzymes that rise with damage.
questions.strategy: Name the tissue the symptoms point to. Find the abnormal value from that tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Trouble with stairs and overhead reach is proximal muscle weakness.
Calcium, alkaline phosphatase and phosphorus are normal bone markers.
Only CK is abnormal. It is a muscle enzyme.

elimination.verdict: D. The elevated CK needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A patient of 62 with a family history of osteoporosis asks how to protect bone and muscle over the coming years. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will walk on most days of the week."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Loading bone is what keeps mineral in it. Loading muscle is what maintains strength. Both are named among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: "I will make sure I get enough calcium and vitamin D."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Appropriate intake is listed among the measures that maintain bone over time.

options.text: "I will stop smoking."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Avoiding tobacco is named directly among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: "I will switch from walking to swimming to spare my joints."
options.rationale: Needs further teaching. Swimming is good conditioning but removes the weight bearing that maintains bone density. It supplements rather than replaces.

questions.takeaway: Activity, weight bearing, calcium with vitamin D, no tobacco, limited alcohol. Non-weight-bearing exercise does not protect bone.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. Swimming sounds healthy, which is exactly why it works as the trap.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that would not protect bone.
Bone keeps mineral only when it bears weight.
D replaces weight bearing with a non-weight-bearing activity.

elimination.verdict: D. Swimming does not load bone.

questions.stem: Patient A has full leg strength but needs both armrests to stand and rests twice crossing a room. Patient B has 4 of 5 strength and walks the hall unaided. Who needs walking help?

options.text: Patient A, because function is limited despite full strength
options.rationale: Functional ability is what the patient accomplishes. Rising only with armrests while stopping to rest marks A as unsafe alone.

options.text: Patient B, because strength is below normal
options.rationale: B's reduced grade does not limit function. B walks the hall unaided.

options.text: Both patients, because each has an abnormal finding
options.rationale: An abnormal number alone does not set the need for help. Function does.

options.text: Neither patient, because both have at least 4 of 5 strength
options.rationale: Strength does not predict function. A needs armrests to rise and rests twice crossing a room.

questions.takeaway: Strength is a number at rest. Function is what the patient accomplishes. Plan help around function.
questions.strategy: Ignore the strength grades at first. Ask which patient completes the task.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and B each name one patient. Decide which one fails the task.
A needs armrests to stand and stops twice. B walks the hall.
C and D judge by strength numbers, not by what the patients do.

elimination.verdict: A. Function, not strength, sets the need for help.

questions.stem: A nurse in a senior health clinic assesses several adults over 75 years of age. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walks more slowly than a year ago with a steady, even gait
options.rationale: Movement slows with age. The gait is steady and symmetric, so it is expected.

options.text: Shoulder range of motion slightly reduced on both sides with no pain
options.rationale: Cartilage becomes less elastic and ROM decreases. Symmetry and no pain keep it in the expected range.

options.text: Right knee hot, red and swollen since yesterday
options.rationale: A sudden, one-sided inflammatory joint is not aging. Infection or gout has to be ruled out.

options.text: Thigh muscles visibly smaller on both sides with strength 4 of 5
options.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Equal loss with good strength fits.

options.text: Lost 4 cm of height with new mid-back pain that began without injury
options.rationale: Pain with no injury plus height loss suggests a vertebral compression fracture from osteoporosis.

options.text: Left calf 3 cm larger than the right after a week of limited activity
options.rationale: One-sided calf swelling after reduced activity is a clot until proven otherwise.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual, symmetric and painless. Sudden onset, one side only, heat or pain without injury moves a finding out of the expected group.
questions.strategy: Look at three features in each option: speed of onset, symmetry and pain. Any one that is abnormal is enough to require follow-up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Both sides equal points to aging. One knee or one calf does not.
Since yesterday or new pain points to a problem.
Painless decline is expected. New back pain without injury is not.

elimination.verdict: Follow up on the hot knee, the height loss with back pain and the larger left calf.

questions.stem: After 5 days of bed rest for a pelvic fracture, a patient is cleared to walk with a walker. The nurse takes a lying blood pressure and pulse, then helps her sit at the bedside. Which action is next?

options.text: Have her straighten each knee and point the toes
options.rationale: This tests leg strength. It comes after sitting tolerance is confirmed.

options.text: Have her rise and hold the buttocks off the bed for a count of five
options.rationale: Standing before the sitting recheck risks a fall from orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Recheck blood pressure and pulse after 1 minute and confirm sitting balance
options.rationale: This screens for orthostatic hypotension and sitting balance at once. If either fails, you stop here.

options.text: Have her march in place, then walk with the walker
options.rationale: Stepping is the last stage, not the next one.

questions.takeaway: Get up in stages and test each stage before the next: baseline, sit and recheck, legs, stand, step.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real step. The question is which one comes next after she sits.

strategies: Priority key word
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: She just moved from lying to sitting.

steps.action: Find the check that belongs here
steps.detail: Repeat the vital signs and confirm balance.
Leg test, stand and step come after.

elimination.verdict: Recheck vital signs after sitting and confirm balance.

questions.stem: On day 10 of bed rest after a stroke, an 84-year-old has sacral nonblanchable redness, no stool for 4 days, an ankle fixed in plantar flexion and SpO2 falling from 97% to 93%. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Declining oxygenation from poor lung expansion
options.rationale: A steady fall in SpO2 points to atelectasis. Each value looks acceptable alone, but the trend threatens breathing.

options.text: Early pressure injury over the sacrum
options.rationale: A real complication that needs repositioning. It does not threaten gas exchange.

options.text: Constipation from slowed bowel motility
options.rationale: Needs treatment, after breathing is addressed.

options.text: Plantar flexion contracture of the ankle
options.rationale: It develops over days and leads to foot drop. It is not the immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Immobility reaches nearly every system. When several complications are present, the ABCs pick the first, and the trend matters more than one value.
questions.strategy: Every option is a true complication of immobility. Only one involves breathing.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Skin, bowel, joint and lungs are all affected.
Falling SpO2 is a breathing problem.
A fall from 97 to 93 is a decline even though 93 alone looks fine.

elimination.verdict: Declining oxygenation comes first.

questions.stem: On day 4 after bowel resection, a patient passes sit and shake and stretch and point. He lifts off the bed but sits back down at a count of two with trembling legs. Which transfer method is most appropriate?

options.text: Walk him to the chair with a gait belt and one person
options.rationale: Walking requires holding a stand for a count of five. He could not.

options.text: Use a sit-to-stand lift for the transfer
options.rationale: He has partial leg strength. This lift lets him bear some weight while the device supports the rest.

options.text: Use a full-body mechanical lift for the transfer
options.rationale: Safe but too restrictive. It takes away the weight bearing he can do.

options.text: Keep him in bed until he can hold a stand for five
options.rationale: Bed rest deepens the weakness that caused the failed stand.

questions.takeaway: The first failed test picks the equipment. The plan should use every bit of strength the patient has.
questions.strategy: Two options are too much help and one is too little. Match the device to what he can do.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: He could not hold the stand.
Walking requires a held stand.
A full-body lift and bed rest waste his strength.

elimination.verdict: Sit-to-stand lift.

questions.stem: On day 5 of bed rest after a pelvic fracture, a patient with compression devices on both legs has a left calf 3 cm larger than the right that is warm and tender. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue the compression devices on both legs as prescribed
options.rationale: Squeezing a leg that may already have a clot can dislodge it.

options.text: Perform active range of motion of the left ankle
options.rationale: Leg exercise prevents clots. Once a clot is suspected, working the calf can break it loose.

options.text: Help the patient sit at the bedside to begin activity
options.rationale: Progressive activity is prevention. It is the right action at the wrong time.

options.text: Remove the left leg device, keep the leg at rest and notify the provider
options.rationale: One-sided swelling, warmth and tenderness after immobility suggest a deep vein thrombosis. Stop anything that squeezes or moves the leg, then report.

questions.takeaway: Compression devices, leg exercises and activity prevent a thrombus. Once one is suspected, stop them on that leg and report.
questions.strategy: Three options are good prevention measures. The new finding turns them into hazards.

strategies: Odd man wins
Priority key word

steps.detail: One calf is larger, warm and tender.
Three options move or squeeze the leg.
Rest the leg and report.

elimination.verdict: Remove the device, rest the leg and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse on a medical unit plans morning hallway walks for four patients. Which patient's walk does the nurse postpone?

options.text: A 70-year-old with coronary artery disease: heart rate 78, blood pressure 132/80, no chest pain since admission
options.rationale: Stable numbers with no symptoms. CAD calls for monitoring during the walk, not for holding it.

options.text: A 64-year-old with COPD: SpO2 91% at rest, which matches a charted baseline of 90 to 92%, no increased work of breathing
options.rationale: A saturation of 91% looks low. It is this patient's baseline. Nothing has changed. Walk with oxygen available and watch the recovery time.

options.text: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes: fingerstick glucose 146 mg/dL, ate breakfast 30 minutes ago
options.rationale: A safe glucose before exercise with a recent meal. There is no reason to hold.

options.text: A 61-year-old with hypertension: blood pressure 188/104, up from 150/88 yesterday, reports a new headache
options.rationale: The pressure is high and climbing. A new headache is a symptom. Exercise raises blood pressure further, so the walk waits while the nurse reassesses and reports.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness modifies an activity plan. A new, worsening, symptomatic finding stops it.
questions.strategy: The COPD patient's number looks the worst. Ask which patient has changed from baseline and has symptoms.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: CAD, COPD and diabetes patients are all at their usual state.
Blood pressure rose from 150/88 to 188/104 overnight.
A new headache with a rising pressure makes this unstable.

elimination.verdict: Postpone the walk for the patient with hypertension and a new headache.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD has a resting heart rate of 78 and SpO2 of 94%. After a short hallway walk, which finding indicates he tolerated the activity?

options.text: HR 94, back to 80 after 3 minutes of rest
options.rationale: A modest rise with activity is expected. Return toward baseline with rest shows recovery.

options.text: SpO2 87% with dizziness at the end of the walk
options.rationale: Oxygenation fell and he is dizzy. Oxygen delivery did not meet the demand.

options.text: HR 118, still 112 after 5 minutes of rest
options.rationale: The rate rose sharply without recovering. Failure to recover signals intolerance.

options.text: Says he feels fine after stopping twice to catch his breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea that forces rest shows intolerance. His words do not match the data.

questions.takeaway: Judge activity tolerance by the whole response. Above all, look for the ability to recover after rest.
questions.strategy: Three options show a body that could not keep up. Only one shows a modest rise followed by recovery.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A modest rise with effort, then recovery with rest.
Low SpO2, a rate that stays high and forced rest all fail.
Only A returns toward baseline.

elimination.verdict: A.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old on bed rest for 5 days has a lying BP of 136/80. The nurse raises her in stages before standing. Which finding indicates orthostatic hypotension was not prevented?

options.text: Sitting BP 132/78 with no dizziness
