questions.stem: A 74-year-old with heart failure is being discharged after community-acquired pneumonia. His home plan includes a fluid restriction of 1.5 L per day. Which statement indicates the need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll drink at least 3 liters of water every day to keep my mucus thin."
options.rationale: 3 L a day is the pneumonia teaching unless fluids are restricted. He is restricted to 1.5 L, so 3 L could push him into heart failure. The exception decides this item.

options.text: "I'll get my pneumonia and flu vaccines when my provider says it's time."
options.rationale: Vaccination is a core prevention measure.

options.text: "I'll stay out of big crowds during flu season."
options.rationale: Correct prevention teaching.

options.text: "I'll do my deep breathing and coughing several times a day and walk around the house."
options.rationale: Coughing, turning, moving and deep breathing help prevent another pneumonia.

questions.takeaway: Standard pneumonia teaching includes 3 L of water daily. That advice applies only when the patient has no fluid restriction.
questions.strategy: Every option is standard teaching for pneumonia. Read the stem for the detail that makes one of them wrong for this patient.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Heart failure with a 1.5 L restriction.
Only the 3 L statement conflicts with the restriction.

elimination.verdict: The plan to drink 3 liters a day.

questions.stem: A nurse makes a home visit to a 71-year-old who uses oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The oxygen cylinder is stored upright in a wheeled stand
options.rationale: Securing cylinders prevents them from falling and damaging the valve. This is correct.

options.text: A water-based gel is used on her dry nostrils
options.rationale: Water-based products are safe with oxygen and help with dryness.

options.text: The patient rubs a petroleum-based vapor rub on her chest at bedtime
options.rationale: Petroleum products are flammable in an oxygen-rich environment and sit right under the oxygen flow. Easy to miss because it looks like an ordinary cold remedy.

options.text: An "Oxygen in use" sign is posted on the front door
options.rationale: Correct fire safety practice.

questions.takeaway: Keep oxygen away from flames and smoking. Keep petroleum-based products away from the face and chest. Water-based lubricants are the safe choice.
questions.strategy: Look for the petroleum product hiding in something familiar. Vapor rub does not look like a fire hazard until you think about what it is made of.

strategies: Negative polarity
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Flame, smoking or petroleum near oxygen.
Vapor rub is petroleum-based.
Secured cylinder, water-based gel, posted sign.

elimination.verdict: The petroleum-based vapor rub.

questions.scenario: A 76-year-old with type 2 diabetes is on day 4 after a hip repair. At 0800 she was oriented x3 with BP 142/84. At 1400 she knows only her name. Temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 112, respirations 28, BP 98/58, SpO2 89% on room air. Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe. WBC 15,800/mm3. Lactate 3.1 mmol/L.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen as prescribed
options.rationale: Improving gas exchange is the first goal of the pneumonia plan. Upright positioning helps the lungs expand.

options.text: Obtain blood and sputum cultures, then give the first antibiotic dose promptly as prescribed
options.rationale: Cultures before the first dose keep results accurate. Prompt antibiotics are how you prevent sepsis from progressing.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.rationale: Her crackles are on one side with a raised WBC, which fits infection rather than overload, and her blood pressure is falling. Restricting fluids worsens perfusion.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until culture results return
options.rationale: Cultures take days. Waiting lets the infection spread.

options.text: Keep her flat in bed to reduce oxygen demand
options.rationale: Lying flat makes breathing harder. Rest is good and it is done sitting up.

options.text: Hospital-acquired pneumonia with signs of early sepsis
options.rationale: Onset after 48 hours in hospital, crackles, low SpO2 and a high WBC point to pneumonia. Falling BP, fast heart rate, new confusion and a raised lactate are sepsis cues.

options.text: Postoperative delirium from pain medication
options.rationale: Explains confusion only. It does not explain crackles, hypoxemia or a high lactate.

options.text: Pulmonary edema from fluid overload
options.rationale: Overload raises the blood pressure. Hers is falling. The crackles are also on one side.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Diabetes makes it worth checking. It does not explain fever, crackles, high WBC or hypoxemia.

options.text: SpO2 trend with respiratory rate and work of breathing
options.rationale: Tells you whether gas exchange is improving.

options.text: Blood pressure, mental status and lactate
options.rationale: Tell you whether sepsis is progressing or responding.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.rationale: Reflects three months of glucose control. It will not change during this event.

options.text: Incision appearance
options.rationale: Worth routine checks. Her cues point to the lungs, not the incision.

questions.takeaway: The pneumonia plan is to improve gas exchange, prevent airflow obstruction and prevent sepsis. In an older adult, new confusion and a falling BP may be the loudest cues, even with a low fever.
questions.strategy: The low temperature and the diabetes are there to pull you toward delirium or hypoglycemia. Only one condition explains every cue.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Global or umbrella option

steps.action: Pick the condition that explains every cue
steps.detail: Lungs, blood pressure, brain and labs all fit pneumonia with early sepsis.

steps.action: Choose actions for gas exchange and sepsis
steps.detail: Upright with oxygen. Cultures, then antibiotics.
Oxygenation for the lungs. Blood pressure, mental status and lactate for sepsis.

elimination.verdict: HAP with early sepsis; oxygen upright, cultures then antibiotic; oxygenation trend and perfusion markers.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old had a bronchoscopy with biopsy 2 hours ago. The nurse reviews the latest findings. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Coughing up about 30 mL of bright red blood in the last 15 minutes
options.rationale: Bleeding is a biopsy complication. Bright red blood in a measurable amount is active bleeding, not streaking. It can block the airway.

options.text: Sputum streaked with small amounts of blood
options.rationale: Expected after a biopsy. Monitor it.

options.text: A sore throat with a hoarse voice
options.rationale: Expected after a scope has passed through the throat.

options.text: Gag reflex not yet returned, so she has not been given anything to drink
options.rationale: Correct care. She stays NPO until the gag reflex returns.

questions.takeaway: After a bronchoscopy with biopsy, streaked sputum is expected and frank bleeding is not. Keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns.
questions.strategy: Two options mention blood. The amount and the color decide which one is expected.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Streaks, sore throat and an absent gag reflex are expected early.
Streaks versus 30 mL of bright red blood.
Active bleeding can fill the airway.

elimination.verdict: The 30 mL of bright red blood.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with a history of heart failure has received IV fluid at 150 mL/hr for 2 days for dehydration. Her weight is up 1.8 kg since admission. The nurse auscultates her lungs. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider now?

options.text: Soft, low-pitched sounds heard over both lung bases
options.rationale: Vesicular sounds. Normal at the bases.

options.text: Medium-pitched sounds heard near the sternum
options.rationale: Bronchovesicular sounds. Normal in that location.

options.text: Coarse sounds over the trachea and large airways that clear after she coughs
options.rationale: Rhonchi from secretions. They cleared with coughing, so the nurse manages them with coughing and deep breathing.

options.text: Fine crackles in both bases that remain after coughing, new since yesterday
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways. They are new and they do not clear. They fit her weight gain on steady IV fluids. With her heart failure history, the fluid rate needs review now.

questions.takeaway: Crackles mean fluid, wheezes mean narrowed airways and rhonchi mean secretions. New crackles that do not clear in a patient receiving IV fluids are a report-now finding.
questions.strategy: The rhonchi are abnormal too. What tips it is that they cleared with coughing while the crackles did not. They also match the weight gain and the IV rate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: Vesicular at the bases and bronchovesicular near the sternum.
Rhonchi cleared. Crackles persisted.
Weight up 1.8 kg on IV fluids with heart failure.

elimination.verdict: New crackles that persist after coughing.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman with pneumonia is newly confused, with an SpO2 of 86% and accessory muscle use. The nurse applies oxygen by nasal cannula. Which finding 30 minutes later indicates the therapy is effective?

options.text: SpO2 95%, oriented, breathing unlabored
options.rationale: Saturation, work of breathing and mental status all improved. The number matches the patient.

options.text: SpO2 96%, hard to wake, RR 10
options.rationale: This is deterioration. Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation or CO2.

options.text: She says the cannula feels comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort supports adherence. It says nothing about her oxygenation.

options.text: SpO2 95% on a cold finger, still restless
options.rationale: Cold extremities make the reading unreliable. Restlessness shows she is still struggling.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate oxygen therapy by the patient and the number together. Better SpO2, easier breathing and a return to baseline mental status mean it worked.
questions.strategy: Three options show a good number or a good report. Only one shows every cue improving.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: RR 10 and restlessness are not improvement.
It is not an oxygenation finding.
Only A improves SpO2, breathing and mental status.

elimination.verdict: A. Treat the patient, not the number.

questions.stem: A man who smokes plans to quit using counseling, a nicotine patch and bupropion. Which statement indicates he needs further teaching?

options.text: "I will use the patch and go to counseling."
options.rationale: Correct. Combining counseling with medication is the recommended approach.

options.text: "I can smoke one cigarette with the patch on if cravings are bad."
options.rationale: Smoking on nicotine replacement raises nicotine levels. That increases the risk of stroke and heart attack.

options.text: "My wife will report any change in my mood."
options.rationale: Correct. Bupropion carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts.

options.text: "The clinic will call me the first week after I quit."
options.rationale: Correct. Arrange, the last of the 5 As, schedules early follow up.

questions.takeaway: Nicotine replacement plus smoking stacks nicotine and raises cardiovascular risk. Teach the patient not to smoke while using NRT.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: find the unsafe statement. Three match the plan. One creates risk.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Combined treatment, mood monitoring and early follow up are correct.
Smoking on the patch raises nicotine levels.

elimination.verdict: B. It is the only statement that puts him at risk.

questions.stem: During a new respiratory virus outbreak, a 35-year-old arrives with fever and cough after international travel. The virus type is unknown. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Place a mask on the patient and start contact and airborne precautions
options.rationale: Correct. With an unknown type, you protect others first. The slide calls for contact and airborne precautions until the type is known.

options.text: Collect a nasal swab for viral testing
options.rationale: Needed to identify the virus, but it can wait until the patient is isolated.

options.text: Auscultate the lungs for adventitious sounds
options.rationale: A key assessment that you do once precautions are in place.

options.text: Obtain a detailed list of every country visited
options.rationale: The travel clue already triggered isolation. The details can follow.

questions.takeaway: When a possible pandemic virus is unknown, isolate first. Contact and airborne precautions come before testing or a full exam.
questions.strategy: All four actions belong in this visit. The travel history plus unknown type decides the order: stop spread before anything else.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An unknown outbreak virus threatens staff and other patients.

steps.action: Find the action that controls it
steps.detail: Masking and airborne precautions stop spread.
Swab, lung exam and history all follow isolation.

elimination.verdict: Mask the patient and start contact and airborne precautions.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old had a right thoracentesis for a pleural effusion. Before the procedure, breath sounds were absent at the right base with respirations of 28. Which finding indicates the procedure was effective?

options.text: Breath sounds heard at the right base with respirations of 18
options.rationale: Correct. Air now reaches the lung that fluid had compressed. Breathing is easier.

options.text: A dry dressing over the puncture site
options.rationale: Shows no leak or bleeding. It does not show that breathing improved.

options.text: The patient rests quietly on the unaffected side
options.rationale: Positioning is not an outcome. It tells you nothing about the lung.

options.text: Heart rate of 112 at 1 hour
options.rationale: A fast heart rate after thoracentesis can signal bleeding or a pneumothorax. It is a warning sign.

questions.takeaway: Judge a procedure by the problem it was meant to fix. Compare the same finding before and after.
questions.strategy: The stem gives you the baseline: absent sounds and a fast rate. The right answer shows both returning toward normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Absent right base sounds with respirations of 28.
Sounds return and respirations slow.
A dressing and a position are not outcomes. Tachycardia is a complication cue.

elimination.verdict: Returned breath sounds with a normal rate. The lung has reexpanded.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with pneumonia has a weak cough. Coarse rhonchi clear after coughing. SpO2 is 96% on room air. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Ineffective airway clearance from retained secretions
options.rationale: Correct. Rhonchi are secretions in the larger airways. They clear with coughing. A weak cough leaves them behind.

options.text: Impaired gas exchange at the alveoli
options.rationale: An SpO2 of 96% on room air shows oxygen is crossing the alveolar membrane well right now.

options.text: Upper airway obstruction
options.rationale: That presents with stridor, not rhonchi that clear with a cough.

options.text: Fluid in the alveoli
options.rationale: Fluid produces crackles, not rhonchi, and the slide does not say crackles clear with a cough. The stem describes rhonchi that clear with coughing.

questions.takeaway: Rhonchi mean secretions in the airways. A normal SpO2 points you to clearance, not gas exchange.
questions.strategy: Use every data point. The sound tells you where the problem is. The saturation tells you what it is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Rhonchi that clear with a cough are airway secretions.
96% on room air rules out a gas exchange problem for now.
Stridor and crackles are not in the stem.

elimination.verdict: Ineffective airway clearance. The cough is too weak to move the secretions.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with pneumonia is on a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. SpO2 is 94%. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: The reservoir bag collapses completely with each breath
options.rationale: The bag must stay at least partly inflated. A collapsing bag means the flow is too low or the patient is drawing in room air, so delivered oxygen drops.

options.text: The mask fits snugly over the nose and mouth
options.rationale: A tight seal is what lets this device deliver a high concentration. This is correct setup.

options.text: SpO2 of 94% on this device
options.rationale: Acceptable for most patients with pneumonia. Watch the trend, but it is not the problem here.

options.text: The patient says the mask feels warm
options.rationale: A common comfort complaint. Offer skin and mouth care, but it does not threaten oxygen delivery.

questions.takeaway: On a nonrebreather, check the reservoir bag and the one way valves. A bag that collapses on inspiration means the device is failing.
questions.strategy: Ask which option shows the equipment not doing its job. The others describe a device that is working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: The slide says check the reservoir and the one way valves.
A snug seal is expected.
94% and a warm mask need no urgent action.

elimination.verdict: The collapsing reservoir bag. The device is not delivering what was ordered.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old is going home after community acquired pneumonia. She has no fluid restriction. Which statement indicates understanding of the discharge teaching?

options.text: "I will drink about 3 liters of fluid every day."
options.rationale: Correct. Without a restriction, generous fluids thin secretions so she can cough them up.

options.text: "I will stay in bed until my cough is gone."
options.rationale: Rest matters, but bed rest lets secretions pool. She should keep moving within her tolerance.

options.text: "I will skip deep breathing when it makes me cough."
options.rationale: Coughing and deep breathing are how she clears the lungs. Avoiding them raises the risk of relapse.

options.text: "I can stop my antibiotic once the fever is gone."
options.rationale: Stopping early lets the infection return. She finishes the full course.

questions.takeaway: After pneumonia, the plan is fluids, movement, cough and deep breathing and the full antibiotic course. Fluid limits apply only if prescribed.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you she has no restriction. That detail is there to make the fluid answer safe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: No fluid restriction means 3 liters a day is appropriate.
Bed rest and skipping deep breaths both let secretions pool.
Fever resolving does not mean the infection is gone.

elimination.verdict: Drinking about 3 liters a day. It thins secretions and matches the class plan.

caseStudies.title: Older adult with community acquired pneumonia
caseStudies.intro: An 84 year old man is admitted from home with a 3 day cough. His daughter brought him in because he has been confused since yesterday.

entries.text: Admitted from home. Oriented to person only; daughter states he is normally oriented x3 and pays his own bills. Coughing up rust colored sputum. Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe. Vesicular breath sounds at the left base. Speaks in short phrases. Mouth dry.
T 37.9 C; HR 112; RR 28 with accessory muscle use; BP 102/58 (usual 136/78); SpO2 88% on room air
Lactate 2.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2)
Sodium 138 mEq/L (135 to 145)
Potassium 4.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0)
Hypertension treated with lisinopril.
Former smoker, 30 pack years; quit 15 years ago. No chronic lung disease.
Pneumonia vaccine not documented.
Lives with his daughter. Independent in ADLs until this week.

question.nursesNote: 0800: 84 year old admitted from home with a cough for 3 days. Oriented to person only; daughter states he is normally oriented x3. Coughing up rust colored sputum. Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe. Vesicular breath sounds at the left base. RR 28 with accessory muscle use; speaks in short phrases. HR 112. BP 102/58 (usual 136/78). SpO2 88% on room air. Pupils equal and reactive to light. Denies chest pain. Daughter at the bedside asking questions.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Oriented to person only; daughter states he is normally oriented x3
segments.rationale: An acute change from his baseline. Older adults respond less to hypoxia, so confusion may be the first sign you get.

segments.text: Coughing up rust colored sputum
segments.rationale: Rust colored sputum points to bacterial pneumonia. It also needs a sputum culture.

segments.text: Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe
segments.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways. One lobe fits pneumonia.

segments.text: Vesicular breath sounds at the left base
segments.rationale: Soft low sounds at the bases are the expected normal.

segments.text: RR 28 with accessory muscle use; speaks in short phrases
segments.rationale: Increased work of breathing. He is working hard to move air.

segments.text: HR 112
segments.rationale: Tachycardia. It can come from hypoxemia or fever. It is also an early sepsis cue.
Well below his own baseline. Compare to his usual, not to a normal range. A falling pressure is an early sepsis cue.

segments.text: SpO2 88% on room air
segments.rationale: Below 90% in a client without chronic lung disease needs immediate assessment and intervention.

segments.text: Pupils equal and reactive to light
segments.rationale: A normal neurologic finding.

segments.text: Denies chest pain
segments.rationale: Nothing to act on.

segments.text: Daughter at the bedside asking questions
segments.rationale: Worth answering later. It is not a physiologic finding that needs follow up.

question.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion is a vital sign. Low SpO2, fast breathing, crackles and a pressure below his baseline all need follow up.
question.strategy: Compare each finding with his own baseline. His blood pressure looks acceptable until you see his usual of 136/78.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: SpO2 88%, RR 28 with accessory muscles and crackles all belong to gas exchange.
Confusion and the blood pressure are abnormal for him.
Vesicular sounds at the base, reactive pupils, no chest pain and a visiting daughter need no follow up.

elimination.verdict: Confusion, sputum, crackles, work of breathing, HR, BP and SpO2.

question.scenario: The nurse reviews the admission data for the client with pneumonia.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is a cue of impaired gas exchange, a cue of early sepsis or not related.

rows.text: SpO2 88% on room air
rows.rationale: Low oxygen saturation is hypoxemia.

rows.text: Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe
rows.rationale: Fluid in the alveoli blocks diffusion across the alveolar capillary membrane.

rows.text: RR 28 with accessory muscle use
rows.rationale: He is breathing harder to make up for poor oxygenation.
A fall from his baseline during an infection is an early sepsis cue.

rows.text: Lactate 2.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2)
rows.rationale: A raised lactate means tissues are not getting enough oxygen. It is on the pneumonia lab list for this reason.

rows.text: Potassium 4.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0)
rows.rationale: Within the normal range.

question.takeaway: Pneumonia threatens two things at once. The lungs cannot exchange gas. The infection can spread into sepsis.
question.strategy: Ask whether each finding comes from the lungs or from the circulation. Lung findings mean gas exchange. A falling pressure and a raised lactate mean the circulation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: SpO2, crackles and breathing effort describe gas exchange.
Blood pressure below baseline and lactate describe early sepsis.
Potassium 4.0 is within range.

elimination.verdict: Gas exchange, gas exchange, gas exchange, sepsis, sepsis, not related.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence:
The client is most likely experiencing [[1]].

The nurse's priority problem is [[2]].

His temperature of 37.9 C [[3]].

options.text: community acquired pneumonia with early sepsis cues
options.rationale: New confusion, crackles, low SpO2, a high WBC and a falling blood pressure all fit. He became ill at home, so it is community acquired.

options.text: progression of dementia
options.rationale: His daughter says he is normally oriented x3 and pays his own bills. His confusion started yesterday.

options.text: expected changes of aging
options.rationale: New or severe shortness of breath is never normal aging. Neither is new confusion.

options.text: hospital acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: Hospital acquired pneumonia starts 48 hours or more after admission. He was sick before he arrived.

options.text: impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: Breathing comes first. The pneumonia plan starts with improving gas exchange.

options.text: risk for falls
options.rationale: Real because he is confused. It is a potential problem. The hypoxemia is actual.

options.text: deficient knowledge about vaccination
options.rationale: Teaching matters at discharge. It does not outrank oxygenation.

options.text: anxiety of the family
options.rationale: Supporting the daughter matters. Physiologic needs come first.

options.text: does not rule out a serious infection because older adults often do not mount a high fever
options.rationale: A low grade temperature in an older adult can hide a serious infection.

options.text: shows the infection is mild
options.rationale: His other cues say otherwise. Older adults often do not run a high fever.

options.text: means the nurse should wait for a fever before calling the provider
options.rationale: Waiting for a fever in a newly confused older adult is a known trap.

options.text: explains his confusion without other causes
options.rationale: A temperature of 37.9 C does not explain new confusion. Hypoxemia can.

question.takeaway: Name the problem from the cluster of cues. Put gas exchange first. Do not let a low grade temperature reassure you in an older adult.
question.strategy: Two distractors blame his age. New confusion and new shortness of breath are never normal aging.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Crackles, rust sputum, low SpO2 and a high WBC mean pneumonia. The pressure and lactate add early sepsis.
Breathing outranks falls, teaching and family anxiety.
Older adults often do not run a high fever.

elimination.verdict: Pneumonia with early sepsis cues; impaired gas exchange; does not rule out serious infection.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Upright positioning helps the lungs expand. It costs nothing while you wait for orders.

options.text: Apply oxygen as prescribed and monitor the SpO2 trend
options.rationale: Oxygen treats the hypoxemia. The trend tells you whether it is working.

options.text: Obtain sputum and blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Cultures drawn after the antibiotic may not grow the organism.

options.text: Encourage him to cough and deep breathe
options.rationale: Moves secretions out of the airways. Part of the pneumonia plan.

options.text: Check mental status and vital signs often
options.rationale: Tells you whether he is improving or sliding toward sepsis.

options.text: Keep him flat in bed to rest
options.rationale: Lying flat makes breathing harder.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: His mouth is dry and nothing in his history calls for a restriction. The pneumonia plan encourages fluids unless they are restricted.

options.text: Reorient him and recheck vital signs at the next routine time
options.rationale: Treats his confusion as a behavior. It is a sign of hypoxemia that needs action now.

question.takeaway: The pneumonia plan: improve gas exchange, clear the airway, prevent sepsis. Position, oxygen, cultures, coughing and close monitoring.
question.strategy: Each wrong option looks restful or cautious. Flat in bed, fewer fluids and waiting all make him worse.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head of bed up, oxygen, cough and deep breathe.
Cultures before antibiotics. Frequent vital signs and mental status.
Lying flat, a fluid restriction and a delayed recheck.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Provider notified by SBAR. Prescriptions received: oxygen by nasal cannula at 2 L/min, titrate up to 6 L/min to keep SpO2 95% or higher. Blood cultures x2. Sputum culture. Ceftriaxone IV. Chest x ray.
Back from x ray and lying flat. SpO2 89% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. RR 28. Lips dry. Blood cultures and sputum specimen not yet collected. First dose of ceftriaxone has arrived from pharmacy.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler position
options.rationale: Lying flat after the x ray is making his breathing harder. Sitting up is the fastest fix.

options.text: Increase the oxygen within the prescribed range
options.rationale: His SpO2 is below the goal of 95%. The titration order lets you go up to 6 L/min.

options.text: Collect the blood cultures and sputum specimen
options.rationale: They come before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can still grow.

options.text: Start the ceftriaxone as soon as the cultures are collected
options.rationale: Antibiotics should not be delayed once cultures are drawn.

options.text: Hold the ceftriaxone until the culture results return
options.rationale: Results take days. Waiting lets the infection progress toward sepsis.

options.text: Apply petroleum jelly to his dry lips
options.rationale: Petroleum products are not used with oxygen. Use a water based product.

options.text: Switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
options.rationale: Outside the prescription. The ordered device still has room to titrate.

options.text: Reposition the probe and recheck the SpO2 in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The reading matches his breathing. Rechecking the number alone delays treatment.

question.takeaway: Position first, then titrate oxygen within the order. Draw cultures before the first antibiotic. Then give the antibiotic without delay.
question.strategy: Two options sound careful. Holding the antibiotic and rechecking the probe both delay treatment for a client who needs it now.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sit him up. Increase the oxygen within the prescribed range.
Cultures first. Antibiotic right after.

steps.action: Cut the unsafe and the unordered
steps.detail: Petroleum near oxygen and a device that was not prescribed.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

entries.text: VS: T 37.6 C; HR 96; RR 20 without accessory muscle use; BP 100/56; SpO2 95% on 3 L/min by nasal cannula.
Oriented to person and place; daughter says he is still not himself. Coughing up thick sputum with encouragement. Crackles in the right lower lobe less coarse.
Repeat lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2).

question.scenario: The nurse reassesses the client at 1200.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the care has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: SpO2 95% on 3 L/min by nasal cannula
rows.rationale: Meets the prescribed goal. Gas exchange has improved.

rows.text: RR 20 without accessory muscle use
rows.rationale: His work of breathing has come down from RR 28 with accessory muscles.

rows.text: Coughing up thick sputum with encouragement
rows.rationale: He is clearing his airway.

rows.text: Oriented to person and place
rows.rationale: Better than this morning. He is still not back to his baseline of x3.
Still well below his usual 136/78. Report it.

rows.text: Repeat lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2)
rows.rationale: It rose from 2.6. His tissues are getting less oxygen, which is a sepsis warning.

question.takeaway: Better breathing does not mean the infection is under control. A rising lactate and a low pressure need a call to the provider even when the SpO2 looks good.
question.strategy: Judge each finding against its goal. Improvement that falls short of baseline is not effective yet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: SpO2 at goal, a slower RR and a productive cough show improvement.
Orientation and blood pressure are still short of his usual.
Lactate went up, not down.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, not effective, not effective, not effective.

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client with a very dark skin tone has a rising bilirubin level. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Yellow tint over the callused soles of the feet
options.rationale: Calluses on the palms and soles can look yellow without jaundice, so this finding does not confirm anything.

options.text: Brown pigment flecks at the outer edges of the sclera
options.rationale: Scleral pigment at the edges is a common normal variant in dark skin.

options.text: A dark band running the length of one fingernail
options.rationale: Melanonychia is common in people with dark skin and is unrelated to bilirubin.

options.text: Yellowing of the hard palate and of the sclera next to the cornea
options.rationale: These low pigment areas are where jaundice shows most accurately in dark skin, so this is true jaundice to report.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, confirm jaundice at the sclera closest to the cornea and the hard palate. Yellow calluses and scleral pigment are not jaundice.
questions.strategy: Three options are normal findings in dark skin that look abnormal. Ask which one sits in a low pigment area that reliably shows bilirubin.

strategies: Odd man wins
Priority key word

steps.detail: Callus color, scleral flecks and nail bands are common in dark skin.
The hard palate and the sclera next to the cornea show bilirubin.

elimination.verdict: Yellow hard palate and sclera next to the cornea.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client how to perform a monthly skin self exam. Which statement indicates the client understood the teaching?

options.text: "I'll have a mole checked if it grows bigger than a pencil eraser."
options.rationale: Diameter greater than 6 mm, about a pencil eraser, is the D in ABCDE.

options.text: "A mole that is two shades of brown is normal for me."
options.rationale: Color variation within one lesion is the C in ABCDE and needs evaluation.

options.text: "I only need to check the skin that gets sun."
options.rationale: The exam covers all skin, including areas that rarely see sun.

options.text: "A mole that changes slowly over months is not a concern."
options.rationale: Evolving is the E in ABCDE. Any change needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm, evolving. Any one feature means the lesion gets checked.
questions.strategy: Three options talk the client out of getting a lesion checked. The correct statement is the one that sends the lesion for evaluation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Two colors is C. Change over months is E.
"Only" sun exposed skin is too narrow.

elimination.verdict: The pencil eraser statement matches D, greater than 6 mm.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with thin, transparent skin needs to be moved up in bed. Which action best protects the client's skin?

options.text: Pull the client up by the upper arms
options.rationale: Grasping and dragging causes skin tears, often on the upper arms.

options.text: Have the client push up with the heels
options.rationale: Heels drag across the sheet, which creates friction and shear.

options.text: Slide the client up on a dry draw sheet without lifting
options.rationale: Sliding without lifting still drags the skin across the sheet.

options.text: Use a lift sheet with a second staff member
options.rationale: Lifting rather than dragging prevents shear on fragile skin.

questions.takeaway: Aging flattens the junction between epidermis and dermis, so shear tears skin easily. Lift, never drag.
questions.strategy: Option C sounds close because it uses a sheet. The key word in the slide is lift.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Thin skin plus shear means tears.
Arms, heels and sliding all drag.

elimination.verdict: Lift sheet with two staff.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old has a warm, tender area on the lower leg with only faint redness and mild swelling. The client asks if this means the infection is mild. How does the nurse interpret the findings?

options.text: The infection is likely mild because redness is faint
options.rationale: This trusts the inflammatory signs that aging blunts.

options.text: Faint redness may underestimate how severe the infection is
options.rationale: Older adults have fewer immune cells in the skin, so redness and swelling understate the problem.

options.text: Faint redness means the infection is resolving
options.rationale: Nothing in the data shows improvement. Warmth and tenderness are present now.

options.text: The findings are expected aging changes
options.rationale: Warmth and tenderness are not aging changes. They point to inflammation.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, do not judge the severity of infection or injury by how red or swollen it looks.
questions.strategy: The client's question invites reassurance. The data do not support it.

strategies: Favor qualifiers
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fewer immune cells means a weaker inflammatory response.
Faint redness may hide a serious infection.

elimination.verdict: Faint redness may underestimate severity.

questions.stem: A bedbound client with a dark skin tone has a sacral area warmer and firmer than surrounding skin, without visible redness. The client reports pain there. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Reposition the client off the area and report it as possible pressure injury
options.rationale: In dark skin, warmth, firmness and pain may be the only signs of early or deep tissue pressure injury.

options.text: Document the sacrum as intact with no redness
options.rationale: Absent redness does not rule out pressure injury in dark skin.

options.text: Recheck the area at the end of the shift for redness
options.rationale: Waiting for redness that may never appear delays care.

options.text: Apply tape to hold a gauze pad over the area
options.rationale: Tape adds friction and does not relieve pressure.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, stage 1 and deep tissue pressure injury may show no redness. Palpate for warmth and firmness and ask about pain.
questions.strategy: Two options wait for redness. That is the trap the slide warns about.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Warmth, firmness and pain over a bony prominence.
Get the client off the area and report.

elimination.verdict: Reposition off the sacrum and report.

questions.stem: A client is having a punch biopsy of a draining leg lesion, with one sample for pathology and one for culture. The client says, "I signed the form, but I don't know what you are removing." Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the provider to explain the procedure again before starting
options.rationale: The client signed but does not understand, so consent is not yet informed. Explaining the procedure is the provider's job.

options.text: Place the pathology sample in 10% formalin
options.rationale: Formalin preserves tissue for the pathologist.

options.text: Place the culture sample in sterile saline
options.rationale: A draining lesion is cultured to find organisms, and saline keeps them alive.

options.text: Set up a sterile field before the procedure
options.rationale: A biopsy breaks the skin, so it is done with sterile technique.

options.text: Place the culture sample in formalin with the pathology sample
options.rationale: Formalin kills the organisms, so the culture would grow nothing.

options.text: Tell the client the numbing injection will not hurt
options.rationale: Local anesthetic stings briefly. Honest preparation builds trust.

questions.takeaway: Before a biopsy, confirm the client understands what was signed. Formalin goes with pathology and sterile saline goes with culture.
questions.strategy: Use the client's statement. A signature without understanding is not informed consent, so it has to be resolved before anything else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Not knowing what is being removed means consent is not informed.

steps.action: Match each sample to its purpose
steps.detail: Tissue for pathology goes in formalin. Organisms for culture go in saline.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old is receiving IV fluids for dehydration. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand stays tented
options.rationale: Tenting means poor turgor. Aging skin on the hand also loses elasticity, so it misleads.

options.text: Skin on the lower legs is dry and flaky
options.rationale: Dry skin is common with aging and does not show hydration status.

options.text: Skin over the abdomen returns immediately when pinched
options.rationale: Turgor is checked on the abdomen or radial wrist in older adults. Immediate return shows improved hydration.

options.text: The client is sweating more than before
options.rationale: Older adults sweat less, so sweating is not a reliable indicator.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, check turgor on the abdomen or radial wrist so lost elasticity is not mistaken for dehydration.
questions.strategy: Option A is the expected site for younger adults. In an older adult, the site matters as much as the result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Abdomen or radial wrist.
Immediate return.

elimination.verdict: Abdominal skin returns immediately.

questions.stem: The nurse performs skin assessments on four hospitalized older adults during morning care. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Cherry angiomas scattered on the trunk of a 70-year-old
options.rationale: Benign proliferation of capillaries common with aging.

options.text: Yellow gray thickened toenails in an 80-year-old
options.rationale: Expected aging change. Monitor for fungal infection.

options.text: Brown age spots on the backs of the hands
options.rationale: Sun related melanocyte hyperplasia. Track for change.

options.text: New petechiae on the abdomen below the nipple line
options.rationale: Petechiae below the nipple line may signal a serious problem such as DIC. Report immediately.

questions.takeaway: Petechiae below the nipple line are an action alert. Report them right away.
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected aging changes. Look for the one that is new and points to bleeding.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Angiomas, thick toenails, age spots.
New petechiae below the nipple line.

elimination.verdict: Petechiae below the nipple line.

questions.stem: A client develops an itchy rash on the trunk. The client started a new blood pressure drug 5 days ago and changed laundry detergent last week. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply an over the counter anti itch cream
options.rationale: Treats the symptom before the cause is known.

options.text: Ask when the rash began in relation to each change
options.rationale: Timing links the rash to the drug or the allergen. Assessment comes first.

options.text: Tell the client to stop taking the new drug
options.rationale: Stopping a prescribed drug is not the nurse's call. Assess and report.

options.text: Reassure the client that detergent rashes are harmless
options.rationale: Assumes a cause without assessing.

questions.takeaway: When a skin change appears, ask whether it began after a new drug or a new product. Timing guides the provider.
questions.strategy: Two causes are in the stem on purpose. You cannot pick one without asking about timing.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New drug and new detergent.
Ask about timing.

elimination.verdict: Ask when the rash began in relation to each change.

questions.scenario:
A client with a very dark skin tone has the following findings.
Platelets 18,000/mm3 and hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL.
Left calf warm and firm compared with the right, with no redness seen.
A dark band in one fingernail that the client says has been there since adolescence.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is appropriate or not appropriate for this client.

rows.text: Inspects the conjunctiva and oral mucosa for petechiae
rows.rationale: With platelets this low, bleeding into the skin is likely, and petechiae show best in mucosa and conjunctiva in dark skin.

rows.text: Judges pallor from the color of the sun exposed forearm
rows.rationale: Sun exposure darkens the forearm and hides pallor. Use mucous membranes instead.

rows.text: Inspects the mucous membranes for an ash gray tone
rows.rationale: With a hemoglobin of 7.4, pallor is expected, and in very dark skin it shows as ash gray mucosa.

rows.text: Documents no inflammation in the left calf because it is not red
rows.rationale: Inflammation in dark skin may not look red. The warmth and firmness compared with the right calf need follow up.

rows.text: Reports the fingernail band as an urgent new finding
rows.rationale: The band has been present since adolescence, and melanonychia is common in dark skin. Document it as baseline.

questions.takeaway: Let this client's labs and history direct where you look. In dark skin, check mucosa and conjunctiva, compare warmth and firmness side to side, and separate a long standing variant from a new finding.
questions.strategy: Tie each action to a line in the excerpt. Low platelets and low hemoglobin send you to the mucosa, the calf needs palpation, and the nail band is old.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Low platelets mean petechiae. Low hemoglobin means pallor. Look in mucosa and conjunctiva.
Warmth and firmness on one side are the cue in the calf.
A band present since adolescence is baseline.

elimination.verdict: Appropriate, not, appropriate, not, not.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches an older adult with very dry skin. Which statement shows the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I'll take a hot shower every day to soften my skin."
options.rationale: Hot water and daily bathing dry the skin further.

options.text: "I'll use plenty of soap all over to stay clean."
options.rationale: Soap dries skin. Use it only on the axillae, groin, scalp and soles.

options.text: "I'll bathe in warm water three times a week and moisturize while I'm still damp."
options.rationale: Less frequent warm baths with moisturizer on damp skin hold in water.

options.text: "I'll let my skin air dry fully before using lotion."
options.rationale: Moisturizer works best on skin that is still damp.

questions.takeaway: Dry aging skin: warm baths about three times a week, limited soap, emollients on damp skin.
questions.strategy: Hot and daily sound clean and soothing. Both dry aging skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Hot daily showers and soap everywhere.
Apply while damp.

elimination.verdict: Warm baths three times a week, moisturize while damp.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with thick, yellowed toenails has an SpO2 of 89%. How does the nurse assess for cyanosis and perfusion?

options.text: Check capillary refill on the great toenail
options.rationale: Thick toenails hide the nail bed. The reading is unreliable.

options.text: Inspect the skin of the lower legs for color
options.rationale: Lower leg skin is not where cyanosis shows reliably.

options.text: Wait for the toenail beds to turn blue
options.rationale: Reduced nail bed blood flow in aging makes this late and unreliable.

options.text: Use fingernails for capillary refill and inspect the oral mucosa
options.rationale: Fingernails are thinner. The oral mucosa shows cyanosis more reliably in older adults.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, use fingernails for capillary refill and the oral mucosa for cyanosis.
questions.strategy: Toenails are the obvious choice because the stem mentions them. That mention tells you not to use them.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Oxygenation is the concern.
Fingernails and oral mucosa.

elimination.verdict: Fingernails for refill, oral mucosa for cyanosis.

questions.stem: A client with pale patches on the back is about to have a Wood lamp examination. She is anxious and asks the nurse to keep the overhead lights on. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the overhead lights on to ease her anxiety
options.rationale: The patches will not show under the lamp in a lit room, so the exam would be wasted.

options.text: Explain that a dark room lets the patches show, and stay with her during the brief, painless exam
options.rationale: The exam needs a darkened room. Explaining why and staying with her addresses her anxiety without spoiling the result.

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative before the exam
options.rationale: The exam is noninvasive and painless. A sedative adds risk for a problem that reassurance can solve.

options.text: Postpone the exam until she feels calmer
options.rationale: Delays the diagnosis when a simple explanation is enough.

questions.takeaway: A Wood lamp exam is painless and noninvasive, and it only works in a darkened room. Meet anxiety with explanation and presence.
questions.strategy: Two needs compete: the client's comfort and a valid exam. Look for the option that meets both.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The lamp only works in the dark.
Explain and stay with her instead of sedating or delaying.

elimination.verdict: Darken the room, explain why and stay with her.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old who gardens daily receives teaching on skin cancer prevention. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I'll wear a hat and SPF 30 sunscreen and stay out of the midday sun."
options.rationale: Aging skin has less melanocyte activity and burns more easily. Hats, SPF 30 or higher and midday avoidance protect it.

options.text: "A base tan from a tanning bed will protect me."
options.rationale: Tanning beds add UV damage.

options.text: "I only need sunscreen when I go to the beach."
options.rationale: UV exposure happens in daily life, not only at the beach.

options.text: "My skin is darker now, so I won't burn."
options.rationale: Aging decreases melanocyte activity, which raises sunburn risk.

questions.takeaway: Teach adults to use sunscreen and limit sun and UV exposure. Older adults burn more easily.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option gives the client a reason to skip protection.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tanning bed.
"Only" and "won't".

elimination.verdict: Hat, SPF 30, avoid midday sun.

questions.stem: A client's palms and the skin around the mouth look yellow orange. The sclera and oral mucosa are not yellow. The client drinks carrot juice daily. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: Jaundice from liver disease is likely
options.rationale: Jaundice shows in the sclera and mucous membranes, which are clear here.

options.text: Carotenemia from diet is likely
options.rationale: Carotene colors the palms and perioral skin and spares the sclera and mucosa.

options.text: Uremia from kidney disease is likely
options.rationale: Urochrome gives a generalized color without this dietary link.

options.text: Pallor from anemia is likely
options.rationale: Pallor is white or ash gray, not yellow orange.

questions.takeaway: Yellow skin with clear sclera points to carotene. Yellow sclera points to bilirubin.
questions.strategy: Yellow skin tempts you toward jaundice. The clear sclera rules it out.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear sclera rules out jaundice.
Daily carrot juice.

elimination.verdict: Carotenemia.

caseStudies.title: Older adult with pressure injury risk after a fall
caseStudies.intro: A 79-year-old with a dark skin tone is admitted after lying on the floor at home for about 12 hours.

entries.text: 79-year-old with a dark skin tone admitted after lying on the floor at home for about 12 hours. Area over the sacrum is darker than surrounding skin, warm and firm. Client reports pain over the sacrum. Skin on forearms is thin and transparent. Bruises on both upper arms. Dark band in one fingernail, present for years per client. Alert and oriented x4.
T 37.0 C; HR 92; RR 18; BP 118/70; SpO2 95% on room air
Lives alone. Hypertension. Poor oral intake for 2 days. Turgor on abdomen tents briefly.

question.nursesNote: 0800: 79-year-old with a dark skin tone admitted after lying on the floor at home for about 12 hours. Area over the sacrum is darker than surrounding skin, warm and firm. Client reports pain over the sacrum. Skin on forearms is thin and transparent. Bruises on both upper arms. Dark band in one fingernail, present for years per client. Alert and oriented x4.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Area over the sacrum is darker than surrounding skin, warm and firm
segments.rationale: In dark skin, a darker, warm, firm area over a bony prominence may be early pressure injury.

segments.text: Client reports pain over the sacrum
segments.rationale: Pain often comes before visible change in deep tissue pressure injury.

segments.text: Skin on forearms is thin and transparent
segments.rationale: An expected aging change. It guides gentle handling.

segments.text: Bruises on both upper arms
segments.rationale: Bruising where a client is grasped points to shear risk and possible skin tears. Assess the cause.

segments.text: Dark band in one fingernail, present for years per client
segments.rationale: Melanonychia is common in dark skin and is unchanged.

segments.text: Alert and oriented x4
segments.rationale: Normal.

question.takeaway: In dark skin, a darker, warm, firm, painful area over a bony prominence is a pressure injury until proven otherwise.
question.strategy: Two findings are expected or long standing. Follow up what is new or tied to injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Thin skin and the old nail band are baseline.
Sacral changes, pain, bruises.

elimination.verdict: Sacral area, sacral pain, upper arm bruises.

question.scenario: The nurse reviews the admission findings.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate what it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Warm, firm sacral area darker than surrounding skin
rows.rationale: Twelve hours of pressure on the sacrum with darker, warm, firm tissue.

rows.text: Pain over the sacrum without visible redness
rows.rationale: Pain and temperature change can precede visible deep tissue injury.

rows.text: Thin, transparent forearm skin
rows.rationale: Epidermal and dermal thinning with age.

rows.text: Long standing dark band in a fingernail
rows.rationale: Melanonychia is common in dark skin.

question.takeaway: Twelve hours of pressure plus warmth, firmness and pain at the sacrum point to pressure injury even without redness.
question.strategy: Ask what is new and linked to the fall. That is the injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Twelve hours on the floor means sacral pressure.
Thin skin and nail band.

elimination.verdict: Injury, injury, aging, variant.

question.stem: Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Disturbed body image related to bruising
options.rationale: Real but not the threat to tissue.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about monthly skin self exams
options.rationale: Health promotion can wait.

options.text: Impaired tissue integrity related to pressure and shear
options.rationale: Ongoing pressure and shear can turn early injury into an open wound.

options.text: Risk for sunburn related to aging skin
options.rationale: Not relevant to a hospitalized client now.

question.takeaway: Physical threat to tissue comes before body image and teaching.
question.strategy: Body image is the emotionally compelling distractor.

strategies: Priority key word
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Tissue breakdown can progress.
Body image and teaching come later.

elimination.verdict: Impaired tissue integrity.

question.stem: Which interventions does the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Relieves pressure on the sacrum.

options.text: Use a lift sheet when moving the client
options.rationale: Prevents shear on thin skin.

options.text: Position to promote air circulation to skinfolds
options.rationale: Prevents moisture buildup that leads to breakdown.

options.text: Encourage protein and fluid intake
options.rationale: Supports healing in fragile skin.

options.text: Secure dressings on the forearms with adhesive tape
options.rationale: Tape tears thin skin when removed.

options.text: Judge improvement by the amount of redness
options.rationale: Redness may not appear in dark skin. Use warmth, firmness and pain.

question.takeaway: Pressure relief, lift sheets, air to skinfolds, protein and fluids. No tape on fragile skin.
question.strategy: Each wrong option uses a habit that fails thin or dark skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Turn, lift, air, nutrition.
Both fail this client.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

entries.text: Client restless. SpO2 89% on room air. Toenails thick and yellowed.

question.stem: Which action does the nurse take to assess for cyanosis?

options.text: Check capillary refill on the great toenail
options.rationale: Thick toenails make the reading unreliable.

options.text: Inspect the lips, tongue and conjunctiva for a gray or bluish tinge
options.rationale: In dark skin, cyanosis shows as gray lips and tongue or a bluish conjunctiva.

options.text: Look for blue color on the face
options.rationale: Facial skin color hides cyanosis in dark skin.

options.text: Pinch the skin on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Turgor checks hydration, not oxygenation.

question.takeaway: In dark skin, look for cyanosis in the lips, tongue, conjunctiva and fingernail beds.
question.strategy: The toenail detail in the update is there to steer you away from toes.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Oxygenation first.
Lips, tongue, conjunctiva.

elimination.verdict: Inspect lips, tongue and conjunctiva.

entries.text: Sacral area same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin. Denies sacral pain. Turgor on abdomen returns immediately. New skin tear on left upper arm noted after transfer. Lips and conjunctiva pink, SpO2 96%.

question.scenario: The nurse reviews the client's status on day 3.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the plan of care was effective or not effective.

rows.text: Sacral area same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin
rows.rationale: Pressure relief allowed the tissue to recover.

rows.text: Denies sacral pain
rows.rationale: Pain was an early cue. Its absence supports recovery.

rows.text: Turgor on abdomen returns immediately
rows.rationale: Fluid intake has restored hydration.

rows.text: New skin tear on left upper arm after transfer
rows.rationale: Shear prevention failed during transfer. Review use of lift sheets.

rows.text: Lips and conjunctiva pink, SpO2 96%
rows.rationale: No signs of cyanosis.

question.takeaway: Evaluate each goal separately. One new skin tear means shear prevention needs review.
question.strategy: Four findings improved. The new injury is the one that tells you the plan has a gap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Sacrum, pain, hydration and oxygenation improved.
Skin tear after transfer.

elimination.verdict: Effective except the new skin tear.

chapters.title: Care of Clients with Conditions of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client on bed rest has a Braden score of 13. The head of the bed is at 45 degrees and the client keeps sliding down. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Place a donut cushion under the sacrum
options.rationale: Donut devices compress the surrounding tissue and cut off capillary flow.

options.text: Reposition the client every 4 hours
options.rationale: Turning is at least every 2 hours. A Braden of 13 means higher risk, not a longer interval.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less
options.rationale: Sliding down with the head raised creates shear. Keeping the head at 30 degrees or below prevents it.

options.text: Massage the sacrum after each position change
options.rationale: Massage damages fragile capillaries. Never massage reddened or at risk skin.

questions.takeaway: A low Braden score plus sliding in bed means shear. Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or less.
questions.strategy: The sliding is the cue. Ask what force is acting on the sacrum, then pick the action that removes it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Skin stays put while deeper tissue slides. That is shear.
Donuts and massage injure tissue.
Every 4 hours is too long for a high risk client.

elimination.verdict: Lower the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less.

questions.stem: A client started allopurinol 10 days ago. Today the client has painful red skin with blisters on the trunk and erosions in the mouth. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply a topical corticosteroid to the blisters
options.rationale: Does nothing about the cause. The reaction keeps progressing while the drug continues.

options.text: Hold the allopurinol and notify the provider
options.rationale: This looks like SJS. Stopping the triggering drug is the first step.

options.text: Give a warm colloidal oatmeal bath
options.rationale: Comfort care for itching. It does not stop a life threatening drug reaction.

options.text: Teach the client to avoid sun exposure
options.rationale: Unrelated to a drug triggered cutaneous reaction.

questions.takeaway: In SJS or TEN, the first step is to stop the suspected drug. Then support airway, fluids, temperature, pain, eyes and infection prevention.
questions.strategy: Allopurinol is a high risk drug for SJS. Mucosal erosions with blistering skin point to it. Remove the cause before treating the skin.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Link the drug to the rash
steps.detail: Allopurinol is on the high risk list.
Only one option stops the trigger.
Steroid cream and baths come later, if at all.

elimination.verdict: Hold the allopurinol and notify the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses the sacrum of a client with dark skin who has been on bed rest for 3 days. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Skin color matches the surrounding area
options.rationale: Expected. No color difference from nearby skin.

options.text: Skin is dry and intact
options.rationale: Intact dry skin is the goal.

options.text: Client reports no discomfort when turning
options.rationale: Absence of pain is reassuring.

options.text: Area feels warmer and firmer than nearby skin
options.rationale: In dark skin, redness is hard to see. Warmth, induration, edema and pain are the early signs of damage.

questions.takeaway: In darker skin, assess temperature, firmness, edema and pain. Do not wait for visible redness.
questions.strategy: Three options describe normal skin. The finding that differs from the surrounding tissue is the one to act on.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Recall what changes in dark skin
steps.detail: Redness may not show. Feel the skin instead.
Matching color, intact skin and no pain are normal.
Warm and firm compared with nearby skin.

elimination.verdict: Warmer and firmer than nearby skin.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with fair skin and several moles about skin cancer prevention. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "A base tan from a tanning bed will protect me."
options.rationale: Tanning beds are UV exposure. Avoid them.

options.text: "I only need sunscreen on beach days."
options.rationale: Sun exposure happens daily, including at work and on errands.

options.text: "I will check my skin monthly and photograph my moles."
options.rationale: Monthly self exam with photos or a body map helps catch change early.

options.text: "I will schedule my outdoor runs around noon."
options.rationale: Midday sun is the strongest. Run early or late.

questions.takeaway: Prevention means avoiding midday sun and tanning beds. Use sunscreen and protective clothing. Do a monthly self exam that tracks moles.
questions.strategy: Three statements increase UV exposure. The correct one adds early detection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Tanning bed and noon runs add UV.
"Only" beach days leaves daily exposure unprotected.
Monthly checks with photos track change.

elimination.verdict: Monthly skin checks with photographs.

questions.stem: A stage 3 sacral pressure injury measured 3 x 2 x 1 cm last week. Today it measures 4 x 3 x 2 cm with new foul smelling drainage. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the changes to the provider
options.rationale: A larger, deeper wound with a change in odor and drainage is deterioration and possible infection. Report it.

options.text: Continue the current dressing plan
options.rationale: The plan is failing. Continuing ignores deterioration.

options.text: Document the findings and recheck next week
options.rationale: Documenting alone delays care for a worsening wound.

options.text: Massage the wound edges to improve circulation
options.rationale: Massage damages tissue and does not treat infection.

questions.takeaway: Sudden enlargement or a change in exudate amount, color or odor gets reported to the provider.
questions.strategy: Compare the two measurements. Growth plus a new odor means the wound is getting worse.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every dimension grew.
New foul odor suggests infection.
Waiting or continuing does not address a worsening wound.

elimination.verdict: Report the changes to the provider.

questions.stem: A client develops raised red wheals and itching 1 hour after a first dose of an oral antibiotic. Breathing is unlabored. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the wheals
options.rationale: Heat dilates vessels and makes hives worse.

options.text: Encourage moderate exercise to distract from itching
options.rationale: Overexertion dilates vessels and worsens hives.

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider
options.rationale: Hives come from an allergen. Removing the trigger comes first.

options.text: Apply a scented lotion to soothe the skin
options.rationale: Perfumes irritate skin and do not address the cause.

questions.takeaway: Urticaria treatment starts with removing the trigger, then antihistamines. Avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion.
questions.strategy: Breathing is fine, so the airway is not the issue. The new drug is the likely trigger.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unlabored, so no emergency step needed.
A new antibiotic 1 hour ago.
Heat and exercise worsen hives.

elimination.verdict: Hold the next dose and notify the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse turned a client off a reddened sacral area 30 minutes ago. Which finding indicates the repositioning plan is working?

options.text: The redness blanches with pressure and color returns
options.rationale: Blanching shows capillaries are refilling. Perfusion is adequate.

options.text: The redness stays when pressed with a gloved finger
options.rationale: Nonblanchable redness means tissue damage. That is a stage 1 injury.

options.text: The area has become maroon in color
options.rationale: Maroon or purple suggests deep tissue pressure injury.

options.text: The area is cooler and firmer than nearby skin
options.rationale: Change in temperature and firmness can precede tissue damage.

questions.takeaway: Blanchable redness means perfusion is intact. Nonblanchable redness means damage has started.
questions.strategy: Three options describe tissue injury. Only one shows blood flow returning.

strategies: Odd man wins
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Blanches versus stays red.
Capillaries refill when pressure is released.
Maroon color and firmness are damage.

elimination.verdict: Redness that blanches and returns.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has thick, long toenails and asks the nurse to trim them. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Trim the nails straight across with clippers
options.rationale: Cutting can break the skin in a client with diabetes. Infection heals poorly.

options.text: Soak the feet and file the nails short
options.rationale: Shaping thick toenails still risks a break in the skin. For clients with diabetes, toenail care is referred to podiatry.

options.text: Teach the client to trim the nails at home
options.rationale: Clients with diabetes should avoid cutting their own toenails.

options.text: Arrange a referral to a podiatrist
options.rationale: Podiatry handles toenails in diabetes to avoid breaks in skin.

questions.takeaway: In diabetes, nobody but a podiatrist cuts the toenails. A small break in the skin can become a nonhealing wound.
questions.strategy: Diabetes is the cue. Ask who can safely do this, not how to do it.

strategies: Global or umbrella option
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diabetes slows healing and dulls sensation.

steps.action: Cut every option that cuts nails
steps.detail: Clipping, filing and home trimming all risk a break in the skin.
Podiatry.

elimination.verdict: Refer to a podiatrist.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with pressure injuries. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Stage 1 heel injury on heel protectors
options.rationale: Intact skin with a plan in place. Stable.

options.text: Stage 2 coccyx injury with scant serous drainage
options.rationale: Expected for a partial thickness wound.

options.text: Unstageable heel with dry, stable eschar
options.rationale: Stable eschar is left alone. No urgent need.

options.text: Stage 4 sacral injury with new fever of 101.8 F
options.rationale: Exposed tissue plus a new fever suggests spreading infection such as osteomyelitis or sepsis.

questions.takeaway: A new fever in a client with an open wound signals systemic infection. That client is unstable.
questions.strategy: All four have a pressure injury. Look for the new systemic change.

strategies: Priority key word
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Only one client has a new change.
Fever with a deep wound is unstable.
Heel protector, serous drainage and stable eschar are expected.

elimination.verdict: The stage 4 client with a new fever.

questions.stem: An incontinent client has redness in the perineal area. Which plan best protects the skin?

options.text: Clean promptly with mild soap, pat dry, apply a zinc barrier cream
options.rationale: Removing moisture fast and adding a barrier protects the skin.

options.text: Scrub with deodorant soap after each episode
options.rationale: Scrubbing and deodorant soaps damage skin.

options.text: Check the incontinence brief every 4 hours
options.rationale: Check under incontinence products at least every 2 hours.

options.text: Leave the skin open to air without cream
options.rationale: Leaves the skin unprotected from the next episode.

questions.takeaway: Clean promptly with mild soap and warm water, pat dry, apply a barrier cream and check briefs every 2 hours.
questions.strategy: Moisture is the problem. Pick the option that removes it gently and blocks the next exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Moisture and incontinence.
Scrubbing and deodorant soap.
Every 4 hours is too long.

elimination.verdict: Clean, pat dry and apply barrier cream.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 3 pressure injury is on a high protein diet and negative pressure wound therapy. Which finding indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Yellow slough covers half the wound bed
options.rationale: Slough is dead tissue. It slows healing.

options.text: Wound bed is beefy red, moist and smaller
options.rationale: Healthy granulation and a shrinking wound show healing by second intention.

options.text: Redness extends 2 cm beyond the wound edge
options.rationale: Spreading redness suggests cellulitis.

options.text: Drainage has turned greenish with a fruity odor
options.rationale: Suggests Pseudomonas infection.

questions.takeaway: Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist and slightly spongy. Healing open wounds get smaller as they contract.
questions.strategy: Three options describe worsening or infection. The right one describes new tissue and a smaller wound.

strategies: Odd man wins
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beefy red, moist, slightly spongy.
Spreading redness and green fruity drainage.
Slough is necrotic.

elimination.verdict: Beefy red, moist and smaller.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 4 pressure injury eats about 25% of meals and has a low prealbumin. Which referral does the nurse request?

options.text: Registered dietitian nutritionist
options.rationale: Severe protein deficiency stops healing. The RDN sets protein, calorie and fluid goals.

options.text: Social worker
options.rationale: Helps with cost and resources, not the intake problem.

options.text: Physical therapist
options.rationale: Helps offload pressure and mobility. It does not fix protein deficit.

options.text: Occupational therapist
options.rationale: Helps with ADLs. Not the problem in this stem.

questions.takeaway: Poor intake and low protein markers in a client with a wound means an RDN consult. Healing stops without protein.
questions.strategy: The data in the stem are all about nutrition. Match the referral to the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Priority key word

steps.detail: 25% of meals and low prealbumin.
Nutrition.

steps.action: Keep the others for other problems
steps.detail: PT, OT and social work have roles, not this one.

elimination.verdict: Registered dietitian nutritionist.

questions.stem: A client has an unstageable heel pressure injury covered by dry, hard, intact eschar. There are no signs of infection. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Soften the eschar with a wet dressing
options.rationale: Stable heel eschar is left in place. It acts as a natural cover.

options.text: Leave the eschar intact and float the heel
options.rationale: Avoid disturbing stable eschar on the heels. Offloading prevents further damage.

options.text: Gently peel the edges of the eschar
options.rationale: Disrupts a stable barrier and invites infection.

options.text: Request mechanical debridement
options.rationale: Contraindicated for intact eschar without infection.

questions.takeaway: Dry, stable, intact heel eschar without infection is left alone. Offload the heel and watch for infection.
questions.strategy: The phrase "no signs of infection" decides it. Debridement is for necrosis with infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Odd man wins

steps.detail: Dry, hard, intact, no infection.
Softening, peeling and debriding all remove eschar.
Leave it and offload.

elimination.verdict: Leave the eschar intact and float the heel.

questions.stem: The nurse observes an assistive personnel caring for a client with a Braden score of 12. Which actions indicate the AP understands pressure injury prevention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lifts the client up in bed with a draw sheet
options.rationale: Lifting instead of dragging prevents friction.

options.text: Positions the client in a 30 degree side tilt
options.rationale: A 30 degree tilt keeps weight off the trochanter.

options.text: Places a pillow under the calves to float the heels
options.rationale: Floating heels removes pressure.

options.text: Checks under the incontinence brief every 2 hours
options.rationale: Matches the every 2 hour check.

options.text: Massages a reddened area on the sacrum
options.rationale: Massage damages capillaries. Never massage reddened areas.

options.text: Places a donut cushion under the coccyx
options.rationale: Donut devices compress surrounding tissue.

questions.takeaway: Lift, tilt to 30 degrees, float heels, check briefs every 2 hours. Never massage red areas or use donut cushions.
questions.strategy: Two actions feel kind but cause harm. Massage and donuts are the classic traps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Does it reduce pressure, friction or moisture?
Massage and donut cushions.
Lift, tilt, float, check.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.scenario: A client has a stage 3 pressure injury. The nurse reviews today's wound assessment at the dressing change.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected healing or requires reporting to the provider.

rows.text: Moist, beefy red granulation tissue
rows.rationale: Healthy granulation.

rows.text: Greenish drainage with a fruity odor
rows.rationale: Suggests Pseudomonas infection.

rows.text: Length and width smaller than last week
rows.rationale: The wound is contracting.

rows.text: Redness spreading 3 cm beyond the wound edge
rows.rationale: Possible cellulitis.

rows.text: Granulation tissue turning pale and dry
rows.rationale: A change in granulation color or texture signals a problem.

rows.text: Scant serous drainage
rows.rationale: Small clear drainage is normal.
