questions.takeaway: Always use a leading zero before a decimal. Never use a trailing zero after one. A leading zero is always placed in front of a decimal, so write 0.25 rather than.25. A trailing zero is never written after a decimal point in a drug dose, because a missed decimal means the patient receives ten times the dose. Write 2 mg, not 2.0 mg.
questions.strategy: Both rules exist because of the same failure: a decimal point that does not reproduce or is not seen. The trailing zero is the more dangerous because the error is always a factor of ten upward.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three of four orders contain one.
No leading zero.
A trailing zero.
Also a trailing zero, with the same tenfold risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: A leading zero is always placed in front of a decimal so the point is not missed.

questions.concept: A leading zero is always placed in front of a decimal, so write 0.25 rather than.25. A trailing zero is never written after a decimal point in a drug dose, because a missed decimal means the patient receives ten times the dose. Write 2 mg, not 2.0 mg.

skills.title: Head-to-Toe Assessment
skills.subtitle: Sequence, the general survey, breath and heart sounds, and assessing with privacy and respect

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a sore throat and difficulty swallowing has a harsh, high-pitched sound over the upper airway audible without a stethoscope. His respiratory rate is 28 and he is sitting forward. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Reposition the patient and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Defers an airway emergency.

options.text: Respond immediately, assess the airway, obtain vital signs, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Stridor is turbulent airflow through a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often a medical emergency.

options.text: Document the finding and continue the head-to-toe examination
options.rationale: Completing the examination while the upper airway is obstructing prioritizes the routine over the emergency.

options.text: Ask the patient to cough and re-auscultate
options.rationale: Coughing clears secretions in the lower airways and does not relieve upper airway obstruction.

questions.takeaway: Stridor is caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often a medical emergency.
questions.strategy: Stridor is the one adventitious sound on this list that stops the assessment. Every other abnormal sound is documented and reported; this one is acted on now.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: High-pitched, upper airway, audible without a stethoscope.
Both continue or defer during an airway emergency.
Coughing does not clear an upper airway obstruction.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: stridor is turbulent airflow through a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often a medical emergency.

questions.concept: Stridor is caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often a medical emergency.

questions.stem: A nurse begins an admission assessment on a 57-year-old who has arrived from home by ambulance. Before examining any body system she completes the general survey. Which elements does it include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Vital signs
options.rationale: Part of the survey that opens the review of primary health problems.

options.text: Height and weight
options.rationale: And both are needed for weight-based dosing later.

options.text: General behavior and appearance
options.rationale: What you notice before any equipment is used.

options.text: A safety scan of the room for potential hazards
options.rationale: Correct, and it is the part students skip because it is not about the patient's body.

options.text: A complete neurological examination including cranial nerves
options.rationale: A detailed system examination that follows the survey rather than forming part of it.

questions.takeaway: The general survey begins the review of primary health problems and includes vital signs, height and weight, general behavior and appearance, and a safety scan of the room for potential hazards.
questions.strategy: The safety scan is easy to forget because nothing about it is clinical. It is also the part that prevents the fall you would otherwise be documenting later.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An overview, not a system examination.
A detailed neurological examination comes later.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: The general survey begins the review of primary health problems and includes vital signs, height and weight, general behavior and appearance, and a safety scan of the room for potential hazards.

questions.stem: A nurse places her stethoscope at the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line to count an apical pulse before administering digoxin. The patient has an irregular rhythm. Which valve and sound correspond to this location?

options.text: The pulmonic valve, where S2 is best heard
options.rationale: Pulmonic is the second left intercostal space at the left sternal border.

options.text: Erb's point
options.rationale: Erb's point is the third left intercostal space.

options.text: The mitral valve, where S1 is best heard
options.rationale: S1 is the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, and the apical site is the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

options.text: The aortic valve, where S2 is best heard
options.rationale: Aortic is the second right intercostal space at the sternal border.

questions.takeaway: S1 is mitral and tricuspid closure. S2 is aortic and pulmonic closure. The apical site is the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line. S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves; S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. Aortic: second right intercostal space at the sternal border. Pulmonic: second left intercostal space. Erb's point: third left intercostal space. Tricuspid: fourth left intercostal space.
questions.strategy: The landmarks run down the chest in order: aortic and pulmonic at the second space, Erb's at the third, tricuspid at the fourth, mitral at the fifth.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fifth left intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Both sit at the second intercostal space.
Erb's point is the third space.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: mitral, where S1 is best heard.

questions.concept: S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves; S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. Aortic: second right intercostal space at the sternal border. Pulmonic: second left intercostal space. Erb's point: third left intercostal space. Tricuspid: fourth left intercostal space. Mitral or apical: fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews abnormal lung sounds with a student before a clinical shift on a respiratory unit, where four patients have different presentations. The student asks how to tell the sounds apart at the bedside. Which descriptions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Crackles result from sudden reinflation of groups of alveoli and are not cleared by coughing
options.rationale: The failure to clear with coughing is what separates them from secretions in larger airways.

options.text: Rhonchi arise from muscular spasm, fluid, or mucus in the larger airways
options.rationale: Also from new growth such as a tumor or from external pressure causing turbulence.

options.text: Wheezes are high-pitched sounds from airflow through a severely narrowed or obstructed airway
options.rationale: The narrowing produces the pitch.

options.text: A pleural friction rub comes from inflamed pleura rubbing against each other
options.rationale: Parietal pleura against visceral pleura.

options.text: Crackles clear readily once the patient coughs
options.rationale: The defining feature is that they do not clear with coughing.

questions.takeaway: Crackles come from alveoli and do not clear with coughing. Rhonchi come from larger airways. Wheezes come from narrowing. A rub comes from inflamed pleura. Crackles come from sudden reinflation of alveoli and are not cleared by coughing. Rhonchi come from spasm, fluid, or mucus in larger airways. Wheezes come from airflow through a severely narrowed airway. A pleural friction rub comes from inflamed parietal and visceral pleura rubbing together.
questions.strategy: Where the sound originates tells you whether coughing will help. Larger airway sounds may shift with a cough; alveolar crackles will not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alveoli, larger airways, narrowed airways, pleura.
Crackles not clearing with coughing is the defining feature.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Crackles come from sudden reinflation of alveoli and are not cleared by coughing. Rhonchi come from spasm, fluid, or mucus in larger airways. Wheezes come from airflow through a severely narrowed airway. A pleural friction rub comes from inflamed parietal and visceral pleura rubbing together.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultates the peripheral lung fields of a healthy adult during a routine assessment. She hears soft, breezy, low-pitched sounds with an inspiratory phase about three times longer than expiration. Which breath sound is this?

options.text: Rhonchi
options.rationale: An adventitious sound rather than a normal one.

options.text: Bronchovesicular
options.rationale: Medium-pitched and blowing, with inspiration equal to expiration, created by air moving through the large airways.

options.text: Vesicular
options.rationale: Created by air moving through the smaller airways, and heard over most of the peripheral lung fields.

options.text: Bronchial
options.rationale: Loud, high-pitched, and hollow, with expiration longer than inspiration in a 3 to 2 ratio, created by air moving through the trachea.

questions.takeaway: Vesicular is soft, low-pitched, inspiration three times expiration. Bronchovesicular is equal. Bronchial has expiration longer than inspiration. Vesicular sounds are soft, breezy, and low-pitched with inspiration three times longer than expiration, from smaller airways. Bronchovesicular are medium-pitched with inspiration equal to expiration, from large airways. Bronchial are loud, high-pitched, and hollow with expiration longer than inspiration in a 3 to 2 ratio, from the trachea.
questions.strategy: The inspiratory to expiratory ratio identifies all three at once: three to one is vesicular, one to one is bronchovesicular, two to three is bronchial.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inspiration three times longer than expiration.
Their ratios are 3 to 2 expiration-long and 1 to 1.
An adventitious sound.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: vesicular.

questions.concept: Vesicular sounds are soft, breezy, and low-pitched with inspiration three times longer than expiration, from smaller airways. Bronchovesicular are medium-pitched with inspiration equal to expiration, from large airways. Bronchial are loud, high-pitched, and hollow with expiration longer than inspiration in a 3 to 2 ratio, from the trachea.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient's neurological status. He states his name and that he is in the hospital, identifies the month and year correctly, and explains that he came in after a fall at home. How does the nurse document his orientation?

options.text: Confused, since he required prompting
options.rationale: Nothing in the description indicates prompting or an incorrect answer.

options.text: Alert and oriented times four
options.rationale: Person, place, time, and situation are all intact, which is what times four records.

options.text: Alert and oriented times three
options.rationale: Would mean one of the four is absent, and he has answered all four correctly.

options.text: Alert and oriented times two
options.rationale: Would leave two components unaccounted for.

questions.takeaway: Alert and oriented times four: person, place, time, and situation. Alert and oriented times four covers person, place, time, and situation, along with the ability to follow commands and clarity of speech. PERRLA records pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation.
questions.strategy: Situation is the component most often left out, and it is often the first to go. A patient can know who and where he is and have no idea why he is there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Name, place, date, and reason for admission.
Both undercount what he demonstrated.
No prompting or error is described.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: oriented times four.

questions.concept: Alert and oriented times four covers person, place, time, and situation, along with the ability to follow commands and clarity of speech. PERRLA records pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation.

questions.stem: An admission physical examination is due for a 63-year-old who speaks limited English, appears uneasy, and is sharing a room separated only by a curtain. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask permission before touching the patient
options.rationale: And it is what turns an examination into consented care.

options.text: Drape the patient thoroughly and use the bedside screen or curtains
options.rationale: Exposing only the area you are examining keeps him covered the rest of the time, which matters as much for dignity as for warmth.

options.text: Ask a family member to remain to help interpret
options.rationale: A family member may lack medical vocabulary and may alter the message. A qualified interpreter is required.

options.text: Use a gender-congruent provider to perform the physical assessment where indicated
options.rationale: Some patients will decline or hold back during an intimate assessment unless the examiner matches their preference, so asking costs nothing.

options.text: Complete the examination as quickly as possible to limit exposure
options.rationale: Speed does not reduce unease and it compromises thoroughness.

options.text: Proceed without explanation to keep the examination brief for an uneasy patient
options.rationale: Removes the explanation that would reduce the unease, and it bypasses consent.

questions.takeaway: Ask permission, drape thoroughly, use a professional interpreter, consider gender congruence, and attend to how you speak and stand. Ask permission before touching a patient, drape thoroughly and use the bedside screen or curtains, use a professional interpreter familiar with the patient's culture, use gender-congruent providers where indicated, and communicate respect through distance, attention, eye contact, tone, and volume.
questions.strategy: The wrong option sounds considerate. Shortening the encounter for an anxious patient removes exactly what would have made it tolerable.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Language and unease.
Speed is not the remedy for unease.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Ask permission before touching a patient, drape thoroughly and use the bedside screen or curtains, use a professional interpreter familiar with the patient's culture, use gender-congruent providers where indicated, and communicate respect through distance, attention, eye contact, tone, and volume.

questions.stem: A student asks why the abdominal assessment is performed in a different order from every other body system. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Palpation and percussion alter bowel sounds
options.rationale: The abdomen runs inspection, auscultation, then palpation and percussion, because touching changes what you would have heard.

options.text: Bowel sounds are loudest before any contact
options.rationale: The issue is that they are altered, not simply quieter.

options.text: Percussion is not used on the abdomen
options.rationale: Percussion is used on the abdomen. It comes after auscultation, because pressing on the abdomen first changes the bowel sounds.

options.text: Palpation is too uncomfortable to perform first
options.rationale: Tenderness is a finding rather than the reason the order changes.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, then auscultate, then palpate and percuss. Touching first changes the sounds you were about to assess. The abdominal assessment begins with inspection and follows with auscultation, because palpation and percussion alter the frequency and character of bowel sounds. Listen in each quadrant for at least 30 seconds.
questions.strategy: The reason matters more than the exception. Once you know palpation alters bowel sounds, the reordering follows without memorizing it as a separate rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Palpation and percussion change bowel sounds.
Tenderness is a finding rather than the reason the order changes.
The issue is that they are altered, not simply quieter.
It is used, and it is performed after auscultation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the abdomen runs inspection, auscultation, then palpation and percussion, because touching changes what you would have heard.

questions.concept: The abdominal assessment begins with inspection and follows with auscultation, because palpation and percussion alter the frequency and character of bowel sounds. Listen in each quadrant for at least 30 seconds.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a physical examination on a newly admitted patient, working through each body system in turn. She has completed the general survey and is beginning the respiratory assessment. In which order does she use the examination techniques?

options.text: Palpation, inspection, auscultation, percussion
options.rationale: Inspection always opens the examination.

options.text: Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
options.rationale: Auscultation comes first only during the abdominal assessment.

options.text: Percussion, auscultation, inspection, palpation
options.rationale: Reorders the sequence entirely.

options.text: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
options.rationale: The standard order for every system, and the abdomen is the single exception.

questions.takeaway: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, in that order, for every system except the abdomen. Examination techniques are used in the order inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation for every system except the abdomen.
questions.strategy: Inspection always comes first because looking costs nothing and changes nothing. The rest of the order runs from least to most disruptive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inspection opens every examination.
Look, feel, tap, listen.
That order belongs to the abdomen only.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the standard order for every system, and the abdomen is the single exception.

questions.concept: Examination techniques are used in the order inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation for every system except the abdomen.

questions.stem: A nurse is taking an admission history from a 71-year-old when he becomes acutely short of breath and is unable to answer further questions. His daughter is at the bedside. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Respond immediately to the identified need
options.rationale: Acute distress interrupts the assessment. The presenting problem is assessed and addressed first.

options.text: Obtain vital signs
options.rationale: Vital signs tell you how far he has moved from where he was ten minutes ago, which is what you need before you call anyone.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: Acute shortness of breath mid-assessment is a change the provider needs to know about now, not at the end of your round.

options.text: Complete the remaining systems before addressing the distress
options.rationale: Acute distress interrupts the assessment. The presenting problem comes first.

options.text: Ask the patient to rate the distress from 0 to 10
options.rationale: He is unable to answer questions, which is why the assessment stopped.

options.text: Ask the daughter to step out before assessing him
options.rationale: Removes a source of history at the moment it is most useful, and does not address the distress.

questions.takeaway: Acute distress: respond immediately, obtain vital signs, notify the provider. Unable to give information: family caregivers and the record. If a patient demonstrates acute distress: respond immediately to the identified need, obtain vital signs, and notify the provider. If a patient is unwilling or unable to provide information: seek it from family caregivers if present and review the record for baseline data.
questions.strategy: The examination is organized, and the organization yields to what the patient is doing. Prioritize based on presenting signs and symptoms.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Acute distress mid-assessment.
Completing the sequence while the patient is in distress.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: If a patient demonstrates acute distress: respond immediately to the identified need, obtain vital signs, and notify the provider. If a patient is unwilling or unable to provide information: seek it from family caregivers if present and review the record for baseline data.

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews assessment technique with a student after observing her examine two patients on a medical unit. She asks the student to describe the order she used and why. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I palpate the abdomen first so I know where the tenderness is before I listen."
options.rationale: The abdominal assessment begins with inspection and follows with auscultation, because palpation and percussion alter the frequency and character of bowel sounds.

options.text: "Every other system runs inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the abdomen is the single exception.

options.text: "Crackles are not cleared by coughing, which separates them from larger airway sounds."
options.rationale: Accurate. They arise from sudden reinflation of alveoli.

options.text: "Stridor is the one adventitious sound that stops the assessment."
options.rationale: Accurate. It indicates a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, auscultate, then palpate and percuss. Touching first changes what you were about to hear.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is efficient and defensible for any other system. The abdomen is the exception.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the incorrect sequence.
Auscultation precedes palpation in the abdomen.
General order, stridor, and crackles are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: palpation alters bowel sounds.

skills.title: Infection Prevention and Control
skills.subtitle: Chain of infection, hand hygiene, medical and surgical asepsis, and health care-associated infections

questions.stem: A student sets up a sterile field for a dressing change on a wound with a temperature of 38.4 C, then reaches across the field to retrieve gauze from the far side. Nothing visibly touched the drape. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Cover the field with a second sterile drape and proceed
options.rationale: Adding a drape over a contaminated field does not restore sterility.

options.text: Continue, since nothing visibly touched the field
options.rationale: You cannot tell by looking whether a field is contaminated. If there is doubt about whether something crossed it, treat it as contaminated.

options.text: Remove only the item nearest where she reached
options.rationale: The field is treated as a whole rather than as separate zones.

options.text: Consider the field contaminated and set up a new one
options.rationale: Reaching over a sterile field is a common error. Contamination has occurred whether or not anything was touched.

questions.takeaway: Common sterile technique errors: reaching over the sterile field, talking or coughing over it, and dropping items below waist level.
questions.strategy: Sterility is not a judgment call. Once a rule is broken the field is contaminated regardless of whether anything was seen to touch it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reaching over the field.
Visibility is not the test.
The field is whole, and a drape does not restore it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: start again.

questions.concept: Common sterile technique errors: reaching over the sterile field, talking or coughing over it, and dropping items below waist level.

questions.stem: A quality committee reviews the unit's health care-associated infection data for the past quarter, which shows a rise in central line and urinary catheter infections. The committee is identifying contributing factors before proposing changes. Which factors contribute to these infections? Select all that apply.

options.text: Invasive procedures
options.rationale: They bypass the body's normal barriers and create a portal of entry.

options.text: Antibiotic administration
options.rationale: Disrupts normal flora and selects for resistant organisms, which is why it appears as a cause rather than only a treatment.

options.text: Multidrug-resistant organisms
options.rationale: Organisms resistant to multiple drugs need contact precautions because the usual antibiotics will not clear them if they spread.

options.text: Breaks in infection prevention and control activities
options.rationale: The category that covers missed hand hygiene, broken technique, and inadequate cleaning.

options.text: Community-acquired infections present on admission
options.rationale: By definition not health care-associated, since they were not acquired during care.

questions.takeaway: HAIs arise from invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention. Health care-associated infections occur as a result of invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention and control activities.
questions.strategy: Antibiotics appearing as a cause is the counterintuitive one. They disrupt normal flora, which is one of the body's own defenses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Acquired during health care.
Present on admission means it was not acquired here.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Health care-associated infections occur as a result of invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention and control activities.

questions.stem: A patient's wound swab grows MRSA. He is afebrile, the wound is clean and granulating, his white cell count is normal, and he has no systemic symptoms. Which term describes his status?

options.text: An infectious disease requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Treatment decisions rest on clinical evidence of disease rather than on the culture alone.

options.text: Colonization, because the organism is present without producing disease
options.rationale: Organisms are present and multiplying without a host response or clinical signs. Contact precautions still apply.

options.text: Infection, because MRSA has been identified
options.rationale: Infection requires the organism to produce a host response and clinical signs.

options.text: A health care-associated infection
options.rationale: Would require an infection acquired during care, and no infection is present.

questions.takeaway: Colonization is the organism present without a host response. Infection produces signs and a response. Colonization is the presence and multiplication of organisms without a host response or clinical signs. Infection produces a host response and clinical evidence of disease.
questions.strategy: The practical consequence is that precautions and treatment separate. A colonized patient still needs contact precautions and does not necessarily need antibiotics.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Organism present, no host response, no clinical signs.
Both require evidence of disease.
No infection has occurred.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: colonization.

questions.concept: Colonization is the presence and multiplication of organisms without a host response or clinical signs. Infection produces a host response and clinical evidence of disease.

questions.stem: A patient on a surgical unit develops a wound infection. The nurse plans interventions and is asked which links in the chain of infection each one breaks. Which are links in the chain of infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reservoir
options.rationale: Where the organism lives and multiplies.

options.text: Portal of exit
options.rationale: How the organism leaves the reservoir.

options.text: Susceptible host
options.rationale: The person in whom the organism can establish itself.

options.text: Incubation period
options.rationale: The interval between exposure and symptoms. It describes the course of an infection rather than a link in the chain.

options.text: Virulence
options.rationale: How readily an organism causes disease. A property of the agent rather than a separate link.

options.text: Antibody titer
options.rationale: A laboratory measure of immune response, not a link in the chain.

questions.takeaway: Six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
questions.strategy: Three distractors describe properties of an organism or a lab value. A link is a stage in how infection travels from one place to the next.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A stage in the journey from source to host.
An interval and a property of the organism.
A laboratory measure of the host response.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: The chain of infection has six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Nursing interventions work by breaking a link.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old receiving chemotherapy has a white cell count of 0.8. He is afebrile with no identified source of infection. Which type of precaution does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Droplet precautions
options.rationale: Also directed at protecting others from a patient with a transmissible organism.

options.text: Contact precautions
options.rationale: Protects others from the patient, and he is not the source.

options.text: Protective isolation
options.rationale: Also called reverse isolation. The direction of protection reverses: the patient is protected from the environment.

options.text: Standard precautions only
options.rationale: Severe immunocompromise calls for more than the baseline.

questions.takeaway: Protective or reverse isolation reverses the direction, protecting an immunocompromised patient from organisms in the environment. Every other precaution protects others from the patient. Transmission-based precautions protect others from the patient.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction the protection runs. That question sorts protective isolation from every other category in one step.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient, from organisms around him.
Protects others from the patient, and he is not the source.
Also directed at protecting others from a patient with a transmissible organism.
Severe immunocompromise calls for more than the baseline.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: also called reverse isolation.

questions.concept: Transmission-based precautions protect others from the patient. Protective or reverse isolation reverses the direction, protecting an immunocompromised patient from organisms in the environment.

questions.stem: Infection control practice is discussed at a staff meeting after an audit found variation in hand hygiene practice on a unit caring for several patients with C. difficile. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Alcohol-based rub is fine after C. difficile care as long as my hands are not visibly soiled."
options.rationale: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill. Soap and water is used for visibly soiled hands and for C. difficile and norovirus.

options.text: "If I reach across a sterile field, it is contaminated even if nothing touched it."
options.rationale: Accurate. Contamination is not judged by what is visible.

options.text: "Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why it sits at the top of standard precautions.

options.text: "Standard precautions apply to every patient, not only those with a known infection."
options.rationale: Accurate, and transmission-based precautions are added on top.

questions.takeaway: Alcohol does not kill spores. Soap and water for C. difficile, norovirus, and visibly soiled hands.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement applies the general rule correctly to the one organism where it fails.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the incorrect practice.
Spore-forming organisms need soap and water.
Hand hygiene, standard precautions, and the sterile field are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: spores survive alcohol.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews with a student what standard precautions require on every patient, every shift, regardless of whether a diagnosis has been confirmed. The unit has several admissions with results still pending. Which elements are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand hygiene
options.rationale: The foundation, and the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections.

options.text: PPE selected according to the anticipated exposure
options.rationale: The task determines the PPE, not the diagnosis.

options.text: Safe injection practices
options.rationale: Never reusing a syringe or needle between patients, and never re-entering a vial with a used needle, prevents bloodborne transmission.

options.text: Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette
options.rationale: Including ensuring patients cover mouth and nose, use tissues, and dispose of them in a waste receptacle.

options.text: An N95 respirator for every patient encounter
options.rationale: Respirator use belongs to airborne precautions rather than to routine care.

questions.stem: A nurse sets up a sterile field for an invasive procedure at the bedside. The overbed table has been cleared and dried, and she has opened the sterile pack in the center of it. Which principles apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Only sterile items may touch other sterile items
options.rationale: Sterile-to-sterile is the governing rule, and any contact with a non-sterile surface contaminates.

options.text: The outer one-inch border of the field is considered contaminated
options.rationale: Which is why items are placed toward the center rather than near the edge.

options.text: Reach across the field only when retrieving sterile items
options.rationale: Reaching over a sterile field contaminates it regardless of what is being retrieved.

options.rationale: A field you cannot see cannot be confirmed sterile.

options.rationale: Anything below waist level is out of view and considered contaminated.

questions.stem: A nurse is administering an intramuscular antibiotic into the ventrogluteal site. She aspirates before injecting and sees blood return in the syringe. The patient reports no pain at the site. Which action is correct?

options.text: Continue the injection slowly, since a small amount of blood return is expected in vascular tissue
options.rationale: Blood return is never expected and injecting would deliver an intramuscular medication intravenously.

options.text: Immediately stop the injection, remove the needle, and prepare a new syringe of medication
options.rationale: Blood return means the needle is in a vessel. The medication and the syringe are discarded and the dose is prepared again.

options.text: Inject the medication and apply firm pressure to the site afterward to limit any bleeding
options.rationale: Pressure afterward does not undo an intravascular injection.

options.text: Withdraw the needle slightly and continue the injection in the same site at a shallower depth
options.rationale: Repositioning within a site where a vessel was entered does not make it safe.

questions.takeaway: Blood on aspiration means stop, remove, and start again with a new syringe of medication. If blood is aspirated during an intramuscular injection, immediately stop the injection, remove the needle, and prepare a new syringe of medication.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Blood return means a vessel.

Repositioning in the same site is not a remedy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: stop, remove, start again.

questions.stem: A nurse selects a subcutaneous injection site for a patient receiving twice-daily heparin. He has bruising over both sides of the abdomen from previous injections and reduced circulation in both lower legs. Which statements about site selection are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The outer aspect of the upper arms is a recommended site
options.rationale: One of the three recommended sites.

options.text: The abdomen from below the costal margins to the iliac crests is a recommended site
options.rationale: The largest available area and the one with the fastest absorption.

options.text: Inject into an area of lipohypertrophy to reduce discomfort
options.rationale: Hypertrophied tissue absorbs unpredictably and is avoided for six months.

options.text: Subcutaneous injection is contraindicated where conditions impair blood flow
options.rationale: Absorption depends on perfusion, meaning blood flow to the tissue, so a poorly perfused site makes the dose unpredictable.

options.text: The subcutaneous route is suited to large volumes of medication
options.rationale: The subcutaneous route takes small volumes, generally 1 mL or less. Larger volumes go intramuscularly or intravenously.

options.text: Use the deltoid for routine subcutaneous heparin
options.rationale: The deltoid is an intramuscular site. Subcutaneous sites are the abdomen, upper arms, thighs, and buttocks.

questions.takeaway: Best sites are the outer aspect of the upper arms, the abdomen from below the costal margins to the iliac crests, and the anterior aspects of the thighs. options.rationale: Holding steady prevents tissue damage and withdrawing at the same angle reduces trauma.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four orders before her morning round: a PPD intradermally, heparin subcutaneously, an intramuscular antibiotic for an adult, and vitamin B12 intramuscularly. She selects the syringe, gauge, length, and angle for each. Which selections are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heparin 5,000 units subcutaneously: 1 mL syringe, 27 gauge, 1/2 inch, 90 degrees

options.rationale: A longer 22 gauge needle at 90 degrees reaches muscle in an average adult, and 3 mL holds the volume.

options.text: Vitamin B12 intramuscularly to an adult: 1 mL syringe, 28 gauge, 3/8 inch, 45 degrees

questions.stem: Enoxaparin is due subcutaneously for a patient on the second postoperative day. The medication is supplied in a prefilled syringe with a small air bubble visible at the top. Which action is correct?

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her medication list for the shift and matches each order to the correct route before she prepares anything. The list includes a skin test, an insulin dose, a vaccine, and a thick antibiotic suspension. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
